Revision 0: April 3, 2012.
Place of publication: India, p. 3) The Vīrāgama.
May Vighneśa, the remover of obstacles, who is saluted by all the gods, be present before me;
and may my speech, which is honored throughout the three worlds, be established. (1)
Seated in the midst of Mount Meru, surrounded by hosts of sages,
and attended by throngs of beings, including bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas.
Then Brahmā, having risen and bowed down to the Lord— who was accompanied by the Gandharvas and whose crest was adorned with the offering of Soma— praised Him.
Be gracious, O Lord of the gods of gods! Be gracious, O Supreme Lord!
Be gracious, O Protector of the worlds! Be gracious, O Imperishable Bestower of Bliss! || 4 ||
Salutations to you who possess a thousand heads, salutations to you who possess a thousand eyes;
salutations to Śarva, the Supreme Self, who is endowed with a thousand feet.
Salutations to you, the Great Lord who possesses a thousand forms, who is peaceful, the wielder of the Pināka bow;
salutations to you, the embodiment of the syllable *huṃ*, and salutations to you, the embodiment of the syllable *vaṣaṭ*.
Salutations to you who utter the sound *phaṭ*; salutations again and again to you who utter the sound *svāhā*.
Salutations to you, the omniscient, the refuge, and the one born in an instant. (7)
Salutations to you, Tatpuruṣa, to Śrīkaṇṭha, to Śikhaṇḍin;
to the one seated upon Ananta, to Ananta, the bringer of the end.
Salutation to you who are Vimalā, Viśālā, and Viśākhā;
salutation to the Yogi who dwells within the seat of yoga and bestows yoga.
Salutations to You who abide in the hearts of yogis and are attainable through yoga;
salutations be to You, the Supreme, the Highest Lord, who is devoid of qualities.
Salutations to you, who stand above the three selves, who are partless, who wear matted hair, who bestow the path, and who are the six paths themselves. (11)

Salutations to you who are eternally for the sake of withdrawal; salutations to you who are for the sake of withdrawal. And salutations to the one established in those who are established in withdrawal, and to the one who abides in those who abide.
Salutations to you, O Dhāraṇā, and to the one who bears the name Dhāraṇā; salutations to the one who stands before those engaged in the practice of dhāraṇā.
Salutations to you who are meditation, who are the form of meditation, and who are attainable through meditation;
salutations to you who are the object of meditation, who are attainable by the object of meditation, and who are both the meditator and the object of meditation. || 14 ||
Homage to You, the most worthy of being meditated upon among all objects of meditation;
homage to You, who are attained through meditative absorption and who are the very embodiment of composure. || 15 ||
To you, Śiva, who dwells in the hearts of those devoted to meditative concentration, the god of a thousand syllables, whose form consists of ten thousand syllables. || 16 ||
"O God of ten thousand syllables, salutations to you, O you of ten thousand syllables!
O Supreme Lord, tell me their Vīra-tantras;
O Grandfather of great wisdom, listen as they are recounted by me. (18)
Endowed with the four pillars of knowledge, conduct, ritual action, and yoga, listen now, O ascetic, to the sixty-four locations.
Mahādeva is at Vārāṇasī, Maheśvara is at Prayāga, Devadeveśa is at Naimiṣa, and Prapitāmaha is at Gayā.
(5) They know Sthāṇu at Kurukṣetra, Śaśibhūṣaṇa at Prabhāsa,
Jaraja at Puṣkara, and Viśvaṃtavimaleśvara at Gandha. || 21 ||
At Mahendra is Aṭṭahāsa, which is greatly surrounded;
at Ujjayinī is Mahākālī, and at Mahākaṭa is Madotkaṭa.
At Śaṅkukarṇa is Mahādeva; at Gokarṇa is Mahābila;
at Rudrakoṭi is Mahāyogin; and at Sthaleśvara is Mahāliṅga.
One should worship Śambhu as Īśāna at Kedāra; Rudra at Rudrahimālaya;
Sahasrākṣa at Svarṇākṣa; and Vṛṣabhadhvaja at Vṛṣa.
They know Bhairava to be at Bhairava, and Bhava at Bhavaprada;
Sūrya at Kanakhala, and Sadāśiva at Bhadrakarṇa. (25)
In the Devadāru forest, one should worship Śaṅkara as Daṇḍin; in Varujaṃkara, as Ūrdhvaretas; in Trisiddhā, as Kāraṇḍa; and in Kāraṇḍa, as Kapardin.
One should visit Kṛttivāsa at Vāmoḍhra, [and] Kṣmā-leśvara;
Śuddheśvara at Dhyāna, and Muktakeśvara at Gāyatrī.
Vijaya is indeed in Kāśmīra, Jayantī in Marukeśvara;
Samaliṅga and Virasthāṇu are in Karavīraka, as is Kapālī.
Tryambaka is to be known at the three junctions of the day; Trilocana at Vīrajā;
Marukeśvara in Dīpta; and Paśupati in Nepāla. || 29 ||
At Śrīkāyārohaṇa, Lakulī; at Devikā, Umāpati;
at Gaṅgāsāra, Amara... [at] Mokāra, Amara.
At Hariścandra there is Abdhīśvara, at Kuruścandra Vṛṣaṅkara; at Jaṭila there is Vāmeśvara, and at Kakuda there are Saumyeśvara and Kakudeśvara. || 31 ||
At Saptagodāvara is Bhīma; Svayaṃbhū and Nāgaleśvara [are at their respective sites];
Triśūla at Japyeśvara; and Tripurāntaka on Śrīśaila.
He appointed Karṇikāra as the superintendent over the mountains, Tura as the lord of the Gaṇas on Kailāsa,
Virūpākṣa on Hemakūṭa, and Bhūbhuj on Gandhamādana.
One should worship Anala with ashes on his body at Bhūteśvara, Gandhavaha at Mukha,
and Vārāha for the sake of slaying the Dānavas at Vinya-keśvara.
On Mount Śliṣṭakoṭīśvara is the holy site; on Miṣṭakāpara is the most excellent one;
in Laṅkā is Ardhadevasaṃ; and in Pātāla is Hāṭakeśvara.
O sinless one, I have thus declared to you the sixty-eight names of the water-loving Malliṅga at Liṅgeśvara, which bestows boons.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Sixty-eight Sites," in the Vīratantra. || 1 ||
Having prostrated before the Blessed One, the Grandfather indeed questioned him:
"O Lord, tell me all that regarding the origin of the tantras."
Īśvara said: O Lotus-seated One, listen as I shall declare all of that in its entirety; this mantra bestows vast benefits upon those who have taken refuge in it. (2)
And because it provides protection for men, it is known as *tantra*. [The five sections are:
Kāmika, Yogaja, Cintya, Kāraṇa, and likewise Ajita. (3)
Dīpta, Sūkṣma, Sahasra, Aṃśumān, Suprabhedaka, Vijaya, Niśvāsa, Svāyaṃbhuva, and likewise Anala.
Vīra and Raurava, as well as Makuṭa and Vimala;
Candrajñāna and Bimba, and likewise Prodgīta and Lalita. || 5 ||
The Siddha, Santāna, Śarvokta, and Pārameśvara, as well as the Kiraṇa and Vātula— these are the twenty-eight Saṃhitās.
Listen now, O best of Brahmins, to their divisions beginning with the Kāmika;
the Kāmika is said to have three distinct divisions.
And that which is born of yoga is specifically said to be of five kinds;
the object of contemplation is declared to be sixfold, and the cause is sevenfold.
O Lotus-seated One! Aṃśumān is declared to be the twelfth division;
there is no other famous division of the Suprabheda known to exist. (9)
The division of Śiva has been proclaimed by me; now listen to the division of Rudra, which is pure and especially distinguished, as well as the Aṃśumat and Suprabhedaka.
Vijaya, Niśvāsa, Svāyambhuva, and Anala; Vīra, Raurava, Makuta, and likewise Vimala.
The Candrajñāna and the Bimba are said to be distinct from the remaining [tantras];
they will be explained specifically according to that same method in the Svāyaṃbhuvatantra.
(8) The Āgneya and the Ekarudra—no other division exists besides these.
And the Vīratantra, O best of Brahmins, is said to be the thirteenth division. || 13 ||
The Raurava, with its sixfold division, has been described by me in its entirety;
the great tantra called Makuṭa is declared to be of two kinds. (14)
The great tantra known as Vimala shall be of fourteen types;
likewise, Candrajñāna and Bimba shall each be of fourteen types. (15)
And the Mukhabimba, O best of Brahmins, is the fifteenth division;
the great tantra named Prodgīta is said to be the sixteenth division.
The great tantra known as Lalita is said to be divided into three ways,
O best of Brahmins, and it is also said to be of four kinds in the Siddhatantra.
The great tantra known as Santāna is said to have seven divisions;
however, the great tantra spoken by Śarva is said to have five divisions. (18)
The Pārameśvara Tantra will be taught in seven divisions,
while the great tantra known as the Kiraṇa is said to have nine divisions.
The Vātula Mahātantra is said to be the twelfth division;
out of special affection for you, I shall specifically proclaim the body of tantras. 20.
The hands and feet should be positioned straight and upright;
the face is said to be like that of a god, adorned with a crown of matted hair. 21.
He should be dressed in white garments and wear a white sacred thread;
he should have three eyes upon his face and be endowed with all the auspicious marks of the limbs.
(9) The deity situated above the *pada* is adorned with all ornaments;
therein the Body is said to be great, the means for accomplishing all desires and aims. (23)
And hear, O Lotus-seated One, the measurement of the book:
it should be either fourteen finger-breadths or fifteen finger-breadths. (24)
Or likewise sixteen finger-breadths, or seventeen finger-breadths, or even eighteen finger-breadths, or nineteen finger-breadths. || 25 ||
Alternatively,
O best of Brahmins, the most excellent preceptor should cause twenty, or indeed twenty-one, or twenty-two [pots] to be prepared.
In this manner, one should have the book made according to the *mānāṅgula* measurement;
having divided the height into eight parts, the width should be one *aṅgula*.
The thickness is said to be half the width; one should carve away the two sides by one part each.
A cavity is prescribed in the middle, measuring three parts or four parts [of the width]. (28)
In that case, multiply by eight and then divide by three;
the remainder is declared to be the *āya*, and one should exclude it by means of the qualities (*guṇa*) themselves.
One should divide by fourteen; the remainder is here called the expenditure (vyaya).
For each quality (guṇa), there is an increase of one unit; thereafter, one should decrease it by eight.
The remainder is known as the *yoni*; multiplied by eight, it is the *pada*.
Divided by twenty-seven, the quotient is remembered as the *iṣṭa*. || 31 ||
The remainder is declared to be the lunar mansion itself; when divided by eight, it is the *pada*.
One should subtract thirty from those [padas]; the remainder here is called the lunar day (*tithi*).

O best of Brahmins, listen now to the measurement of the book, beginning with the first [chapter] and so forth; one should divide the attained height by the measurement in finger-breadths (mānāṅgula).
A footprint of one finger-breadth is prescribed, and one that is deficient in finger-breadths should be avoided;
if it is even, it should be accepted, for the matter of income and expenditure is discussed here.
Having increased that by eight, one should then decrease it by seven;
the remainder is declared to be the day (vāra), as well as the income (āya), the expenditure (vyaya), and the source (yoni).

The lunar mansion (nakṣatra), lunar day (tithi), and day of the week (vāra) are declared to be conducive to longevity; when income is greater than expenditure, it is said here to bring about prosperity.
When income is deficient and expenditure is excessive, it is here called a "mine of defects";
therefore, with every effort, one should not cause [a temple] to be built where income is deficient. || 35 ||
A lion on a banner, a bull, an elephant, and a rising sun;
a smoky-colored dog, a donkey, and a crow—one should avoid these defects. (36)
Having thus examined in many ways whether the lunar mansion of the patron is favorable to the [chosen] constellation, the supreme manuscript should be prepared. (37)
O Lotus-Seated One, I shall now declare the seers, meters, and presiding deities:
Viśvāmitra, Vālmīki, Kāśyapa, and likewise Aṅgiras. (38)
Gautama, Mudgala, Gārgya, Vasiṣṭha, and likewise Uśanas—having thus assigned these starting from fourteen finger-breadths in sequence to the embodied soul; || 39 ||
The *triṣṭubh* is both the original form and the modification;
likewise, the *jagatī* is the *śatvarī* and also the *atiśatvarī*. || 40 ||
Thus, the supreme unmanifest is ordained as the essence of the Vedas;
it is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva himself.
Kālarudra, Nīlarudra, Pralayānila, and Sadāśiva;
here, the measurements of the deities beginning from fourteen finger-breadths are now described.
One should have it written with ink, or indeed write it with colored pigment;
then one should have the book written in six lines or five lines. (43)
The Ṛṣis, the Vasus, the planets, the directions, and the single Śūdra—thus is the row (paṅkti) described, along with their respective presiding deities according to their names. || 44 ||
O best of the twice-born, one should have this [mantra], endowed with such characteristics and increasing the prosperity of kings and kingdoms, written upon birch bark by the sages.
The preceptor should always cause it to be written on palm leaves with gold ink;
it should have two margins provided with lines, and its dimensions should be equal to those of a book.
I shall now proclaim the ritual procedure for consecration, endowed with its defining characteristics:
one should construct a pavilion in front of Śiva, or in the northeast or the south. (47)
The wise one, having constructed an altar within the center of the pavilion in three parts,
should cause five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) to be made all around the exterior of the altar.
One should have these sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) constructed as either circular or square;
or else, an altar (sthaṇḍila) should be prepared, endowed with the proper characteristics.
In the south-western part of the pavilion, prepare a sacrificial altar (sthaṇḍila) with rice;
there, one should perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) either on the fifth day or even on the third day.
And in the center of that [should be placed] a jar of Soma, together with its cloth, its lid, its gold, and its ritual grass-bundle, having King Soma as its presiding deity. (51)
Having prepared a nine-square grid there, one should specifically place a jar of Soma in the center and pitchers in the eight directions.
One should sow black gram, mung beans, horse gram, and mustard seeds;
then, one should plant these seeds while reciting the heart mantra. (53)
Having consecrated the jars with water from the deity,
one should then lift them up in the place where [the deity] slept and subsequently install the *pālikās*.
There, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited; one should sprinkle [the area] with the *pavamāna* mantra.
O Brahmin, one should bind the marriage-thread (*kautuka*) with a golden thread while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra.
One should smear the book with elā, lavaṅga, takkola, uśīra, and sandalwood; then, one should place it upon that bed.
One should strew the altar with śāli rice and draw an eight-petaled lotus;
having placed half as much unhusked rice as the śāli rice, one should place half as many sesame seeds as the unhusked rice.
Having prepared a fivefold bed, one should then lay down the book; one should lay it upon the bed with the seed-syllable (bīja) of each respective Āgama.
The Brahman is declared to be short, while the limbs are said to be long;
it is joined with the first syllable and endowed with the anusvāra.
This is declared to be the limb of Brahman and is prescribed for all;
one should especially wrap the book there with a cloth.
And likewise, O best of Brahmins, one should place the mirror in that same sequence;
then, one should install Sarasvatī there in the middle of the book.
And one should place a water-pot in the northeastern direction of the book,
filled with pure water, containing a bundle of kuśa grass, and provided with a lid.
Then he should place a garment and gold upon Sarasvatī;
having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the root mantra, he should worship her especially. (63)
One should place [the vessels] in the *vardhanīs* starting from the east and ending with the northeast;
one should also place a cloth, gold, and the *kūrca*-grass bundles therein.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, and likewise Kalavikaraṇī, Balavikariṇī, Balapramathinī, and Sarvabhūtadamanī. (65)
Having placed [the letters] beginning with 'pūrva' and [the goddess] Manonmanī upon the book,
one should worship [them] according to the rule with the groups of six starting from the Heart-mantra.
One should offer the sacrificial oblation there and afterwards perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
A palāśa branch should be placed in the eastern part, and likewise an aśvattha branch in the south.
Likewise, one should offer *bilva* in the west, *apāmārga* in the north, and *udumbara* in the northeast; or indeed, the oblation may be offered with *pālāśa* wood.
One should offer fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds;
the fuel-stick with the Sadyojāta mantra and the clarified butter with the Īśāna mantra.
One should indeed offer the *caru* with the heart-mantra, the parched grains (*lāja*) with the left [hand],
the mustard seeds with the *sadyojāta* mantra, and likewise the barley with the eye-mantra.
Having offered sesame seeds with the Kavaca mantra, the seven substances are here described;
one thousand, or half of that, or even half of that again, may be offered.
Having offered one hundred and eight, or fifty, or twenty-five oblations of the materials with the Vyāhṛtis, he should touch the book with his heart.

Immediately after that, while reciting the mantra "Sviṣṭam agne," one should offer oblations into the fire, which carries the offerings, while uttering [the name] joined with all the ritual substances. (73)
Then, at the clear dawn, having especially performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
one should sprinkle the vardhanī vessel with the seed-mantra of the respective Āgama.
Having placed a mirror in close proximity, one should perform the consecration;
thereafter, one should offer the sacrificial food and then cause betel-leaf to be given.
Thereafter, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings;
one should honor the Brahmins there, and one should also honor seven maidens.
The Buddhist, the Arhat, the Śaiva, the Pāśupata, as well as the Kāpāla and the Pañcarātra—these six are remembered as the religious systems (samayas). || 77 ||
The confusion of these very [duties] is called *tantra-saṃkara* (confusion of systems);
by the fault of *tantra-saṃkara*, the king and the kingdom perish. (78)
Therefore, with every effort, one should never cause confusion;
the division of the Śaivas is prescribed as being of twenty-eight kinds.
Furthermore, for a consecrated person, a true hero, and one devoted to the worship of Śiva, even the intermixture of these [practices] does not result in any fault. (80)
To such a person it should be given, and from him it should be received; thus the tantra is described here.
It must not be heard by one who is uninitiated, nor should it be given to just anyone.
The mortal who performs it in this manner shall attain the world of Śiva.
Thus has the introduction of the Tantra been declared; now hear the five-syllabled mantra. (82)
Thus ends the second chapter, "The Introduction to the Tantra," in the *Vīratantra* consisting of six thousand verses. || 2 ||
The Grandfather said:
Having paid homage to the Lord of the World, the Grandfather questioned him.
O Lord, tell me all of that, including the ritual manual of the glorious five-syllabled mantra! || 1 ||
Īśvara said:
I shall declare all of that in its entirety; listen, O Four-faced One!
The two syllables "Śi-va," joined with a salutation, [constitute the name]. (2)
The fourth letter of the first group, the second group consisting of the *ya*-class, and the seventh letter at the end of that same class—this is remembered as the five-syllabled [mantra]. (3)
Having recollected this mantra, which is joined with the Bindu and the Nāda and conjoined with the dative case-ending,
it is known as the five-syllabled mantra.
The letter *na*, the letter *ma*, the letter *śi*, and the letter *va*, joined with the letter *ya*—this is called the five-syllabled [mantra] here. || 5 ||
Joined with the Praṇava, it is remembered as the five-syllabled mantra.
O Brahmin, the Ṛgveda is born; the syllable "na" is said to be its expression. (6)
The letter *ma* is the Yajurveda; the letter *śi* is the Sāmaveda;
the letter *va* is in the Atharvaveda; and the letter *ya* is in the Itihāsas.
The letter *na* should be known as earth, and the letter *ma* as water;
the letter *śi* is joined with fire, and the letter *vā* as air itself. (8)
The letter *ya* is born from space and is established within each of those elements;
the letter *na*, white in color, is joined with Īśvara.
Joined with the Sāvitrī meter and associated with Gautama, the station known as Sadyomukha is said to consist of the syllable "Na. || 10 ||
The letter *ma* is yellow in color and has Brahmā as its presiding deity;
it is joined with the *anuṣṭubh* meter and is associated with the practitioner. (11)
The station is Vāmadeva, which is said to be the syllable *ma*;
the syllable *vā* is red in color, and Skanda is the presiding deity there. (12)
Joined with the Bṛhatī meter and associated with Aṅgiras, the mouth is the station of the Puruṣa; it is said that the syllable is the letter Vā. || 13 ||
The letter *ya* is white in color; Vighneśa is its presiding deity.
It is joined with the Sāvitrī meter and associated with Bhāradvāja.
The syllable *ya* is said to be the location of the mouth of Īśāna; it is proclaimed as the five-syllabled mantra. Now hear the Praṇava according to its true nature.
The letter *a*, the letter *u*, and the letter *m* constitute the threefold [syllable].
The letter *a* has Brahmā as its deity; the letter *u* has Viṣṇu as its deity. || 16 ||
The letter *ma* is proclaimed there as Maheśvara, the presiding deity;
the letter *a* is the Ṛgveda, and the letter *u* is the Yajurveda. (17)
The letter *ma* is the Sāmaveda; listen now to this other [teaching]:
one should know the letter *a* to be *sāttvika*, while the letter *u* would be *rājasa*.
The syllable *ma* should be known as pertaining to *tamas*; the syllable *a* is pacificatory (*śāntika*).
One should know the syllable *u* to be nourishing (*pauṣṭika*), and the syllable *ma* is for malevolent rites (*ābhicāraka*). (19)
The syllable *a* shall be white in color, the syllable *u* red in color, and the syllable *m* yellow in color; thus indeed is it according to the sequence.
Through the quality [of union], it becomes the *saṃdhikāra*; the syllable *oṃ* is said to be Śiva.
When joined with the syllable *oṃ*, it is here called the six-syllabled [mantra]. (21)
One should perform the recitation (japa) with a rudrākṣa bead while joined with the five-syllabled mantra.
Reciting it once with a finger is equivalent to five recitations performed with an earthen bead.
It is declared that [the merit] from lines is eightfold; it becomes tenfold by means of seeds;
it should be known as hundredfold by means of [beads] numbering a hundred, and thousandfold by means of coral.
With crystal beads, [the merit is] ten thousandfold; with pearls, one hundred thousandfold;
with lotus seeds, it is multiplied by ten million; and with golden beads, it is ten times ten millionfold.
With Rudrākṣa beads numbering one hundred crores, it becomes infinite.
Then the practitioner of mantra should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa); here, the five-syllabled mantra is now declared. (25)
The placement starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger is declared to be the *sṛṣṭi-nyāsa* (creation placement);
that starting from the little finger and ending with the thumb is called the *saṃhāra-nyāsa* (dissolution placement).
O Brahmin, the wise one should finally merge the letter *ya* into the palm of the hand;
having first performed the assignment of the hands (*karanyāsa*), hear now the assignment of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).
Having placed the syllable *ya* upon the head, one should place the syllable *vā* on the forehead, the syllable *śi* in the region of the ears, and the syllable *ma* on the heart. (28)
One should especially place the syllable *na* at the region of the navel;
then, O best of Brahmins, one should place the syllable *oṃ* upon all the limbs.
One should perform the recitation specifically one thousand times, or half of that, or one hundred and eight, or fifty, or twenty-five. (30)
O best of Brahmins, one should perform the recitation endowed with the *prāsāda* mantra and the *hṛdaya*, combined with the *praṇava*. (31)
In one's own home, the fruit shall be single; in a cow-pen, it becomes tenfold;
on a riverbank, one should know it to be a hundredfold; and in a temple of the deity, it is a thousandfold.
Having recited it twenty lakhs of times, one shall personally attain the status of a king;
thereafter, with twenty-five lakhs, one shall attain the station of Viṣṇu.
Then, having recited it one hundred thousand times, one shall attain the state of Rudra;
one shall enter the auspicious Lord Śiva and [be liberated] from the ocean of saṃsāra.
"The Śrīpañcākṣara itself has been declared; now hear the extraction of the mantra from that.
Thus ends the third chapter, the Śrīpañcākṣarakalpa, in the Vīratantra, the Saṃhitā of Six Thousand Verses. 3.
For all living beings submerged in the ocean of ignorance, how may this extraction of the mantra be accomplished for the purpose of destroying all sins? (1)
The Lord said:

In that very place, the extraction of the splinters from the body of the site (vāstu) should be performed in due order:
the splinter of bone is removed by touching the head, and both of those [other types] by measuring from below. || 23 ||
Likewise, when the touch reaches the ear or the throat, it is "grown" (vṛddha) due to the measure of those three;
at three cubits, there is the Śṛṅgalā-śalya, and the preceptor [perceives] it from the touch of the body.
At a distance of one cubit (hasta), by the touch of the hand, one should predict the arrival of a wicked woman;
at three cubits, however, it is said that the touch of the arm indicates [the arrival of] Aṅgāraka.
That which is measured from the ankle to the foot is called one *ekāṅga* when it is one *vitasti* in length; that which reaches from the little finger to the thumb is called half a *karārdha-ekāṅga*.

Furthermore, iron [is purified] by contact with the hip; [the body] up to the height of two palms from the hands; and [the area] from the navel to the elbow, as well as the hands, is purified by contact with the knees. || 27 ||
Having thus examined it in many ways, O best of Brahmins, one should extract the splinter from the body; then, having cleansed the wound, one should smear it with cow dung.
There, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited; then, with ninety-six [mantras], one should sprinkle [the site].
After that, one should have a stake made of either *aśvattha* or *udumbara* wood driven in.
It should be twelve finger-breadths in length and six finger-breadths in circumference;
one should place a peg in its center and rotate it around with that same measurement.
And by means of two sūtras, one should not [measure] from that point;
rather, one should observe the shadow of the gnomon (śaṅku) in both the forenoon and the afternoon. || 31 ||
There, one should cast two threads from the center of the peg toward the east;
then, having worshipped the Vāstu deities, one should subsequently worship Puruṣa.
For the benefit of the Asuras, Śukra performed great penance;
from that great austerity was born one of immense strength, possessing a physical form like a living being.
On the ground, that site (vāstu) should be situated facing downwards; it should be made by a man standing in the center, using the respective measurements beforehand.
Having laid out the north-south thread here and thus formed a square,
one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow while reciting the ninety-sixfold mantra.
Having understood this sequence in this very way, one should prepare the site;
likewise, one should lay down ten lines, both oriented toward the east and toward the north.
Having divided [the site] into eighty-one squares, one should assign the Vāstu deities;
having set aside nine squares in the center, one should arrange them in the four directions.
Brahmā is in the eastern part, occupying six squares including his attendants; Vivasvān is in the south, likewise occupying six squares. || 38 ||
And furthermore, O best of Brahmins, in the fifth [section] is Mitra and likewise Ṣaṭpada;
in the north, Pṛthivīdhara indeed enjoys a six-pada space.
Āpa and Apavatsa occupy two squares in the northeast;
Sāvitra and Savitṛ likewise occupy two squares in the southeast. || 40 ||
Indra and Indrajaya are in the two squares of the southwest;
Rudra and Rudrajaya are in the two squares of the northwest. (41)
Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, Mattendraka,
Āditya, Satyaka, Bhraṃśa, and Antarikṣa are in the east. (42)
Agni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, Graha, Kṣata, Yama, Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, and Bhṛṅga are likewise situated in the south. (43)
Pitṛdauvārika, as well as Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, Varuṇa, and likewise the Apsaras; || 44 ||
Wasting disease and consumption are established in the western [directions];
likewise, in the northern [directions], there is the chief nāga, Roga. (45)
Likewise, Bhallāṭa and Soma, as well as Ṛg, Aditi, and Diti;
Pūtanā in the southwest (Nairṛta), and the evil Rākṣasī in the northwest (Vāyu). || 46 ||
For all the guardians of the site (vāstupas), [the placement] is indeed facing toward Brahmā;
having thus arranged the deities, I shall now describe the Puruṣa.
Having gathered the filaments, one should know that the body of Bṛja is then spoken of;
O Brahmin, in the Āpāpavatsaka [mantra], it is remembered as the left arm.
Sāvitrī and Savitṛ are said to be the right arm;
Rudra and Rudrodaya are proclaimed to be the left foot. (49)
Indra and Indrajaya are said to be the right foot;
Mitra is the penis and the back of the linga.
Thus has this fixed site (vāstu) been declared; now hear about the moving site (caravāstu).
In the month of Bhādrapada, beginning with the first day, it is said that the head is toward the east.
(38) Beginning with the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the three months up to Kumbha are the right [side]; the three months beginning with Phālguna are called the western head.
The northern head should be known for the month of Jyeṣṭha and so forth;
the eastern head is for midday, while the southern head is for evening.
O best of Brahmins, at midnight it is said that the head is in the west;
at the time of dawn, for all [the days], the head is said to be in the north.
Thus one should worship well with flowers, incense, and lamps. O ascetic, I shall now describe the ritual for the bali offering; listen to that as well. 55.
An offering should be given consisting of milk-rice (pāyasa) soaked in ghee;
furthermore, one should especially offer fruits and edible foods along with mārkava seeds.
Then, one should offer the bali-oblation beginning with Vivasvat, combined with sesame, mung beans, and rice;
likewise, curd for Pūṣan and buffalo milk for Mitra.
In Parjanya there is ghee, and in Jayanta fresh butter;
likewise, in Mahendra there is flour, which is called *madhu*. (58)
Madhu produced the fruit of the Aru tree; Bali is said here to be in the truth.
Kakvāna [produced] the Bimba fruits, and he is seized by the planets and stars.
O best of Brahmins, *kṛsara* is for Yama; likewise, the *khila* is said to be for the Gandharvas; then follows the *samudramatsya* and the offering (*bali*) of *bhṛṅgarāja*.
One should offer curd-rice to Mṛga, and to Pitṛ, piṇyāka (oil-cake) with oil;
to Iṣṭa, śatapiṣṭa (hundred-fold flour); and to Dauvārika, gravel.
One should know that at Puṣpadanta there is a flower, and likewise milk-rice at Varuṇa;
at Asura there is madhuka, and at Śoṣa there is sesame and rice.
For a disease, one should offer dry meat, as well as a bali-offering of goats and low-caste persons;
even for a primary [deity], however, there should be powdered grain mixed with curd.

At the Bhallāṭa [shrine], there should be rice with jaggery (gulānna), and at the Soma [shrine] likewise rice with jaggery; at the Ṛgveda [shrine], jaggery, and at the shrine of the gods of the Daityas, sweetmeat balls (modakas).
On the Diti days, one should eat sesame; on the Kṣīrānna day, mustard and śīraka; likewise on the Āpi and Pavatse days, goat meat and fish.
One should offer *jaṅgagandhodana* to Savitṛ and Sāvitrī;
likewise, one should give an oblation (*bali*) of rice to Indra, and *mudga* beans to Indrajaya.
To Rudra and Rudrajaya, one should offer meat and an oblation of milk;
to Carakī, clarified butter; and likewise, salt to Pitṛrāja.
One should likewise offer as an oblation (bali) sesame paste, Pūtanā, Gulamāṃsa, Pāparākṣasī, Sphaṭita, and one who has observed a fast. 68.
Combined with the names of the deities and accompanied by mung beans and black gram, the preceptor, having become pure and observing a fast, [should perform the rite]. (69)
Clad in new garments, wearing a turban and an upper cloth,
the twice-born one should offer the oblation (bali) to Śiva, preceded by the syllable Om.
Having honored the preceptor with garments, grain, gold, and other offerings,
there shall likewise be great peace for the sake of attaining all prosperity.
Thus, the mortal who performs these acts pertaining to the deity attains the world of Śiva and rejoices forever like Śiva himself. (72)
The procedure for ploughing has been declared; now hear the characteristics of the preceptor.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, on the ritual of ploughing, in the Vīratantra, the compendium of six thousand verses.
The Grandfather said:
O Lord, what kind of teachers are to be known? How are the Śaivas of seven types? In which lineage were they born? Tell me all that!
Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom, for that which has been requested by you!
I shall explain it in brief; listen as I speak.
Because he points out the way, he is therefore known as the "Guide" (deśika);
and because he is the teacher of all, he is designated as the "Guru. || 3 ||
Because he is worthy of installing the *liṅga*, he is called an "installer" (*sthāpaka*);
he should always be vigilant and constantly devoted to the worship of his guru. || 4 ||
Thus has the teacher endowed with these characteristics been described.
The Śaivas are to be known as being of seven kinds; now hear their distinctions.
The first is the Anādiśaiva; the second is the Ādiśaiva;
the third is the Mahāśaiva; and the fourth is the Anuśaivaka.
The fifth is the intermediate Śaiva, and the sixth is called the Pravara;
the seventh is the Vanya-Śaiva—these are said to be the divisions of the Śaivas.
The eternal Śaiva is Śiva; the initial Śaiva is the twice-born Śiva;
the great Śaiva is the solitary Brahmin, as well as the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya. (8)
The Anuśaiva is declared to be among the Śūdras,
while the Savarṇa, Ambaṣṭha, Kulāla, and Pāraśava are situated between them.
O best of Brahmins, I have described to you the Prāvaraṇa-Śaivas in their entirety;
now another Śaiva tradition among those born here [in this land] shall be told.
But because he was a Śaiva from the very beginning, he is remembered as Ādiśaiva;
likewise Kauśika, Kāśyapa, Bhāradvāja, and Tri. (11)
Gautama—these five have been initiated into the five faces;
those who have been initiated by Śiva are indeed called Śiva-brāhmaṇas.
Śiva, Śikha, as well as Jyotis, Sāvitrī, and Vyoma;
Kauśika facing north, and Kāśyapa on the south. (13)
Bhāradvāja is to be known as being in the east, and likewise Gautama in the west; Atri is to be known as facing upward; thus are those who have been initiated among these [directions].
The self whose five spheres of perception were purified...
Kauśika was a devotee of Śiva, while Kāśyapa was [ordained] by Īśvara.
Bharadvāja was initiated by Īśāna, while Gautama was the embodiment of Brahman; Atreya was Sadāśiva himself, and Dīkṣita was Umādhūrta.
The five sages are said to be those whose selves are purified by the five objects of sense;
one who is born from the initiation of Śiva is called a Śiva-brāhmaṇa.
The earth of Kauśika is wonderful; that of Pāṇḍarīka belongs to Kāśyapa;
Bharadvāja is at Gokarṇa, while Gautama is at Nāgarika. || 18 ||
One should designate this as being equal to the Varaṇḍas for the purpose of eating:
the fourfold [traditions], namely Śaiva, Pāśupata, Soma, and Lākula. || 19 ||
This should be known as a division of Śaivism; one should not practice a mixture [of these]. Even among these tantras, however, there is a mixture of only one with the ninth.
One should not perform a mixture of tantras nor practice that which is joined with them;
through the fault of mixing tantras, the king and the kingdom perish. (21)
The division of Śaivism is established through twenty-eight branches:
Kāmika, Yogaja, Cintya, Kāraṇa, and likewise Ajita; || 22 ||
Dīpta, Sūkṣma, Sahasra, Aṃśumān, Suprabha, Vijaya, Niśvāsa, Svāyaṃbhuva, and Anala. (23)
Vīra and Raurava, Mākuṭa and Vimala as well, Candrajñāna and Bimba, and likewise Prodgīta and Lalita. || 24 ||
The Siddha, the Śārvokta, the Pārameśvara,
the Kiraṇa, and the Tula— these are the twenty-eight Saṃhitās.
One should not consider the intermingling of these [qualities] to be a fault;
they say that the teacher is indeed Śiva, and Śiva is said to be the teacher. (26)
He who understands non-differentiation is said to be free from these distinctions:
the son of Subhadrā, those called Viṣaya, the Kauśalas, and likewise the Māgadhas.
The Mālavas, the Pāñcālas, the Kaliṅgas, and the Pulindas; Kerala and Āryadeśa, as well as Mālava and Maru. (28)
Furthermore, the Pañcas, the Ketus, the Siṃhalas in the south, the Jonakas, the Tuluvās, and the Karṇāṭakas by region. (29)
The classification of the regions has been fully declared; I shall describe them to you in brief:
Kumārī is in the midst of the Himavat mountains... [30]
Therefore, O Puruṣottama, with every effort,
one should avoid that region of Haihala-Baghara in the performance of rites related to the liṅga.
One should know that the householder is superior, or else the student (brahmacārin);
however, he who is born in a family of the primary Śaivas is called a Vaidika.
He may have his hair tied in a topknot or be one whose body is smeared with ashes;
he must be born into a family of initiated practitioners and be proficient in all the Agamas. || 33 ||
He should always be vigilant, worshipping the gods, the fire, and his guru;
he should be complete in all limbs and endowed with all auspicious marks. || 34 ||
He should be skilled in ritual action, possessed of virtuous conduct, and proficient in the knowledge of the tantras, from the rituals up to the ultimate gnosis. || 35 ||
Thus has the teacher been described as endowed with these characteristics;
likewise, one who is a kinsman, one with deformed nails, a child, or an old man [is not to be appointed]. (36)
He is merciless, abstains from food, and is habituated to reviling others;
he is excessively tall or excessively short, and likewise excessively stout or emaciated. (37)
The skull and the *hāpra* [are used], as well as those of others in equal measure;
likewise, the radiance of the naked one is free from intoxication, facial hair, body hair, and the like. (38)
And likewise, O best of Brahmins, there were blameless astrologers as well. || 39 ||
O best of Brahmins, one should avoid those who maintain no sacred fire, as well as those who are one-eyed;
likewise, those addicted to vices, those of cruel deeds, adulterers, and thieves. (40)

Those afflicted with skin diseases, those scattered abroad, those who are two-footed [human beings], as well as those with leprosy, the sightless, the deaf, and those whose hearing is impaired; || 41 ||
However, those possessed of these characteristics should not perform the installation or worship;
otherwise, the king and the kingdom will perish, and it will not rain in that land.
Therefore, with every effort, an Ādiśaiva should perform all rites— from the installation (pratiṣṭhā) to the final worship— for an Ācārya who possesses the required characteristics.
Furthermore, one who would act otherwise for the sake of practicing with a Māhiṣī should never form a matrimonial alliance through lineage with her. 44.
In that regard, O best of Brahmins, among these sages who are born again and again, the family of one who is born does not increase.
One should never perform the initiation (dīkṣā) of Śiva-dvijas;
rather, at the conclusion of the time for the sacred thread ceremony (upanayana), one should worship Śiva within a mandala.
A Śiva-brahmin should cause the ritual bathing (snapana) to be performed for the sake of purifying the limbs;
however, a fixed linga (sthiraliṅga) may be touched by Śūdras when it is intended for malevolent magic (abhicāra).
(45) It would be a marvel if that place were destroyed;
one should always worship for one's own sake, as well as for the sake of all beings. 48.
Therefore, with every effort, the preceptor should not cause [the image] to be made;
he should instead place it in the hands of the teacher, and thus he shall attain the world of Śiva.
For that distinction among all the lineages born of the sages does not, in any way, result in fault for any of the twice-born who are devoted to Śiva. (50)
O best of the twice-born, for the sake of the Lord, one should place all things, such as land and so forth, into the hands of the preceptor; thus one shall attain the world of Śiva.
I salute Āvṛttavaṃśa, Vandāha, and Ṣaṇḍaka;
and the fallen Anucāṇḍāla, Dhūpadeśevika, and Śivi.
Having touched one who has fallen from a high position, and especially a mendicant, as well as a village cock, and likewise fire; 53.
O best of Brahmins, if one sees a horse or an ass while eating, one should indeed abandon the meal; having performed a bath, one becomes endowed with grace.
By reciting the three "Mānas" mantras, one certainly becomes pure.
One should practice this three times in the morning, three times in the evening, and likewise [three times] at midday and when not begging for food.
But after three days, a man should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
likewise, he should first perform the sixteen purificatory rites (kriyās).
The characteristics of the teacher have been declared; now hear about the mandala for initiation.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, concerning the characteristics of the Ācārya, in the Vīra-tantra, the compendium of six thousand verses.
The Grandfather.
For the sake of the welfare of all living beings and for liberation from all sins, O Lord, tell me everything regarding what kind of maṇḍala it is, O Master. (1)
The Lord.
Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! That which has been requested by you, I shall explain in its entirety; listen, O Lotus-seated One.
On the bank of the Gaṅgā, or at the ocean, or at a river, or even at a pond; in a garden, or in a cow-pen, or on the shore of a great lake. || 3 ||
Then, one should have a pavilion constructed near a temple, on the bank of a sacred river, or even in a pure dwelling.
A pavilion, a peaked structure, or likewise a water-shed (prapā) should be constructed;
it should measure four cubits, five cubits, or six cubits, with the latter three being the lowest grade.
Seven cubits or eight cubits [is the smallest]; nine cubits is the medium;
ten, eleven, or twelve cubits shall be the best.
In this very same sequence, one should construct the measurement in finger-breadths (mātrāṅgula);
it should be provided with sixteen pillars, according to the measurement of the rows and the height.
A *jāti* flower, or even a *campaka*, a pillar of *khadira* wood, or a *kramuka* nut, a bamboo staff, as well as a *vakulī* and a *ketakī*; || 8 ||
Then, the covering should be made from trees suitable for sacrificial rites, measuring twenty finger-breadths in width, and not with a coconut leaf.
One should wrap the body with cloth, adorned with four archways,
provided with banners in the cardinal directions, and beautified by a canopy above.
Having adorned it with strings of pearls and hanging garlands of flowers,
one should first examine the ground in this very same sequence. (11)
The earth of a Brāhmaṇa is white; that of a Kṣatriya is indeed red;
the earth of a Vaiśya is yellow; and that of a Śūdra is known to be black. (12)
The earth is sweet for a Brāhmaṇa, indeed astringent for a Kṣatriya;
it should be known as having six tastes for a Vaiśya, while for a Śūdra it is remembered as pungent.
The Brahmin woman has the scent of clarified butter, the Kṣatriya woman the scent of blood,
the Vaiśya woman the scent of urine, and the Śūdra woman has the odor of excrement.
And for those with crooked odors and tastes, it should be according to their respective species.
One should dig the ground to the depth of one cubit and fill it back with that same soil. (15)
One should know that [a site] with an excess of dust is the best; one with an equal amount of dust is middling;
and one with less is to be known as inferior; one should avoid the inferior.
Then, from each of those tufts of hair on the head of the elephant,
the preceptor should sprinkle [the area] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), while reciting the Śiva-mantra.
One should cast the five jewels there with the ninety-six-fold mantra;
then, having covered it with dust, one should properly prepare the sacrificial altar (dhiṣṇya).
It should be square on all sides, resembling the surface of a mirror;
it should be seven cubits long, with its front facing either east or north.
Having prepared two black threads, the root-mantra is recited before them:
Īśa, Jayanta, Āditya, Satyaka, and likewise Bhṛśa.
Agni, Vitatha, Gṛhakṣata, and Yama; Bhṛṅga, Pitṛ, Sugrīva, Varuṇa, and Asura; || 21 ||
Roganāśa, Mukhya, Soma, and Ādita from the very beginning—these, together with Marīcaka, enjoy the eastern quarter consisting of two and a half padas. || 22 ||
Vivasvat indeed rules the south, and Mitra the west;
while Pṛthivīdhara enjoys half of each of the two quarters in the north.
Āpāpavatsa, Sāvitrī, and likewise Indrajaya,
as well as Rudrajaya, O best of Brahmins, are all stationed upon the single foot of Īśāna.
Brahmā enjoys four quarters along with the one who possesses thirty-six quarters;
likewise Carakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, and the sinful Rākṣasī.
One should place [the elements] there upon the four-pronged [diagram] and worship them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
having first conceived Puruṣa, his head should be in the Pūruṣa-ṛk.
It is proclaimed that Brahmakāya occurs in the year Vāma;
O best of Brahmins, Sāvitrī and Candra are said to be Dakṣiṇa and Bahuruci respectively.
Likewise, the left foot is proclaimed as the wife of a Śūdra;
similarly, Indrajaya is said to be the right foot. (28)
The Mitra-liṅga should indeed be downward-facing;
it should be worshipped with perfumes, flowers, incense, and Varuṇa.

The wise one should enlarge the mandala and then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited; he should then divide it into eighteen parts in the east and likewise in the four quarters.
One should rotate a single portion there, turning it inward, toward the middle, and so forth;
in this very manner, one should rotate it in sequence through all four directions. || 31 ||
Having grasped the ear from the middle and drawing it with that very line, one should rotate it;
thus, one should fashion the petal at the position of the inner ear.
In this very manner, the four-fold staff (daṇḍa) is described in due order;
one should likewise draw a circle with half [the measure] at the outer corner of the square.
In this manner, one should join the tips of the petals with eight petals;
and one should fashion the line of the protective border (prativāraṇa) with a width of one finger-breadth.
One should avoid the action of three fingers as well as their mere beauty;
having measured the ground with a single finger... || 35 ||
O best of Brahmins, one should fashion the *śobhā* at a distance of three finger-breadths [from the previous],
and one should fashion the *upaśobhā* at a distance of exactly one finger-breadth.
Then, from the center to the edge of the eastern petal, one should draw the filaments;
one should fashion the filaments as one-third of a part and likewise the pericarp.
In this very manner, one should construct the pavilion step by step;
thus the mandala that bestows liberation has been described. Now, listen to that which is for the purpose of pacification (śāntika).
One should stretch two threads, one from east to west and the other from north to south; or [one may stretch them] from the southwest to the northeast, or from the northwest to the southeast. (39)
One should stretch the cord there and fix a stake right in the middle;
the stakes should be made of khadira wood, or of bilva, mango, and kadamba.
p.
50) [One should use] madhuka, devadāru, or indeed a sacrificial tree;
its height is said to be eight finger-breadths, and half of that is the width. || 41 ||
O best of Brahmins, the pericarp should be made four finger-breadths wide, the filaments six finger-breadths,
and the length of the petals should be fourteen finger-breadths.
One should fashion the *prativāraṇa* as one finger-breadth, the *vidha* as three fingers,
and both the *śobhā* and *upaśobhā* with a space of one finger between them.
In this very manner, one should proceed with the mandala in due order;
thereafter, I shall fully describe the mandala joined with pearl powder.
With the flour of rice and wheat, with powders of the five colors, with the powder of red chalk and bricks, and with the powder of sapphire; || 45 ||
Then, one should place within the mandala a mixture of powdered black charcoal, powdered emerald, and powdered turmeric.
At the base of the filament (kesara), however, it is proclaimed to be white in color;
in the middle it is yellow, and at the tip it is said here to be white.
On the eastern petal, it is remembered as being white in color;
on the southeast it is red, and on the south it is said here to be black.
O best of Brahmins, one should place white [powder] with the mouth in the western direction;
then, having placed turmeric at its end, one should place rice-flour at the end of that.
A twice-born devotee of Śiva should have it drawn provided with four doors,
measuring either one cubit, two cubits, or even four cubits.
It should be eight, twelve, sixteen, or twenty cubits;
or even thirty cubits, but one should not construct it beyond this.
The number of petals is prescribed as eight, or sixteen, or thirty-two, or even one hundred and eight. || 52 ||
I shall now proclaim the ritual placement of the mantras; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
Having placed Puruṣa on the eastern petal, place Aghora on the southern petal.
Having assigned Sadyojāta in the west and likewise Vāmadeva in the north,
one should assign the Heart in the southeast and the Head on the petal of Īśāna.
O Brahmin, one should worship the Śikhā-mantra on the southwestern petal;
the Kavaca-mantra in the region of the wind (northwest), and the Netra-mantra in the region of Īśāna (northeast). 55.

Having worshipped the weapon (astra) in the directions, one should likewise place it in the sequence; and on the spot designated for the Daitya, there shall be the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the disciple.
A *kuṇḍa* may also be used for a human [initiate], while for a *paiśāca* one, the Guru should remain present;
likewise, in the *brāhmīka* mandala, one should act according to this same sequence.
Having worshipped Śiva in the pericarp, one should place [the deity] upon the filaments in the northeast;
then, having sprinkled it with water, one should cause the declaration of "an auspicious day" (puṇyāha) to be recited.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and incense using the *hṛdaya* mantra;
then, one should invoke the deity by means of the *sadyojāta* mantra. (59)
One should establish [the deity] with Vāmadeva and restrain it with Aghora;
one should effect its presence with Puruṣa and worship it with Īśāna.
One should worship according to the prescribed ritual by means of the path of the five coverings (pañcāvaraṇa).
Therefore, one should offer food accompanied by all kinds of side dishes. 61.
One should offer half to the deity, half of that half as an oblation (bali) to the fires,
and one-fourth of what remains in the vessel should be given to the disciple.
Having recollected [the deity] with the five Brahmans, then form the five lumps;
having sipped water according to this rite, without touching it with the teeth, one should consume them.
There, having sipped water according to the rule, one should recite the *vyomavyāpin* mantra;
then one should take a tooth-stick twelve finger-breadths in length.
One should have a tooth-stick made from the pippala, the vaṭa tree, or even the khadira; the apāmārga from a milky tree is also said to be suitable for cleaning the teeth. (65)
Then, having recited the Pāśupatāstra mantra, one should have [the earth] dug;
O Brahmin, having thus purified the impurity and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules.
There, one should mutter the Vyomavyāpin mantra and then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the limbs of Śiva;
then, with the Aghora mantra, one should apply ashes to the head.
Then one should offer the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) accompanied by the Śiva-mantra;
having recited it while joined with the Brahma-mantras that are the limbs of Śiva, one should cause [the disciple] to consume the five [products].
Having sipped water according to the rule, one certainly becomes purified;
then the mantra-practitioner should consecrate the disciple to the south of the mandala.
Seated upon ashes and darbha grass, devoted solely to the meditation on Śiva,
one should prepare a fire-pit measuring either thirty-two or sixteen [units].
One should cause all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) to be made as eight, five, or four in number; they may be circular or square. (71)
The Bilva, Udumbara, and Śamī, as well as the Vaikaṅkata and Śamī;
the Pālāśa, Khadira, Aśvattha, Plakṣa, and Nyagrodha. || 72 ||
And the well-known apāmārga is prescribed as the sacrificial fuel (samidh);
likewise, one should prepare the fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice (caru), parched grain (lāja), the offering (bali), and mustard seeds.
O best of Brahmins, the master of the tantra should offer barley grains as an oblation;
he should offer fuel sticks with the Sadyojāta mantra and clarified butter with the Hṛdaya mantra.

One should perform the oblation of cooked rice (caru) with the *śikhā* [mantra], and likewise the oblation of parched grains (*lāja*) with the *vāma* [mantra]; one should offer stone and other items with the *yantrī*, and rice (*śālī*) with the *puruṣa* [mantra].
One should offer mustard seeds with the *śiras* mantra and likewise barley with the *kavaca* mantra; ten oblations should be offered to Śiva, which shall be double the number for the *vidyeśas*.
Then the best of preceptors should offer oblations three times for Gaṇeśa and the world-protectors (lokapālas),
and he should offer oblations three times for the weapons of the world-protectors.
To the east of the maṇḍala, one should arrange nine water-pots, provided with cloths, covered with lids, and entirely joined with gold. (78)
O best of Brahmins, one should place the nine gems into the ninth pitcher;
it should be filled with sandalwood water and placed upon a heap of grain.
Having established the principal water-pot with the Śiva-mantra, one should likewise place Puruṣa to the east and Aghora to the south.
Having established Sadyojāta in the west and Vāmadeva likewise in the north,
one should place Īśāna in the northeast with the Īśāna mantra, and Hṛdaya in the southeast with the Hṛdaya mantra.
The preceptor, joined with the respective mantras, [should place] the *śikhā* mantra in the southwest and the *kavaca* in the northwest, into their corresponding jars.
With perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and especially with water-offerings (arghya),
one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented to Śivā while reciting the heart-mantra.
One should, however, carefully examine auspicious and inauspicious dreams. || 83½ ||

Mounting bulls, elephants, palaces, mountain peaks, and trees; being smeared with excrement, the flow of blood, and approaching a woman who should not be approached; and [the acquisition of] grain—[these are auspicious]. (84½)
If one sees a Piśāca in a dream, one will encounter great misfortune. || 85 ||
A lotus, a flower, a bull, or a crown that grants the acquisition of land—whether offered, crushed, or ripened on an auspicious tree—[brings success]. (86)
When it rains, one obtains the fruit of rain here without a doubt;
in a field of rice, when the great crop is seen ripe, it brings the gain of rice.
If one sees a great body of water in a dream, one shall obtain wealth and grain;
if a garland of flowers is seen, one should predict the acquisition of wealth.
O Brahmin, if one sees various kinds of sweet fruits even in a dream, one should predict the acquisition of wealth.
Whether it be a cow, or an excellent horse, or a parrot, or even a deer; or a myna bird, or even a hawk—one should see them as signs of the increase of one's family.
But he who sleeps and is seen by one with a serpent on his right arm will obtain either a leaf or a gain of wealth; of this there is no doubt. (91)
Whether it be *gandhaśāli*, *mahāśāli*, *kalamāśāli*, or even *meya* rice,
these should indeed be given— even in a dream— for they truly bring about the destruction of suffering.
If one beholds a Surabhi cow with her calf, his lifespan increases;
likewise, if he sees a person, or even a monkey, or a serpent. (93)
A man obtains wealth and grain that increase his sons and grandsons;
he may even ascend a palace or behold the ocean.
That man certainly obtains the kingdom;
if he sees the orb of the sun in a dream, he shall attain sovereignty through that vision. || 95 ||
Whether it be an astrologer or even a king’s daughter who is exceedingly beautiful, one obtains gain of wealth; by seeing them, one shall attain wealth. (96)
If blood, wine, or even a drink is seen, there will be the acquisition of knowledge for the twice-born, while another shall obtain wealth. (97)
If one crosses a river of blood, one shall attain great wealth;
if one sees or eats impure things, one should predict the acquisition of wealth. (98)
Drinking milk leads to a great disease; drinking ghee leads to great fear;
drinking blood leads to a great disease; and eating curd brings sovereignty. 99.
If one dreams of milk-rice or a dog, half of that merit dissolves;
yet one attains great happiness and shall meet death after a month.
Whether it be a hawk, a donkey, a cat, or an owl—
if a fool hides among their wings, he shall meet death within a month. (101)
If one's own tooth falls out, one will meet with the death of a kinsman;
if a chain is seen there, one will incur a great disease. (102)
If a woman wearing red garments or garlands stands at the feet of one who is black, death shall occur for those afflicted by disease.
If one sees oneself being led to the abode of Yama, mounted upon a chariot yoked with black horses, within a month death shall befall him, even if this is seen at the end of a dream. (104)
When the visible form has fallen away, one should declare his death;
for a renunciant, a mendicant, or a bodhisattva, death is seen to occur [in this manner]. (105)
If one sees a great woman at the end of a dream—other than a Śaiva, or even a twice-born man, wearing red garments and being most auspicious—one attains [great fortune]. (106)
One should therefore avoid the fruit of the palmyra tree among fruits;
one should also avoid the kiṃśuka, red flowers, and the karavīra.
O Brahmin, a white flower is praised when its stalk is hard;
among men, the Brāhmaṇa is the best, while the king would be middling. (108)
One should display a parrot among birds, as well as a cow, a bull, a lion, and likewise a deer. (109)
O Brahmin, even in a dream, seeing mustard seeds or mung beans growing on one's own family land increases longevity; however, if they are seen growing elsewhere, one will incur disease. (110)
(57) Having seen the fruit of a plantain, a coconut, a jackfruit, or a citron, one shall obtain wealth and grain. || 111 ||
Whoever sees at the end of a dream a deity or a sage, or the wife of a god or an apsaras, shall obtain wealth, long life, and fame. (112)
If one sees weapons or vehicles, or the expansion of one's family;
or if meat or fish is obtained, it shall bring auspicious results. (113)
Whether it be a thief, a great sage, or even a tiger, the king suffers affliction; one should indicate disease through the portents of crossing over [obstacles]. (114)
If one performs the rite of bathing, one is immediately freed from disease;
yet, one may see a widow, a shaven-headed woman, or even a naked woman. (115)
There will be a depletion of his grain even at the end of a dream; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, he should not discharge feces or urine in a dream. || 116 ||
If an object perishes at the end of the dream, one will suffer loss of wealth;
however, he who eats rice cooked with milk increases his lifespan, prosperity, and fame. (117)

One should enter the initiation (dīkṣā) during an auspicious [lunar day] after having had auspicious sexual union with women who are highly auspicious; however, during an inauspicious [day], one should perform a fire-oblation (homa).
The goddess Dūrvā, who has a thousand as her limit, a hundred roots, and a hundred sprouts—may she, the destroyer of evil dreams, take away all my sin. (119)
Having recited this mantra, one should place *dūrvā* grass upon the head;
a dream seen during the first watch of the night bears fruit within three years.
By the second [practice], one attains both; by the third, in one year;
and by the fourth, in the Viśvayāma, one achieves success after six months. || 12 ||
If performed at dawn, success is attained in ten days; if in the early morning, in fifteen days;
and if at the time of sunrise, one attains perfection in seven days.
In this very manner, one should examine the dream step by step;
having examined the dream in many ways, the ritual bathing should take place at dawn.
Having explained initiation and the maṇḍala, now hear from me the path of initiation as it has been taught. || 123½ ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the Ritual for the Initiation Mandala, in the Vīratantra, the Compendium of Six Thousand Verses.
The Grandfather.
O Lord, how is the path of initiation? O Master, how is the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa)?
The Śaivas are to be known as being of seven kinds; tell me all of that, O Lord! (1)
Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! That which has been requested by you, I shall explain all of it in its entirety; listen, O Lotus-seated One.
The true essence of knowledge is bestowed and the cage of bonds is destroyed;
having thus brought about this union, it is called initiation (dīkṣā). || 3 ||
The Śaiva [system] has been taught by me in seven ways; listen to it with a focused mind.
First is the Anādi-Śaiva, and the second is the Ādi-Śaiva.
The third is Mahāśaiva, the fourth is Anuśaivaka,
and the wise know the intermediate Śaiva to be the fifth.
The sixth is the Pravara-Śaiva, and the seventh is another, the Śaivaka. Thus the Śaivas are said to be of seven kinds; hear now their distinctions. (6)
The Anādiśaivas are to be known as being conjoined with the scriptures alone;
O best of Brahmins, the Śivadvijas are proclaimed as the Ādiśaivas.
Kauśika, Kāśyapa, Bhāradvāja, Atri,
and Gautama— these five were initiated into the five faces.
For these sages who have been born as Śiva-brahmins, the Śiva-initiation must not be performed; if it were performed, it would be utterly fruitless.
Having led [the disciple] forward at that time, one should worship Śiva within the mandala;
and for the sake of purifying the limbs, one should cause the twice-born Śiva-adepts to perform the ceremonial bath (snapana).
The Great Śaivism belongs to the Brahmins who are endowed with Śiva-initiation;
one who is uninitiated, even if he knows the four Vedas, should not perform the worship of Śiva.
O Supreme Lord, twice-born men who perform initiation for the sake of gain fall after six months; they are remembered as *devalakas* (temple-priests). One should not worship them. || 12 ||
If a Brahmin, having been initiated even for the sake of a mere smile, serves for three years for the purpose of maintenance, he indeed becomes a *devalaka*.
And for all these people, and especially for all these worlds,
they never perform worship at the fixed lingas.
The Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya are said here to be Anuśaivas;
the Śūdra, whether he be an insider or an outsider, is called an Antaraśaiva.
The Savarṇa, Ambaṣṭha, Madhyastha, Kulāla, and likewise the Pārakī—this is known as the Pravara-Śaiva; now hear this other [account] as well. (16)
And for other castes as well, another Śaiva [tradition] is taught here;
he who causes it to be performed otherwise shall obtain nothing but fruitlessness.
The divisions of the Śaivas have been declared by me; now hear the rule for initiation (dīkṣā). || 18 ||
Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Ārdrā, the three Uttarās,
Puṣya, and Śatabhiṣaj are said to be the lunar mansions for initiation (dīkṣā).
Or a bull, or a lion, or a scorpion, or a jar; or a Gemini, or a Virgo, or a Sagittarius, or a Pisces. (20)
For these are declared to be the fixed signs (rāśis); one should avoid the movable sign (cararāśi).
Specifically, the second, fifth, or even the sixth [tithi] is preferred. (21)
It should be performed on the twelfth day, or even on the thirteenth;
for these lunar days have been declared. Now listen also to the [appropriate] weekdays. || 22 ||
Or when the Moon, Venus, Mercury, Jupiter, or Saturn [are favorable], or during the rising of Jupiter, or even the rising of Venus. (23)
One should perform either the rising of Mercury or the rising of the Moon;
meanwhile, let the planets remain in the eighth house, and afterwards, [initiate] the disciples who have fasted.

Having purified himself and controlled his senses, he should wash the feet of the devotees whose hearts are pure, and then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the prescribed rule.
p.
61) One should perform the binding of the eyes with the *hṛdaya* mantra, using either a silk cloth or one made of cotton. (26)
The best [measure] is twelve cubits, the middling ten cubits, and the lowest nine cubits; it should be four tālas in width. || 27 ||
The vessel should be made of crystal or of copper;
one should then cause the binding of the eyes with a new, unwashed cloth. || 28 ||
One should recite the Netra-mantra ten times accompanied by the collection of weapons (astras);
there, one should recite the Vyomavyāpin mantra conjoined with Tatpuruṣa.
The blindfold should be prepared together with golden flowers;
ten niṣkas is the best, while eight niṣkas is the middling.
The lowest [image] is said by me to be five niṣkas in weight;
however, for all those who are poor, one should have it made according to whatever wealth they possess.
Facing north, the wise man, with a single-minded focus,
should place a flower in his hand while reciting the Īśāna mantra.
Having performed three circumambulations with the Vāmadeva mantra,
the wise one should meditate upon the Supreme Lord Śiva with the Śiva-mantra.
The wise one, having meditated upon the Supreme Lord Śiva with the Śiva-mantra, should scatter flowers upon the mandala while reciting words of auspiciousness and benediction.
In whichever mantra, at which word, the flower is offered— whether that be the name or the lineage— his mantra is perfected, or those two grant him grace.
(62) For Īśāna, it bestows the portion of the eastern petal;
likewise, in the south-east it is said to bring prosperity, while in the north-west it brings a loss of longevity. (36)
O best of Brahmins, it is remembered that if the flower falls upon the pericarp in any of the four directions, then there will indeed be happiness. (37)
On the petal of Īśāna, the "Eye" is indeed named here;
one should apply ashes mixed with water to the head. (38)
Having worshipped with *sugandhī* and other offerings according to the mantra of the Heart,
one should place the water-pot upon rice grains in front of Śiva.
He should place the water-pot itself, complete with its cord, its lid, its cloth, and its gold, while reciting the Śiva-mantra.
O best of Brahmins, he should sprinkle water on the head of the disciple;
having placed Īśāna on the head, he should place Tatpuruṣa on the face.
Having placed Aghora in the heart, one should assign Vāma to the secret organ;
one should place Sadyojāta on the feet, and thus perform the ritual placement upon the body of the disciple.
Having placed the heart-mantra upon the heart, one should place the head-mantra upon the head;
having placed the crest-mantra upon the crest, one should place the armor-mantra in the middle of the hands.
One should place the weapon (astra) on the region of the hand and the eye (netra) on the eyes;
and on the right side of the deity, one should place a palāśa leaf.
That seat is proclaimed to be joined with a *kūrca* [grass mat];
and the disciples, seated upon it, should indeed face the east. (45)
O best of Brahmins, when the triangular maṇḍala is established by means of the seed-syllable of fire,
one should burn [the body] starting from the big toe up until the end of the head. (46)
The wise one should not fixate upon what is unreal there with a single-pointed mind;
rather, [he should contemplate] the letter A, which resembles the orb of the moon and is self-arisen. 47.
The principle of Vidyā (vidyā-tattva) is the syllable *u*, while the principle of Śiva (śiva-tattva) is the syllable *m*.
With the single syllable *oṃ*, one [visualizes] the impurity (*mala*) upon the yoga-seat (*yogapīṭha*), facing downwards.
One should contemplate the water of nectar [flowing] through the Suṣumnā, piercing the crown of the head; one should contemplate oneself being flooded by it, up to the very end of the heart. 49.
He who constantly practices this concentration which destroys death shall never experience anger; this is the certainty of the scripture. (50)
Thereafter, one should specifically perform the deposition (*nyāsa*) of the six paths upon the body of the disciple:
the path of mantra, the path of words, the path of principles (*tattva*), and that consisting of the worlds (*bhuvana*).
The path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) and the path of kalās, the twenty-onefold state of Śiva, as well as sattva, rajas, and tamas—these indeed constitute the triad of selves (ātmatraya). || 52 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara, along with the eight Śaktis,
[worship] the Prāsāda, which consists of the five Brahmans and the limbs of Śiva, as Sadāśiva.
O Brahmin, one should place [the mantras] upon the body of the disciple, beginning with the Praṇava and ending with "Namaḥ";
recollecting each respective mantra, one should join them to the disciple's body.
One should place the path of mantra upon the head, and the path of kalā upon the mouth;
having placed the path of tattva at the heart, one should place that which consists of the worlds (bhuvana) at the navel.
The path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) is in the region of the genitals, while the path of kalās (kalādhvan) is in the two feet.
Furthermore, the path of the feet (pādādhvan) should be joined starting from the feet and ending at the head. (56)
Immediately [he should worship] Vāmadeva with eight kalās as the thirteenth,
Aghora with eight, and likewise Tatpuruṣa.
One should assign the five kalās of Īśāna and the thirty-eight kalās;
likewise, the eight of the Vidyeśvaras and the four of the Gaṇeśas.
Having thus laid out the path of the *padas*— the two *padas* of the world-protectors and each single *pada* of the weapons— one should then lay out the path of the *tattvas*.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space;
and the ear, the eye, the tongue, the nose, and the skin as the fifth. (60)
Speech, feet, hands, the anus, and the genitals as the fifth;
and sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth.
The mind, ego, and intellect, as well as primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa);
passion, illusion (māyā), knowledge (vidyā), limited agency (kalā), and necessity (niyati). || 62 ||
He is Gṛheśvara and Kāla, as well as Śuddhamāyā; likewise Śuddhavidyā, Śuddhakalā, Sadāśiva, and the supreme Śiva. (63)
One should thus deposit the thirty-six principles (tattvas) in their proper sequence;
thereafter, one should deposit the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan), beginning with the Kalās and ending with Śiva.
Thereafter, one should deposit the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) in sequence upon the penis;
then, the best of those skilled in ritual procedures should arrange the heart and the other centers below it.
Kālāgni and Andhakāra, those twenty-one hells: Raurava, Kumbhīpāka, and Mahāraurava; (66)
He was not satiated by hunger, nor by water that was both bitter and cold;
likewise, he performed the heat-penance of the heated iron, which causes burning with its warmth.
And the well of the Kūṭaśālmalī tree, the machine of the sesame presses, the bow-hell with its foundation, and that which is like a razor-edged blade. 68.
Pāṣāṇa, Taptapāṃsu, and likewise Taraṇī;
also Tala, Vitala, Nitala, and Talātala. (69)
Aṭala, Talātala, Rasātala, Mahātala, and likewise Pātāla;
as well as Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, and Paraloka. || 70 ||
Maharloka is to be known, as well as Janaloka;
then Tapoloka, Satyaloka, and the imperishable world of the Gandharvas. || 71 ||
And the world of the Vidyādharas, as well as the world of Soma, the world of Īśāna, and likewise the world of Brahmā. || 72 ||
Above the world of Brahmā is the world of Viṣṇu;
beyond that is Satyaloka in Ananta, and above that is Sūkṣmaloka.
The world of Śivottama, the world of Ekanetra, as well as Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin. (74)
The world of Maheśvara, the world of Sadāśiva, Goloka, and Śivaloka—their sequence is thus proclaimed. (75)
Above the world of Śiva, however, no other world exists.
[This extends] starting from the root of the navel up to the region of the heart. (76)
O Brahmin, one should perform the placement of the path of letters (varṇādhvan), beginning with the letter 'ka' and ending with the letter 'pa'.
One should place the letter 'a' on the region of the head and the letter 'ā' on the forehead.
The letter *i* is in the right eye, the letter *ī* in the left eye;
the letter *ḷ* is in the right cheek, and the letter *ḹ* in the left cheek.
And having assigned *e* and *ai* to the cavity of the palate, *o* and *au* to the two lips, and the two syllables *aṃ* and *aḥ* to the two rows of teeth; || 79 ||
The *ka*-group [of consonants] on the right hand, the *ca*-group on the left hand;
the *ṭa*-group on the right foot, and the *ta*-group on the left foot. (80)
One should place the *pavarga* on the right side; it shines upon the left side as well.
Having placed the letter *ma* in the heart, one should likewise assign the letter *ya*. (81)
The letter *repha* is said to be blood, and the letter *la* is indeed flesh;
having placed the letter *la* in the fat, one should place the letter *śa* in the presiding deity.
In the region of the anus is the letter *ṣa*, and the letter *sa* is indeed white;
they say the letter *ha* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the letter *la* is the penis.
The syllable *kṣa* is said to be on the testicles; one should place all of these [syllables] together.
O Brahmin, one should place the thirty-nine *kalās* beginning with *ka* and ending with *pa*. (84)
Rāsvatā, Ādhāra, Maṇītā, Paṅkti, Dāruṇī, Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti. || 85 ||
Having sequentially deposited the principles (tattvas) up to the supreme ether beyond peace (śāntyatīta),
one then [deposits] delusion, hunger, sleep, death, illusion, and old age. (86)
One should delight in protecting the king and guarding those to be protected; one must not neglect the precious opportunity for practice.
Furthermore, one should maintain steadfastness during the night, as well as employ the wandering and the deluding [practices]. || 87 ||
We meditate upon that which is pervaded by the thirty-nine digits (kalās)—Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Śānti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Svadhā, and Sthiti—by the God of gods. 88.
Having placed fire in the heart, one should place [the element] in the mouth;
having placed space in the head, one should place the five principles (tattvas) in their proper order.

The path of mantras is by means of the Sadyojāta mantra; the path of words (pada) is indeed by means of Vāmadeva; the path of principles (tattva) is by means of Aghora; and the path of worlds (bhuvana) is by means of Puruṣa.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) with Īśāna for both the path of the phonemes (varṇādhvan) and the path of the kalās;
then, in this very same sequence, one should place them upon the body of the disciple.
Having placed Īśāna on the head, Viṣṇu is remembered for the mouth;
that of Brahmā is declared for the heart, and one should place [the deity] in the hands during the Aśvinī constellation.
O Brahmin, that mortal who acts in this manner on earth becomes a human being who is himself a spiritual guide; Śiva himself abides right there.
Therefore, with every effort, one should thereafter worship the preceptor;
whatever substance remains in the vessel and so forth belongs to Śiva, the Supreme Lord.
Even for a teacher, it should not be considered a fault to offer oblations;
indeed, everything—clothing, grain, gold, and so forth—should be offered with Śiva in mind.
If one places [the offering] into the hand of the preceptor, one shall attain the world of Śiva.
Thus has been declared the procedure for initiation; now hear about the consecration (abhiṣeka). || 96 ||
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the procedure for initiation, in the Vīratantra.
The Grandfather.
O Lord, O Master, tell me all about how the consecration (abhiṣeka) is performed for initiated disciples for the sake of purifying their evil karma. || 1 ||
The Lord.
Whatever has been seen by others shall now all be told;
[this occurs] at an auspicious moment, in a favorable planetary alignment (lagna), and in a conjunction endowed with the proper astrological divisions (karaṇa).
One should construct a pavilion in front of the deity according to the previously mentioned procedure;
then, one should perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) endowed with its proper characteristics.
The *pālikā*, the *ghaṭikā*, and the *śarāva*—these three types [of vessels] should be used; likewise, wild rice, barley, *śālī* rice, sesame, and bamboo [vessels]. (4)
White rice, great rice, mung beans, black gram, and horse-gram;
or what is called kalama rice, barley, mustard, or even peas.
O Brahmin, one should cause a Niṣpāva and a Priyaṅgu tree, endowed with auspicious marks, to be taken; one should wash them with milk and plant them toward the east and other directions.
O best of Brahmins, one should place a water-pot in the very center,
provided with a cloth, gold, a tuft of kusha grass, and a lid.
The preceptor, having become pure, wearing a turban and an upper garment, should cause the seeds to be sown there; thereafter, he should cause betel to be offered.
Then, one should perform the consecration of the pavilion and have the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana) recited;
this should be done either one hundred and eight times, or fifty, or twenty-five times.
