The supreme preceptor should place nine inferior jars;
then a cord-receptacle must be prepared, and he should scatter rice there.
One should prepare [the altar] with eight *droṇas* of rice, or half of that amount;
one should then strew it with half as much rice, sesame seeds, parched grain (*lāja*), and *darbha* grass.
In the center, one should place the Śiva-pitcher with the Śiva-mantra; it should be provided with threads, a lid, cloth, and gold.
To his left, he should place the *vardhanī* vessel conjoined with the seed-syllable of Gaurī;
then, from the south to the northeast, he should establish eight water-pots (*kumbhas*).
Śiva is to be worshipped in the principal pitcher (kumbha), and one should place Ambikā in the vardhanī;
likewise Ananteśa, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, and Ekanetraka.
Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin are declared to be the presiding deities; now listen also to those of the ritual substances. || 15 ||
O Brahmin, one should then place the nine gems into the principal pitcher;
one should cast gold into the *vardhanī* with the *gaurī* seed-mantra.
Then, one should first place in abundance gold, silver, copper, lead, tin, brass, and bell-metal. (17)
O Brahmin, one should place the nine minerals into the pitcher in the southeast:
yellow orpiment, [and so on], along with chickpeas and sesame seeds. (18)
Then one should specifically place a *māṣaka* of *saurāṣṭra*, followed by a single lump of *rasa-paṅka*; and likewise, one should especially arrange nine [parts] with *rasa*. (19)
And, O best of Brahmins, one should place a leaf from each of these trees upon the southern pitcher:
the Palāśa, the Khadira, the Tārkṣya, and the Nyagrodha.
One should place a set of nine flowers— pippala, panasa, bilva, śirīṣa, and campaka— into the pitcher situated in the southwest.
On both banks of the river, betel vines should be planted;
and when the pitcher has been placed in the western direction, one should place a set of nine flowers within it—
either lotuses, campakas, water-lilies, or blue lotuses.
The *pāṭalī*, the *karavīra*, the red lotus (*raktotpala*), the *nandyāvarta*, and the *ghāta*—these are here called the "nine flowers. (24)
And in the northwest, one should place perfumes, flowers, and so forth within the water-jars;
[namely] sandalwood, saffron, blue lotus, the elephant, and the monkey.
One should place a copper leaf inscribed with one's own name [in the vessel];
and when the water-pot has been established in the north, one should deposit the nine seed-syllables within it.
Barley, bamboo seeds, priyaṅgu, śāli rice, and nīvāra grain; likewise, wheat, barley, mung beans, and mustard seeds in their proper order. (27)
In the northeast, one should likewise place a water-pot and arrange the medicinal herbs in their proper order:
Lakṣmī, Sahādevī, Viṣṇukrānti, and Trayambalā. (28)
One should specifically place the *indraparṇa*, *śaṅkhapuṣpa*, *sūryāvarta*, and *gandhikā* flowers, consecrating each with its own respective name-mantra. (29)
One should especially have eighty-one jars prepared;
furthermore, a fire-offering (homa) should be performed in the eight directions according to the prescribed characteristics.
Alternatively, there may be five oblations, and fourteen in the northeast,
using wood from the Palāśa, Khadira, Aśvattha, Plakṣa, Nyagrodha, and Bilva trees.
One should arrange the Audumbara and Śamī wood, as well as sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, barley, śāli rice, and sesame seeds, starting from the east.
One should offer one thousand oblations each of *priyaṅgu* and *siddhārthaka*,
continuing until the number of oblations is equal to the number of jars.
Or one hundred and eight, or fifty, or twenty-five [times],
[he should perform this] to the west of the sacrificial site for Mahādeva.
O best of Brahmins, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) accompanied by the initiation of Śiva;
and study of the four Vedas should be conducted in the four directions.
Then, one should worship Śiva with perfumes, flowers, and incense, in the western direction of the sacrificial site and to the east of Mahādeva. (36)
There, one should perform the consecration with the mantra of the Prāsāda,
joined with the Brahma-mantras and their limbs, and accompanied by the Vyomavyāpin.
There, one should especially perform the consecration upon the body of the disciple,
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, by means of the mantra of the Prāsāda.
In that very place, the preceptor, together with his disciples, should feed the Brahmins;
that meal, [performed] today on this day of the lion, is the end of the coloring. (39)
One should cause the preceptor to receive all the implements for initiation, as well as sandals,
a buffalo, a goat, a cow, a female slave, grains, and garments in their entirety.
One should present it to the teacher and announce the honorarium. || 41 ||
One should offer as food milk-rice (pāyasa) filled with milk,
combined with jaggery, mixed with cow's ghee, and accompanied by plantain fruit.

The preceptor, together with the disciple, should cause [the guests] to eat according to the prescribed ritual, accompanied by various side dishes and served from the beginning with the mantra of the temple.
One should feed [the deities] there according to the ritual convention (samaya), and at the front, one should cast the bali offering,
consisting of fried grain (lāja) combined with cakes (apūpa) mixed with ghee.
The preceptor should offer a bali-oblation consisting of sacrificial porridge mixed with curd at the crossroads, on the main road, and likewise at each single path, according to the prescribed rule.
One should worship the abode of all the gods according to the Pañcarātra;
in this very sequence, one should indeed cause the consecration to be performed.
For one who causes this— the most auspicious of all auspicious things and the warder-off of all diseases—
to be performed according to the prescribed rite, death does not exist.
The mortal who performs this in such a manner shall attain the world of Śiva.
I have thus declared the consecration; now hear from me the conduct of a Śaiva.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "Consecration," in the Vīratantra, the compendium of six thousand verses. 10.
(73) O Teacher, you ought to explain here everything concerning those such as the Ādiśaiva, the Mahāśaiva, and the Anuśaiva— what they are like in this world. 1.
Īśvara said: O Lotus-seated One, listen to the sixteen rites of conduct for the Śaivas of the three castes, beginning with *niṣeka* and ending with *sapiṇḍana*.
In this very context, O best of the twice-born, they cite this [example]:
having prepared a level spot in a pure place, one should then place white [materials] there.
O best of Brahmins, having removed husks, charcoal, iron, hair, and insects,
one should then prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit.
One should draw three lines facing east and north upon the entire surface;
then, having wiped away the water from the jar, one should wash both hands there.
Alternatively, having approached the fire in the house of a Vedic scholar (śrotriya),
one should cause the fire to be brought forth with the Vyāhṛtis and then kindle it with six fuel-sticks (ulmuka).
And he performs the ritual attendance with the mantra "juṣṭo damūnā," having then strewn darbha grass around the four directions to the extent of one cubit.
Then, one should place nine [vessels] in the four directions starting from the east;
thereafter, one should place those facing south, north, and downwards.
One should arrange the darbha grasses toward the east and north, and then arrange the enclosing sticks (paridhis) to a length of one cubit.
Then one should place the darbha grass in the south, the west, and the north; the enclosing sticks (paridhis) together with the crest-blade (śikhā) should be placed with the heart-mantra.
O Brahmin, one should place two joints above with the *śiras* mantra; then,
one should place a shallow bowl (*śarāva*) upon the *darbha* grass along with sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*).
O best of brahmins, one should prepare the clarified butter (ājya) with the heart-mantra;
one should sprinkle it with water and worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Having silently lifted the vessel and sprinkled it again with water,
one should then feed the Brāhmaṇas on the southern side of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Having placed the *praṇītā* vessel on the north, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
one should then set down the *tiras-pavitra*, joined with two tips of *darbha* grass.
One should place the clarified butter (ājya) in the vessel for ghee (ājyasthālī), and afterwards place it over the embers;
O best of Brahmins, one should then place a single blade of darbha grass [upon it], and thus the heating of the ghee (ājyādhiśravaṇa) shall take place.
Then, having joined it with the tips of two *darbha* blades, the most excellent preceptor should illuminate it with fire; he should likewise purify both the *sruva* ladle and the *darbha* blades.
Therefore, one should offer oblations with the sūtra, especially into the mouth of the fire;
thereafter, one should perform the sprinkling (pariṣecana) accompanied by the Hṛdaya mantra. || 17 ||
One should silently place the fuel-wood, consisting of sixteen pieces, into the fire; then one should perform the oblation with the *sruva* ladon using the mantra, "To Prajāpati, svāhā! (18).
Saying "svāhā," while touching the junction of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), she [should offer];
then the portion of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) is to be offered with the mantra: "To Agni, svāhā! (19).
And having offered the northern oblation rich with worship, one should perform the purification in sequence by means of the six [mantras] beginning with Vahni. || 20 ||
One should offer the *vyāhṛtis* there, and one should perform the oblation with grace. Thus ends the "Face of Fire" (*agnimukha*).
And hear now concerning the seasonal union with women who have bathed after their menses. || 21 ||
One should also consecrate with the heart-mantra a woman who has bathed after her menses;
there, the fire-mouth should be fashioned as upward-facing and four-armed.
Thus, it should be joined with the three eyes; one should offer ten oblations to Śiva.
By means of the heart mantra, the purification is performed in sequence.
With the *sruva* ladle, one should pour the clarified butter from the *ājyasthālī* onto the ground in the southwest direction;
in this very manner, for the satisfaction of the *rākṣasas*. (24)
Having offered the after-sacrifices (anuyāja), he should deposit the Āmopayāma vessel there;
and by the command of Agni, he should fashion the body [of the cake] with the verses beginning "ayantayoni."
Thus, there should be no self-identification with these [deities] through mantra;
rather, having rinsed the lips of the consecrated [offering], one should sprinkle [them] with water from the *prokṣiṇī* vessel.
Then, O Grandfather, having cast [the water] in the ten directions and upwards as well,
one should cause the vardhanī vessel to pervade that area and then sprinkle it with water.
On that night, an excellent meal of milk should be served to the women;
there, one should have them lie down upon the bed together with the husband and wife.
Prajāpati, the bed being threefold, should consecrate it with mantras;
indeed, the primary linga is established with the mantra "viṣṇur yoniḥ. (29)
Thinking, "I am depositing the embryo; I am within this," he becomes joined;
he should perform the union of the womb as prescribed, being thus joined.
If on an even day a male is conceived, and on an odd day a female,
it is said that he will increase the moon-like [splendor], and his body shall endure. (31)
This consecration has been described for you specifically out of affection.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the ritual for union during the seasons, in the Vīra-tantra. || 11 ||
I shall now describe the procedure for conception (garbhādhāna) in brief; listen at once.
[The auspicious asterisms are] Rohiṇī, Revatī, Hastā, Śravaṇa, and Anurādhā (Ananāyaka). || 1 ||
The constellations Svātī, Śatabhiṣaj, and the three Uttaras; and the final decan and the final portion of the signs of Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and the Moon. (2)
Thinking "I shall conceive a fetus," one should meditate upon the fetus in its true nature;
then, one should perform a circumambulation of the person named Jīva.
Even when the fetus has not yet been conceived, one should arrange the fire-mouth;
there, one should perform twenty-five oblations with the Sadyojāta mantra.
One should likewise offer oblations during Jyeṣṭhā, Śreṣṭhā, and Śraviṣṭhā;
thereafter, O best of Brahmins, one whose body has been made complete [performs] the Paṅkti rite.
Indeed, conception occurs when a man touches her [the woman] with water.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, the procedure for the rite of conception, in the Vīra-tantra.
77) Now I shall describe the *puṃsavana* rite; listen to its true nature, O ascetic.
It should be performed at the end of the second month, accompanied by all ornaments. || 1 ||
A wise man should perform the *puṃsavana* rite under the asterisms of Puṣya or Śravaṇa;
likewise, the rising of Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon is highly commended.

Indeed, the rising of the moon is auspicious, but the planets are not desired in the eighth house; here, the sowing of sprouts should be performed, and thereafter one should cause the proclamation of a "holy day" (puṇyāha) to be recited.
One should tie the protective amulet there with the mantra "viśve tvā" (VS 10.25). Having spread out the mouth of the fire, one who is disciplined performs the oblation and other rites.
O Prajāpati, one should not perform these *caru* oblations;
rather, one should cause the *garbha* [rites] to be performed in the fire according to the injunctions and then offer oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*). || 5 ||
Eight hundred oblations are offered with the Vāmadeva mantra,
using fuel-sticks of Nyagrodha, Udumbara, Aśvattha, Palāśa, and Khadira wood together.
With clarified butter and the Vāmadeva hymn, one should cause a new cloth to be placed;
and on the right side of his nose, he should offer to these deities according to the mantra.
O best of Brahmins, there was no mortar here, nor was a woman present to grind;
therefore, I saw only the cutting [of grain] facing either eastward or northward.
Having released the breaths through the five Brahmans,
he should then show [the pole star] while saying, "This is Dhruva," and "This is Arundhatī."
Then that [image] is seen to be composed of gold, copper, or silver;
it brings about the fulfillment of the threefold dharma for women—of this there is no doubt. || 10 ||
Carrying away [the water], binding it, or even causing it to overflow—these are the functions [of the deity].
Furthermore, there is the scratching of the nails and the opening of the sheaths of the sacred fords (*tīrtha*). (11)
From that time on, he should not bathe with water nor have his hair shaved;
the husband of a pregnant woman should not do these things, for otherwise the offspring will not be healthy.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, the procedure for the *puṃsavana* rite, in the *Vīratantra*.
I shall now describe the parting of the hair (sīmanta); listen, O Lotus-seated One!
It should be performed when the fourth month has arrived, or even in the sixth month.
Then one should perform the *garbha* (conception) and *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair) rites under Rohiṇī, Puṣya, Uttarā-phalgunī, or Punarvasu. || 2 ||
One should perform the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) under the asterisms of Hasta, Śravaṇa, Revatī, or Mṛgaśīrṣaka, during an auspicious lunar day and at a favorable planetary conjunction.
If the eighth house is occupied by Leo or Scorpio and is devoid of planets,
one should have the auspicious day proclaimed (puṇyāha-vācana) there and perform the rite of the mouth of fire (agnimukha).
One should perform the Jaya-oblation [with the mantra]: "May Dhātṛ grant us wealth;
I shall perform the oblation of clarified butter... || 5 ||
Then, one hundred oblations are offered with the Aghora mantra;
one should cause [the deity] to desire [the goal] with the "Kāmayet" mantra, and one should sacrifice at the peak of the night.
One should draw the lines with a sprout of darbha grass while reciting the *vāstospataye* mantra;
one should perform the fire-oblation with a piece of udumbara wood while reciting the *sinīvālī* mantra.
One should have it written by a Yavana alone with the mantra "Rudradeva";
then Vanavāsī and Āsīva, having bound the hair on the left side, are [subdued] by Keśarvanila. (8)
O best of gods, one should have women perform [the rite] with the words, "Soma alone is our king"; the remainder of the ritual should be performed exactly as in the Puṃsavana. || 9 ||
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the Ritual for the Parting of the Hair, in the Vīratantra. || 14 ||
O Grandfather, listen as I describe the Viṣṇubali;
having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), one should then worship Viṣṇu.
One should invoke Viṣṇu there with the Vyāhṛtis and the Ghoramantra;
and having prepared the mouth of the fire (Agnimukha) as before, endowed with the prescribed characteristics.
Having especially offered the water of honor (arghya) with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā," [he should worship] Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Govinda, and likewise Mādhava.
Viṣṇu, Madhusūdana, Trivikrama, Vāmana, Śrīdhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, and likewise Padmanābha. (4)
O best of Brahmins, one should also worship Dāmodara by his twelfth name,
and a meal of sacrificial porridge (caru) should be prepared at the conclusion of the vow.
With the six verses beginning with "Viṣṇornukaṃ," the oblation of food is here prescribed;
likewise, there should be an oblation of clarified butter, and then one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (Puṇyāha) to be made.
One should especially feed eight celibate students.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the ritual for the Viṣṇu-bali offering, in the Vīratantra. || 15 ||
I shall describe the ritual procedure for the birth-ceremony (jātakarman), which accomplishes all desires and aims; one should show the newborn boy with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Having specifically severed the navel with the Astra-mantra alone,
one should bathe it according to the prescribed ritual with the mantra "adbhyaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ."
The preceptor smells [the disciple] from limb to limb, beginning with the head;
by smelling the head with the Īśāna and other mantras, he is said to be liberated.
Then one should mutter the *tatpuruṣa* mantra at the right ear;
having especially muttered the *aśvābhidhānī* and the *paraśubhadā*, [one should proceed]. || 4 ||
I shall now declare the names of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) according to the mantras for each day;
having honored them with the word "brūhi" at the end, they should be worshipped together with gold.
Furthermore, one should bathe [the child] again with the Vyāpaka [mantra] according to the prescribed rule;
then, one should have him consume [the medicinal substance] while reciting: "Long life, health, and intelligence."
Saying "I give [it] into the hand of the mother," or reciting the *vitatvam* mantra, one should give the breast to the mother with her left breast using this mantra: "yaste stane. || 7 ||
One should place a full water-pot in the position of the head;
having established it in this manner, one should then prepare the mouth of the fire.
The offering of cooked oblations (pakvāhuti) here is said to be performed with water while reciting the mantra;
likewise, one should release Hari, Hara, and [the other deities].
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the Īśāna mantra,
and [offerings] for Sadyojāta joined with *aśvattha* leaves.
O best of Brahmins, one should offer the remainder of the oblation as a *bali* and enter [the ritual space].
There, one should perform the fire-offering (*homa*) for the sake of the entry and the attainment of the fruit of the woman. (11½)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the ritual for the birth-ceremony, in the Vīratantra. || 16 ||
I shall now describe the naming ceremony; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
[The auspicious asterisms are] Uttarā, Revatī, Hastā, Śatabhiṣaj, Mūla, and Puṣya. (1)
Punarvasu, Śravaṇa, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśīrṣaka, Śraviṣṭhā, and Uttarā [Phalgunī]—these constellations are recommended for the naming ceremony. (2)
Having likewise formally conceived of the fire as the mouth according to the rules, the preceptor performs the naming ceremony for Īśāna under the constellation Prājāpatya. || 3 ||
Having recited "Svasti" at the beginning and the mantra ending in "Śiva" consisting of four syllables, one should worship Puṣyeśa in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa; he is remembered as Śambhu.
In Māgha one should worship Mahādeva by the name Maheśvara; in Phālguna, the Great God (Mahādeva);
in Caitra, the one named Sthāṇu; and likewise in Vaiśākha, Śiva.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship the deity named Paśupati; in Āṣāḍha, the one named Ugra;
in Śrāvaṇa, the one named Sarva; and in the month of Bhādrapada, Triyambaka.
The name of Aśvinī is Īśvara, and that of Kṛttikā is Rudra;
having uttered these names, one should cause the name of the preceptor to be recited.
And the naming ceremony for me should be performed in this manner, O best of gods. (7 ½)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, the ritual for naming, in the Vīratantra. || 17 ||
I shall describe the procedure for the departure; the rosary is said to be the Śāru.
Aśvinī has Soma as its deity, as do Revatī and Punarvasu. (1)
Śravaṇa, Śraviṣṭhā, Hasta, Svāti, Anurādhā, Citrā and the others, the Uttarās, as well as Śatabhiṣaj and Rohiṇī. (2)
The Puṣya asterism is indeed praised for the Great Departure;
furthermore, planets situated in the tenth house are not desired by all means.
At an auspicious and propitious moment, one should perform the rite with the fire as the mouth;
and with the Īśāna mantra, one offers oblations with one's own [prescribed] ghee.
Outside, having smeared an area the size of a cow-hide with gorocanā and having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with sand, one should then place an aśvattha tree there.
"They cause [the senses] to bend toward their own objects through restraint"—it is thus that it is prescribed. || 5½ ||
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, the ritual for the going-forth, in the Vīratantra. || 18 ||
Now, O ascetic rich in penance, I shall describe the first feeding with solid food (annaprāśana) in brief:
it is performed when the sixth month has arrived. || 1 ||
Aśvinī, Mṛgaśiras, Revatī, and Punarvasu; Śravaṇa, Śraviṣṭhā, Hasta, Svātī, and Anurādhā. || 2 ||
Citrā, the three Uttarās, Śatabhiṣaj, Rohiṇī, and Puṣya— these lunar mansions are likewise recommended for the consumption of food. (3)
All planets situated in the tenth house are undesirable by every means. On the previous day, one should feed an even number of Brahmins, beginning with those who are not the eldest.
Having especially adorned the son with perfumes and other such things,
one should worship him there auspiciously and likewise cover him with a variegated cloth.

The father, however, should go again for the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra; then the Lotus-born One should smell the head of the son in the middle [of the forehead] with the *atijighra* mantra.
Having conceived Agni as the mouth [of the sacrifice], accompanied by the Agnisūkta and joined with the Pañcabrahma mantras, one should offer seven oblations into cow dung.
With the mantra "I am this," he should place [the materials] combined with curd, clarified butter, and honey;
and with the mantra "Whatever herbs there are," he should pour honey upon the honey.
Then, at an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction of planets, one should feed them milk-rice (pāyasa);
there, one should feed the Brahmins and then worship the preceptor (ācārya).
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, the ritual for the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), in the *Vīratantra*.
I shall describe the procedure for the *caula-karman*, which increases longevity and health.
The asterisms of Citrā, Śraviṣṭhā, Hasta, Revatī, and Śravaṇā are auspicious;
as are Puṣya, Punarvasu, and Mṛgaśīrṣa. (2)
These very [days] are declared inauspicious when occurring on the eighth lunar day;
therefore, one should have the *puṇyāha* (declaration of auspiciousness) recited there and provide a feast for the Brahmins. || 3 ||
Having spread out the mouth of the fire (the sacrificial ground), one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
then, having offered an oblation with the mantra "eke sinī'tinaktaṃ ca," one should subsequently offer the [main] oblation.
One should perform the offering of clarified butter upon the *proṣṭha* with the *hṛdaya-mantra*;
thereafter, one should offer fifty oblations with the *īśāna-mantra*.
Then, on the northern side of the boy, the mother should prepare a ball of cow dung mixed with unbroken grains (akṣata) in a shallow dish (śarāva).
With cold and warm water, they should dispel [the afflictions] so that he may live;
one should sprinkle the hair there and then consecrate it with *kuśa* grass.
The preceptor should first cause [the hair] to be shaved, followed by the barber;
having left a tuft of hair (śikhā) in the middle of the work, he should then face toward the cows.
Then, at the root of a Darbha or Udumbara tree, he should offer the hair;
there he should bathe the boy and sprinkle him with water while reciting the Hṛdaya mantra.
Accompanied by the recitation of auspicious verses, he should give the teacher’s sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 9½ ||
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, the Ritual for Tonsure, in the Vīratantra.
I shall now describe the initiation ceremony (upanayana), which increases longevity and health:
for Brahmins it is in the eighth year from conception, and for Kshatriyas, eleven years thereafter.
Then, for the Vaiśyas, one should have it performed in the twelfth year during the spring;
likewise, having performed the sixteen-year rite, one should thereafter feed the Brāhmaṇas.
In Rohiṇī, Hasta, Citrā, the two Uttarās, Anurādhā, Svātī, Mṛgaśiras, and Punarvasu— these are proclaimed [as auspicious]. (3)
O best of Brahmins, having performed one's ablutions during the months of Taurus, Gemini, Virgo, and Cancer, one should perform a complete circumambulation.
One should present the sacred thread with the *yajñopavīta* mantra;
having performed the ritual dedication (*saṃkalpa*) for the commencement of the fire-rite, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
To the north of the fire, one should press down upon the measuring-mark and the base;
then, with a cord of that same length as the spear-point, one should wrap it around the pair of cloths.
One should bind [it] with the mantra beginning "yāduktena";
then, one should give a black antelope skin to the student (ācamitra) after the water-offering (āpaḥ). || 7 ||
One should cause a palāśa staff to be placed in the hand and also cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given;
then, with the left hand, one should perform the cooked oblation (pākāhuti) while reciting "devasya tvā."
If one should perform an oblation of clarified butter with the *aghora* mantra,
having offered with the *brahmasūkta* and having offered by means of the *vyāhṛtis*.
One should cause food to be offered on a Palāśa leaf with the mantra "Nīlagrīva";
four Palāśa fuel-sticks should be offered as oblations by one who lives in a lowly state.
"O Agni, Lord of Vows," and "O Vāyu, Lord of Vows," and "O Āditya, Lord of Vows," and also "O Lord of Vows of Vows. || 11 ||
One should be able to fashion that; then one should offer oblations into the fire in due order.
Having placed it to the south of the fire, one should then sprinkle it with water using the Astra-mantra.
One should offer the Jaya and other oblations, as well as the Rāṣṭrabhṛt oblations;
then, facing the student, one should recite the Sāvitrī. (13)
Then, one should have the student who has observed celibacy consume the remnants of the oblation with the Sāvitrī mantra;
at that time, having drawn a mandala according to the prescribed rules.
One should worship Śiva there and offer the food oblation (naivedya) to Śiva;
then, one should place the water-pots (kalaśas) on the northern side of the mandala.
One should place it in the midst of śāli rice and bathe it with the Śiva-mantra,
together with nine fuel-sticks consecrated by the Īśāna-mantra and the vyāhṛtis.
One should perform the fire-oblation there according to the prescribed rules,
and one should honor the preceptor with gifts such as cows, land, gold, and other riches.
Having brought the alms-bowl, he should place it in the hand of the young brahmin;
then, with the arghya water itself, he should offer the māyās to the young brahmin.
Or his teacher, having performed purification especially well, having bathed in the morning and sipped water, should drink water while reciting the mantra "Sūryaśca. (19)
Then, at each appropriate time, one should drink water with the mantra "āpaḥ punantu," combined with the heart-mantra, and with "agniśca" and "sāmnā. 20.
Having sprinkled himself with water while reciting the mantra "dadhikrāvṇo," he should then take water in his cupped palms and,
facing the sun, discharge it while reciting the Vyāhṛtis.
One should cause water to be held in the hand and sprinkle it with the Astra-mantra;
having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should recite the Sāvitrī mantra one hundred and eight times. (23)
Rising from his previous position, or likewise remaining seated,
a friend who has approached should perform the established rite of attendance at the twilight prayers according to the rules.
The wise man should enter his own home and perform his daily rites;
having strewn grass around the fire, he should perform the ritual sprinkling. || 25 ||
One should apply the sacred ash with the mantra "juṣasva naḥ" and likewise wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra);
in this very sequence, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) both evening and morning.
The teacher should instruct him especially in the Vedic scriptures;
meanwhile, he should avoid alkaline substances, honey, meat, salt, and the like.
They never desire him while he is asleep during the day;
in this very manner, strength generally belongs to the night in due succession. (28)
To the north of the fire, prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with rice;
having adorned two women, [address them] as "Śraddhā" and "Medhā. (29)
Having adorned [the deity] with perfumes and garlands, one should offer incense, lamps, and an oblation;
by performing the ritual in this very sequence, one shall obtain longevity and strength. || 30 ||
On the fourth day, O best of Brahmins, one should worship the Brahma-tree and,
having consecrated the fire-mouth, [worship] the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with the mantra.
One should perform the touching of the *palāśa* leaf and observe the *sāvitra* vow;
then, one should offer four fuel-sticks as before and burn incense.
One should perform the circumambulation in a clockwise direction, beginning from the northeast (Īśāna).
At the root of a Palāśa tree, he should place his staff, deerskin, girdle of muñja grass, and rosary, with a friend [to assist]. (33)
One should deposit [the offerings] with the Sadyojāta mantra and hold one another;
having sipped water (ācamana), O best of Brahmins, the Jaya and other oblations are then offered.
There, one should feed Brahmins who have received the initiation of Śiva.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, the ritual for the initiation [upanayana], in the Vīra-tantra. || 21 ||
And on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, I shall speak specifically;
having gone to a riverbank or a lake, one should then offer libations to the nine Ṛṣis.
In this very manner, one should satisfy Prajāpati, the seer of the section;
and having designated Agni as the mouth, an oblation is offered to the seers.
Then, having become one with Savitṛ, he should offer the beginnings of the Vedas in their proper sequence;
having again performed the sprinkling around according to the rule, the oblation is offered.
Having shaved his hair, beard, and body hair, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the preceptor then offers a thousand fuel-sticks (samidh) into the fire in succession.
Alternatively, Sāvitrī herself would always perform the recitation in this manner.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, the Procedure for the Upākarma, in the Vīratantra.
I shall now describe the Śukriya rite on the bank of a river or a pond;
having bathed, wearing clean garments, and having offered oblations according to the Śukriya ritual procedure.
p. 89) It should be offered as an oblation with the *brahmāṅga* mantra together with *palāśa* fuel-sticks;
and the preceptor should wrap the body with a new cloth. || 2 ||
One should remain awake there during the night, and at dawn one should begin the ritual;
one should feed Brāhmaṇas there who are endowed with devotion to Śiva.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, the ritual procedure for the Śukriya-vrata, in the Vīra-tantra.
O Lotus-born One, listen as I describe the procedure for the return home (samāvarta) in brief: Svāti, Mūla, Anurādhā, and so forth.
Hasta, Revatī, Rohiṇī,
and the three Uttaras— these are the constellations, O best of gods, which are devoid of the seventh planet.
Having mentally conceived Agni as the mouth [of the sacrifice] and having especially offered clarified butter,
he should place [the sacrificial grass] bound with a muñja-grass cord into the hand of the student.
At the root of an udumbara tree, however, a wise man should deposit the girdle of muñja grass and so forth,
as well as black hair and body hair.
Having indeed purified his vision and bathed,
he who meets his end has fulfilled the vow of a *snātaka* and has especially performed the fire-oblation.
The Arhatī, having drunk the yellow liquid, should then perform the cooked oblation;
thereafter, she should offer all the oblations of clarified butter and meat.
Having thus recollected the mantra, one should cast the *bilva* fruit— remaining from the oblation (*hutaśeṣa*)— onto the thousand-branched *bilva* branch.

90) Or, as it is said: she should display the *caru* while reciting the *pravadīyantī* mantra;
and she should consecrate her belly with the *prativeśā* mantra. || 8 ||
One should show the collyrium and the mirror with the Īśāna mantra;
in the eastern direction, one should worship that [mirror] with the Śāstra mantra.
Having gone facing north, equipped with shoes and an umbrella,
an oblation of clarified butter is offered with the *vyāhṛtis* during ceremonies such as the return home (*samāvartana*) and rites for prosperity (*vṛddhi*).
Nine oblations are offered with the Pañcabrahma mantra;
and for the sake of the marriage ceremony, grains such as rice are weighed on a scale.
"To Agni, svāhā!"—thus it is offered to Prajāpati in the evening;
"To Sūrya, to Prajāpati"—thus it is offered in the morning. || 12 ||
Those who desire long life should offer oblations with the mantra beginning "ayāścāgne."
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, the procedure for the return ceremony, in the Vīratantra.
I shall now describe the auspicious marriage ceremony under favorable constellations:
Svātī, Mūla, Anurādhā, Maghā, and likewise Mṛgaśiras. (1)
In the asterisms Hasta, Revatī, Rohiṇī, and the three Uttaras, as well as in the signs Kanyā, Mithuna, Tulā, Makara, and Kumbha, [these acts] are auspicious. || 2 ||
The most excellent characteristic of these [planets] is that they are free from [malefic] planets in the seventh house;
one should indeed take a maiden who is endowed with all auspicious marks.

The illustrious one, facing north, should recite the Prājāpatya mantra three times accompanied by the Brāhmaṇas; then, having performed worship, he should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (Puṇyāha) to be proclaimed.
Afterwards, one should tie the *kautuka* (sacred thread) and then recite the mantra consisting of Śiva;
O Brahmin, with the mantra "viśve tvā" [one binds] the head with the *sāman* chant.
In this very manner, one should gradually perform the *tuṅgamāna* and other rites;
having bathed and put on a garment, one's body becomes adorned with splendor.
Endowed with these characteristics, he gazes upon the bride;
then, having entered his father's lap, he [recites] the mantra for that person.
One should purify her with the mantra "darbheṇa mālinīm" and the "aghora" mantra, saying "may she not be a killer of her brother.
There, while the husband stands to the south, he should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
Having placed the wife to the north and facing eastward,
they should together perform the *hūṃ-saṃ* and especially the *haṃtalā* rites.
He should visualize [the deity] facing him, situated in the western direction;
then, having offered the Sāvitra [mantra], he should place the apahāṃsi [waters] upon his head.
Then, while meditating upon him with the right hand, one should place seven or five blades of darbha grass, joined at their tips and roots. || 11 ||
In one desired [rite], the Viṣṇu-mantra and so forth are recited seven times;
likewise, the "seven-step friend" (sakhā saptapada) rite is performed specifically to its west.
Having placed the husband in the north, one should place the lotus in the south;
then, with the mantra beginning with "hṛdayena," one should touch the heart.
Then, with the mantra "tatas tena," the preceptor should always perform the fire-oblation;
he should specifically establish the place to the north of the fire.
With the mantra "ātiṣṭhena," he should touch the foot of the girl;
there, he should wash his hand and fill both hands with parched grains (lājā). || 15 ||
The noble one addresses you with the auspicious mantra beginning with "Agra," followed again by the mantra "Patnī" conjoined with the *hṛdaya* [mantra]. (16)
One should perform the oblation of clarified butter (ājyahoma), and then offer the vyāhṛtis;
furthermore, the jaya-oblations and others, as well as the rāṣṭrabhṛt-oblations, are offered.
O best of Brahmins, having especially offered the *vyomavyāpin* mantra, one should then offer the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with the verse beginning "yad asya. (18)
There, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and display incense and lamps;
and Arundhatī should be shown with the mantra, "Thou art the Pole Star" (*dhruvosi*). || 19 ||
One should wash the feet with milk for seven days and then have [the devotee] consume it;
thereafter, one should prepare a bed with the four auspicious verses.
Then, he should have the couple lie down together on the bed;
and on the fourth day, the oblation is offered into the mouth of the fire.

The oblation beginning with "O Agni, for atonement" (agne prāyaścitta) is offered to Havyavāha and the others; then the Jaya and other offerings, the placing of the fire, and the Night-rite are performed in sequence as they are sacrificed.
Having accepted [the offering], it is offered; one should perform the oblation (homa) in due order.
One should present [the fruit] to Śiva and cause the seed of the couple to be sown.
A man should mutter [the mantra] there, especially into his two ears;
having touched the secret place with his left hand, he endures the approach of the fertile season. || 24 ||
O best of Brahmins, on the fifth day, you should then sow it;
go from the village toward the east until the Udumbara tree is seen.
Having performed three circumambulations, Arundhatī is also seen;
standing in knee-deep water, one should cause her to accept the garments and the other items.
On the tenth day, O best of Brahmins, one should especially offer a bali-oblation at the root of an Udumbara tree, and one should also arrange for the fire-offering (agnimukha).
"O All-Gods, you who are cooked by the Truth, let the oblation be offered to us.
Then, having reached the house, the preceptor should perform the *daśabali* offering. (28)
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, the Ritual for Marriage, in the Vīratantra.
I shall now describe the funeral rites for a deceased person; one should bathe the body silently, and with a branch of the Udumbara tree, one should purify it according to the prescribed rule.
One should have a pit dug there, and then, having strewn darbha grass over it, one should cast [the body] into it with the mantra: "To Yama, the lord of the burning ground, svāhā."
Having spread out the funeral pyre, he should then sprinkle it with water;
having placed the deceased upon the pyre, he should sprinkle him with water while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra.
This [offering] must be performed by you yourself, and likewise it must be offered;
with the mantra "vātās te pasatīsvī," one should also cause a new [vessel] to be made.
With the mantra *imā apaḥ*, the breaking of the jar is here described;
then, having cast the fire [into the water] with the words *asmāt tvam abhijāto 'si*, the preceptor [proceeds]. (5)
Then, with the mantra *athagheha*, the instructor of the mantra should depart;
he should cast a shallow bowl joined with a stone at the left side of the door.
One should perform the *bali* offering for seven nights and likewise cause it to be performed for ten days;
on the eleventh day, one should perform the *ekāddiṣṭa* rite at its proper place using this very same [procedure].
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, the ritual for the consecration of the deceased, in the Vīra-tantra.
I shall describe the consecration of the grass; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
Having first shown it to a Śūdra or others, one should indeed perform the consecration for those of the same caste.
He [is the destroyer] of the streams of sins in other lands by means of the weapon that slays;
likewise, he is devoid of ritual action regarding cows, serpents, and the like.
Then, one should fashion the body with either *darbha* or *kuśa* grass;
the limbs and minor members [of the body] are fashioned with three-pointed leaves of the *pālāśa* tree.
In this manner, one should likewise [dispose of] the body of a preta, as well as its clothing and ornaments;
then, by means of a cloth and a fan, one should mutter the Karṇasūkta.
Having performed the cremation as before, the stone was prepared as previously described;
having offered the oblation for ten nights, it was performed for seven days as before.
On the eleventh day, one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite at that very same place.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter of the Vīratantra, the ritual procedure for the consecration of grass.
95) Now, therefore, I shall describe the ritual purification for pregnant women. Having performed a bath with the Aghora mantra, O best of Brahmins, [one should proceed]. (1)
Having adorned the corpse with garments and garlands as before, one should lift it up;
having thus placed the corpse [on the pyre], one should sprinkle it with the Puruṣa-sūkta.
Then, having depicted the womb with the art of craftsmanship, one should show it;
if it is filled with yellow food, death will occur, and there will be density [of suffering].
Then, with the Hiraṇyāvarta mantra,
one should bathe my young son, who is indeed alive, along with a woman of the same caste.
One should cause the breast to disappear with the mantra "yaste stane," and having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the Tatpuruṣa mantra.
And for the purpose of setting forth, one should then perform an oblation of clarified butter with the mantra:
"To Prāṇa, Apāna, Vyāna, Udāna, and Samāna, Svāhā! (6)
Whatever belongs to him, one should offer that into the fire;
then, having placed the deceased upon a wooden plank, one should cremate him according to the prescribed rite.
Then, one should have all the ritual actions performed as previously described.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, the ritual for the consecration of the pregnant woman, in the Vīratantra.
I shall describe the ritual for the Aṣṭakā; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
It is performed on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, or even on the fourteenth day.
On the seventh, the ninth, and also on the fourteenth day,
as well as on the preceding day, the Śaiva teachers perform the preparatory rite (kṣaṇa).
Now, two things must be performed: the Viśvedevas in the north and the ancestors in the south; likewise, perform the washing of their feet. (3)
Having offered betel-leaf and having performed a special bath,
O Grandfather, one should then perform the fire-offering for the ancestors.
Then, O best of Brahmins, the great-grandfather should sprinkle water;
he should then perform the cooked oblation consisting of boiled rice and cakes.
O Venerable One, the guides there grant a moment to the Brahmin;
one should worship him with garments, flowers, incense, and garlands.
One should offer boiled rice mixed with clarified butter as a libation to the two ancestors;
one should place it upon a single blade of darbha grass on the southern side of the fire.
One should offer the rice-ball (piṇḍa) with the Aghora mantra; what indeed is Agni like?
One should cause to be given boiled rice mixed with water, which carries nourishment (ūrja).
Expiatory offerings are being made; let them be offered now in due order.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, the Ritual of the Aṣṭakā, in the Vīratantra.
I shall describe the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite; it is likewise performed on the twelfth day, as well as on the fourth and the twelfth month. Perform that *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. (1)
Having designated the fire as the mouth [of the sacrifice], one should begin with the Viśvedevas;
then, having invoked the fathers and grandfathers with the mantra "May the ancestors come," [one proceeds]. (2)

Then, with the mantra for the barley-leaf garment (*yavaparṇavāsa*), one should offer oblations into the fire with the right thumb and the *bhīma* [mudrā], saying "Svāhā to the ancestors and the Rudra-deities."
One should fill forty śarāvas with water alone,
[reciting] "śanno yava" and "asīti," as well as for oneself and for Mahantura.
One should offer sesame, salt, honey, wind [incense], and liquor;
then the tongue [offering] should be given with the mantra "vāmasya tvitāvaśca. || 5 ||
He should likewise offer the *svadhā* invocation in the eight directions and perform the ritual scattering (*nirasana*),
accompanied by perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps.
Having invoked his father and grandfather, the preceptor should scatter [the offerings] there, joined with heated sesame seeds, while reciting the mantra beginning with "apahanta."
Having summoned the Brahmins, they indeed perform the consecration ceremony there;
they offer the arghya water with the mantra "ye divyā āpaḥ" at that very place.
He should offer gold and garments while reciting the Pañcabrahma mantra,
and likewise perform seven oblations of clarified butter with the mantra "yan me mātā."
There, one should feed the ancestors and then offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa),
consisting of rice mixed with sesame seeds, along with curd combined with honey.
Having formed a ball of food (piṇḍa) and joined it with the name of the deceased, O best of Brahmins,
one should offer it to the father and grandfather with the mantra beginning with "pṛthivyai" (to the earth).

Having brought [the water] together with the *samānīyam* mantra, one should pour water there into the vessel for the deceased ancestors (*pretapitṛ*), along with honey and the three [other substances]. (12)

The preceptor should offer the *preta* [portion] into the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) of the ancestors while remaining fixed in the leftward direction; then, having performed a circumambulation and a salutation, he should proceed. (13)
Having thus offered oblations especially, one should unite the ancestors with Śiva,
as well as the Ādiśaivas and Anuśaivas in every respect.
And one should practice proper conduct according to the mantra spoken by the god. || 14 ½ ||
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, the procedure for the Sapindikarana rite, in the Viratantra. || 30 ||
I shall now describe the supreme conduct of the various Śaiva sects,
following that which was spoken by Maheśvara himself with his own heart-mantra.
One should offer oblations to the two Iṣṭakās by their respective names;
and after the period of sorrow, one should arrange the festival of lights.
Having worshipped Śiva upon a pedestal, one should hold him above the head—
two-eyed, four-armed, and endowed with a sacred thread.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks, bearing a compassionate and pure [form], and graced with earrings, pendants, necklaces, waist-bands, and girdles; || 4 ||
O best of Brahmins, having likewise meditated upon Śiva— endowed with the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), wearing celestial garments,
and seated in the lotus posture—
the traveler should offer a lamp at whatever age is appropriate for the devotees of Śiva.
It was beautified by the spreading sounds of the resonance of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments.
Provided with various items and accompanied by trident-lamps,
one should give a feast for the Śaivas who are worthy, and offer a sacrificial fee according to one's capacity. (5½)
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, the procedure for the intermediate Śaiva conduct, in the Vīratantra.
I shall now describe the consecration of the planets; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
Having made the ground level in a pure place, one should smear it with cow dung. (1)
Having prepared a sacrificial mound with śāli rice,
one should then place upon it water-jars together with threads, lids, gold, and cloths.
One should place the nine planets on the right side of the pitcher;
having placed Āditya in the center, one should install Śukra in the east.
One should place nine jars: one dedicated to the deity Candra in the southeast, Aṅgāraka in the south, and the others from the center up to the northeast.
One should place the pitcher in the center and worship it with fragrances, flowers, and so forth;
likewise, one should place Ketu in the northwest and Bṛhaspati in the north.
In the northeast, one should establish the deity Budha together with kuśa grass,
joined with his own name and accompanied by the Hṛdaya mantra.
O best of Brahmins, one should worship and then offer oblations;
[using] bilva leaves, śirīṣa, and likewise the eastern palāśa leaf.
Viṣṇukrānti, Śamī leaves, and likewise lotus petals, as well as Bakula leaves, and those of the Aśvattha and Udumbara trees. (8)
One should place a *karavīra* flower and a water-pitcher (*bhṛṅgāra*) into each jar;
having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) on the preceding day.
Then, at the clear dawn,
one should cause the consecration to be performed with the hymns "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ" and "tāṃ samandī".
One should perform the consecration with the mantra for pure water for the feet and so forth;
having thus worshipped according to the rule and having dispelled the affliction caused by the planets.
One should likewise consecrate him through rites such as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*);
all defects are destroyed in this very way—one should act accordingly. || 12 ||
There, one should honor the teacher with garments, grain, gold, and other such offerings.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, the Ritual for the Consecration of the Planets, in the Vīratantra.
The Grandfather.
What are all the characteristics of the mudrās as they are described here?
O Blessed One, you should explain all of this to me in brief.
The Blessed One said:
O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, O four-faced one, O Brahmin, I shall explain all of that which has been urged by you in its entirety.
The Surabhimudrā, Liṅgamudrā, Mukulī, Śaśakarṇikā,
Āvāhanī, and Nirvīramudrā are the five mudrās of the Five Brahmans.
Likewise, O King, [there is] the Ṣaḍaṅga, as well as Mudrā, Śodhanī, and Kalyāśa. || 4 ||
The lotus, the trident, the axe, the sword and noose, as well as the goad,
the bow and arrow, the pestle, and likewise the thunderbolt seal (vajramudrā). || 5 ||

Having formed the hands with the palms facing upward, the tips of the index fingers should rest upon the middle fingers; the little finger and the ring finger should likewise be positioned upon the middle finger.
The tip joined with the tip; thus, the four breasts shall always cause the nectar to flow. This is the Surabhi-mudrā, which destroys all misfortunes. || 7 ||
On the right hand, positioned on the middle finger,
one should purify the ring finger and wrap it around the index finger.
One should especially encircle the thumb with the tips of the little fingers;
this shall be the Liṅga-mudrā, which accomplishes all desires and purposes.

Having joined the two hands together with a hollow space in the middle, this is called the *mukula* (bud) mudrā; it becomes the *mukulī* mudrā when [the fingers] are formed like a bud in the presence of a righteous king.

Both hands have the little fingers [joined], and the index fingers are likewise bent over the heads of their respective thumbs; the remaining fingers, beginning with the middle fingers, remain straight.
When both [hands] are joined at the wrists, this mudrā is called Śaśikarṇikā;
both hands have the little fingers and the base of the thumbs joined together.
And one should perform the placement in this manner, O best of Brahmins! This is known as the *āvāhanī* (invoking) mudrā;
it consists of both hands joined in fists, with each [thumb] pressing against the other.
This mudrā is indeed soundless and crushes all enemies;
it is formed by extending the right hand with the thumb joined upward. (15)
This is the Sṛṣṭimudrā, which brings benefit to all.
One should extend the right hand with the thumb raised upward. (16)
O best of Brahmins, having formed a fist, this is said to be their withdrawal;
then, having extended both hands, the thumb is placed upon the head. (17)
This shall be the Sadyomudrā; now hear concerning Vāmadeva:
having placed the hands with palms facing upward, one should extend the ring fingers and the others. (18)
Now listen to the mudrā of Vāmadeva and then that of Aghora:
one should join the two hands at the wrists and extend the two middle fingers. (19)
This is the mudrā of Aghora, which crushes all enemies:
one should join the two hands at the wrists and extend both index fingers. (20)
The Mahāmudrā of Tatpuruṣa accomplishes all desires and goals.
As before, having joined the hands, one should then extend the two little fingers.
Then the mudrā of Īśāna and the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) are described:
having extended both hands and then interlaced them with one another.
Having slightly bent the two thumbs, this is the mudrā of the heart.
Having extended both hands, [one should place] the ring fingers and the middle fingers [together]. (23)
O best of Brahmins, having placed the two hands together,
one should position the tip of the thumb at the base of the little finger.
When the two hands and three fingers are likewise joined together, this shall be the *śiro-mudrā*, which accomplishes all desires and purposes. (25)
Having placed the two hands palm-upward and concealed the index fingers with the thumbs, and having joined the remaining fingers together, these are known as the *śikhā-mudrā*. (26)
Having placed the two palms face upward, adorned with the thumbs in the middle, and having interlaced the remaining fingers, this is proclaimed as the armor mudrā (kavaca).
Having placed the two hands palms upward, one should join the wrists;
then the index and middle fingers should be turned face downward. || 28 ||
The two thumbs should be concealed; this is proclaimed as the Netra-mudrā (Eye Gesture).
Then, having extended both hands, the little fingers and thumbs are joined together.
This [mudrā] shall be the Astra (weapon), which crushes all enemies;
the two hands, joined at the wrists, are positioned at the heart.
One should clap the two hands there; this mudrā becomes one of purification.
Having placed the hands with palms facing upward, one should join the wrists. || 31 ||
Then, one should place the right hand above the left;
one should place the right thumb above the middle of the left thumb.
One should make a hollow in the middle and bind it with the index finger;
this is the Kalaśa-mudrā, which one should employ at the time of bathing.
O best of Brahmins, one should join both hands at the wrists;
when both hands are thus formed into buds, they are known as the Padma-mudrā (Lotus Gesture).
Having extended the right hand and concealed the little finger with the thumb, this shall be the Śūla-mudrā, which crushes all enemies. (35)
Having placed the two hands palms upward, one should cause everything to be directed upward;
the two backs of the hands should then be joined closely together with one another. (36)
This shall be the Paraśu-mudrā, which bestows the fruits of all desires;
having placed both hands palm-upward, the two index fingers remain [erect]. (37)
Having formed a fist with the remaining [fingers], these indeed become the sword mudrās (khaḍgamudrā).
Having turned both hands upward, one should raise them above.
Furthermore, by specifically spreading both hands wide to the right, this becomes the noose mudrā (pāśamudrā), which crushes all enemies. (39)
The right hand should be turned upward with the two index fingers bent;
likewise, having joined the remaining fingers into a fist, one should form the *mukulita* (bud-like) gesture for the slender [deity].
Having placed both hands palms upward, one should extend the left hand while placing the right at the root of the ear; these indeed constitute the bow mudrā (dhanurmudrā). || 41 ||
Having placed the two palms face upwards with the two index fingers standing erect and having clenched the remaining fingers into fists, these indeed constitute the arrow mudrā.
Having made the right hand open with the fingers closed into a fist in a circular shape, and then making it move unsteadily, one likewise forms the bell-mudrā (ghaṇṭāmudrā). || 43 ||
Having placed both hands palm-upward and pressed the little fingers and thumbs together,
with the two hands joined to one another, they indeed become the Vajra-mudrā.
The characteristics of the mudrās have been declared; now hear concerning the food offering (naivedya). || 44½ ||
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, the ritual for the characteristics of the mudrās, in the Vīra-tantra.
The Grandfather.
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Protector of the world, Master of the universe!
O Supreme Lord, tell me what is the ritual procedure for the food offering (naivedya). || 1 ||
The Lord.
Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! That which has been requested by you, I shall explain all of that; listen, O Lotus-seated One.
For as many grains of rice as there are in that food offering by count,
for that many thousands of yugas he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Milk-rice is superior to a thousand servings of *śuddhodana*; and rice cooked with jaggery is superior to a thousand servings of *kṛsara*. (4)
Mudga-rice is superior to a thousand servings of rice from Gauḍa;
in this very same sequence, the fruit increases a thousandfold at each step.
White rice, great rice, red rice, and likewise barley; black rice, wild millet, bamboo grain, and wheat as well. (6)
And the priyaṅgu, O best of brahmins, is said by me to be of nine kinds;
one should take half a grain of rice, which is declared to be the best. || 7 ||
One should designate all grains as being of three types: middling, and the lowest, which bears the name "bird"; therefore, one should avoid them. || 8 ||
O best of Brahmins, one should smear the courtyard with cow dung;
one should sprinkle all the rice with the Heart mantra and place it with the Netra mantra.
Then, one should perform the cutting [of the hair] for those scorched by the rays of the Sun;
first by the women of the twice-born (Brāhmaṇas), and then by the daughters of the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.
The middle method of cutting is proclaimed; the lowest would be performed by Śūdra women.
Then, one should place [the substance] into a mortar or an earthen vessel with the heart-mantra itself. || 11 ||
The mortar has Brahmā as its presiding deity, the pestle has Śiva, and the winnowing basket has Viṣṇu;
these are the presiding deities.
Having winnowed away the husks with a winnowing basket, one should discard the chaff and the broken grains.
Two hundred and twenty-five grains of rice are said to constitute a *śukti*.
The *tala*, the *prasṛti*, and likewise the *kuḍuba*;
the *añjali* as well, O best of Brahmins, and the *prastha* as well. (14)
In that regard, there shall be the measurements of vessels:
the *āḍhaka*, and likewise the *śiva*, the *droṇaka*, and also the *khārī*. || 15 ||
O best of Brahmins, there shall be one añjali, one prastha, and likewise the number of vessels; each āḍhaka shall be double [the preceding measure].
And it shall increase gradually from now on;
a *prastha* combined with a *kuḍava* shall become the offering for the *piśācas*. (17)
Two *prasthas* of *caru* and one *āḍhaka* of sacrificial oblation (*havis*) are prescribed;
the best of those skilled in ritual procedures should prepare the food offering (*naivedya*) in nine varieties.
Two *prasthas* at the three junctions of the day, and likewise one *āḍhaka*, as well as *śiva*—this is to be known as the triad of middling [measures]. (19)
The droṇa, the khārī, and the hāra—these three constitute the middle set; now hear about the superior set. || 20 ||
O best of Brahmins, that which is endowed with eight *droṇas* and two *bhāras*, and three *bhāras*, is called the "triple supreme" (*uttamatraya*). (21)

One should not offer oblations such as the *āḍhaka* measure, nor should one perform the *śrībali* offering; however, there is no fault in accepting rice grains, and one should indeed perform the ritual scattering (*nirvāpana*).
Having placed [the materials] in a new vessel, one should wash them with the Astra-mantra;
after washing three times, the water should be more than half-full.
There, upon the vessel, the preceptor should place [the materials] with the mantra of Īśāna;
he should then ignite the fire there with the seed-syllable of Agni.
The preceptor, having placed pure food with the *sadyojāta* mantra, [should select one] that is free from worm-holes and devoid of ants and the like. (25)
One should not kindle the fire with wood that emits sparks;
nor [should one use wood] that is overcooked, undercooked, smelling of smoke, or cold. (26)
O best of Brahmins, one should avoid [impure things] and offer well-cooked food;
one should perform the sequence of external purification and apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the body in the proper direction.
One should especially cause [the patient] to rise by means of the Vāmadeva mantra.
O Lotus-seated One, listen as I shall describe the treatment for venereal disease (upadaṃśa). 28.
The plantain, the breadfruit, the cucumber, the gourd, the two types of brinjal, the pumpkin, the large mung bean, and the bottle gourd. (29)
Kośātakī, ṛtāṃśa, and likewise palyagandha;
śiśuka, bṛhatkanda, and the kanda of sāraṇa. || 30 ||
The *śambaka*, *kadamba*, and *līkanda*, as well as the two types of *karkandhū*, *rājamāṣa*, *āḍhakī*, the pod of *mudga*, and *kulasthaka*. (31)
The fruit of the *kukkuṭāṇḍa* is said here to be a side-dish (*upadaṃśa*);
these are the chest-side-dishes, as is the *kāravallī*. (32)
One should increase [the dose] by three palas for each prastha according to the sequence;
in this very manner one should proceed, and one should administer it according to what is obtained. || 33 ||
Combined with salt and mixed with black pepper,
along with thirty-two grains of rice— this is here called an *upadaṃśa*.
Having prepared a soup especially with sixteen parts of gulma-beans, one part of muṣṭa, combined with curd, and mixed with flour... 35.
One should offer sugar combined with plantain fruit, along with jackfruit, as well as soup and clarified butter.
It was well-cooked with ghee and joined with the *hāṭa* [mixture], along with two betel nuts accompanied by eight petals. (37)
A portion mixed with some powder is prescribed for two *prastha*s;
one should offer ripe fruits such as the *mātuluṅga* and others. (38)
In this very manner, O best of Brahmins, one should perform [the rite] gradually according to one's effort;
having then placed everything in a single location.
One should sprinkle water there with the heart-mantra using kusha grass,
and one should worship well with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps.
One should worship there with the six limbs; many lamps are prescribed, as well as a stand made of gold, silver, or even bell-metal. (41)
It may also be made of copper; one should perform purification with ashes.
Alternatively, one should place a plantain leaf upon a cloth. (42)
One should sprinkle it with water and indeed drench it with ghee;
then, with the Vāmadeva mantra, one should place the food into the vessel.
One should offer [the oblation] combined with various condiments along with the heart-mantra;
one should offer four parts of the *caru* and two parts of the [other] offering.
One should offer the remnant from the vessel at the portion belonging to Agni;
furthermore, one should give water with the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Having purified the ground, one should discard the floral remains (nirmālya);
then, having sprinkled [the area] with water, one should offer betel leaf (tāmbūla). || 46 ||
The mortal who performs [this] in this manner shall attain the world of Śiva;
thereafter, he should perform the fire-ritual according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures.
In this very manner, pure food is described by me in due order;
I shall now describe the sequence for milk-rice (pāyasa), wherein mung beans are indeed half the measure of the rice.
It is said that twice as much milk should be used to cook it into a milk-rice (pāyasa) preparation;
O Brahmin, the preparation of gulānna will now be described, wherein the milk is indeed half the measure of the rice.
Half a *taṇḍula* is said to be a *guḷa*, and clarified butter (*ājya*) is half a *guḷa*; this is to be known as *gulānna*. Now hear about *kṛsarānna*. || 50 ||
(110) One should indeed add powdered sesame seeds there, one-fourth the amount of rice,
and half as much ghee; this is here called *kṛsarānna*.
One should add one-fourth part of mung beans to that same quantity of rice;
this is proclaimed as *mudgānna* (mung bean rice) when combined with coconut fruits.
Having stirred together marīca, ajamodā, jīraka, and sarṣapa,
this is indeed cooked along with kadalī and the two types of bṛhatī.
For this is indeed the best of side dishes; one should also offer pure food.
Three and three-quarter *ghaṭikās* remain here at the end.
The three middle periods are said to be the time of twilight;
one should perform the Śrī-bali at that time, which is joined with the watch (yāma) of the night.
The triad of supreme [mantras], joined with ten *nāḍikās*, is thus declared.
One should discard the *nirmālya* and offer it to Caṇḍeśa.
Stepping over, giving away, or eating the remains of an offering (nirmālya) are all equally [forbidden];
by stepping over or giving away the nirmālya, one goes to hell at that very moment.
Therefore, with every effort, it must be avoided for consumption by people in every way;
one should either bury it in the ground there or burn it with fire.
The best of preceptors should offer water, or even animals and elephants, into the river;
this is the offering for all, while the food is for the Śūdras and others.
The food offering for Vināyaka is for the Brahmins and others to eat;
the food offering for the goddess Umā is for everyone to eat. (60)
The food offering of Divākara shall be the meal for all;
however, it is not to be eaten by the devotees of the Sun, as is Jyeṣṭhā Sarasvatī herself. (61)
The food offering (naivedya) for Śrīdevī and Bhūmidevī shall be edible;
however, the food offering of others is not to be eaten by any embodied beings.
In this very sequence, one must not eat with those born of other castes;
[this applies] at the eastern gate, then the southern, or indeed the western gate. (63)
The northern gate should likewise be so; this applies especially to other palaces.
Among the various types of gates, there is no difference in the method of worship.
One should offer the food oblation at each respective doorway;
however, he who causes it to be done otherwise shall surely go forth to perform malevolent magic.
Therefore, with every effort, one should indeed cause an offering (naivedya) to be made;
the mortal who acts in this way is liberated from all sins. || 66 ||
Having delivered twenty-one generations of his lineage, he shall attain the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, the Chapter on the Ritual of Food Offering, in the Vīratantra.
The Grandfather.
Having performed purification and the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), what is the procedure for the act of bathing?
O Blessed One, you should explain all of this to me in brief.
The Lord.
O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, that which has been questioned by you—I shall explain all of it in its entirety; listen, O Lotus-seated One.
p.
112) Having risen at dawn, equipped with his leather water-skin (*carman*) and other items, the teacher, in particular, should go from the village toward the east or the north. (3)
Facing either north or south,
one should likewise discharge excrement while standing facing toward the east.
O best of Brahmins, one should not discharge feces or urine on ground infested with insects or ants, nor on barren soil,
nor in the vicinity of a sacred field of Śiva.
Having turned his right side toward the sun, avoiding the discharge of feces and urine during the day,
and covering his head, he should perform the evacuation in silence.
Then, with his right hand, he should cause him to take up the earth;
with his left hand, he should hold the penis, the ear, and the sacred thread.
Whether at a river, a pond, a lotus-lake, or even a deep pool,
having obtained pure water for bathing, one should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) according to the prescribed rules.
One should apply cow dung ten times, and especially jaṭāmāṃsī;
one should wash the left hand five times with [cow dung] and seven times with clay.
One should apply a single application of clay to the penis and wash the hands five times;
thereafter, one should wash the feet with water sufficient for a single *āmalaka* fruit.
Having performed the *āpośana* rite twice, having wiped [the mouth] twice, and having sipped water according to the rule,
one should divide the lump of clay into three parts with the heart mantra.
The first ball of food (piṇḍa) should be divided into three parts with the Tatpuruṣa mantra;
the southern part with the Ghora mantra, and the northern part with the Vāma mantra.
One should offer [the oblation] with clay using the Astra-mantra in the ten directions;
indeed, in the south with the Ghora-mantra, and in the north with the Vāma-mantra. (13)
One should indeed offer [oblations] in the ten directions starting from the east with the Heart-mantra;
and with the Heart-mantra from the south, one should perform the initiation of Śiva (śivadīkṣā).
The preceptor, remaining in the midst of water with the five Brahmans,
should smear oil mixed with *āmalaka* over his entire body.
Furthermore, having smeared [the image] again with cow dung, one should bathe it;
one should cleanse the head with Īśāna and then the face with Puruṣa.
The best of preceptors should cleanse the heart with the Saura mantra, the secret place with the Vāma mantra, and the two feet with the Sadyojāta mantra.
Having performed the purification there, the knower of mantras should recite the *vyomavyāpin* mantra;
then, having formed the *kālamudrā*, he should consecrate [the disciple] with the *prāsāda* mantra. || 18 ||

One should smear all the limbs with cow dung and earth while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra; then, standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should perform the ritual ablution according to the prescribed rules.
Having sipped water three times and wiped [the mouth] twice, one should touch the eyes once with the thumb and ring finger, while reciting the *ūrdhvāghora* mantra.
One should touch both nostrils and the ears with the middle finger;
then, one should touch the arms with the thumb and forefinger.
One should touch the head with all the fingers;
then, with the right hand, one should cause [the disciple] to take up water.
One should drink water with the mantra "sūryaśca" joined with the Vāmadeva [section];
one should drink water in the evening with the mantra "agniśca" joined with the Īśāna [section]. || 23 ||
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rule, joined with the Īśāna mantra,
and having recited the Sāvitrī there, one should offer the "Sūrya-water."
One should indeed satisfy the gods there with the Vāmadeva mantra;
one should cause the sages to receive offerings there with the Aghora mantra. || 25 ||
There, the preceptor should offer libations to the ancestors with the Sadyojāta mantra,
as well as the Sāvitrī mantra accompanied by the Prāsāda mantra, one hundred and eight times.
The preceptor, endowed with truthfulness, speech, and a sincere heart,
should recite mantras there and wrap [the image] in a washed cloth.
There, wearing his turban and upper garment, he should sip water as before;
having made the riverbank level, he should smear it to the depth of one cubit.
One should invoke the Sun there with the six-syllable mantra;
one should then offer him water for his feet, water for sipping, and the respectful oblation (arghya). || 29 ||
Then, one should satisfy the gods with the *daivika* (divine) *tīrtha*,
and likewise satisfy the sages with the *ārṣa* (sage-related) *tīrtha*.
He should satisfy his ancestors and forefathers with the ancestral offering (paitṛka);
there, the wise man, with flowers in hand, should enter the celestial chariot (vimāna).
Having performed three circumambulations, one should enter the door-panel;
having prostrated like a staff upon the ground, one should worship the door-panel.
Then, O Brahmin, one should worship the deities stationed at the door-panels according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, using the *hṛdaya* mantra. (33)
One should also worship Bhujaṅga and Pataṅga, the presiding deities of the door-panel;
then, having gone into the inner sanctum and bowed in this manner, he who performs this daily is liberated from all sins. (34)

One should maintain silence during bathing, the worship of the deity, meditative absorption, as well as during recitation, eating, and religious rites; thus, silence is prescribed in these six instances.
Bathing is known to be fivefold: the Vāruṇa bath, the Āgneya, the Divya, as well as the Vāyavya, and the Mānasa is traditionally taught.
The ritual act of bathing is Vāruṇa, and the bath itself is indeed Vāruṇa;
the Āgneya bath is with ashes—she should avoid that path thereafter. (37)
"May the winds carry away the dust-born [impurity];
by means of mantras, the mental bath is declared"—thus the fivefold bath is prescribed. (38)
In this very manner, the best of preceptors should indeed perform it;
thus has the bath been described by me as the means for accomplishing all desires and goals. (39)
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, the procedure for purification, sipping water, and bathing, in the Vīratantra. || 35 ||
The Grandfather.
O Lord, how is the ash-bath performed, and what is that bath like?
O Supreme Lord, tell me all of this in brief.
The Lord.
I shall now describe the ash-bath; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
Because it shines (bhāsa), it is called *bhasma* for human beings. || 2 ||
When all diseases have arisen, and in the face of all fears such as tigers and other wicked,
malevolent wild beasts, they are destroyed by the ash-bath. (3)
The first is indeed Āgneya, the second should be Ananta;
the third is said to be Śaiva, and the fourth is the bestower of enjoyment (bhoga). || 4 ||
The fifth is declared to be Śrīkara; now listen to these as well: Nandā, Bhadrā, Surabhi, Suśīlā, and likewise Sumanā. (5)
One should collect the cow dung produced from among these groups;
that which is white in color is the best, while the red is middling.
One should avoid the lowest [type], which is black in color, as well as any other [inferior] color; O best of Brahmins, one should also avoid those with deformed limbs and those lacking limbs.
One should take fallen cow dung while reciting the mantra of the heart;
indeed, the cow dung of a tawny cow (kapilā) is said to be the most excellent of all.

Cow dung connected with the wind [element], when consecrated by the mantras of the peaceful wind, should be grasped by the limbs of the practitioner through the space [element] using *darbha* grass; that shall be the rite for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*).
Those who have fallen upon the ground because of a palace [collapse], or [those who die] on the full moon day, the new moon day, or the sixth day of both the bright and dark fortnights; || 10 ||
Having burned [the image] with the Śiva-fire, or even with husks,
the preceptor, having fashioned a *piṇḍa*, [should worship] the heart [of the deity] with the *śikhā-mantra*.
In this manner, having dried it with the head-mantra and likewise burnt it with the crest-mantra,
one should especially cause [the disciple] to grasp it with the mantra of immediate birth.
The best vessel is made of gold, the middling one should be of silver, and the lowest should be a copper vessel; in the absence of these, it may be made of clay. (13)
Having collected [the substances] in a gourd vessel with the Vāmadeva mantra, this is called the Āgneya; now hear the Māruta.
Then one should burn [the body] with the limbs, with a ladle, or with the fire produced therefrom;
this is called the method known as Māruta, and the characteristics of Śaiva are now being stated.
O best of Brahmins, ashes produced in the sacrificial fire-pit of Śiva grant worldly enjoyment;
I shall now describe those from the kilns of potters as well. (16)
Thus has the fourfold [rite] been described; now listen to that which brings prosperity (śrīkara), which is joined with four divisions and especially characterized by the use of ashes. || 17 ||
In this very manner, one should then smear it with ashes;
it is pervasive like the sky and joined with the limb of Brahmā.
Then, one should smear the head with the Īśāna mantra;
likewise, the face with the Tatpuruṣa mantra, and the two thighs and the waist with the Sadyojāta mantra.
On both sides and on both feet as well,
one should especially sprinkle [ashes] with the Sadyojāta mantra.
One should smear the entire body with ashes, especially in the case of Brāhmaṇas;
one should likewise apply the Tripuṇḍra mark there for kings and Vaiśyas as well.
And for all Śūdras as well, it is exactly the same in this sequence;
however, one should avoid that water which is mixed with rainwater from midday.
(118) I shall explain the distinction of the locations: the crown of the head and the forehead, the two ears, the two eyes, the two nostrils, and the mouth. || 23 ||
In the neck, the shoulder, the two arms, the two elbows, and likewise the wrists;
in the heart, the navel, the genitals, the thighs, the shanks, and the knees—24.
Having applied [the ashes] to the two calves, leaving out the feet, and likewise to the two backs, these thirty-two places are said to be smeared with ashes. Then, one should smear them.
