And at the junction of the forehead and neck, as well as at the arms and elbows;
likewise in the heart, the belly, the navel, the sides, and the back. (26)
O best of Brahmins, the sixteenth station is said to be on the two sides;
likewise, it is on the head, the forehead, the throat, and the arms. (27)
O best of Brahmins, one should apply sacred ash specifically to eight locations: in the heart, at the navel, and especially on the back.
Brahmā, Skanda, Viṣṇu, Vighna, and likewise Śiva, as well as Vasundharā and the two Parents (the Sun and Moon), are proclaimed as the presiding deities. || 29 ||
The width for the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas should be six finger-breadths, four, three, or even one finger-breadth respectively. || 30 ||
Then, in the same manner, one should smear [the ground] with ashes along the path;
having likewise smeared it with sandalwood paste for the sake of a Vaiśya, it should be complete.
O best of Brahmins, one who desires victory should smear [the image] with red sandalwood;
for all preceptors, however, the ring finger, middle finger, and forefinger [are used]. (32)
One should smear that [area] with ashes; thereby one is liberated from all sins, as well as from bad dreams, contact with wicked people, and in all cases for those who are afflicted by illness. (33)
They are purified by bathing with ashes; this is prescribed here for the sake of protection. Furthermore, [food] containing husks, hair, charcoal, or even fingernails [is impure]. 34.
One should apply mantras everywhere, especially over a mixture of curd, milk, ghee, and oil. || 35 ||
Through the ash-bath one attains purity, just as an elephant does through the lion's snort;
this applies equally whether it is performed in the forenoon, at the time of eating, or while traveling.
In this very manner, one should apply the ashes in due order with devotion. || 37 ||
Freed from all sins, one shall attain the world of Śiva.
I have thus declared the ritual bath with ashes; now listen to the placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa).
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, the Ritual for the Ash-Bath, in the Vīra-tantra.
Having bowed his head to the God, the Grandfather (Brahmā) questioned him:
"O Lord, how is the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) performed? O Master, tell me all of that."
The Lord.
Whatever I have asked for the benefit of mortals, I shall speak out of affection for you; listen, O Lotus-seated One.
One should construct a pavilion in front of Śiva, and then another to the south of that pavilion;
O best of Brahmins, one should smear the pavilion with cow dung.
Having offered incense, flowers, and likewise a lamp prepared together,
and having placed a *kūrca* [grass-bundle] according to the ritual procedure previously taught by the Lord, (verse 4).
Facing north, one should sprinkle water there with the Sadyojāta mantra using a bundle of kuśa grass held in the middle of the kuśa mat, starting from the left.
Then, O Brahmin, one should worship one's own goddess with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
one should contemplate the Śiva-tattva at the tip of the flame of ghee, twelve finger-breadths in height.
One should unite one's own self there and then burn the body;
within the triangular mandala, one should contemplate the non-dual Vidyā.
Beginning from the big toe, one should burn this body up to the head;
having meditated on Śiva as it has become ashes, perform the immersion with nectar.
One should visualize [the deity] above the crest by a measure of one cubit;
above that is a white lotus, and upon it a lunar disc facing downwards.
One should meditate upon the fourth state, the immortal, conjoined with the syllable Om;
one should contemplate that immortal water as it pierces through the head via the Suṣumṇā.
One should contemplate oneself being washed by that [water] and being filled;
for this indeed is the destruction of death—such is the certainty of the scripture. (11)
Afterwards, having visualized one's own body, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Recaka, pūraka, and kumbhaka are considered the three types of breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 12 ||
The breath neither releases nor grasps that which is situated inside or outside; for one who is motionless, the kumbhaka remains like a completely filled jar. (13)
In this very manner, the supreme instructor should cause [the disciple] to perform [the ritual];
first, he should touch [the body] with both hands, beginning from the letter *ka* at the feet and ending at the head. (14)
With the thumb and forefinger, joined with the Astra mantra, one should bestow [the protection] in the sky and in all directions, and likewise place it above and below. (15)
The earth element is known to extend to the knees; the accomplishment of water [is attained] from the region of the navel;
from the throat, the purification of fire occurs; and from the forehead, the air element is purified. (16)
Twelve finger-breadths above that, the purification of space (gaganaśuddhi) is proclaimed;
first is the placement of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa), and the second is the placement of persistence (sthitinyāsa).
The third, however, is withdrawal (saṃhāra), which is said by me to be threefold:
the householder follows the path of creation, while the student (brahmacārī) abides in the state of maintenance (sthiti).
For forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas) and ascetics (yatīs), the withdrawal-assignment (saṃhāranyāsa) is prescribed;
the creation-assignment (sṛṣṭinyāsa) is declared to extend from the thumb to the little finger.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the five mantras beginning with Īśa on the thumb and the other fingers;
having placed Īśāna on the head, one should place Tatpuruṣa on the face.
Having placed Aghora on the heart, one should assign Vāma to the secret place;
one should place Sadyojāta on the feet, and then again assign the limbs.
One should then assign the six limbs; now hear the assignment of the deities.
Having assigned Brahmā to the head, Viṣṇu is said to be on the forehead. (22)
The moon and sun are the two eyes, the earth is likewise in the nose;
Sarasvatī is in the uvula, and the Lord (Īśvara) is in the heart. (23)
The two hands have Indra as their presiding deity, and Vāyu is the deity of the belly;
likewise, Subrahmaṇya is in the *liṅga* and Ambikā is in the two sides.
One should likewise place the Maruts on the two feet in their proper order;
having placed the letter *a* on the head, one should place the letter *ā* on the forehead.
The letter *i* is in the right eye, the letter *ī* in the left eye;
the letter *u* is in the right nostril, and the letter *ū* in the left nostril.
The syllable Ṛ is in the right ear, and the syllable Ṝ is in the left ear;
the syllable Ḷ is in the right cheek, and the syllable Ḹ is in the left cheek. || 27 ||
And here (ca), in the cavity of the palate (tālurandhra); and o and au in both lips;
having assigned them in the two rows of teeth, aṃ and aḥ are proclaimed [as the final ones]. (28)
The *ka*-group [of consonants] is on the right hand, the *ca*-group on the left hand;
the *ṭa*-group is on the right foot, and the *ta*-group on the left foot. (29)
One should place *pa* on the right side and *pha* on the left side;
having placed *ma* in the heart, one should assign *ya* to the skin.
The letter *repha* is said to be blood, and the letter *la* is indeed flesh;
the letter *va* is in the region of the fat, while the letter *śa* is in the region of the bones.
They say that the letter *ṣa* is in the region of the marrow, the letter *sa* is the semen,
the letter *ha* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the letter *kṣa* is the penis.
One should place the letter *la*, the *vṛṣaṇa*, and all these others in their respective order.
This is declared to be the Sṛṣṭinyāsa; now hear the Nyāsa of Stiti.
One should place the five Brahmans in sequence starting from the center and so forth:
one should place Īśāna in the center and Puruṣa with the ring finger. (34)
One should not place [the mantra] on the little finger; the fierce one should be placed on the left thumb.
One should place Sadyojāta on the index finger, and likewise on the back [of the hand]. (35)
Having placed the Heart mantra on the middle fingers, the Śiras mantra on the ring fingers,
the Śikhā mantra on the little fingers, one should place the Kavaca mantra on the thumbs.
Having placed the Netra-mantra on the index finger, one should place the Astra-mantra on the palm;
having thus performed the assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), one should then assign the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas).
Having placed Ananta on the crown of the head, Sūkṣma is said to be on the forehead;
having placed Śivottama on the mouth, Ekanetra is on the two ears. (38)
One should place Ekarudra on the arm and Trimūrti in the heart;
Śrīkaṇṭha is said to be placed on the linga, and one should place Śikhaṇḍin on the feet.
Having placed the heart-mantra on the heart, one should place the head-mantra on the head;
having placed the crest-mantra on the crest, one should place the armor-mantra between the breasts.
One should place the Astra-mantra on the region of the hands, the Netra-mantra on the eyes,
and likewise the Īśa and Brahmāṇi mantras on the wrists of both hands.
This is declared to be the placement of maintenance (sthiti-nyāsa); now hear about the placement of withdrawal (saṃhāra).
Sadyojāta is on the little finger, and Vāmadeva is on the ring finger.
Having assigned Aghora to the middle finger and Puruṣa to the index finger,
and having assigned Īśāna to the thumb, one should then assign the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
Having placed the *kaniṣṭhikā* [finger] on the heart, the *kavaca* [mantra] between the breasts,
and the *śiromantra* on the nose.
The śikhā-mantra should be in the middle, and the kavaca [in the next]. || 44 ||
One should place the *tarjanī* [finger].
Having placed the *netra* [mantra] on the thumb, one should place the *astra* [mantra] on the palm.
Then, one should place the *sadyojāta* mantra on the two feet and the *vāmadeva* mantra on the belly. (45)
Having placed Aghora in the heart, one should place Tatpuruṣa in the mouth;
having assigned Īśāna to the head, one should place Hṛdaya on the feet.
One should place the Śiraḥ-mantra on the penis, the Śikhā-mantra on the belly,
the Kavaca-mantra on the heart, and the Netra-mantra on the two arms.
It is taught that the Astra-mantra is to be placed in the mouth, while the Śiva-mantra is to be applied everywhere; one should assign Indra to the feet and Pāvaka to the penis.
Having placed Yama in the belly, one should place Nirṛti in the heart;
the deity Varuṇa is assigned to the two arms, and Vāyu is traditionally taught to be in the throat. (49)
One should place the deity Soma in the mouth and Īśa on the head;
having understood this sequence, the preceptor should likewise perform the placement.
The preceptor should be an adherent of Ādiśaiva, a householder, and the best among the twice-born;
being wise, he should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) regarding emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal.
Having thus performed the ritual placement according to the prescribed rule, the preceptor shall become a destroyer of sins;
he should then worship his own body with perfumes, flowers, and water for the feet, using the heart-mantra.
Having worshipped the gatekeepers with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should likewise worship the gatekeeper in the east, as well as Nandi and Kāla.
The two gatekeepers of the southern door are Daṇḍin and Muṇḍin;
the two gatekeepers of the western door are Bhṛṅgin and Vijaya. (54)
As for the two gatekeepers of the northern door, they are Nanda and Paśupati;
having placed Nandin on the south, endowed with a dark complexion. (55)
The syllable *la*, joined with the staff in hand (*daṇḍahasta*), is said to be the mantra;
it is black, the color of saffron, and established in the north.
Having first placed Daṇḍin in the east—one who is endowed with weapons such as the banyan tree and possesses the mantra consisting of the syllable *hrīṃ*—who resembles an *indragopa* insect; || 57 ||
The mantra associated with the sword-weapon is said to be the syllable *Hrauṃ*.
Having placed the one with the shaven head (*Muṇḍī*), who resembles pure crystal, in the west... (58)
The mantra is said to be accompanied by the *bhindipāla* and the *sṛṅkāra*;
one should place the *bhṛṅgiṭi*, which resembles the neck of a peacock, on the right side. (59)
The mantra is said to be the syllable *hrīṃ*, joined with the weapon *śakti*;
and having placed Vijaya in the north, he is endowed with a red color.
The mantra is said to be the syllable *hrīṃ* joined with the trident weapon;
likewise, one should place Ananta, who has the luster of gold, in the western position.
The mantra is said to be the syllable *hrīṃ* joined with the vajra weapon;
having placed Paśupati, endowed with a blue form, in the east. (62)
The mantra is said to be the syllable *hrīṃ* joined with the weapon *pāśa*;
having established [the deity] in this very manner through these successive steps, one should worship with these mantras.
(126) All are endowed with four arms and three eyes;
all have arrived straightway in their posture, inspiring fear with their cruel gaze. 64.
Adorned with crowns, earrings, necklaces, and hero-belts, they were equipped with various ornaments and were terrifying and fearsome.
All [the deities] have their feet slightly contracted and are endowed with beauty and youth;
the preceptor should always worship them in this very sequence.
This placement of the mantras has been declared; now hear the ritual worship according to its true nature.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter on the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) in the Vīratantra. || 37 ||
The Grandfather.
Having prostrated before the Blessed One, the Grandfather indeed inquired:
"O Lord, how is the worship of Śiva performed? O Master, tell all of that to me. (1)
The Lord.
O Lotus-seated One, hear all this in brief:
one who is not Rudra himself cannot remember Rudra; one who is not Rudra cannot worship Rudra.
One who is not a devotee of Rudra should not recite the Rudra-hymn; one who is not a devotee of Rudra cannot attain Rudra.
It removes all sins and yields the fruit of all sacred pilgrimage sites.
One who has not been initiated, even if he is a knower of the four Vedas, should not touch the Śivaliṅga;
nor should a Brahmin who has been initiated fail to worship it for the sake of his livelihood.
(127) Having prioritized the performance of one's own duty at all times, a follower of Śiva should worship Śiva;
the performance of one's own duty during the transitional periods (saṃdhi) does not result in fault. || 5 ||
One should worship them for one's own sake according to the path of the scriptures,
whether at that specific time or at any other time, following this very same sequence.
Having first performed the purification of oneself, the second is the purification of the place;
the third is the purification of the materials, and the fourth is the purification of the liṅga.
Fifth, the purification of the mantra is taught; these are the five purifications.
One should perform the purification of the self according to the procedure previously described. (8)
The most excellent of teachers should indeed perform the purification of the site as the second step,
employing it together with the syllable *huṃ* and the syllable *phaṭ*.
Then one should perform the purification of the site in all ten directions;
having smeared it with cow dung, one should sprinkle it while reciting the heart-mantra.
The water-vessel, the vardhanī, the vessel for foot-washing and sipping, the arghya-vessel, the flower-vessel, and the vessels for incense and the lamp. || 11 ||
Having washed the vessel for the sacrificial porridge (carusthālī), the water jar,
and the vessel for the lustration rite (nīrājana) with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), one should then purify them with the weapon-mantra (astra).
One should place [the vessel] upon *darbha* grass there and veil it with the *kavaca* mantra;
thereafter, one should sprinkle water with the *pañcabrahma* mantra.
One should offer perfume with the heart-mantra and apply fragrant paste with the head-mantra;
one should then sprinkle the ritual substances there with the heart-mantra.
Thus the purification of the substances is accomplished; now hear the purification of the *liṅga*.
One should strike the bell with the heart mantra itself. (15)
One should lead [the deities] to the Kāpāpa [mandala] with the mantra *huṃ*;
one should dismiss those who have been served the worship with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*). || 16 ||
One should place a flower on the head with the Sadyojāta mantra;
then, having removed the faded garland (nirmālya), one should cause it to be offered to Caṇḍeśa.
Having made the top of the linga non-empty, the practitioner should perform the consecration;
he should then wash the linga there with the Hṛdaya mantra.
Whether in a linga, or in a ritual image (kautuka), or in a wall-painting, or in a mandala—
one should perform the purification of the linga according to this very same sequence.
The supreme preceptor should then perform the fifth [rite], the purification of the mantra,
together with the five Brahmans, the Śiva-aṅgas, and the Prāsāda-mantra.
He is joined with Vyomavyāpin and likewise with the Vidyeshvaras,
the Ganeshas, the Lokapalas, and the weapons of the Lokapalas.
Having placed the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and joining it with the word of salutation (*namas*) at the end, the mantra becomes purified; thus should the supreme preceptor perform it. (22)
He who knows the five purifications is worthy to perform the worship. The wise one should arrange the seats, ending with Ananta, in their proper order.
The first is the Anantasana, the second is the Yogāsana;
the third should be the Siṃhāsana, and the fourth is the Yogāsana. (24)
(129) The Vimalāsana is in the fourth [position], while here the Padmāsana is said to be joined with the Śakti-syllable and endowed with the ninth sprout.
It is proclaimed that [the lotus] is joined with the seed-syllables up to the stalk;
in the center, it is joined with the stalk and possesses fifty pericarp-petals.
Above that, one should place the pericarp with lotus-seated figures of the same length;
[one should place] Ananta in the eastern portion and Vāsuki in the southeast.
Having placed Takṣaka in the south, Kārkoṭaka in the southwest, Śaṅkhapāla in the west, and Gulika in the northwest; 28.
One should place a lotus in the northern quarter within the domain of Mahāpadmeśa;
one should provide an Ananta-seat supported upon a tortoise.
Then one should wrap the central stalk, which is indeed a limb of Śiva;
O Brahmin, listen now to the support for the gods as well.
Ananteśa, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetraka, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍika. || 31 ||
Having sequentially placed [the mantras] from the east to the northeast,
the preceptor should likewise place Śeṣa and the lords of the nāgas as pellets in the four directions.
The Anantāsana is proclaimed here; the Yogāsana is spoken of here.
The Yoga [seat] should be square, and one should place it upon Śeṣa.
Having established the prāṇa in the east and the apāna in the region of fire (the southeast),
one should disperse the devadatta and dhanañjaya breaths in the middle.
(130) Now listen as I proclaim the support for the deities:
the *praṇava* (oṃ) is in the central region, and the letter *ā* is in the eastern region. (35)

The letter *na* is in the northern direction, and the letter *oṃ* is situated in the east; with the letter *a* below and the letter *tha* above as the cover, this is known as the yoga-seat (*yogāsana*).
Above the yoga seat, however, the lion throne (siṃhāsana) is described here;
having placed Dharma in the southeast and Jñāna in the southwest. (37)
Detachment is in the northwest, and sovereignty is in the domain of Īśa (the northeast);
in the four corners is the great lion-throne fashioned from the feet.
The color of the lion is white as a conch or crystal, and red;
unrighteousness is in the eastern part, and likewise ignorance is in the south. (39)
Having assigned detachment (vairāgya) in the western direction and sovereignty (aiśvarya) in the northern direction,
one should place the black-colored Ilīkā there.
One should place this tetrad—Avyakta, Niyati, Kāla, and Kalā—in the cardinal directions; Keśava, however, occupies the central position.
Three-eyed and of terrifying appearance, likewise facing the intermediate directions—thus is the lion-throne described; now the lotus-throne is being told.
The earth is on the eastern petal, and the waters are in the southeast;
the form of fire is in the south, and the form of air is in the southwest.
And space itself, O best of Brahmins, is said to be the petal in the western direction;
having placed sattva in the northwestern [direction], one should place rajas in the northern [direction]. (44)
O Brahmin, one should visualize the form of Tamas on the petal in the northeast; endowed with its own specific color, it is called by me the "Support" (Ādhāra). (45)
One should fashion the root with the Sadyojāta mantra and the stalk with the Vāmadeva; they say the Aghora mantra belongs to the petals, while the Tatpuruṣa mantra is for the secret region.
The best of preceptors should indeed create the cavity with the Īśa-mantra;
I shall fully declare the deities: one should first install Kālī in the east.
One should place Kalavikaraṇī in the southeast and Raudrī in the south; Balavikaraṇī in the southwest and Vāmā in the west. (48)
One should worship Balapramathanī in the northwest, Jyeṣṭhā in the northern direction,
Sarvabhūtadamanī in the northeast, and Manonmanī in the center.
Thus the lotus posture (padmāsana) has been described; it is called the stainless seat (vimalāsana).
One should arrange the form of the four Vedas like a tiger skin.
Having placed the deity upon the pedestal, listen now:
having established Ambikā in the east and Gaṇāmbikā in the south. (51)
Having placed Gaurī in the west and Prajñā in the northern direction, this is declared to be the Vimalāsana; now listen to another.
The lotus for invocation, the lotus-seat, and the infinite seat are declared to be pure for acts of worship; however, the food-seat is prescribed according to yoga.
In this very manner, the sequence of postures is described;
one should worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps. (54)
The preceptor, by means of the very first syllable of his own name together with the heart-mantra,
should place sattva, rajas, and tamas one above the other. (55)
Within the circle of fire, and at its center, one should place the solar orb;
thereafter, one should place the lunar disk, and within that, the Self as the Inner Self.
In this manner, one should install the Supreme Self with its own name and so forth;
indeed, the *ātmatattva* is on the right, while the *vidyātattva* is on the left.
One should then place the Śivatattva in the middle according to the proper sequence;
having thus performed the ritual placement according to the rules, one should then worship Śiva.
Resembling pure crystal, throbbing with radiant splendor, he has three eyes and ten arms, and his crest is adorned by the crescent moon. (59)
He is endowed with a crown of matted locks and possesses a beautiful body;
he is the Lord of Gods, having five faces and five heads.
Endowed with all the auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament—namely, a crown, earrings, armlets, and bracelets. (61)
The god has a waist-cord and a bound girdle, is endowed with anklets,
wears divine garments, and is anointed with divine perfumes.
In his right hands he holds a noose, an axe, a sword, and a face that grants fearlessness;
in his left hands he carries a goad, a bell, a serpent, and fire.
Then, O Brahmin, one should place these weapons in the left hand;
having thus meditated upon Sadāśiva, who brings happiness to all the worlds. (64)
Then one should invoke the deity with the *sadyojāta* mantra;
one should establish him with the *vāmadeva* mantra and restrain him with the *aghora* mantra. (65)
One should worship the presence [of the deity] with the mantra of Puruṣa, or specifically with that of Īśāna,
in the eastern gate-house or especially in the southern one.
Having meditated upon the formless within the formed at either the western door-house or the northern door itself, one should likewise prepare the seat.
Then, having placed [the image] facing the door, one should worship it as before;
for even when there are differences in the doors, no difference in the mode of worship exists. || 68 ||
Having placed Īśāna on the head, one should place Tatpuruṣa on the face;
having placed Aghora on the heart, one should assign Vāma to the private parts.
One should place the Sadyojāta mantra on the foot, and then again perform the placement of the limbs (aṅgas);
having placed the Heart mantra on the heart, one should place the Head mantra on the head.

Having placed the *śikhā* [mantra] on the crest-lock, the *kavaca* between the breasts, the *astra* in the region of the hands, and the *netra* in the eyes, one should perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*). (71)
O best of Brahmins, water for the feet should be offered at the five faces and at the fifteen eyes;
the arghya offering should be placed upon the head.
One should know that the sipping of water (ācamana) is performed with the mantra beginning with "hṛdayena";
as for the materials for the foot-water (pādya), they are said to consist of uśīra combined with sandalwood.
The three fruits, camphor, and betel leaf along with lime—
this is declared to be the *ācamanīya* (water for sipping), which one should especially offer into the mouth.
Water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, unbroken grains, barley, rice, sesame seeds, and white mustard seeds— this is declared to be the eightfold *arghya* offering. (75)
O best of brahmins, one should likewise show the eye-gesture (netramudrā) at the eyes;
then, one should fashion the razor-gesture (kṣurikā) on the right side.
One should place the Śivāstra there on the tips of the petals in the ten directions;
one should place the Pāśupatāstra on the right side of Śiva.
Having assigned the Aghora-weapon mantra in the west according to the ritual procedure, using its respective seed-syllable and mantra,
one should then commence the worship.
There, one should perform the consecration with the Heart Mantra;
prior to sunrise, one should indeed perform the fivefold ablution.
Beginning from sunrise, one should consecrate [the deity] with water alone;
then, one should recite the Pañcabrahma mantras, the Ṣaḍaṅga mantras, and the Vyomavyāpin mantra.
Having placed jewel-water, gold-colored water, and water mixed with flowers into a water vessel, one should perform the consecration.
One may perform [the rite] with a single new pitcher, or with sixteen pitchers, or with thirty-two, thirty-four, fifty, or twenty-five. || 82 ||
The preceptor should likewise cause one hundred and eight [offerings] to be made;
the characteristic of the water-pot is that it should be filled with an *āḍhaka* measure.
A water-pot (kumbha) should indeed be prepared, made of gold or silver, or of copper or even clay; with it, one should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka).
Curd, milk, ghee, honey, or the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
as well as coconut water combined with a stalk of sugarcane. (85)
There, one should perform the consecration again with scented water,
accompanied by dance and song, and joined with the sound of hymns of praise.
Accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments according to the path taught by Bharata,
at its conclusion, a Brahmin priest should cause the performer to perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Saffron, sandalwood, agallochum, and indeed khadira; resin, the three myrobalans, and especially uśīra. || 88 ||
Having thus stirred everything together, one should smear the liṅga itself;
the fragrance should be offered with the Heart-mantra, and one should cause the cloth to be given with the Vāma-mantra. || 89 ||
Having wrapped the liṅga with cloths of many colors in great variety,
one should worship the Supreme Lord with various kinds of flowers.
One should offer a flower upon the head of Śiva with the Astra-mantra;
then the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha-pūjā) should be performed according to the prescribed characteristics.
A square wooden plank should be made with a height equal to that of the pedestal;
its width should be the same, and it should be smeared with clay alone.
One should smear the surface of the coconut vessel with the finest rice flour and adorn it with various kinds of flowers. (93)
The Gajasiṃha, the Aṅgāca, the Aśva, and the Padmapuṣpaka;
likewise the Sarvadvaya, the Pīṭha, the Gopura, and the Maṇḍapa.
A celestial chariot, a fish, and likewise the letter *ma*,
a mirror, a full water-jar, a bull, and a pair of chowries. (95)
The Śrīvatsa, the Svastika, the conch, the lamp, and the eight auspicious objects of the gods;
likewise, the thunderbolt, the spear, the staff, the sword, the noose, and the goad.
The mace, the trident, the thunderbolt, and the lotus—these constitute the ten weapons;
one should install them one by one every day until the end of thirty days.
O best of Brahmins, having especially adorned it with flowers and leaves, one should perform the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) according to the heart-mantra (hṛdayamantra). || 98 ||
The wise one should install [the deity] upon the pedestal and worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
this should be performed month after month, again and again. || 99 ||
O best of Brahmins, one should also place incense, and especially the incense vessel, in the east with the Prāsāda mantra.
Having cast in śītāri according to one's means, one part of camphor and four parts of metal [should be added]. (101)
Sandalwood and the six-ingredient [incense] should be prepared seven times;
one should sprinkle it with honey, offer it as incense, and place it within the vessel.
One should especially offer incense consisting of devadāru, meru, sarja, śrīlāsa, kunda, and śrīphala, mixed with clarified butter.
The wise practitioner should hold a bell joined with incense in the left hand,
while in the right hand he should offer an incense burner with the heart-mantra.
The curtain is removed with the mantra *huṃ*;
one should sprinkle water and immediately offer a lamp. (105)
One should sprinkle the flower with water and place it upon the head;
at that time, in particular, a protective lamp should be lit.
O Brahmin, at the time of evening, one should worship the Lord of Yakṣas;
women should indeed hold that lamp upon the sacrificial pedestal.
O best of Brahmins, dismiss them and perform the washing of the feet;
cook one āḍhaka, or even a śiva, or a droṇa measure of rice.
The offering should be prepared with various seasonings, combined with clarified butter and curd, according to the previously mentioned procedure. || 109 ||
One should offer half [of the portion] to the deity, one part to the *bali* and the fire;
the remaining fourth part in the vessel should be presented to the preceptor (*deśika*). || 110 ||
One should offer oblations of five-colored sacrificial porridge (caru) into the five faces;
and, O best of Brahmins, one should cause the remains of the offering (nirmālya) to be given to Caṇḍeśa.
Having performed the washing of the feet, one should indeed wear the hand-gestures (mudrās):
the lotus, the trident, the axe, the sword, the noose, and likewise the goad.
One should display the mudrās of the bow and arrow, the bell, and the thunderbolt;
one should then display the surabhi-mudrā and the liṅga-mudrā according to the prescribed rule.
In this very manner one should perform the sequence; thereafter, one should worship the limbs of Brahmā.
Having worshipped Puruṣa in the east, one should sacrifice to Aghora in the south.
Having worshipped Sadyojāta in the west and Vāmadeva in the north,
the preceptor should always worship Īśāna in the pericarp. (115)
Having worshipped the Heart in the southeast, one should worship the Head in the northeast;
having worshipped the Crest in the southwest, one should worship the Armor in the northwest. (116)
Having worshipped the Astra-mantra in the directions, one should worship the Netra-mantra in the northeast;
the Śivatattva in the center, and the Ātmatattva in the south.
One should worship the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) in the northern direction with perfumes and other offerings;
in the center, however, one should worship the god Śiva, the supreme cause.
Then, having relied slightly upon Īśāna, one should worship Sadāśiva;
one should worship Maheśvara in the center and perform a slight rite toward the southeast (Āgneya).
Know Maheśvara to be the gross form and Sadāśiva to be the subtle form;
the supreme should be known as consisting of Śiva, for there is nothing higher than Śiva. 120.
Thus is the enclosure of the womb; now hear concerning the enclosure of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas):
Ananta is to be worshipped in the east, and Sūkṣma indeed in the south.
Having worshipped Śivottama in the west, likewise Ekanetra in the north, Ekarudra in the northeast, and Trimūrti in the southeast; 122.
Śrīkaṇṭha is in the southwest, and Śikhaṇḍin is in the region of the wind (the northwest).
This indeed is the enclosure of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas); now hear of the enclosure of the Lords of the Gaṇas (Gaṇeśas).
The preceptor should always worship Umādevī in the northern region;
he should worship Caṇḍeśa in the northeastern quarter and Nandīśa in the east.
One should worship Mahākāla in the southeast, Vṛṣabha in the south, Vighneśa in the southwest, and Bhṛṅgīśa in the west. (125)
And one should worship Mahāsena in the northwest with perfumes and flowers;
for this is the Gaṇeśa enclosure—now hear about the world-protectors (lokapālas).
Having worshipped Indra in the east and Śakti in the southeast,
one should worship Yama in the south and Nirṛti in the southwest.
Having worshipped Varuṇa in the western quarter and Vāyu in the north-western quarter, and having fully worshipped Soma in the northern quarter and Īśa in the north-eastern quarter; 128.
Brahmā is in the southwestern quarter, and Viṣṇu is said to be in the northeastern quarter;
this is indeed the enclosure of the world-protectors (lokeśa), and it is called the array of the weapons of the guardians of the quarters (lokapāla). || 129 ||
Having first worshipped the Vajra in the east and the Śakti in the southeast,
one should worship the Daṇḍa there in the south and the Khaḍga in the domain of Nirṛti.
One should worship the noose in the western quarter, the goad in the region of the wind (the north-west),
the mace weapon in the north, and the trident in the region of Īśāna (the north-east).
One should worship the lotus in the south-western quarter and the wheel in the region of the north-east, using perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps. || 132 ||
All the deities of the obstructions are the seat; this is called the *bindu*. One stands facing Śiva, with the deities seated upon that seat. || 133 ||
One should display the Surabhi-mudrā for the five Brahmans and the limbs of Śiva;
one should also display the Liṅga-mudrā for the Vidyeśvaras and the Gaṇeśvaras. || 134 ||
One should display the world-protectors, the hands, and the lotus seal;
at that time, one should strike the bell and dismiss the cloth painting. || 135 ||
O best of Brahmins, one should offer incense with the Hṛdaya mantra;
one should likewise sprinkle water [upon it] and offer a lamp together with the Śikhā mantra.
One should sprinkle it with water, especially with the Īśāna mantra;
then the preceptor should offer oblations of five colors into the five faces.
One should indeed offer water using water purified by a cloth, together with uśīra, kuṣṭha, elā, and sandalwood. (138)
And at that very time, O best of Brahmins, one should cause water to be offered,
as well as mouth-freshener, betel-leaf, camphor, and the three myrobalans.
One should offer fruits such as the mātuluṅga along with betel leaves,
together with cakes (apūpa), flattened rice (pṛthuka), and phaṭkulī.
One should cook it together with sugar and clarified butter along with the *bṛnda*;
one should then offer it to Śarva and worship the guardians of the field (*kṣetrapāla*s). || 141 ||
Tālujaṅgha, Lohajaṅgha, as well as Parvatajaṅghaka, Samudraghoṣa, Vāyughoṣa, Analākṣa, and Pramardana. || 142 ||
Aghoradaṃṣṭra and the others—these eight, with staffs in their hands, are most terrifying;
they resemble dark blue clouds and possess upright hair. (143)
One should worship the Kṣetrapālas, worshipping each by their respective names;
in this very manner and sequence, the best of preceptors should perform the worship.
Having performed three circumambulations, one should perform a prostration with the head,
hands, both knees, chin, and arms joined together. (145)
Now hear concerning the eight-limbed and the five-limbed prostration.
Here, the five limbs are said to be the head, the two hands, and the two knees. (146)
One should worship the gatekeepers and worship the retinue;
this is declared as the fivefold enclosure (pañcāvaraṇa), while the single enclosure (ekāvaraṇa) is now described.
First is the lion-throne, the lotus-throne is second, and the stainless-throne shall be third; one should thus arrange these three seats. (148)
Then, one should worship with the five Brahmans and the limbs of Śiva as before;
thus, only a single enclosure is prescribed, which the preceptor should always worship.
There, one should worship one's own guru with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
thereafter, one should perform the fire-ritual (agnikārya) endowed with the proper characteristics.
Then one should perform the sprinkling with the *hṛdaya* mantra, and likewise worship the deity Agni with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. || 151 ||
The preceptor should always offer oblations ending with clarified butter; for Śiva, he should perform ten oblations with the Prāsāda mantra. (152)
One should offer five oblations with the mantra of the Gaurī-bīja;
then, one should offer one oblation for each of the five Brahma-mantras and the limbs of Śiva.

One should offer a single oblation for each of the lords of knowledge (vidyeśas), the lords of the hosts (gaṇeśas), and the thousand world-protectors (lokapālas), using their respective names as mantras. || 154 ||
Then, having performed the ritual sprinkling, one should conduct the daily festival;
therein, the worship of the book should be performed with perfumes, flowers, and so forth. (155)
O best of Brahmins, one should offer oneself with water from the hollowed palms;
whatever has been stated or unstated, all of that should be offered with the heart.
The wise man should dismiss [the deity] with the heart-mantra;
having entered his own house afterwards, he should worship the household deities.
One should never eat without having first worshipped Śiva out of delusion;
therefore, with every effort, one should worship Śiva with reverence. 158.
There is no one else in the three worlds so devoted to dharma as this man, who constantly worships for his own sake, especially the mobile liṅga. (159)
"Whosoever shall worship by resorting to the seven-fold devotion, I shall perform sorcery against him—once, and then tenfold. (160)
One should also worship the maṇḍala according to the previously mentioned procedure;
in this very manner and sequence, the preceptor should always perform the worship.
The procedure for worship has been declared; now hear the ritual of the fire-offering.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, the Ritual of Worship, in the Vīratantra. || 38 ||
The Grandfather.
Having prostrated before Śiva according to the prescribed rites, the Grandfather (Brahmā) inquired:
"O Lord, tell me all about what kind of fire-ritual (agnikārya) it is."
The Lord.
All this that you have asked regarding the fire-ritual in its entirety, I shall explain in brief; listen, O Lotus-seated One! (2)
During an eclipse, at the equinoxes, during both daily and occasional rites, at the consecration of an image, during festivals, and when confronting enemies; || 3 ||
One should perform it during the solstices, at the new or full moon, during the consecration with mantras,
at the time of initiation, or even during rites for peace or prosperity.

Or one may perform the *snapana* rite, or commence the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) during the initiation (*cauka*), the sacred thread ceremony (*upanayana*), or even the return home (*samāvartana*). || 5 ||
At a marriage, at the first feeding of solid food, and likewise at the *puṃsavana* rite;
at the *sīmanta*, the *jātakarman*, and at sacrifices such as the *agniṣṭoma*.
With a concentrated mind, he should cause the fire-rite to be performed according to the prescribed rule;
likewise, the preceptor should prepare either a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or a leveled altar (sthaṇḍila).
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be one cubit in measure and square; it may also be circular. This is declared here as the procedure for the daily rite (*nityakarman*).
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should have as many corners as there are sides to the pedestal (pīṭha), up to its maximum extent;
it should be provided with three girdles (mekhalā) and endowed with a navel (nābhi) and a womb (yoni).
One should fashion the vulva like a leaf of the aśvattha tree and the girdle around it; then, one should dig a hole one cubit deep, shaped like the surface of a mirror.
Alternatively, a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) should be prepared by those who have gone to a pure location;
it must likewise be dried and baked, as well as purified through drying and baking.

The vessel for clarified butter, the pot for the sacrificial rice-oblation, fuel-sticks, the sacrificial grass mat, kusha-grass, the praṇītā-water vessel, the vessel for the substances to be touched, the girdle, the enclosing sticks, and the offering-spoons. (12)
The ladle (darvī) and the large sacrificial spoon (sruk), all the materials for the oblation, as well as a cloth, a turban, and likewise the water-offering (arghya), perfume, and flowers. || 13 ||
Likewise, one should place incense and lamps, and the fire to the north;
as well as clarified butter, sacrificial porridge (caru), and all other materials for the oblation (homa). || 14 ||
Having placed a blade of darbha grass upon it, one should cover it with darbha blades;
one should consecrate it with the heart-mantra and then sprinkle it with water.
Then, having sprinkled [the area] with the *kavaca* mantra, one should perform the scraping;
first, three lines facing east, and likewise lines directed upwards.
One should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as the presiding deities of the south and other directions, with perfumes and flowers, using the mantra beginning with "Hṛdaya. (17)
Then, one should produce the *jātavetasa* fire from either wood grown in the forest or from a sun-crystal, using the fire of a *śrotriya* who maintains the *agnihotra*.
O best of Brahmins, the lower fire-drill (araṇi) should be sixteen finger-breadths in length,
six finger-breadths in width, and three finger-breadths in thickness.
Then the preceptor should have a fire-drill (araṇī) made from śamī and pippala wood; having churned it with the Pañcabrahma mantra, he should place [the fire] in the vessel.
Therefore, one should cause the fire to be employed in all rites, beginning with the initiation ceremony;
having established the fire with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should then perform the formal installation of the fire (*agnyādhāna*). || 21 ||
The establishment of the fire, the ritual attendance, and the strewing of grass around it; likewise, the placing of the vessels, the sprinkling, and the *prokṣaṇī* water. (22)

The preceptor should perform the placement of the *kūrca*, the *praṇītā* vessel, the consecration of the clarified butter (*ghṛta-saṃskāra*), and the upward entry [of the fire], each with its respective mantra. || 23 ||
The preceptor, having cast a piece of wood into the fire with the *prāsāda* mantra, should perform the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) using the *śiva* mantra. (24)
One should perform the strewing again with the tips pointing eastward and the tips pointing northward;
having strewn it with *kuśa* grass, one should first strew from the east with the tips pointing northward.
Having spread them with the points facing south above that, and with the points facing north in the west,
the preceptor should likewise place them with the points facing east in the north.
One should place the enclosing sticks (paridhis) there on the south, west, and north;
and two should be positioned above, in the southeast and the northeast.
Having specially established Vāgīśī in the center and having performed the ritual resolve (saṃkalpa) for the post-menstrual bath, [the child] is born through the path of the womb. || 28 ||
With the *hṛdaya* [mantra], seven oblations are indeed for the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*);
with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra, the rite for ensuring a male child (*puṃsavana*) is performed. (29)
O best of Brahmins, the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) is offered seven times with the Śiras mantra;
and the birth-rite (jātakarman) is offered with the Vāmadeva mantra.
It has one heart, three feet, two faces, and two nostrils;
it is endowed with four horns and possessed of six eyes. || 31 ||
Having seven tongues and seven hands, endowed with the sacred thread (*upavīta*), possessed of matted hair and a girdle of muñja grass, and clad in a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*). (32)
Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Aruṇā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā,
Atiraktā, and Bahurūpā are proclaimed as the seven tongues of fire.
The tongue in the western [direction] is golden; the one situated in the middle is gold-colored;
the northern is said to be red; and that in the southern is remembered as black.
Suprabhā is situated in the eastern direction, while Atiraktā is established in the southeast;
Bahurūpā is likewise a tongue—thus the seven tongues are proclaimed. (35)
One should perform all the fire-oblations (homa) with the mantra called Kanaka on the tongue;
thus the birth-rite (jātakarma) has been declared by me, while the naming ceremony (nāma) is performed with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
The emergence [from the womb] should be performed with the head-mantra, the first feeding with the heart-mantra,
the tonsure ceremony (caula) with the mantra of that name, and the initiation (upanayana) with the heart-mantra.
Of all vows indeed, it is offered with the head;
but the rites of returning home and marriage are performed with the *hṛdaya* mantra.
For each of the individual rites, there shall be seven oblations;
one should place the station of Brahmā on the south side upon a seat of darbha grass.
Having placed the *praṇītā* vessel on the northern side together with the *pavitra*,
one should worship Viṣṇu, who is its presiding deity (*adhidaivatyam*), with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
O best of Brahmins, taking the vessel for sprinkling water, you should sprinkle water with the heart-mantra using a blade of kuśa grass; thus perform the ritual watering with water.
Having taken the vessel of *praṇītā* water, one should sprinkle water while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Then, one should perform the "floating" rite (*utplāvana*) and finally pour it out with the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*).
Having taken up the vessel for clarified butter,
he should fill it with ghee and place it upon the embers on the northern side of the fire.
One should place it there in its own location; perform the sprinkling with *darbha* grass.
The ghee must be placed on the fire, and one should cast *darbha* grass into the flame.
One should not sprinkle water upon the fire while it is blazing;
rather, O best of Brahmins, one should cleanse the *sruva* ladle with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
One should touch the tip with the tip joined together, the middle with the middle, and the root with the root. || 46 ||
One should sprinkle with water and perform the ritual sprinkling (pariṣecana);
when [the time] has passed, one sprinkles around [the fire], saying "May it be auspicious," on the right side.
He sprinkles water around [the fire] to the west with the words, "O Anumati, grant your approval! and to the north with the words, "O Sarasvatī, grant your approval! (48).
Saying "O God Savitṛ, impel [the sacrifice]," he sprinkles water all around; likewise, he prepares fuel-sticks of Palāśa wood, with the sacrificial faggot consisting of sixteen pieces.
The fuel (idhma) should be offered silently, and the oblation (hūyate) is made with the Aghora mantra;
[the offering] "To Prajāpati, svāhā! is made in the eastern part of the southern half.
With the mantra "Svāhā to Indra," [he offers] in the northern front portion; with the mantra "Svāhā to Soma," in the southern front portion. || 51 ||
One who knows the mantras should offer oblations into the mouth of the fire with the *Pañcabrahma* mantras;
in this very sequence, one who desires long life should perform the offerings. (52)
The daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) must be performed according to the prescribed characteristics;
one should worship the fire with clarified butter (ājya) mixed with sour gruel (vāma).
One should offer a hundred oblations with the *prāsāda* mantra of Śiva,
and likewise with the *bīja* of Gaurī, as well as with the five Brahmans and the limbs (*aṅga*) of Śiva.

O best of Brahmins, one should also offer oblations to the mantras of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) along with the world-protectors (Lokapālas) and their thousands [of attendants]; this is what is called the daily fire-sacrifice (nityahoma).
Having performed the sprinkling again,
the preceptor should then carry out the daily festival and observe the colors, fire, fragrance, and sounds.
It has the luster of the rising sun, a radiance equal to a ruby, resembling a red lotus, and possessing a brilliance like that of the *kiṃśuka* flower. || 57 ||
These twelve syllables, O Jātavedas, bestow success:
uśīra, kuṣṭha-gandha, karpūra, and agaru. (58)
One should cast in sandalwood, nutmeg, *takkola*, *kauśika*, *tuṭi*, lotus, and *kusumagandha*; these are the auspicious substances. || 59 ||
One should observe the crest-line there; in the east and above, it grants success;
in the west, it is said to bring peace; and in the north, it destroys death.
In the upward direction, however, one obtains all desired objects; of this there is no doubt.
In the southeast one encounters being consumed by fire, and in the south, death itself.
In the southwest there is death in battle; in the northwest there will be strife;
in the northeast there is the attainment of knowledge, characterized by the emergence of the crest-lock. (62)
If there is a sound like that of bell-metal, one will meet death within a month;
if there is the hooting of an owl in the fire, one will fall into prison.
If the fire crackles with a tawny sound, the death of the king will occur; if the fire crackles like a bull, there will be sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached.
If the fire sounds like a thunderclap, death will occur within six months;
if it sounds like a donkey, one has fallen under the power of untimely death.
If fire crackles like lightning, the death of one's wife will occur;
if it makes a sound like that of a cow or a donkey, one's own property will be seized by thieves.

If the sound is like the roar of the ocean, one will meet death by water; if there is a sound like that of a cow, death will come from fire; and if it is like a serpent, death will occur from a snake. || 67 ||
If there is a sound like that of a jhallarī drum, it indicates sexual union with a Caṇḍālī;
if the fire makes a sound like a musical vessel (bhāṇḍa), disease will certainly arise. 68.
If the fire makes a sound like a dog's bark, one incurs the sin of killing an embryo; if it makes a sound like a tawny cow (kapila), one incurs the sin of drinking liquor. || 69 ||
If the fire makes a sound like that of a child, death by cholera will occur;
if there is a smell of garlic in the fire, one will contract the disease of consumption (kṣaya).
If the fire has the smell of asafoetida, urinary disorder (prameha) arises;
if the fire has an excessive smell, one shall suffer from a great fever.
If there is the smell of fat in the fire, there will be death from fistula-in-ano;
if there is the smell of urine in the fire, one shall incur jaundice. (72)
O Brahmin, by the odor of a corpse one indeed incurs a gathering of diseases;
by the odor of body hair, O Brahmin, one incurs a disease of the stomach.
Therefore, O lotus-born one, the preceptor should always observe with every effort the auspicious and inauspicious signs of the god Agni as proclaimed by me.
During the aforementioned times for the planets, one should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) and other rites at an auspicious moment (muhūrta);
furthermore, one should perform a ritual sprinkling (pariṣecana) to pacify those planetary defects.
O best of Brahmins, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) endowed with the proper characteristics,
using sacrificial fuel (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), cooked rice (caru), parched grain (lāja), mustard seeds (sarṣapa), barley (yava), and sesame seeds (tila).
One should offer fifty fuel-sticks with the Prāsāda mantra;
one should perform the oblation of clarified butter with the Heart mantra, and the oblation of caru with the Śikhā mantra.
Having offered parched grain with the Vāma mantra, mustard seeds with the Sadyojāta mantra, barley with the Aghora mantra, and sesame seeds with the Kavaca mantra; 78.
Then, one should offer fifteen oblations with seven substances,
reciting the mantra for the fire-god while combining all the ritual materials.
Immediately after that, one should offer an oblation with the mantra "sviṣṭam agne";
and at the end, having performed [the rite], the Sviṣṭakṛt offering is indeed made with the mantra "yad asya".
One should offer oblations in the east, the south, the west, and likewise in the north,
as well as in the northeast, either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a consecrated mound (sthaṇḍila).
When this has been performed, there is great peace, bringing happiness to the king and the kingdom;
and upon seeing a rainbow, one should likewise perform it for the pacification of its defects. (82)

Having proceeded in this very manner, and having performed the worship of the teacher with garments, rings, and other such items, [one should proceed] with the other defects and possible occurrences. || 83 ||
The fire-ritual has been declared by me; now hear the daily festival as it is understood.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, the Ritual for Fire-offerings, in the Vīra-tantra. || 39 ||
The Grandfather.
Then, having bowed to the Lord of the World, Brahmā spoke these words:
"O God, O Lord, tell me all about how that eternal festival is to be celebrated."
The Lord.
Listen, for I shall describe in detail the eternal festival,
which is meritorious, removes all sins, and brings happiness to all the worlds.
It brings about all peace and destroys all misfortunes;
one should always perform the perpetual festival at the conclusion of the daily worship.
Rākṣasas, asuras, piśācas, and brahmarākṣasas, as well as ucchiṣṭas, vetālas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and arhat-tathāgatas [were there]. (4)
Likewise, the dwellings of Māra, other spirits, and the hosts of Maruts,
upon hearing the sounds of the eternal festival, indeed roar there.
O Brahmin, first perform a circumambulation to the right for the sake of pleasing you,
and a second circumambulation for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu.
And this third circumambulation is indeed for my great delight;
in the forenoon, it brings you joy when accompanied by an offering of flowers at the *liṅga*. (7)
At midday, the food-liṅga is a great source of delight for me;
at evening, the rice-grain liṅga is likewise dear to Nārāyaṇa.
O best of Brahmins, one should indeed perform the Śrī-bali offering at a fixed liṅga;
however, one should not perform the Śrī-bali offering at any of the movable liṅgas.
One should not perform the food offering (*naivedya*) or the *śrībali* using less than an *āḍhaka*;
in this very manner and sequence, one should indeed conduct the daily festival (*nityotsava*). || 10 ||
The vessel for the sacrificial offering (balipātra) should be made of gold, silver, copper, or even bell-metal, and it must be endowed with the proper characteristics.
It should be made according to the measurement of the finger-breadth; the best [vessel] shall be two tālas, while that which is deficient by one tāla is called the middling vessel.
The middle bowl is said to be two finger-breadths less [than the large one];
the three bowls and the triple-tiered pavilion should be made, and one should fashion a lotus in the center.
The wise one should fashion it with the middle finger;
here, the height of the lotus is said to be one finger-breadth.
One should fashion it joined with eight lotuses, with the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) as the deities therein;
in this very same sequence, one should likewise cause the vessel for the sacrificial offering (balipātra) to be made.
One should cook the sacrificial oblation (caru) according to the previously mentioned procedure;
two prasthas are declared to be the minimum, while one āḍhaka is the medium amount.
(153) They say that the supreme [food] is indeed auspicious; one should cook it with rice.
It should be very hot, or even very cold, sour, and devoid of salt. (17)
One should designate as lethal a stone that is diseased, causes grief, or is covered in husks, yet is possessed of the [auspicious] marks of an ear and a conch. || 18 ||
Having understood this sequence in this very way, one should cook [the offering] according to the prescribed rite;
having constructed a pavilion in front of Śiva, [one should do so] in the northern direction of that pavilion.
Then, having smeared [the ground] with cow dung, one should place the offering vessel with the heart mantra;
one should sprinkle it with water using kusha grass while reciting the weapon mantra.
One should indeed place the sacrificial oblation (caru) into the vessel for offerings by means of the heart-mantra alone;
it may consist of milk, or curd combined with clarified butter.
One should fashion the food-offering (annaliṅga) from mixed and equal portions of grain;
its height should be eight finger-breadths, and its base should be twice that measure.
The topmost part should be eight finger-breadths in circumference, and it should gradually diminish;
this is called the inferior linga. Now hear about the middling one.
The height should be ten finger-breadths, its base twice that [twenty], and its tip eight finger-breadths in circumference; hear now the description of the best [type] according to reality.
With a height of twelve finger-breadths and a base circumference double that,
and a top circumference of ten finger-breadths— this is here called the *anna-liṅga*.
Three-eyed, four-armed, fierce, with hair standing erect and fangs bared;
his right hand [is raised] and his left hand touches his hip. (26)
Having thus meditated upon the deity situated in the center of the lotus, adorned with all ornaments and possessing such a form, one should then deposit the offering (bali) into the liṅga. || 27 ||
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps;
perfume is offered with the heart-mantra, and it is said that flowers are offered with the crest-mantra.
One should have it made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay;
the staff should be one cubit in length, and there should be two wheels at its tip.
Thus, the wise one, holding a staff in his hand, should sprinkle that which is endowed with these characteristics with water, reciting the mantra of the heart.
Having placed Īśāna on the head, one should place Tatpuruṣa on the face;
having placed Aghora on the heart, one should assign Vāmadeva to the private parts.
One should place Sadyojāta on the two feet; then one should again perform the placement of the limbs (aṅgas):
having placed the Heart-mantra on the heart, one should place the Head-mantra on the head.
Having placed the *śikhā* on the crest, the *kavaca* between the breasts, the *astra* in the region of the hands, one should place the *netra* upon the eyes. (33)
Then, O best of Brahmins, one should place the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) upon all the limbs;
and having lifted up the small vessel with the heart-mantra, [one should proceed].
One should place it upon her head, joined with the Śiras-mantra;
one should mutter the Pāśupatāstra mantra and proceed slowly in circumambulation.
One should not stand still, nor should one walk too quickly at every step;
rather, one should move forward facing the image, while following after the liṅga.
One should not walk with sandals on one's back;
rather, one should smear the ground with cow dung facing toward Śiva. (37)
Having placed the drum right there with the heart mantra,
and having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should then worship the musical instrument.
There, one should cause musical instruments to be played, endowed with the five types of sound:
the hollow-sounding, the singing-like, and likewise the various other distinctions of sound. (39)
Then, an instrument made with strings is called "five-toned" (pañcadhvani) here; having thus performed the prescribed rite, one should then cause the musical instruments to be played.
First, one should perform the *dakṣiṇa* [movement] with the *aṅgiṇī* palm-clapping;
second, one should perform the *dakṣiṇa* accompanied by the eight-fold *tāla*.
In the east, however, there should be Samahasta, and likewise Bhṛṅgiṇī in the southeast;
in the south, Kaduvādya should be present, and likewise Saṃkarī in the southwest.
In the west (vāruṇī) there is Utkaṭa, and in the northwest (vāyavyā) Kubjatālaka;
Naṭaprahāra is in the north (saumyā), and Mallatālaka is in the northeast (aiśānī). || 43 ||
The gateway, silent of musical instruments yet accompanied by the sound of conchs, having circumambulated the temple three times in sequence upon the outer pedestal, [should be entered]. || 44 ||
The sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) may be of three kinds, located in the east, the south, or the west; one should then perform circumambulation during the three junctions of the day.
In the forenoon, one should offer the bali-oblation on the eastern seat; likewise at midday on the southern;
and in the evening on the western; thus one should dismiss the offering.
Alternatively, it is said that on the front pedestal (agrapīṭha), the southern side is for the offering (bali);
however, at every door, the offering pedestal (balipīṭhaka) should be constructed on the eastern side.
The *balitāla* belongs to Indra, while the *madhyavaṇa* belongs to Agni;
the *bhṛṅgiṇītāla* belongs to Yama, and the *mallatāla* is in the south-west (Nairṛtya). || 48 ||
In the west there is Navatāla, in the northwest Nāgatālaka;
in the north Koṭikās are proclaimed, and likewise in the northeast is Aṇḍakarī.
In this very manner, one should circumambulate the temple three times in due order;
singing first the Gāndhāra [scale], and likewise the Kauśika on the right.
In the west is Kāntamara, and likewise Takkārāga in the north; in the southeast is Kollī, and in the southwest is Nāṭṭa in the local dialect.
Takkeśī is in the quarter of the wind (the northwest), within the domain of Śākāpāṇi and Īśa;
having reached the gateway, she is the presiding deity of the bull.
One should place the sandals there and then sprinkle them with water;
having discarded the remains of the previous offerings (nirmālya), one should then perform the consecration in the water.
With the Aghora mantra one should offer the lamp, and with the Sadyojāta mantra one should cause the arghya to be given;
the wise one should worship the two sandals for both [deities].
One should place Dharitrī in the east, Dharaṇī in the south,
Pṛthivī in the west, and Medinī in the north.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavikariṇī, Balavikariṇī, Balapramathinī, and Sarvabhūtamanonmanī. (56)
One should place [the deities] with the eight Śaktis from the east to the northeast;
one should place Manonmanī in the center and worship them with perfumes and flowers. (57)
One should enter the abode there and place [the deity] within the previously prepared maṇḍala; one should dismiss [the deity] with the Astra mantra and perform a salutation.
At the conclusion of that, one should have a dance performed according to the path taught by Bharata;
there, one should bathe a courtesan and worship her with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Then, having prepared a mandala before him, one should worship Śiva;
thereafter, one should worship Brahmā on his right side.
One should not cross over the middle there; from crossing it, a ritual bathing occurs.
Then, one should contemplate the dance of the Gaṇikā one hundred and eight times.
O best of Brahmins, at the conclusion of the dance, one should dismiss the God and the Goddess;
that which is the ritual of making Agni the mouth [of the sacrifice] is then called the "mounting" (vāhana).
Upon the completion of the worship, one should dismiss that [deity] with its face turned away, having performed three circumambulations and likewise a prostration. (63)
One should perform the circumambulation clockwise around the *liṅga* and counter-clockwise around the *prāsāda* and other structures;
the mortal who acts in this manner shall attain the world of Śiva.
And then, by performing the ritual placement (nyāsa) of those [mantras] along with their attendants and retinues, one attains the world of Śiva and rejoices forever like Śiva himself. || 65 ||
This is declared to be the perpetual festival; now hear concerning the retinue.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, the ritual for the perpetual festival, in the Vīra-tantra.
Having bowed his head to the God, the Grandfather (Brahmā) asked:
"O Lord, how is it that [the world] has a retinue? Tell me all of that, O Master. (1)
The Lord.
O Lotus-seated One, listen to all that you have asked;
I shall describe the retinue according to the prescribed ritual sequence.
Within the inner circle, one should construct the temple of Caṇḍeśvara;
then, in front of it, one should establish the station of the bull and place the bull there.
Having specifically installed Durgā in the southeastern quarter,
O best of Brahmins, one should then place Bhāskara in the northeastern quarter.
In this manner, one should install the eight deities within the enclosure;
O Four-faced One, I shall now describe another method.
One should place the bull in the western part of the house at the western gate;
likewise, one should place the Mother-deities in the south and Vighneśa in the southwest.
One should install Kumāra there in the western quarter (vāruṇī), or it may be Aja;
Jyeṣṭhā in the north-western region (vāyavya), and Viṣṇu in the northern region.
The preceptor should install Jyeṣṭhā with all possible effort in the northwestern direction,
and he should also install the goddess Durgā in the northern direction.
O best of Brahmins, Kṣetrapāla is ordained in the northeast; in the east is the station of Bhārgava, and [there is] Kumāra... || 9 ||
One should place Durgā in the north-eastern direction and Bhāskara in the east;
having established Gaṇapati in the south-east, one should then install the deities.
To the north of the northern gate-house is the domain of Taurus;
to the south of the southern gate-house is the abode of the Bull. (11)
Mātṛsthāna is in the southwest, Subrahmaṇya in the west, Jyeṣṭhā in the region of Vāyu (the north), and Viṣṇu is said to be [in the northeast]. 12.
Having placed Bhāskara in the northeast, Viṣṇu is said to be in the east;
one should place Durgā in the southeastern quarter and Kṣetrapāla in the southeast.
One should install the two Aśvins between Indra and Agni;
the boundary markers are in the direction of the heroes (the north), and the groups of Mothers are traditionally placed in the south.
The wise one should especially install Vighnarāja in the southwest, Kumāra in the west, and Jyeṣṭhā in the northwest. || 15 ||
In this very manner, O best of sages, one should install [the deities] in sequence within the inner enclosure; I shall now describe the sixteen door-deities.
One should place the seven Rohiṇīs between the southern and southern-fire (southeastern) quarters;
and one should place the eight Vasus between Yama and Nairṛta (the south and southwest).
Between Soma and Īśāna, the host of Apsarases is said to dwell;
between Varuṇa and Vāyu, the station of the Ṛṣis is said to be located. || 18 ||
One should place the eight Vasus between Vāyu and Soma;
one should arrange the eight Nāgas between Soma and Īśāna. || 19 ||
Between Indra and Īśāna, one should likewise place the twelve Ādityas;
in this very manner, one should also arrange them at the boundaries.
The Grandfather.
Having bowed his head to the God, the Grandfather (Brahmā) questioned him:
"O Lord, tell me all about how this protective lamp [is to be used]. || 1 ||
The Lord.
O Lotus-born One! Listen to all that you have asked;
I shall describe in detail the threefold protective lamp.
It is threefold: pacifying (śāntika), nourishing (pauṣṭika), and that which grants desires (kāmada).
It may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay. (3)
And a vessel (sthālikā) should be fashioned with a width of thirty finger-breadths,
[measured] from the east to the south, and likewise from the west to the north.
In the middle [section], however, one should arrange five pitchers joined together;
they should be eight finger-breadths in height and [possess the other required characteristics]. || 5 ||
Then, having placed the lamp above the *kumbha*, one should have it fashioned by a craftsman;
the height of the base (*pāda*) is prescribed to be ten finger-breadths.
They say its width should be exactly that; one should also have a lamp-vessel made.
This is called the rite for pacification (śāntika); now hear about the rite for nourishment (pauṣṭika).
Its width, however, should be twenty-four finger-breadths, and it should be raised up.
Rice flour [mixed with] * * * * * * * * * * * is said to be nourishing (*pauṣṭika*); now hear from me about that which grants desires (*kāmada*). || 9 ||
Having established [the vessel] as before, one should arrange seven vessels;
and upon those seven vessels, one should likewise place [the ritual items].
(162) This is said to be the bestower of desires; it is declared by me to be threefold. One should perform it with devotion; its food is called Nandīpa. || 11 ||
In the evening, one should perform the rites upon the bed and worship the Mistress of the Yakṣas;
O best of Brahmins, one should kindle the perpetual fire in the sacrificial pit.
On its southern side, however, there is a square mandala;
one should place a small mound there, conjoined with the śikhā-mantra.
Then, one should light a wick there, combined with either cow's ghee or sesame oil.
With the Prāsāda mantra, the lamp is said to be in the center;
with Puruṣa in the east, and Aghora in the south.
Having placed Sadyojāta in the west and Vāmadeva in the north,
one should perform the rite with the Īśāna mantra, accompanied by the Vyomavyāpin.
One should worship especially and cause [the lamp] to be held above the head;
a courtesan or a female servant should hold the excellent lamp.
Accompanied by songs set to mantras, joined with the dances of courtesans,
and endowed with the sounds of drums, mṛdaṅgas, and hymns of praise,
go there and perform circumambulation, concluding it in the presence of Śiva.
Having placed the tripod in the center and sprinkled it with water while reciting the Astra mantra,
one should worship the lamp itself with the Īśāna mantra.
Having joined the flower with the lamp, one should place it upon the top of the *liṅga*.
Then, one should perform either one or three circumambulations. (21)
One should discard the floral remains (nirmālya) and place them upon the outer pedestal;
this is called the rite of pacification (śāntika). Now hear concerning the rite of nourishment (pauṣṭika).
One should construct a pavilion in front of Śiva and place a tripod right there;
one should then place a small pedestal there with the Hṛdaya mantra.
Having placed the ground flour on the left side, one should likewise sprinkle it with water while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra; then, one should place the wick upon the upper part of the inner sanctum.
One should worship with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) and then sprinkle [the offerings] with water;
then, with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra), one should offer a lamp to Śiva.

One should perform the circumambulation of one or even three lingas of Śiva for the protection [of the devotee] and for the welfare of all living beings. Thus has the rite for nourishment been explained; now hear in truth about that which grants desires. || 27 ||
One may perform it either at the fire-pit or again in the inner sanctum;
then, O best of Brahmins, one should place the lamp upon seven vessels.
The preceptor should likewise perform the rite of nourishment (pauṣṭika) in the proper sequence;
having properly offered a lamp to Śiva, he may then dismiss it as prescribed.
This is called the "Bestower of Desires"; I shall describe it to you in brief.
It is declared to be the supreme lamp, seven finger-breadths in height.
The middle [size] should be five finger-breadths, while the lowest height is three finger-breadths;
the best [ointment] is indeed cow’s ghee, and the middling is that produced from sesame. (31)
They say that oil alone is the lowest [offering]; however, one should have it strained through a cloth.
It should be joined with dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains, a mirror, and sacred ash.
After the appearance of the lamp, one should especially offer water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), the respectful offering (arghya), fragrance, flowers, and incense to Śiva.
O Lotus-seated One! Listen now to the true form of Yakṣeśvarī, which is joined with that very [letter] followed by the vowel sound 'ī'. (34)
Beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, with the seed-syllable of the Lord of Yakṣas in the middle—this supreme secret mantra has been revealed out of affection for you. (35)
He has two arms, one face, two feet, and two eyes;
he is endowed with a crown and a casket, possesses a gentle form, and has beautiful eyes. (36)
One should place the Goddess in the center of the lamp with palms joined in reverence and a focused mind;
having meditated upon her in such a form, one should then perform worship.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavikariṇī, Balavikaraṇī, Balapramathinī, and Sarvabhūtadamanī. (38)
One should worship with perfumes and flowers from the east up to the northeast;
having placed Manonmanī in the center, O Goddess, one should worship her externally.
O best of Brahmins, one should then worship Soma, Aṅgāraka, Budha, Jīva, Śukra, Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and Ketu on the outside of that.
Then, one should worship Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, as well as Soma and Īśāna, joined together on the outside of that [circle]. (41)
In this very same manner, one should worship Yakṣeśvarī in due order;
one should apply the ashes there to Śivā and give the remainder to the people.
In the evening, one should perform [the ritual] on the bed in this very same sequence;
however, at the time of the sprinkling, he who provides a protective lamp [is blessed]. || 43 ||
Freed from all sins, one shall attain the world of Śiva.
I have thus described the protective lamp; now hear about the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa).
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, concerning the ritual for the protective lamp, in the Vīratantra.
Having bowed his head to the God, the Grandfather (Brahmā) asked:
"O Lord, what is this 'offering of the sprouts' (aṅkurārpaṇa)? Tell me all of that! || 1 ||
The Lord.
O Lotus-seated One, listen as I shall explain in its entirety that entire ritual for the auspicious sprout which was requested by you. || 2 ||
The first is to be known as the sprout of the banner (dhvajāṅkura), the second as the sprout of the festival (utsavāṅkura);
and the third is specifically declared to be the sprout of the festival itself.
The fourth is Tīrthāṅkura, while Caṇḍāṅkura is the fifth;
alternatively, one should know Tryaṅkura, which is also called Dhvajāṅkura.
That which is joined with the sprouts of the sacred sites (tīrtha) is called the "sprout of sprouts" (aṅkurāṅkura),
whether for the installation, the sprinkling, the sacrifice, the festival, or even the ritual bathing.
Furthermore, in rites for auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), it is called the "Sprout of Auspiciousness" (*maṅgalāṅkura*);
it is threefold: that which brings fortune (*śrīkara*), that which is the abode of fortune (*śrīnivāsa*), and that which bestows fortune (*śrīprada*). (6)
Having drawn four lines with their tips pointing east and likewise four with their tips pointing north, thus forming nine squares there, listen now to the deities [to be assigned]. (7)
In the eastern quarter, however, is the Ṛgveda; in the southeast, brilliance is said to reside. In the south is the Yajurveda, and in the southwest is the letter E.
In the western quarter, one should likewise place the Sāmaveda;
in the north-western quarter, Pavana (the Wind-god), and in the northern quarter, the Atharvaveda.
The waters are established in the northeast, while the Vāma is established in the center;
and in the central position itself, the Soma-kumbha is established.
Having placed a *ghaṭikā* in the cardinal directions and a *pālikā* in the intermediate directions, this is called *śrīkara*; now hear from me the *śrīnivāsa*.
The five lines should have their tips pointing eastward, and likewise their tips pointing northward;
they say there are sixteen such squares—now hear about the divine feet.
Īśāna, Jayanta, Āditya, Agni, Vitatha, Yama, Sugrīva, Varuṇa, Śoṣa, Mukhya, Soma, and Āditi; || 13 ||
Brahmā is established in the center of the four-footed [mandala],
while Īśāna, Agni, and Sugrīva occupy the positions of the principal [deity].
One should place the *pālikā* there; this is said to be the location for the water-jar (*ghaṭikā*).
Jayanta, Vitatha, Varuṇa, and Soma [are the deities]. (15)
p.
167) The location of the *ghaṭikā* has thus been described; now hear about the location of the *śarāva*.
Āditya, Yama, and Śoṣa are situated in Diti. || 16 ||
Now listen to this account of Śrīnivāsa, which bestows prosperity. || 17 ||
Having likewise laid out six lines with their tips pointing east and north,
and having divided [the space] into twenty-five squares, one should worship them in due order.
Īśa, Jayanta, Āditya, Bhrama, Agni, Nirṛti, Yama, Svabhṛṅga, Sugrīva, Varuṇa, Śoṣa, and Māruta. (19)
Soma and Aditi are proclaimed as the primary external deities;
[the others are] Āpa, Vatsāri, Sāvitrī, Vivasvat, Indra, and Mitra.
Between Rudra and Bhūta, in the middle, the Brāhmaṇa is said to be located;
one should place the Soma-pitcher at the very station of Brahmā.
Īśāna, Jayanta, Agni, Vitatha, as well as the Pitṛs, Dauvārika, and the chief Maruts. || 22 ||
One should place the *pālikā* there, and then listen to [the placement of] the *śarāva*:
Āditya, Prathas, Yama, and Bhṛṅgarāja. (23)
Varuṇa, Śoṣa, Soma, and likewise Aditi—one should place these in the shallow bowls (śarāva); now listen to [the arrangement of] the small jars (ghaṭikā) as well. || 24 ||
Water, fire, wind, and so forth—the eight [elements] are said to be the locus.
O Four-faced One! Listen as I shall fully explain their characteristics. (25)
