One should have [the vessels] made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay; indeed, the *pālikās* and other such items should be fashioned there according to the measurement of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*). (26)
The width of the opening of the *pālikā* is twenty finger-breadths for the best, sixteen finger-breadths for the middling, and ten finger-breadths for the lowest. (27)
Its width is equal to its height, half of that is the width of the base,
and around it, O best of Brahmins, there are eight [parts], while one-sixth is traditionally prescribed.
In the middle [section], it should be joined with the *bali* and made like the surface of a mirror;
its height should be equal to that of the *pālikā*.
The width of the belly of the jar is said to be twelve finger-breadths,
and its mouth six finger-breadths, provided with five faces.
One should fashion the characteristics of the jar like those of the *pālikā* pedestal;
its mouth should be six finger-breadths wide and provided with five faces. || 31 ||
The width at the mouth of the shallow bowl (śarāva) should be eight finger-breadths;
its base width is said to be half of that, or three-quarters.
One should avoid [a vessel] that is cracked, chipped, old, or perforated.
A *ghaṭikā* has Brahmā as its presiding deity, while a *pālikā* is said to have Viṣṇu as its deity.
Śarāvasyeśvara is proclaimed [as the deity]; thus these are the presiding deities (adhidaivatas). One should designate this collection of twenty-four as the most excellent. || 34 ||
One should designate that which possesses sixteen *pālikās* as the middling;
that which is joined with eight *pālikās* is here called the lowest. || 35 ||
On the first night of the festival, the sowing of the seed is prescribed;
it should be performed on the ninth or the seventh [night], accompanied by the trident. (36)
One should place the image joined with Caṇḍeśa,
and at its end, one should have the devotees of Śiva hold the *pālikā* vessels and other items.
Facing either the east, the north, or especially the south,
and having reached a thoroughly purified ground, one should sprinkle it with pure water.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), one should worship with the Heart-mantra;
and having fully honored Kuṇḍalī as well, one should do so with the Heart-mantra according to the ritual formula.
The preceptor should cause the ground to be excavated with the *hṛdaya* mantra;
having gathered the earth with his left hand, he should worship that earth with his left [hand].
Accompanied by all musical instruments, he should enter toward the temple,
either in front of the palace, or in the northeast, or in the south.
Or else, O best of Brahmins, one should smear the northern area with cow dung;
then, one should have an altar prepared there using eight *droṇas* of rice.
Having worshipped the eight-petaled lotus, one should sprinkle it with water while reciting the heart-mantra;
then, one should place the soma-vessel in the center using the seed-syllables of Soma.

Having worshipped that [vessel] containing a tuft of grass, gold, and cloth, filled with water, and adorned with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, he should then cause an offering of food (naivedya) to be presented.
Having first arranged the *pālikā* vessels and all other items outside of that on every side,
one should place a hollow made of *darbha* grass and fill it with earth right there.
One should worship [the image] smeared with cow dung while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*;
one should then perform the *puṇyāha* rite and subsequently cause betel-leaf to be offered. (46)
Mudga beans, māṣa beans, and kulattha; sesame and nīvāra grain; niṣpāva, along with śimba, apāmārga, and mustard seeds. || 47 ||
One should wash the barley and bamboo stalks combined with green wheat there with milk, while reciting the mantra of the Heart.
Facing either east or north, the preceptor, whose very form is the mantra, should have [the hair] shaved with the Śiva-mantra; and he should also have those devoted to Śiva shave it.
A female attendant of Rudra and a maidservant should especially cause [the hair] to be shaved;
then, having sprinkled water from a jar presided over by Soma.
Having placed all the vessels, beginning with the *pālikā*, in a well-concealed location protected from wind and sun, together with the *soma* jar, [he should proceed]. (51)
From that day until the conclusion of the pilgrimage site, the preceptor of Somarāja should present the sacrificial offering there,
and thereafter cause betel to be given.
If it resembles a black thread, one should offer a hundred oblations with the *prāsāda* mantra;
O best of Brahmins, one should likewise offer cakes (*apūpa*) as the sacrificial offerings.
In this very way, the offering of the sprouts is said to be performed in due order;
for if the offering of the sprouts is omitted, it causes harm to the king and his kingdom.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the auspicious rite of the sprout (*maṅgalāṅkura*).
The mortal who acts in this manner shall attain the world of Śiva. || 55 ||
The ritual of depositing the sprouts has thus been described; now hear the procedure for the festival.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, the Ritual for the Planting of Sprouts, in the Vīratantra.
Having bowed his head to the God, the Grandfather (Brahmā) questioned him:
"O Lord, what is the procedure for the festival? Tell me all of that! (1)
Out of special affection for you, O Lotus-seated One, I shall tell you in its entirety everything regarding that festival about which you have asked; listen!
All suffering is fully described as that which obstructs all prosperity;
because all [prosperity] has emerged from it, therefore it is called a festival (utsava).

At the conclusion of initiation, at the conclusion of consecration, and likewise at the conclusion of the sprinkling rite, let the Jvara-māryās perform [the ritual], even for the purpose of afflicting enemies. || 4 ||
It bestows abundance of wealth and grain, brings about emaciation and destruction [of enemies],
fulfills all desired objects for everyone, and destroys all diseases.
At these times, one should perform the festival according to the prescribed rules.
There are two kinds of festivals; now hear their distinction.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the Śiva festival should conclude with Ārdrā;
in the month of Puṣya, it should conclude with Puṣya; and in the month of Māgha, it should conclude with Maghā.
In Phālguna, it should end with Uttarā; in Caitra, it is said to end with Citrā;
in Vaiśākha, it ends with Viśākhā; and in the month of Jyeṣṭha, it ends with Jyeṣṭhā.
In Āṣāḍha, [the asterism] Uttarāṣāḍhā; in Śrāvaṇa, ending with Śravaṇā;
in Pūrvāṣāḍha, Meṣa is said [to begin]; and the month [of Bhādrapada] begins with Pūrvabhadrapadā.
In the month of Āśvayuja, one should perform the festival until the end of the asterism Aśvinī;
in Kārttika, however, one should perform the Śiva-festival until the end of Kṛttikā.
The festival of Śiva should be performed in all months, ending with the Ārdrā asterism;
or it may be held on the king’s birthday, or under the very nakṣatra of the village. (11)
And on the birth-star (janmanakṣatra) of the performer, one should hold a festival;
it is said [to consist of] the Śaiva, the Gauṇa, the Vibhūti, the Bhauvana, and likewise the Daivika [festivals].
The procedure for the festival of Śiva should be performed according to five divisions;
O Lotus-seated One, listen as I describe these distinctions. (13)
The Śaiva division has been fully described; thereafter, the festival lasting one day, when joined with three days, is designated as the secondary (gauṇa).
The five-day [rite] is declared to be *bhautika*, while the seven-day is remembered as *bhauvana*;
now, the procedure for these sequences shall be explained according to the rule.
Beginning at evening and continuing until before nightfall, the ritual bath (tīrtha) should take place in the morning; on a single day, however, there shall be two offerings (bali).
Listen now to this other method for a one-day festival:
beginning in the evening, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) during that night.
One should perform the *homa* that same night; at the beginning of that, one should offer the *bali*.
I have described this single *bali* for a festival lasting a single day. (18)
O best of Brahmins, the preceptor should likewise perform the rite of the sacred ford (tīrtha) with others as well;
in this very manner, I shall describe the various types in their proper sequence.
O best of Brahmins, one should begin that at evening during the three-day periods;
O Brahmin, on the third day it should be performed in the morning, and there are exactly six offerings.
On the second day, one should indeed cause two offerings (bali) to be made;
on the third day, however, only one offering is prescribed. || 21 ||
And at the conclusion of the *bali* offering, O best of Brahmins, one should perform the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*).
At the end of the powder festival, there shall be a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), which is said by me to be of two kinds.
I shall now proclaim the fivefold rite; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
Beginning at evening, one should first perform the fire-oblation (homa).
O best of Brahmins, one should not perform the bali offering there during the fifth day;
however, on the sixth day, in the forenoon, one should perform the powder festival (cūrṇotsava).
Furthermore, one should prepare the sacred bathing place (tīrtha); listen now to another [instruction]:
beginning at evening, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) during that night.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) every night, and every night one should offer the bali-offering;
on the second day, however, only a single bali-offering is prescribed.
O best of Brahmins, at the conclusion of the *bali* offering, one should indeed perform the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*).
At the end of the powder festival, there shall be a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*); thus, it is said by me to be of two kinds. (27)
I shall now declare the five-day [rite]; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
One should begin that on the preceding day, starting from the evening time.
O best of Brahmins, one should not perform the *bali* offering there during the fifth day;
however, on the sixth day, in the forenoon, one should perform the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*).
Furthermore, a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) must be prepared; listen now to another matter:
beginning at evening time, it should likewise be performed for five days.
One should perform the *homa* that night, and a single *bali* offering is prescribed;
on the second, third, and fourth [nights], two *balis* are offered.
On the fifth day, there should be one bali offering; then one should perform the remaining festival.
One should indeed perform the rite of the sacred ford (tīrthakarma), which is said by me to be of two kinds.
I shall speak on the seventh day; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
On the eighth day, in the evening, one should commence the consecration ceremony (adhivāsana). || 33 ||
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) during that night and offer the bali oblation again and again;
one should present the fourteen-fold bali and cause the powder festival (cūrṇotsava) to be celebrated.
One should especially prepare the sacred bathing place (tīrtha); listen now to this other [instruction]:
having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) on the evening of the seventh day, the wise man [should proceed].
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) during that night and again offer a single bali offering; this should be done on the second day, and likewise on the third and fourth days.
O best of Brahmins, one should perform two offerings on the fifth and sixth days;
thus there shall be an offering every seven days, and at the conclusion of the offerings, the powder is prescribed.
Then, beginning from the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), there is that most excellent [rite];
it is declared to be of two kinds for seven days, so now hear also of the nine-day rite. (38)
One should perform the consecration (adhivāsana) during that night, beginning from the first part of the night;
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) during that night and likewise cause the sacrificial offering (bali) to be given.
From that day forward, at that time, it is called Bali;
then the wise man should perform the Cūrṇotsava festival, and thereafter he should perform the Tīrtha rite.
(175) I shall now declare another matter; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
On the ninth day, at the time of sunset, one should begin the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana). || 41 ||
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) during that night and likewise cause the sacrificial offering (bali) to be given;
and so too on the second, third, and fourth days.
On the fifth day and indeed on the sixth day, one should perform the second bali offering;
and on the ninth day as well, O best of Brahmins, there shall be a pair of bali offerings.
Then one should perform the powder festival (cūrṇotsava) and commence the rites of the sacred ford (tīrthakarma);
O Lotus-seated One, it is said that this lasts for nine days and is of two kinds.
In this very manner, one should perform the fivefold rites in due order.
O Lotus-seated One, listen as I shall now declare the procedure for Sunday. 45.
Beginning at the time of dawn, one should worship Śiva twice as much;
there, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited and then offer the sacrificial oblation (havis).
One should present the bali offering to the world-protectors (lokapālas), beginning with Indra and ending with Īśāna;
at the time of the daily festival, one should perform a circumambulation of the village.
Then, having carried [the deity] on his head in either a chariot or a palanquin,
he should enter the temple there and perform the worship of the sandals (pādukārcana).
This has been declared as Sunday; now listen to [the rules for] Saturday. Herein, an oil massage on a linga or an image is prescribed. (49)
The consecration (abhiṣeka) should be performed with the mantra of the Heart;
afterwards, one should present the sacrificial oblation (havis) and cast the bali-offering to the guardians of the world (lokapāla).
One should honor the Śaivas there and perform the sequence of serving food; one should perform a circumambulation of the village accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments. (51)
I shall proclaim the rite pertaining to Mārtaṇḍa; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
Beginning at the time of evening, one should offer the oblation (bali) at the time of dawn.
At the conclusion of the sacred site (tīrtha), during the first part of the night, one should offer the bali-oblation to the world-protectors (lokapālas).
One should then place nine water-pots (kalaśas) on the southern side of the pavilion (maṇṭapa).
Then the fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed according to the prescribed characteristics;
having offered twenty-five oblations of sacrificial fuel (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), and cooked rice (caru).
O best of Brahmins, one should offer an oblation (bali) accompanied by the Linga of food and endowed with the king of weapons, especially at the time of evening.
Then at dawn, he should perform circumambulation of the image and the village;
thereafter, the wise man should perform the ritual bath at a sacred ford and enter the temple.
In this very manner, specifically on Wednesday, this [rite] pertaining to Mārtāṇḍa is proclaimed; O twice-born one, listen to the account of Rambhā. 57.
I shall describe it as being of three kinds: preceded by the offering of sprouts, preceded by the hoisting of the banner, and preceded by the beating of the drum. (58)
The wise man should offer the sprouts and then raise the banner;
having struck the drum, he should do so preceded by the offering of the sprouts.
The wise man should raise the banner, preceded by the beating of the drum;
in this very sequence, the threefold [rite] is thus described by me.
O best of Brahmins, on that very day one should cause [the pole] to be raised doubled;
or, having doubled it, one should then erect the banner. (61)
The commencement of the festival is said to be the hoisting of the banner at night;
one should perform it during the Bhauvana and Daivika periods, and avoid other times.
When [the time for] bathing in the ocean has arisen, the previously prescribed rule is enjoined:
on whichever lunar fortnight, on whichever day, or on whichever weekday the sun sets.
On that day, when there is a solar transit (saṃkrānti), the division [of time] and the sacred ford (tīrtha) are determined by the daytime;
since it is not touched by other lunar days (tithis), it is therefore prescribed as occurring before them.
O best of Brahmins, one may perform it on those days, or on the day preceding them, or even on the following day;
however, for others, one should not have it performed in those rivers.
On the banks of rivers and lakes, that lunar mansion on which the sun sets during its respective fortnight is called a *tīrtha*. (66)
On that day, at the time of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), it is certain that the holy ford (tīrtha) is during the daytime;
one should perform the vow of Śiva and thereafter the ritual bathing (snapana).
In this very manner, one should then cause the festival to be performed in due order.
Listen now to the description of the commencement of the festival according to the Vṛṣayāga.
I shall proclaim the bull-sacrifice; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
One should construct a square pavilion in front of the temple. (69)
In the center of that pavilion, one should perform the sacrifice to the Bull (Vṛṣayāga),
having encircled it with garlands of *darbha* grass and hung it with flower garlands.
From Indra to Īśāna, one should mark eight banners in the eight directions; presided over by the world-protectors as their presiding deities, they should be marked with their respective emblems. (71)
One should place banners there, adorned with four archways,
covered above with a canopy, and decorated with strings of pearls.
Then, having worshipped Vṛṣadeva with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should offer green-gram rice accompanied by side dishes.
Then, having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before that with pure śāli rice—
specifically eight droṇas of śāli and half of that amount in rice grains (taṇḍula)— 74.
Having placed half of that amount of sesame seeds and having especially fashioned a lotus,
one should place nine water-pots upon it.
One should place one [vessel] in the middle, provided with a thread and a lid;
it should be filled with scented water and gold should be placed therein.
Having recollected the seed-syllable of Vṛṣabha, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
one should then place eight jars starting from the east and ending with the northeast.
One should first place the water for the feet (pādya) there; it is said that the flower belongs in the southeast (āgneyī).
Having placed the water for sipping (ācamana) in the south, one should place the pure water (śuddhodaka) in the southwest (nairṛta).
Having placed the *arghya* water in the west, one should place *bilva* water in the northwest;
one should place the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) in the north, and precious gem-water in the northeast. (79)
There, one should worship the deities with perfumes and other offerings, and then install them;
having installed the bull in the center, one should install the ox in the east.
One should worship Gopati in the direction of Agni (the southeast), Śṛṅgin in the south,
Nandin in the southwest, and Paśupati in the west. (81)
One should place Viṣāṇin in the quarter of Vāyu (the northwest), Śaṅkukarṇa in the north,
and Mahodaka in the northeast within the jars.
To the east of the water-pot, prepare a sacrificial mound with rice;
having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, cover it with *darbha* grass.
One should install a banner-cloth there, endowed with the proper characteristics;
the best is ten cubits long, while the middling is nine cubits.
The lowest [flagpole] is eight cubits, while the middle is nine cubits;
the length of the banner is said here to be three and a half tālas.
Six tālas are declared to be the best, five tālas the middling,
and three and a half tālas are said here to be the inferior.
The width of the cloth should likewise be one-fourth of its length;
for a Brāhmaṇa it should be white, and for a Kṣatriya, red.
The yellow [color] is declared here for the Vaiśya, while the black color is for the Śūdra.
The tail should be equal in width to the body, and the finial (śikhara) should be half the size of the tail.
In the middle [of the mandala], one should place a bull as the emblem, whether standing or reclining;
the bull should be white in color, while its two horns are red.
The hooves are red in color, or perhaps yellow;
the tail is likewise [yellow]; the eye is white, and the middle part is red.
One should place a bull and a lotus-seat adorned with a garland of jewels;
having positioned two lamps at the sides, one should cause a variegated [canopy] to be made above.
Then one should have two sides decorated with chowries,
and thereafter, one should place the form of the bull starting from the east up to the northeast.
On the preceding day, there should be the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) together with the flagstaff;
one should sprinkle it with water while reciting the Hṛdaya mantra.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should then install the form of the Bull (Vṛṣa) starting from the east and ending at the northeast, using the Vṛṣa-Gāyatrī mantra.
At the end of that, one should especially worship the world-protectors (lokapālas);
outside of that, one should worship the weapons of the world-protectors there as well.
In the eastern direction of that very place, prepare a sacrificial mound with rice;
having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, cover it with *darbha* grass.
Above that, one should place the trident and worship it especially;
for the trident is established at the base of the powers (śaktis) such as Vāmā and the others.
One should place Kumāra on a wooden plank, Varuṇa in a water-pot,
Agni as the deity upon the bank, and Sarasvatī upon the staff.
Having placed Pārvatī upon the pedestal and Vasundharā upon the ground, one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, incense, and the ninety-six [articles]. || 99 ||
There, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and then cause betel-leaf (*tāmbūla*) to be offered.
After that, one should perform the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) upon a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).

(181) One should generate the fire of Śiva there, and the "mouth of fire" (agnimukha) is offered into it; sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, and mustard seeds are likewise offered. || 101 ||
Combined with the five Brahmans, the oblations beginning with Īśāna are offered;
each is offered either one hundred times, or fifty, or even half of that.
The consecration of the bull has been declared; now hear about the hoisting of the banner.
O best of sages, I shall describe the hoisting of the banner in this manner. 103.
A white-colored banner increases the king and the kingdom;
a red color indeed [effects] attraction, while a yellow color effects paralyzing.
The *bijaya* [mantra] is tawny-colored, the *kṛṣṇa* is for malevolent rites (*abhicāraka*), and the *dhūmra* brings about disease; thus indeed is it according to the sequence. (105)
Whatever desires one may wish for, those very ones the Banner shall surely accomplish.
For half a year it is dark green in color, while that which resembles the luster of milk brings all-pervading peace.

A conch shell with the luster of crystal or pearl, which grants protection and bestows peace and nourishment, brings satisfaction to Brāhmaṇas when offered in the forenoon and increases royal prosperity at midday. (107)
O Vaiśya, the increase for Śūdras at night is likewise in successive order.
O Lotus-seated One, listen as I describe the location of the flagstaff (dhvaja). || 108 ||
The location for the flagstaff (dhvaja) is prescribed as being between the pedestal (pīṭha) and the gateway (gopura), or in front of the bull,
or at the very front of the pedestal.
Betel nut, bamboo, sandalwood, or even khadira;
campaka, deodar, stambaka, and also bilva—(110)
It should be straight, free from blemishes, and devoid of worm-holes or cavities; it should be level with the temple or even the height of the temple’s neck. (111)
The height of the staff (daṇḍa) is said to be either equal to the Vṛṣasthala, or equal to the height of the gate-tower (gopura),
extending from the base to the top, or from the root to the end of the lineage.
One may construct it measuring eight cubits, or even thirty cubits;
the height of the banner is said to be twelve or ten cubits.
Its circumference (nāha) is prescribed as either thirty-seven angulas, or twenty-four,
or even twenty-two angulas.
Then, having taken a bamboo staff, he skillfully fashioned it;
one [joint] at the front was for the purpose of destruction, while with two [joints] it became terrifying. (115)
Afflicted by disease at the third joint, one suffers the destruction of the fourth;
two sets of five joints bring misfortune in this world, while six joints bring prosperity.
A cow with seven previous joints perverts the eight ancestral lineages;
one with nine joints destroys the family; but one with ten joints indeed grants all desires. (117)
The eleventh [type] is for those desiring a son, and the twelfth bestows nourishment.
Beyond this, one should not construct [an image] larger than the size of a cubit; listen now to that.
One should place a water-pot (ghaṭikā) before it at a height of six or five tālas;
the supporting planks and other items should be made from wood suitable for sacrificial purposes.
The space between them should be known as one cubit, or half a cubit, or even just a span;
it should consist of two hollows joined together, like a betel nut with a bamboo stalk.
O best of Brahmins, one should likewise have it joined by a craftsman;
the circumference of the bamboo staff should be five, six, or seven finger-breadths. (121)
One should bind it there with a cord and then encircle it with *darbha* grass;
a cord is said to be made from a thread the thickness of the little finger.
One should perform [the rite] for one ghaṭikā at the beginning and twice that at the root;
then, having become pure, the student (māṇavaka) should sprinkle it with water.
Clad in new garments, wearing a turban and an upper robe,
at its edge he should place the King of Weapons (Astrarāja), accompanied by the Linga of food,
endowed with various banners and various crests.
It was crowded with various people, provided with various musical instruments, adorned with various umbrellas, and accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas. || 126 ||
Accompanied by auspicious sprouts and provided with dance and song,
the preceptor and the patron proceed, one before and the other behind.
Having circumambulated slowly in a clockwise direction, one should cause it to enter the place for the flag;
there, one should have a pit dug measuring two cubits in size.
At its base, one should construct an altar endowed with the prescribed characteristics,
having placed there a golden tortoise according to the measurement of six *tālas*.
There, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited and sprinkle [the area] with pure water;
then, with the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should wash the flagpole (*dhvajadaṇḍaka*).
Having encircled it with garlands of *darbha* grass and endowed it with flower garlands,
one should sprinkle it with water from the ritual jar while reciting the *vṛṣagāyatrī* mantra. (131)
Having raised the flagstaff while reciting the *Vyomavyāpin* mantra,
one should then fill the pit with sand while reciting the *Hṛdaya* mantra.
At its base, one should construct an altar endowed with the prescribed characteristics,
measuring six tālas, five tālas, or even four tālas.
O Brahmin, the width is declared [to be such], while the height is half of that;
having conceived above that a very beautiful eight-petaled lotus.
There should be either a single girdle or three girdles;
having divided the height into three parts, each individual girdle shall have one such part as its elevation.
One should place Mekhalā below and Bhūmidevī as well;
having worshipped Śrīdevī in the middle, one should worship Sarasvatī in the third [position].
O best of Brahmins, one should fashion three Śaktis for the three girdles;
with one girdle, one should make [the goddess] Bhūmidevī and then install her there.
In this very manner, one should especially prepare the pedestal;
likewise, O God, one should bathe the deity at the place of sacrifice with a ritual pitcher.
During the ritual bath, one should worship Vṛṣabhadeva with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
thereafter, one should thread [the beads] using the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra.
Having raised it by means of a pulley in due order, or by means of a rope-mechanism, one should then hoist the banner. || 140 ||
Kumbhodara and Vṛṣabha, Pāśahasta and Madotkaṭa,
Śūlahasta and Pinākī, as well as Aṣṭanāḍī and Daṇḍamuṇḍiya. (141)
One should place these in the eight directions, starting from the east and ending with the northeast;
one should worship them with perfumes and flowers, accompanied by incense and lamps.
One should have a sacrificial altar prepared there with four *droṇas* of *śāli* rice;
one should perform the *puṇyāha* rite there and arrange nine water-pots.
In the center, one should place a bull-pitcher with the mantra of the Bull;
thereafter, one should place the pitchers from Indra up to Īśāna.
Having established them according to the rule with their respective garments and covers, with the world-protectors as their presiding deities, using the Vṛṣa-gāyatrī mantra. || 145 ||
One should offer rice cooked with mung beans accompanied by curd as a side dish;
at that time, one who desires offspring should then feed the *piṇḍas*.
The preceptor should form a ball of food the size of a hen’s egg;
the preceptor should then offer that ball with the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra.
Having firmly established the bull-pillar and having circumambulated it three times,
one should act in this manner, O best of Brahmins, for women of the four castes; however,
for those of the lowest castes (antyajātis), one should cause them to perform the rite in the reverse order.
Thereafter, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings;
one should offer betel-leaf to him, and especially to all the people.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, the ritual for hoisting the banner, in the Vīra-tantra.
From this point forward, the supreme beating of the drum should be performed;
thereafter, one should hoist the banner in the morning, at midday, and in the evening. (1)
On that night, one should beat the drum endowed with the proper characteristics;
O Lotus-seated One, listen as I explain those characteristics.
One should make a seat, or likewise a sandalwood one, or one of *vakula*, or *śirīṣa*; or one may make it from *vyāghra* wood, or indeed a drum (*bherī*) or a kettle-drum (*paṭaha*).
The length should be three cubits; this is prescribed as the best. The middle [size] should be five tālas, less by six finger-breadths.
This is declared to be the lowest; it is said by me to be of three kinds.
When the circumference is equal to the length, it is called a *paṭaha* in the middle [category].
The mouth should indeed be twelve finger-breadths, or nine, or even seven;
in this very sequence, one should fashion an excellent drum.
On a long journey, however, there should be a binding with cowhide,
accompanied by the sounds of mṛdaṅga drums and hāhala drums, as well as the cry of swans.
One should strike the jhallarī, jharjharī, mohanī, and the karaṇḍikā, along with all other musical instruments as they may be available.
Then, one should have a pavilion constructed in front of the temple;
in the center of that pavilion, one should smear the ground with cow dung.
Having prepared two altars (sthaṇḍila) in that same manner with rice,
one should have two altars made using eight droṇas of rice.
One should place a drum there upon a new cloth;
then, having combined half of that with rice, one should sprinkle it with water.
Having drawn a lotus of the proper measure, one should spread darbha grass in its center;
thereafter, one should have an altar (sthaṇḍila) made in the shape of a drum.
One should place a drum there, covered with a new cloth;
then the preceptor should set up a shield in front of it with the Astra-mantra.
One should offer oblations of cooked rice (caru) along with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps;
thus indeed one should worship the Śūkta, and afterwards one should worship the drum (bherī).
Facing north, one should worship with perfumes and flowers;
having sprinkled [the area] with water mixed with *kuśa* grass while reciting the mantra "Āpo hi ṣṭhā," || 15 ||
One should place the drum there and worship it with the Heart-mantra;
Rudra is to be worshipped on the right, and Viṣṇu is traditionally remembered as being on the left.
One should worship Brahmā in the center, and likewise in due order:
Vāsuki in the leather thong, and the sun and moon as the two bracelets.
One should worship the Seven Mothers with the seven stakes situated in the belly, joined with the staff of the Kaulaṇḍa, using the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra). || 18 ||
Having summoned musicians, one should perform the ritual bathing;
then, wearing white garments, one should apply perfumes, garlands, and unguents.
Then, having worshipped Nandikeśvara with his two arms, accompanied by the Nandi-mantra, according to the prescribed rule with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; ||| 20 ||
O best of Brahmins! Then one should offer the sacrificial oblation to the drum itself;
there, one should worship the preceptor and thereafter worship the musician. || 21 ||
With the Vāmadeva mantra...
[the preceptor], whose body is composed of mantra, should strike with the Śiva mantra. || 22 ||
Afterwards, one born of a noble family, even if poor, should strike the musical instrument while reciting the Nandi mantra; he should likewise strike only according to the rhythmic measure (tāla).
In the first [beat] there is *caccatpuṭa*, and in the second there is *cācatpuṭa*;
with the *samatāla* of Indra, there shall be the sound *vaṇa* when bound in the southeast.
Then, accompanied by these rhythmic beats (tāla), one should play the musical instruments;
thereafter, one should offer the village-oblation (grāmabali) endowed with the proper characteristics.
It was equipped with various banners, provided with various umbrellas, endowed with incense and lamps, and furnished with various peacock feathers. || 26 ||
Resounding with the sounds of conchs and drums, filled with songs and instrumental music,
it was provided with a trident and accompanied by a food-liṅga.
In this very manner, one should perform the circumambulation of the village;
endowed with devotion to Śiva, one should perform the circumambulation of the temple. (28)
One should offer the bali-oblation at the base of the banner and offer the bali-oblation to the retinue;
one should also offer the bali-oblation within the village, starting from Brahmā and ending with Īśāna.
Having announced the day of the sacred ford (tīrtha) and having invoked all the deities,
[one should offer to] all the hosts, as well as the spirits and the piśācas.
From that time forward, one should offer the village-oblation at night at the edge of the sacred site (tīrtha).
Having invoked [the deity] at the base of the banner, one should deposit the oblation right there. || 31 ||
When this great propitiatory rite has been performed, it brings happiness to the king and the kingdom;
the sounding of the drum is thus prescribed. Now hear concerning the sacrificial pavilion.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, the procedure for beating the drum, in the Vīratantra.
I shall describe the sacrificial pavilion for the sacrifice; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
It is required for the installation ceremony, the festival, initiation, and even for the ritual sprinkling.
O twice-born one, I have already previously explained the acquisition of the ground for the sacrificial pavilion used in rites such as the Great Peace (mahāśānti).
Either in front of the temple, or to the south, or even to the west, or between Indra and Īśāna, or between Agni and Śakra. (3)
Between the southern and southeastern [directions], and between the northern and northeastern [directions],
one should cause a pavilion to be constructed there, endowed with the proper characteristics.
The twelfth [type] is ten cubits, or nine cubits, eight cubits, or seven, six, or five cubits; it is also said to be seven [cubits]. || 5 ||
There should be ten threads with their tips pointing eastward and likewise ten with their tips pointing northward;
having thus formed eighty-one squares, one should sprinkle them with fragrant water.
In the center, one should likewise arrange nine squares and construct an altar there; the height of the altar should be one cubit, made smooth like the surface of a mirror.
(190) It is provided with sixteen pillars and endowed with four gates;
and in the central square, the sacrificial fire-pit (homakuṇḍa) is prescribed.
O best of Brahmins, the pit in the east shall be square, as shall those in the south, west, and north;
and in the north, indeed, the pit should be square.
In the intermediate directions, there should be circular kuṇḍas provided with three girdles;
or for all [the deities], they may be square, or for all, they may be circular.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should have the shape of a seat;
it is traditionally taught that a circular pit is located between the northeast (Īśāna) and the east (Indra).
One should cause a single fire-pit to be constructed, either with nine fires or five fires;
it should be provided with three girdles or even just a single girdle.
There, the preceptor should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) and sprinkle the area with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
he should also arrange four archways at the four gates.
The best [image] is five cubits in height; the middling is four cubits;
and that which measures three cubits is said to be the lowest.
The height of the trident should be half its width, increased by one krośa; it should be joined with three palas and be equal to a tāla in measure. || 15 ||

The middle [size] is five finger-breadths according to the measure of a mother's finger (mātrāṅgula), while the best is made with seven darbha grasses and suspended to the length of one cubit (hasta). || 16 ||
And in front of that, one should indeed prepare a cord,
[covered] above by a canopy and joined with garlands of pearls.
One should install a poisoned banner there, measuring four tālas in height;
it should be dark green in color in the east, and red in color in the southeast.
In the south, it is black in color; likewise in the southwest, it has the luster of a pearl;
in the west, it is yellow in color; and in the northwest, it is indeed blue.
In the north it has the luster of crystal, and in the northeast it is said to be smoky;
one should place the forms of the world-protectors in the middle of the banners.
The Darbha grass, the full water-pot, the bull,
the pair of chowries, the Śrīvatsa mark, the Svastika, the conch, and the lamp— these are the eight auspicious objects of the gods.
The vajra, the śakti, the staff (daṇḍa), the sword, the noose, as well as the goad, the mace, the trident, the discus, and the lotus—these are the ten weapons. || 22 ||
There, one should have it fashioned by a craftsman endowed with the proper characteristics; one should have the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala) made with a measurement of one cubit.
Then, one should likewise have the ten weapons fashioned by a craftsman;
thereafter, one should wash them with clay combined with pure water.
There, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and sprinkle [the area] with the *Śiva-mantra*.
Outside the altar, one should place rice (*śāli*) that is equal in amount and well-adorned.
Upon that, one should place the Astra-mantra accompanied by the eight auspicious symbols;
and one should place it upon Darbha grass, having covered it with a tuft of grass (kūrca).
One should place the water-pots for the missile (astra) together with their respective names;
in this very manner, the wise man should also place them in the eighth and ninth [sections].
Having worshipped with incense, flowers, and so forth, according to the mantra of the Prāsāda [hymn],
one should worship the vajra and other implements there with their respective names and mantras. (28)
There, one should present the sacrificial offering (havis) and then cause betel-leaf (tāmbūla) to be given;
thereafter, a fire-oblation (homa) should be performed, either once or on the fifth day.
One should sprinkle the weapons and the eight auspicious symbols with water from the ritual pitcher;
having performed the worship of the preceptor, one should then worship the articles for the feet.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, concerning the characteristics of the pavilion, in the Vīratantra.
I shall describe the procedure for the consecration (adhivāsa); listen briefly, O Lotus-born One! One should commence the consecration on the first night of the festival.
One should likewise prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice in front of the temple;
one should place the pālikās and other vessels there, and the Soma-vessel in the center.
Then, with the heart-mantra, one should sow the *pālikās*;
having established the *pālikās* and other vessels in their proper order in a well-concealed place.
Afterwards, one should tie the protective thread (kautuka) and prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before Śiva;
there, one should place the image and likewise place the weapon-mantra (astra).
One should place a golden woolen thread upon a small pedestal, or one may use a cotton thread; then, one should sprinkle it while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Then, one should bind the protective thread (kautuka) upon the image with the temple mantra;
afterwards, one should cause betel-leaf to be distributed, especially to all the people.
(193) One should prepare a mandala in the center of the altar using eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice; it should be strewn with rice grains mixed with sesame seeds and covered with *darbha* grass.
Having installed the Śiva-pitcher (śivakumbha), one should place the Vardhanī pitcher to its left,
along with [other vessels] provided with cords, lids, and cloths, and filled with water.
One should establish the five jewels with the Śiva-mantra;
one should place the gems and install the gold with the Gaurī-bīja.
Having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should carry it upon the head,
accompanied by various musical instruments and adorned with various peacock feathers.
Accompanied by various songs and provided with various lamps,
one should circumambulate the celestial chariot (vimāna) and enter the sacrificial pavilion.
There, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, and then sprinkle [the area] with water;
thereafter, the preceptor, having become pure and endowed with the body of mantras, [should proceed].
One should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) there according to the previously mentioned procedure,
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the Heart-mantra.
One should place the pitcher in the center of the altar while reciting the *vyomavyāpin* mantra.
I shall now describe the form of the Sacrifice (*yajñamūrti*), which is endowed with a single face. (14)
He has four arms and three eyes, endowed with a gentle form;
he sits comfortably in the midst of a lotus, adorned with a crown of matted locks.
Hara was adorned with all ornaments, holding a black axe,
with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and wearing divine garments.
Having meditated upon the auspicious Śiva in the form of a hand, one should then meditate upon Gaurī,
who has two eyes, a beautiful face, two arms, and is in the full bloom of youth. (17)
One should place Vardhanī, whose mind is perfectly tranquil, whose face is slightly smiling, and who is adorned with all ornaments, in the middle.
Having fashioned the sacrificial pavilion like the door of a palace,
one should install the image of the deity of sacrifice facing the entrance.
One should place the *vardhanī* vessel on the left with the mantra of the Gaurī-bīja.
Then, one should place eight jars in sequence, starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
Then, he should place [the vessels] along with their cloths, covers, gold, and brushes,
as well as the altars in the various directions, and thereafter install the trident.
One should place [the deities] beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin within the center of the jar;
one should worship them specifically with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using their respective names.
The vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, as well as the goad, the mace, the trident, the lotus, and the discus—these constitute the ten weapons. (23)
One should worship [the deities] in the directions from the east to the northeast with their respective mantras;
the Lotus and the Weapon in the southwest quarter, and the Discus in the domain of the northeast.
A mirror, a full water-pot, a bull, a pair of chowries,
the Śrīvatsa mark, the Svastika, a conch, and a lamp— these are the eight auspicious objects of the gods.

The best of preceptors should place [the offerings] starting from the east and ending with the northeast, worshipping each with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the respective name-mantras. (26)
Thereafter, one should place the pitchers at the doors or recite [the mantras] with their respective mantras;
then the preceptor should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the prescribed characteristics. || 27 ||
Every evening and morning, one should perform the burnt offering (homa) accompanied by the materials for the oblation:
sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), cooked rice (caru), parched grain (lāja), mustard seeds (sarṣapa), barley (yava), and sesame seeds (tila).
Bamboo, mung beans, and rice—these ten substances are mentioned here.
The sacrificial fuel (samidh) is offered with the Sadyojāta mantra, and the clarified butter (ājya) is offered with the Vāmadeva mantra.
Having offered the sacrificial oblation (caru) with the Aghora mantra, and the parched grains (lāja) with the Puruṣa mantra;
one should offer mustard seeds with the Īśāna mantra, or barley with the Yama mantra.
Having offered sesame seeds with the *vaiśikha* mantra, or bamboo with the *kavaca* mantra,
and having offered mung beans with the *netra* mantra, one should then offer śāli rice with the *astra* mantra.
Having offered one hundred and eight, or fifty, or twenty-five oblations especially for each specific substance, according to the particular requirements.
Having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblation at the end of each substance,
one should perform the sprinkling (pariṣecana) while reciting the name of the Fire-god (*Havyavāha*) together with all the substances.

Immediately following that, one should offer oblations with the mantra "sviṣṭam agne," and then in sequence, one should perform the Jaya and other offerings, the Abhyādhāna, and the Rāṣṭrabhṛt offerings.
Then, one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented to the deities such as Yāgeśvara;
there, one should perform the study [of the Vedas] with four scholars who have mastered the Vedas.
Having recited the Prāsāda mantra, and especially having recited the hymn of praise,
one should offer the bali oblation in the evening and in the morning, particularly at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice (homa).
(196) I shall explain the procedure for the sequence of offerings; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
A food-liṅga should be fashioned, endowed with the characteristics as previously described. (37)
He has four arms and three eyes;
he holds a trident in his right hand and a noose in his left hand, while his right hand displays the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya).
Having thus meditated upon Pāśupata, who is endowed with a fierce form and holds a boon-granting gesture in his left hand, one should properly offer the bali-oblation to the liṅga.
One should place food mixed with all the necessary substances into the offering vessel;
first for Vighnarāja, and second for Bhūtarāja. (40)
The third is the Brahma-night, while the fourth is called the Garaba;
the fifth would be the Indra-night, and the sixth is indeed the Rishi-night.
The seventh is declared to be Vaiṣṇava, the eighth likewise Rākṣasa, and the ninth they call Śaiva; these are the presiding deities of the nights.
O best of Brahmins, in the case of a seven-day rite, one should increase the presiding deity of Brahma-rātra;
however, in a five-day rite, one should increase the presiding deity of Indra-rātra.
One should cause a festival for the Vaiṣṇavas and others to be held there for three days;
even a single day of festival is traditionally known as Śivarātra.
I shall describe the materials for the bali offering; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
[It consists of] pure food mixed with curd, along with cakes and sweetmeat balls.
On the first day, one should offer [the oblation] while reciting the Viṣṇu-mantra,
consisting of lotus flowers, turmeric, parched grain, and milk-rice (pāyasa).
On the second day, one should offer [the oblation] while reciting the *bhūta-mantra*:
the root of a lotus, the tips of *kuśa* grass, and rice mixed with ghee. (47)
On the third day, while recollecting the Brahma-mantra,
one should offer turmeric rice together with ghee and coconut fruits.
On the fourth day, one should give [the medicine] while reciting the Gandharva mantra:
Indravallī, turmeric, rice, and Priyaṅgu combined with ghee. (49)
On the fifth day, recollecting the mantra of Indra,
one should give food made of *gulodana* (rice cooked with molasses) mixed with clarified butter, along with plantains and jackfruit.
On the sixth day, while reciting the mantra of the sages,
one should offer boiled rice mixed with jujube fruits, ghee, and the fruit of the *bṛhatī* plant.
On the seventh day, while reciting the Vaiṣṇava mantra,
one should offer food made of black gram mixed with ghee, along with meat and *caṃpa*.
On the eighth day, reciting the Rākṣasa mantra,
one should offer pure food mixed with curd, along with parched grain and cakes.
Combined with plantain fruit and thoroughly saturated with ghee,
it should be offered on the ninth day while recollecting the mantra of Śiva.
One should especially offer the bali-oblation in the size of a hen’s egg;
one should cast the bali upon the bali-altar (balipīṭha) from Brahmā up to Īśāna.
The pedestal for the Yantra should be constructed measuring one Tāla in size;
it should be made according to the Mātrā-aṅgula measure, with its width and length being equal to that.
It should be six finger-breadths in height, provided with three girdles;
the height of each girdle is two finger-breadths, and the width of the entrance is likewise the same.
This has been declared as the Yantrapīṭha; now listen to another.
Its width should be one cubit (hasta), and its height one palm (tāla). || 58 ||
Having made it equal to the three girdles, the height is prescribed;
having divided the width into three parts, each part shall be two cubits.
Having specially prepared a pedestal out of either clay or sacrificial wood,
one should then proceed to the festival procession on a stage or upon a chariot.
I shall describe the ritual of the return; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
On the first day there are banners, and likewise on the second, musical instruments.
In the third [stage], he is declared a *samayin*; in the fourth, he is called a *śūlin*.
In the fifth, however, there is the *vānna-liṅga*, provided with a canopy and cloth.
One should hold the ten weapons all around above the head,
accompanied by incense and lamps, and joined with the sounding of a bell.
In this very manner, having performed the bali offering in due order, the preceptor [should offer it] to Caṇḍarudra at the cow-pen and to Vyāpida.
In the well, one should worship Śaṅkukarṇa; likewise, [one should worship] the goddess Gaṅgā in the river.
In the sacred fields (kṣetra), one should worship Kṣetrapāla, and in the assembly hall, Sarasvatī.
One should offer the *jyeṣṭhā*-oblation to Durgā, which brings happiness to all the worlds;
in this very manner, one should perform the oblation and cast it upon the sacrificial pedestal (*balipīṭha*).
O best of Brahmins, on the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), one should especially offer an oblation of food (annaliṅga);
at the conclusion of the offering, one should perform the circumambulation of the village as a rite of auspiciousness.
It was equipped with various kinds of mechanical stages in great numbers,
joined by people from many different regions, and adorned with diverse banners.
It was provided with various musical instruments and adorned with various crests;
in the first [section] were banners, and in the second were musicians.
In the third [section] there were swinging machines (ḍolayantras), and in the fourth horse-machines;
in the fifth were dancing machines, as well as staffs and banners.
In the seventh [month], he is seated comfortably; in the eighth, there are then the testicles;
in the ninth, however, * * * *; and in the tenth, then the bull.
Likewise, Gaṅgādhara is the twelfth, and Nṛttarūpaka follows;
then Bhikṣāṭana at the end, and Arddhanārī is the fourteenth.
Candraśekhara alone is specifically declared as the fifteenth;
in the sixteenth [syllable], Hari occupies half, and at its end, Kālahā shall proceed.
At its end, O best of Brahmins, one should specifically worship the Destroyer of Tripura eighteen times; above the image, one should proceed to that which is beneficial for Umā and Skanda.
One should know that there are twenty Caṇḍeśvaras at the end of that;
then the preceptor, having performed the circumambulation of the village, [proceeds with] the offering of the bali.
It should never be performed in another location because of its impurity; the wise man should enter the abode. Now, the ritual of serving food (pariveṣa) is described.
One should have a pavilion constructed there, or else one should have a water-shed (prapā) built;
it should face either the south or the east. (77)
In front of the temple, or to its south or north,
one should construct the great boundary-markers (maryādau) and the boundary-markers (maryādau), as well as the Nauda pavilion.
One should place the *kautuka* (sacred thread) there and dismiss the *nirmālya* (remnants of the offering).
Then, O best of Brahmins, one should perform the ritual bath and worship the lord with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
The preceptor should be on the right side of the deity and in the south-east;
one should know the king to be in the north, and one should place two women on the two sides.
The dancer and the drummer are in the south; in the north is the lineage of singers.
To the south, however, are those of the Śaivas, and in the north, the smiling followers of the Samaya.
And in the presence of the deity, O best of Brahmins, accompanied by the dances of courtesans, at that very time, according to the previously mentioned procedure.
A protective lamp should be prepared for the trident-bearing God of gods;
one should worship him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and indeed offer incense and a lamp.
Having placed salt along with flowers and other items, as well as flowers for the *arghya* offering, each separately into vessels, the courtesan should hold them in due order. (84)
One should offer the protective lamp to Śivā and dismiss it at the pedestal for the sacrificial offering (balipīṭha);
in this very manner, one should perform the rite every day. || 85 ||
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, the ritual for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*), in the *Vīratantra*.
On the day of Viṣṇu, one should display the form of dance;
on the day of the Rākṣasas, however, one should commence the forest procession. || 1 ||
One should go to the forest in the four directions, starting with the east;
one should assume the form of the Destroyer of Tripura and carry his weapons.
By the power of the commencement of battle, all the people took up every kind of weapon;
some were archers, and others likewise were sword-bearers.
Some should hold tomara-spears in their hands, and others should carry maces;
in this very manner one should perform the rite by day, and the binding of the *kautuka* (protective thread) at night.

Whether it be made of gold or silver, or even of linen or cotton, one should perform the consecration of the amulet and the trident; one should increase the power of the amulet with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
In front of Śiva, within the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*),
one should place a small mound (*sthalikā*) there, and upon it, one should place rice grains.
Having placed the *kautuka* (sacred thread) above it, one should sprinkle it with water while reciting the *Hṛdaya-mantra*;
then, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the *Prāsāda-mantra*.
One should perform the circumambulation of the village while being joined with the ritual spear (śūla),
accompanied by various lamps and provided with various musical instruments.
One should enter the abode there and bind the *kautuka* with the heart-mantra;
then, one should indeed bind the trident with the previously mentioned mantra.
One should perform the collection of sacred sites (tīrthasaṃgrahaṇa) and then construct a pavilion in front of Śiva.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound with śāli rice and strewn it with darbha grass,
one should place a water-pot in the center, provided with a cloth and a lid. (11)
One should place eight jars from the east up to the northeast;
having placed gold therein, one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Whether at the ocean, or a river, or especially a lake,
one should prepare a level surface on the bank and then install [the image] there.
The preceptor should install the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin;
furthermore, the binding of the directions must be performed by the preceptor using the Astra-mantra.
One should then invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas) as well as holy places;
thereafter, one should bathe the trident with the consecrated jars.
One should enter the temple there and worship with incense, flowers, and so forth.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter of the Vīra-tantra, the ritual for the auspicious journey.
I shall describe the powder festival; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
At the conclusion of the offering of the sacrificial oblation (bali), one should perform the circumambulation of the village with festive curiosity.
Thereafter, one should perform the powder festival (cūrṇotsava) either on the roof of the temple,
or even in front of the *kautuka*, having sprinkled powder upon the mortar.
In the northwestern direction, in the southern quarter, or even in the northeast,
having smeared the ground with cow dung, prepare an altar (*sthaṇḍila*) with rice grains.
One should place rice equal to eight *droṇas*, or half of that amount;
having laid down an eight-petaled lotus, one should surround it with *darbha* grass.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before him, and especially a mortar—
made of Plakṣa, Udumbara, or Aśvattha wood, but never of Pada wood.
One should not tie the pestle with [any other mantra];
one should wash it with the Astra-mantra and establish it with the Hṛdaya-mantra. || 6 ||
Having covered it with a cloth and dried it with cow-dung,
one should place it upon a wooden mortar at its center, with the heart [mantra].
Having recited the *vyomavyāpin* mantra, the most excellent of teachers should grind [the ingredients].
I shall now describe all the fragrances: combined with cardamom (*elā*) and cloves (*lavaṅga*), as well as black pepper (*takkoḷa*), jasmine (*jātī*), and *gaṇikā*, he should then grind them.
Having placed the powder in a jar together with a *kūrca* grass-bundle,
a lid, cloth, and gold, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having taken the powder upon your head, perform a circumambulation of the celestial chariot;
then place that powder, as well as the oil, upon the primary image there.
One should cause the king of weapons, Kautuka, to be given by means of the heart-mantra itself;
one should especially give the powder to the devotees and their attendants.
One should perform a circumambulation of the village accompanied by the powder of the trident;
the preceptor should then offer the powder of the world-protectors, beginning with Indra.
One should cause him to enter the house there, and then one should perform the ritual at the sacred site (tīrtha). || 13 ½ ||
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, the Ritual for the Powder Festival, in the Vīratantra.
I shall now describe the sacred site (tīrtha), specifically at the front of the temple;
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice mixed with sesame seeds.
Taking nine jars, one should fill them with fragrant water;
to the left of that, one should fill the *vardhanī* jar with the mantra consisting of the seed-syllable of Gaurī.
But having established them, O best of Brahmins, together with the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras),
one should especially worship each according to their own name and mantra.

Carrying the water-pots upon his head and bearing the eight auspicious symbols and weapons, he should perform the circumambulation of the village while joined with Śiva and the marriage-thread (kautuka).
Whether at the ocean, a lake, or especially at a river,
having made the bank level, prepare a sacrificial altar (sthaṇḍila) with rice.
One should place an image there and set a water-pot (kalaśa) before it;
having worshipped the trident together with the pot using perfumes and other offerings.
Having summoned all the gods and summoned all the sacred fords from every direction, and having indeed released the marriage-thread (kautuka) as well as the image and the trident; || 7 ||
One should indeed bathe the Śūla with jars of water and cause it to engage in water-sports;
that mortal who performs this thousandfold bath is liberated from all sins.

One should cause [the disciple] to enter the house; there, one should cause him to enter the sacrificial hall. Having performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should indeed dismiss the fire. || 9 ||
One should reverently bathe Śiva with pitchers placed upon the altar;
one should perform the ceremonial bath there according to the prescribed characteristics.
Having performed a special worship, O best of Brahmins, one should especially offer a bali-oblation before Śiva on that very night.
O best of Brahmins! One should cut it with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) using a trident alone;
one should also sow it together with oil-cake mixed with clarified butter.
One should especially offer a bali-oblation combined with cakes at the junctions of time,
at crossroads, in a temple, and in a cremation ground.
One should especially offer oblations in the garden, at the well, in the forest, and in the king’s own palace; this brings happiness to the king and his kingdom.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, the Ritual for Holy Places (Tīrthavidhi), in the Vīra-tantra. || 50 ||
I shall describe the lowering of the banner (dhvajāvarohaṇa) correctly and in due order:
either on the day of the pilgrimage, or on the third, fifth, or even the seventh day.
I shall describe the lowering of the banner (dhvajāvarohaṇa) correctly and in due order:
either on the day of the pilgrimage (tīrthāha), or on the third, fifth, or even the seventh day.
One should perform the lowering of the banner accompanied by the Caṇḍayāga rite;
furthermore, one should have a ceremonial bathing performed there after seven days at the very latest.
Then one should perform a peace-offering (śānti-homa) and lower the flag;
furthermore, one should smear the ground in front of Caṇḍeśvara with cow dung.
One should scatter rice there, along with half that amount of husked grains;
having placed sesame seeds, O best of Brahmins, one should further spread them over with *darbha* grass.
Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, one should sprinkle it with water while reciting the heart-mantra;
then, taking nine jars, one should encircle them with a thread.
Having worshipped with scented water while recollecting the Caṇḍa-mantra,
the wise one should bathe Caṇḍeśa with the Caṇḍa-mantra itself.
Thereafter, one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented, and then cause betel-leaf to be offered;
having fashioned the image of Caṇḍeśa, the celibate student (brahmacārī) shall remain pure.
Clad in new garments, wearing a turban and an upper robe, and adorned with flower garlands, perfumes, sandalwood paste, and other such things; || 8 ||
O best of Brahmins, one should feed [the deity] accompanied by all kinds of side dishes,
with a ṭaṅka coin held in hand, and the body smeared with ashes.
One should place the fierce mantra there and cause it to enter the location of the banner;
one should place it above the palanquin and cause it to enter the location of the banner. || 10 ||
Then, one should place an image of Caṇḍeśa upon the top of the palanquin;
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) at the tip of the banner, one should install nine water-pots (kalaśas).
Then, having recollected the Vṛṣa-mantra, he should indeed install the banner, which is provided with cloth, gold, a tuft of grass, and a lid.
Afterwards, one should cause mudga-rice to be offered while recollecting the seed-syllable of Vṛṣa;
then, having performed the bali-offering to the quarters, one should dismiss the banner.
Having performed the lowering of the banner with the Heart-mantra,
one should especially cut the banner-pedestal there with a chisel.
Then, one should offer the village bali together with Śūladeva,
consisting of parched grain (lāja), roasted barley flour (sakthu), turmeric rice, and curd.
One should especially offer an oblation (bali) accompanied by all kinds of side-dishes;
having performed the ritual dismissal (udvāsya) of the pedestal situated at the joint, one should cut it away with the *ṭaṅka* tool alone.
Having entered the temple, one should afterwards offer the oblation upon the sacrificial pedestal.
And thus, O best of Brahmins, the preceptor should say: "Perform the washing of the feet."
One should have the ceremonial bathing performed there according to the prescribed characteristics;
one should honor the preceptor there with garments, grain, gold, and other offerings.
One should cause garments and other articles to be given to the devotees and attendants;
thereafter, one should cause sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to be given to the courtesans and female servants.
Thus, the mortal who performs this festival according to the prescribed rites,
having delivered twenty-one generations of his lineage, goes to the world of Śiva.
Having served humans, elephants, horses, and all other beings in every way,
he shall go to the divine city of Śiva for as long as the dissolution of the world (dhṛtisaṃplava) lasts.
"Everything rejoices in Śiva"—this is the certainty of the scripture.
The procedure for the festival has been declared; now hear the procedure for atonement.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, the Ritual for Festivals, in the Vīra-tantra. || 51 ||
The Grandfather.
Having prostrated before Śiva according to the prescribed rite, Brahmā spoke these words: "O Lord, O Master! Tell me all about how that expiation is to be performed."
The Lord.
"Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! That which has been requested by you, I shall explain in its entirety; listen, O Lotus-seated One! || 2 ||
"Prāya" means destruction; "citta" is said to be the act of mending.
Thus, the mending of what has been destroyed is traditionally known as *prāyaścitta* (expiation). (3)
Due to negligence, impairment of the intellect, or the depletion of ritual materials, an expiation is prescribed for rites that were either left unperformed or became ruined. (4)
When the temple has fallen or been destroyed, one should cause a place for the Child (Bālasthāna) to be established;
(having constructed the temple as before, perform the sprinkling with water). || 5 ||
The palace would surely be destroyed; with [the defect] in the east, there would be a fracture at the head;
in the southeast, it would be consumed by fire; in the south, death would occur. || 6 ||
In the southwest there is the gain of wealth, and in the west, grain;
in the northwest there will be an increase in kinsmen, and in the north, an increase in sons.
In the northeast one attains Śiva; in this very sequence, having removed all impurity from the sun, one should bind [the protection] with the *sakalīkaraṇa*.
There, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made, and then have the ritual bathing (*snapana*) performed;
thus the temple shall be restored, and one should indeed cause the temple to be built.
One should install [the linga] endowed with these characteristics; now hear this other [matter]:
a linga situated in its original place may come to be in another location. || 10 ||
Having then discarded that [old] linga, a new linga was installed; however, in the eastern region, some mobile linga remained established. (11)
The wise one should restore it to its proper place after performing a sprinkling with water,
whether it be the liṅga or the pedestal, even if it is cracked or burnt.
The preceptor should prepare a temporary site for the child and perform worship;
having removed that [old] liṅga, he should install a new liṅga.
Or else, one should have a hundred staffs (daṇḍakas) raised by elephants at a river;
one should install that liṅga, or another endowed with the characteristics of the region.
If one is touched by those in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka), those in a state of death-impurity (pretaka), or by corpses,
then one should perform a sprinkling with water accompanied by this ritual procedure.
One should cause it to be made with eight bindings, free from the eighth binding;
the resin should be actual beeswax combined with the juice of *sajja*.
If one touches the linga of another caste, one should perform a sprinkling with water; bathing [the linga] should take place nearby. (17)
In the inner sanctum (garbhageha) that is devoid of plaster, one should perform the work of whitewashing;
one should cause the proclamation of the auspicious day (puṇyāha) and have a ceremonial bath (snapana) performed there.
Then, one should have the artisan fashion any missing limbs for the image.
O Brahmin, one should join the image and have the ceremonial bathing (snapana) performed there;
and the image of the Lord of Gods should be surrounded by the Viśvadevas.

One should cause the image to lie upon the bed and commence the fire-oblation (homa) around it; having offered the oblations according to the procedure for installation, one should establish it in exactly that same manner. || 21 ||
Then, the artisan should fashion a pedestal that is devoid of radiance;
O Brahmin, one should then join the image to it and perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) there.
Indeed, weapons, deer-skins, and ornaments, when broken, cracked, or even torn through negligence; || 23 ||
The wise one should have it performed by a craftsman in the same manner as before;
having performed the sprinkling with water, he should then cause the *śānti* oblation to be offered.
If negligence should arise during festivals or at [auspicious] times,
one should worship Śiva with incense and other offerings and recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
Then, having gone to the remaining path, one should subsequently enter the temple;
or, after measuring as before, one should perform the sprinkling and other rites.
If the *pūraṇaliṅga* cracks, breaks, or is likewise split,
it causes affliction by fever and other ailments, yet it also brings about pacification.
Then one should perform the Diśāhoma (oblation to the quarters) according to the prescribed characteristics;
thereafter, one should have the study of the four Vedas conducted in the four directions.
The milk-consecration (kṣīrābhiṣeka) is said to consist of one hundred and eight prasthas;
sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, and flour are likewise offered as oblations.
The best of preceptors should offer oblations to Īśāna, ending with [the appropriate mantra], in the northeastern direction;
in this manner, he should perform one hundred and eight oblations.
Then, one should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) there one hundred and eight times;
in this very same sequence, the twice-born should continue the rite for seven days. (31)
And day by day, O best of Brahmins, he should then feed the Brāhmaṇas;
there he should also feed the devotees of Śiva (Śaivas) along with their attendants and servants.
One should feed the preceptor there with garments, grain, gold, and other gifts;
and at the end of the day, O best of Brahmins, one should offer the village-oblation (grāmabali) at night.
One should offer rice mixed with mung beans and curd, along with the leaves of the * * *,
starting from Brahmā and ending with Īśāna, while reciting their respective names.
One should offer the bali-oblation ending with Īśāna in this very sequence;
however, if the daily worship has been omitted, one should perform a propitiatory homa.
If one has transgressed the time for the twilight prayer (saṃdhyā), one should then perform worship twice as much;
and if two or three [prayers] have been omitted, there must be an ablution with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Then one should perform the peace-offering (śāntihoma) and worship Śiva according to the prescribed number [of times],
whether it be on the first day, the third, or even the fifth day, or if the period is shorter.
Then one should perform the *śānti*-oblation and have the ritual bathing (*snapana*) performed there;
likewise, every half-month, one should perform the *diśāhoma* and the ritual bathing as well. || 38 ||
From this point forward, however, for one month you should perform the ritual sprinkling with water.
This has been described as the stationary liṅga; now hear about the mobile liṅga.
If, however, one day or more has elapsed, one should then perform twice the worship;
after thirty days have passed, one should then cause the ceremonial bathing (snapana) to be performed.
O Brahmin! After six months, perform the sprinkling with water;
however, if the daily fire-sacrifice has been neglected, it is said that the *homa* must be performed twice as much. (41)
If the food offering (naivedya) is deficient, one should offer double the amount;
if the retinue is omitted, one should establish the members of the retinue.
Having offered a hundred oblations with that mantra, one should then perform the ceremonial bathing;
in the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), which is devoid of lamps, one should cause the auspicious day (puṇyāha) ceremony to be performed there.
One should join the lamp there with the temple by means of the mantra;
however, if the lamp is absent during the daily festival, one should perform a Puṇyāha ceremony there.
Having again applied the lamp, perform the perpetual festival once more;
however, if it is devoid of pure dance, one should cause the ceremonial bathing (snapana) to be performed there.
During a perpetual festival, if the food-liṅga (annaliṅga) has fallen or become deficient,
one should then perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma) and prepare a new food-liṅga.

The ceremonial bathing (snapana) should be performed there, and thereafter listen to the rules for the daily festival (nityotsava). Even if the image should fall, one should have the ceremonial bathing performed there.
If it is broken or cracked,
having performed the sprinkling with water, afterwards perform the daily festival.
In the absence of musical instruments at that time, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations to Śiva;
likewise, if a linga or even an image has been touched by dogs, crows, or similar creatures.
Having sprinkled [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma).
At a time when there is no festival, one should perform a ceremonial bath (snapana) there.
If the *balikarma* (offering of oblations) is omitted on the day of the ritual bath, one should likewise perform it;
however, if the *bali* is omitted for five days, one should cause the *diśāhoma* (oblation to the quarters) to be performed. || 51 ||
Furthermore, one should perform the ritual sequence for the bali offering according to the previously stated procedure;
however, if the materials for the bali are lacking, one should employ double the amount.
O best of Brahmins, at the time of circumambulating the village, if an auspicious mark or even a trident should fall,
the preceptor [should act] with the Astra-mantra.
Having recited the Śiva-mantra one hundred and eight times, perform circumambulation thereafter;
likewise, do so for each individual trident, even if it is broken or devoid of its limbs.
Having consecrated it with a blade of darbha grass, one should sprinkle it while reciting the Astra-mantra;
having invoked the Trident right there, one should perform the offering of the remaining oblation.
O Brahmin, wash it as before; perform the sprinkling with water, whether the image is of one of the eight auspicious forms or is devoid of weapons.
One should offer oblations separately one hundred and eight times with each respective mantra;
then, having again assumed that [deity's] form, one should sprinkle [it] according to the previous sequence.
If the banner has fallen, broken, been cut, or even lost,
one should perform a ritual ablution there and have a sacrifice to Caṇḍa performed.
The ritual of oblation (homa) to the image must be performed, and one should raise the banner in due order;
however, if the Caṇḍayāga is omitted, one should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) there instead.
If the bathing is deficient in that way, the bathing should be performed twice;
however, if the sacrificial hall is lacking, one should then perform a *śānti*-oblation.
If that place is devoid of a lamp, one should perform a *śānti* oblation;
having placed a lamp in that very spot, it is for the pacification of that defect. (61)
O Brahmin! One should perform the oblation twice as much, especially when there is a deficiency of fuel-sticks, or likewise when it is devoid of scents and flowers, or similarly devoid of incense.
One should cause a Puṇyāha ceremony to be performed there and then cause double the [usual] gifts to be given;
O best of Brahmins, if negligence or the occurrence of disease should happen to the preceptor, [the following should be done].
The wise man should have the ritual bathing performed by others who have arisen from negligence;
however, he should have it performed by his son, grandson, or the like, or indeed by his disciple.
If the bull in front [of the image] is deficient, one should perform a pacifying homa;
