having stationed the bull there, one should establish it according to the prescribed rite.
If the outer pedestal (pīṭha) is missing, one should perform the ceremonial bathing there;
one should have the artisan construct the pedestal and install it with the proper characteristics.
If the worship of the retinue is deficient, one should then perform a *puṇyāha* ceremony;
and for the sake of pacifying that defect, one should commence the worship again.
Moreover, if an occasional rite (naimittika) has been omitted, an interruption may occur here;
one should have the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana) performed there and begin the ritual action once again. || 68 ||
If the festival of the day is lacking, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma);
one should perform a ceremonial bath there and then conduct the festival of the day once again.
If the new moon day (amāvāsyā) is missing, one should perform the ritual bathing there;
then one should perform the pacifying oblation (śāntihoma), and perform [the rite] again on the new moon day.
p.
215) But if the monthly festival has been omitted, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma);
one should perform a ritual ablution there and then conduct the monthly festival once again. || 71 ||
If the transference and bathing are deficient, one should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma);
there, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited and perform the bathing once again.
If an anthill is seen either in a palace or within its inner chamber,
then one should dig it up with the Astra-mantra and subsequently fill it back in with earth from other anthills.
Then one should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) and have a ceremonial bath (snapana) conducted there,
either in the enclosure wall, in a pavilion, or near the temple (prāsāda).
The fourteenth staff-mark belongs to the *dhāman*, and for women, it occurs upon the arrival of their season;
at that time, one should offer the five oblations and then sprinkle it accordingly.
One should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made there, and then have the ritual bathing performed;
O best of Brahmins, the offering to the spirits (bhūtabali) should then be without a lamp.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited, one should again apply the lamp;
however, if the fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa) is lacking, one should perform a propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma).
As before, one should install the fire for the pacification of those defects,
whether during the consecration involving the fire-oblation, or during the sprinkling ceremony, or even during a festival.
In all other rites, the twice-born who is well-prepared for initiation should then perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) and have a ceremonial bath (snapana) conducted there.
Furthermore, one should cause her who is engaged in initiation to perform all the rites; [this applies to] women born in families of the three twice-born castes during their menstrual period. 80.
Whether it be a *liṅga* or a *kautuka*, if conception occurs nearby, it is purified by the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) at the enclosure wall and the city gate. (81)
One should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited there and perform a fire-oblation for peace (*śāntihoma*);
furthermore, a ceremonial bath (*snapana*) should be performed there for the pacification of that defect.
Or even if one should touch it, O best of Brahmins, perform a sprinkling with water!
For that which is deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, and deficient in materials during the appointed time— || 83 ||
One should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited there, and perform [the rite] again in the same manner.
If the side-dishes and so forth are interrupted, one should then cause the declaration of an auspicious day to be recited.
Furthermore, one should provide a snack (upadaṃśa) and likewise clothing;
however, if the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā) has been omitted, one should then have the Puṇyāha recitation performed.
Furthermore, worship should be performed according to the previously mentioned procedure;
however, in the absence of pure dance, one should perform the supreme ritual ablution (snāpana). || 86 ||
At that time, when the courtesan has fallen, a ritual bathing should take place;
then one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) and have a pure dance performed.
Whether in a palace, or within a courtyard, or likewise in a pavilion, or among the circle of courtesans and servants—if [the rite] should occur while being seen by dust; 88.
One should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made there, and then have the ceremonial bathing performed.
Thereafter, one should perform the oblation for the quarters (diśāhoma) and present the great sacrificial offering (mahāhavis). || 89 ||
If a corpse is produced even outside the enclosure,
one should cause an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be performed there and have a propitiatory fire-oblation (*śāntihoma*) performed.
p. 217) This expiation has been proclaimed; now hear the milk-bath. 90½.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, the "Rite of Expiation," in the Vīratantra. 52.
The Grandfather.
O Lord! What are the various procedures here, and what is the supreme rite for the milk-bath? You ought to explain all of this to me in brief.
The Lord.
I shall declare all of that in its entirety; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
[It concerns] times of drought and the like, and the outbreak of fever and pestilence.
When a great disease has arisen, likewise at the commencement of war,
and at a time of oppression by enemies, a milk-bath is prescribed.
The milk of a tawny cow is the best, that of a white cow is middling, and that of a red cow is declared to be the lowest; the most excellent preceptor should bathe [the deity] with it.
Nandā, Bhadrā, Surabhi, Suśīlā, and Sumanas—these five cows were born out of a desire to bestow grace upon the world. || 5 ||
The preceptor, having collected the milk from those born within their respective groups, performs the milk-bath, which is declared to be of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
One should bathe [the image] with lukewarm milk while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra;
this is designated as the lowest [rite], so now hear about the middling one.
Having taken the milk of all [the cows], O Brahmin, one should fill a single vessel with it;
then, in front of Śiva, one should smear the ground with cow dung.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice grains, one should then have the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited;
thereafter, the laying out of the lines (sūtrapāta) should be performed using a thread as prescribed in the scriptures.
The best of instructors should lay down fourteen threads facing eastward, and likewise a thread with its tip pointing north.
Having established nine squares in the center, one should omit one square outside of that;
furthermore, one should reduce the number of squares by one on the outermost enclosure.
And for the sake of the door, one should reduce one square in each of the four directions;
then, one should scatter *śāli* rice upon that central square.
Having placed half a measure of śāli rice, one should place half a measure of sesame seeds;
one should then strew it with darbha grass and sprinkle it while reciting the heart mantra.
He should cause jars that are very firm, stainless, and filled to the brim with an *āḍhaka* measure to be taken up; then he should wrap them with that thread.
One should wash [the vessel] with water and sprinkle it with the Īśāna-mantra;
in the central Śiva-vessel, one should fill it with milk alone.
One should fill the *vardhanī* vessel on his left with milk alone;
then, with the mantra consisting of the seed-syllable of Śiva, one should install the *śivakumbha*.
The best of preceptors should place [the vessel] upon the *vardhanī* with the seed-syllable of Gaurī;
it should be provided with cloth, gold, a tuft of grass (*kūrca*), and a lid.
Having worshipped with incense, flowers, and so forth, one should begin the installation;
and in the first enclosure, one should place eight jars. (18)
In the second enclosure, one should place twenty jars;
and in the third enclosure, one should place thirty-six jars.
In the fourth enclosure, there should be forty-four [pots];
one should fill them with milk, provided they are complete, covered with cloth, and fitted with lids.
Now listen as I describe specifically how one should install the deities:
in the first enclosure, one should install the Vidyeśvaras.
In the second enclosure, Vighneśa is the deity there;
and in the third enclosure, Brahmā is the presiding deity there.
One should present offerings of perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps;
thereafter, a fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed, consisting of nine, five, or even one oblation.
Having prepared either a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila), whether square or circular,
one should perform the rite of invoking the mouth of the fire according to the previously mentioned sequence.
Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, mustard seeds,
barley, sesame seeds, mung beans, and black gram— these are said here to be the nine substances.

Having offered the fuel-sticks with the Īśāna mantra, the clarified butter with the Puruṣa mantra, the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Aghora mantra, and indeed the parched grains (lāja) with the Vāma mantra; || 26 ||
One should offer mustard seeds with the *sadyojāta* mantra, barley grains with the *hṛdaya* mantra, sesame seeds indeed with the *śiras* mantra, and mung beans accompanied by the *śikhā* mantra. (27)
Having offered a māṣa with the eye-mantra, one then performs the oblation in due order—
either one hundred and eight times, or fifty, or twenty-five. (28)
The number of oblations is thus declared; at the end of each substance, one should offer the Vyāhṛtis. Immediately thereafter, one should perform the oblation with the mantra "ghṛtam ikṣe."
Having offered the final oblation with the mantra "yadasya," one should then perform the *pūrṇāhuti*.
There, one should worship the preceptor (*ācārya*) and thereafter worship the ritual materials (*padārtha*).
Immediately thereafter, one should perform the oblation with the Prāsāda mantra;
then, one should bathe the Vardhanī vessel with the Gaurī-bīja mantra.
One should also bathe the remaining jars in due order;
one should perform the bathing with fifty or twenty-five [verses] as prescribed for the ritual bath.
Then, one should bathe the jar according to this aforementioned rite;
likewise, a bath with curd and a bath with ghee should be performed.
The consecration with milk has thus been described; now hear the characteristics of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas). 33½.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, the Ritual for the Milk Consecration, in the Vīra-tantra.
The Grandfather.
Having first prostrated before the God of gods, the Grandfather (Brahmā) inquired:
"O Lord! What are the characteristics of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas)? Tell me all of that."
The Lord.
O Lotus-seated One! Listen now to the characteristics of these [deities], as well as their weapons, the eight auspicious symbols, and the ritual procedure for the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles. (2)
The fire of the machine [yantra] with its fuel-offerings is said to be the burning of the hut;
that which burns everything in its entirety is designated here as the sacrificial pit [kuṇḍa].

During the time of festivals such as the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), likewise during the sprinkling with water, during the ritual bathing, at the time of initiation (dīkṣā), and during the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) and other rites; || 4 ||

During such times as these, one should prepare the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). One should lay down three lines: one pointing eastward and likewise one pointing northward, measuring exactly one cubit in length and provided with the standard measurement of finger-breadths (mātrāṅgula).
One should fashion a square and contemplate it in due order;
all sacrificial pits, beginning with the yoni-shaped, are produced from the square.
In the east, it should be square; in the southeast, like an aśvattha leaf;
in the south, a half-moon; and in the southwest, a triangle.
In the west (Vāruṇī) it is circular, in the northwest (Vāyavyā) it has five corners;
in the north (Saumyā) it has seven corners, and in the northeast (Aiśānī) it has eight corners.
In this very manner, one should then fashion the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in due order;
thereafter, one should place the portion released from the ear-line (karṇasūtra) in the west.
Using that measurement, the best of preceptors should specifically rotate [the compass] to the end of the corner, and cause a circle to be drawn on the south and north sides.
One should divide the perimeter into seven parts and place one part for Indra;
then the best of teachers should lay down the thread there starting from the corner. (12)
In this very manner, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should gradually take the shape of a womb (yoni);
the best of the twice-born should cause the diagonal of the square to be taken up.
Then, having set aside half of the field, one should divide the remainder into three parts;
one part should be placed in the east, and from the center, one should rotate [the cord] toward the east and so forth.
Having thus made it circular, half of that is called the bow (dhanu).
The field is divided into eight parts, and one part is on the south.
O best of Brahmins, one should lay down a cord according to that measurement, placing one part toward the north and one part toward the east.
In this very manner, the triangle is described in due order;
one should first lay out the field divided into seven parts, one by one.
Therefore, having taken the center and drawn a circle, the preceptor should divide half the diameter into eight parts and join them with that half-diameter.
By that measurement, one indeed constructs the five corners starting from the east;
the field shall consist of eight parts, and one should first lay down one part in the east.
Therefore, having taken the center, one indeed constructs a circular pit (kuṇḍa);
one should divide the field into thirty-two parts and join [the cord] with half of the field.

It is said that the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is seven-cornered; one should then arrange it starting from the east. The field is divided into eight parts, and from the southern half-part [the measurement proceeds].
The most excellent of teachers should then place half a portion in the northern part;
having taken the center from that, he should likewise form a hexagon. (22)
Two each in the east and the west are here called the ears;
one each in the south and the north is designated as the corner. || 23 ||
The best of teachers should construct a circular pit as before;
having made it equal to eight petals, it is here called a lotus-pit (padmakuṇḍa).
The preceptor, having thus divided the field into twenty-four parts,
should specifically arrange them within [the central area] in the four directions.
Having taken the karṇa from the middle, one should mark it in the four directions;
taking the koṇaka as the mark, this pertains to the interior.
The preceptor should construct an eight-cornered [altar] according to the measurement of the cord;
or else, the preceptor may construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in another manner.
As many-sided as the pedestal (pīṭha) may be, so many-sided should the fire-pit (kuṇḍala) be;
the girdle (mekhalā) should also be made with its width and height equal to that [of the pit].
O Brahmin, the upper girdle (mekhalā) is said here to be four finger-breadths high, the middle three finger-breadths, and the lower two finger-breadths. (29)
The wise preceptor should fashion the *yoni* above the girdle;
its width should be four finger-breadths and its length seven finger-breadths.
One should dig into the earth a pit one cubit deep and as wide at the base, shaped like an elephant or a camel, with a rim and a stalk-like cord. (31)
One should fashion it with depressions and elevations like the surface of a mirror;
then, having fashioned a navel in the center, there should be a pedestal of one finger-breadth.
The characteristics of the sacrificial pits have been declared; now hear the characteristics of the weapons:
the thunderbolt, the spear, the staff, the sword, the noose, and likewise the goad. (33)
The mace, the trident, the discus, and the lotus—these constitute the ten weapons.
They may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even from a sacrificial tree.
One should fashion an unsurpassed weapon from the wood of the Plakṣa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, Vaṭa, or Khadira, or even one made of Vikaṅkata.
One should make the length thirty-two finger-breadths according to the measurement of one's own fingers;
the width is six finger-breadths, and its thickness is said to be half of that.
Having fashioned a trident measuring six finger-breadths, the preceptor should make the lotus straight in the middle, while making it curved on both sides on the outside.
Below that, one should have a fillet (gaṇḍikā) made one finger-breadth high;
below that, one should make another fillet, having it made half a finger-breadth [in height]. || 38 ||
One should fashion the staff with a circumference of six finger-breadths at its middle;
one should make a knob (gaṇḍikā) at the center measuring two finger-breadths.
Above that and below that, form [the shape] with two fingers;
in this very same sequence, the tips of the two [fingers] should be like a trident.
Thus the vajra has been fully described; now the characteristics of the śakti are stated:
it should be four finger-breadths in width and long, just as before. (41)
O best of Brahmins, the tip of the two [prongs] should be like the middle leaf of a trident;
its height shall be six finger-breadths, and the *gaṇḍikā* shall be one finger-breadth.
One should make the central joint exactly two finger-breadths [in width];
both above and below that, it should likewise be made with two finger-breadths.
A *gaṇḍikā* should be made there; the characteristics of the *śakti* are now described.
It has a blade like a thunderbolt (*vajra*), and above that is a *gaṇḍikā* measuring one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
The width of the staff itself should especially be eight finger-breadths;
the height of the jar should be six finger-breadths, and below that, the neck (gaṇḍikā) should be one finger-breadth.
A staff measuring six finger-breadths is said here to be suitable for a staff;
it should be long as before, and likewise curved in the middle.
The wise one should gradually make it slender from the curve upwards;
having fashioned a flat base at the root, its width should be six finger-breadths.
Above that, one should then have a circular plank made;
having made that plank long, one should draw a noose in its center.
I shall now describe the dimensions of the goad in due order:
having made its length as before, one should then fashion a needle-point at its tip.
Six finger-breadths from the front and below, one should [draw] a circle with a needle;
its length shall be four finger-breadths, and its circumference one finger-breadth.
In this manner, the hook (aṅkuśa) is curved, and its handle is six finger-breadths long;
having fashioned the mace (gadā) like the staff, one should cause a needle-point to be made at its tip.
Having fashioned a trident as before, with three petals and joined by a *pālikā*,
one should then place a bull upon the four-cornered *pālikā*. (52)
Thus the trident has been fully described; now the characteristics of the wheel are being stated.
Here, the measurement of the wheel is said to be circular in form, just like that of the trident. (53)
Endowed with twelve spokes and joined with a hub in the center—thus the wheel has been fully described; now listen to the lotus as well.
The bud (mukula) is said to be eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas), and below that, the knob (gaṇḍikā) is one finger-breadth;
O best of Brahmins, the handle-receptacle (daṇḍanāha) here is said to be five finger-breadths.
Thus the lotus has been fully described; it is called one of the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala).
It should be sixteen finger-breadths in length and eight finger-breadths in width.
Below that, one should indeed fashion a lotus six finger-breadths in size,
as well as a mirror, a full water-pot, a bull, and a pair of chowries.
One should place the Śrīvatsa, the Svastika, the conch, the lamp, and the eight auspicious objects of the gods in the middle of the wooden plank; this is called the Aṣṭamaṅgala.
Having had it drawn with the correct colors by an artisan, one should then have it marked with a length of twenty-six finger-breadths and a width of ten finger-breadths.
One should have that form, joined with a seat, inscribed with the eight auspicious signs (aṣṭamaṅgala).
I shall now describe the characteristics of the *sruva* ladle: it should be twenty-four finger-breadths [in length].
Thus, the length is declared to be six finger-breadths and the circumference likewise;
the ear is said to be three finger-breadths in measure—this worshipful measurement shall be inexhaustible.

O best of Brahmins, having had it engraved, I myself [shall perform the rite]; and having fashioned the sacrificial offering (bali) with six fingers [in length], the characteristics of the *sruva* ladle are now described. (62)
Now I shall describe the characteristics of the *sruk* (ladle); various types will be explained by me.
It should be thirty-six finger-breadths in length and eight finger-breadths in width.
One should have the height made six finger-breadths and the plank likewise;
the tip should be one-third [of that], and its length seven finger-breadths.
Having gradually brought about its destruction, being free from depressions and elevations,
and with a width of one *rasāṅgula*, he, being composed, [should fashion] the ear as well.
The height of the *karṇa* (ear) should be two finger-breadths, and below that there should be a plank (*phalakā*).
The altar (*vedi*) should be eight finger-breadths [in height], and its width should be exactly that much as well.
Outside the altar, all around, with a width of half a finger, one should likewise provide a sacrificial offering (bali) four fingers wide in the middle. || 67 ||
On all sides, outside the lip, there should be a band of half a finger-breadth;
between the two bands, there should be a depression of two barley-corns.
The guide, having made a depression four finger-breadths deep,
should dig from the opening of the pit down to its mouth according to the measurement of the little finger.
It should have the appearance of the back of a lotus, be provided with a lotus below,
resemble the shape of an elephant's or camel's lip, and take the form of the back of a fish.
The *gaṇḍikā* should indeed be made; it is said to be three finger-breadths [in width].
Below that is the outer *gaṇḍikā*; now hear about the *gaṇḍikā* below that. (71)
The staff shall be six finger-breadths in circumference, and at the base of the staff there should be a jar;
having fashioned the jar with a measurement of two finger-breadths, the preceptor [should proceed]. (72)
The characteristics of the sacrificial ladle (*sruc*) have been declared; now hear concerning the arches (*toraṇa*).
The height of the best arch is five cubits in measure. (73)
A height of four cubits is declared to be middling, while that less by one palm is inferior; the width should be half the height, and one should likewise arrange the wooden planks.
Above that, the best of preceptors should place two finger-breadths [of space];
thus the archway (toraṇa) is described. Now listen to the description of the garland of darbha grass.
The best [cord] is made with seven darbha grasses, the middling is said to be with five, and the lowest with three darbhas; at its tip, a string is prescribed.
The wise man should let down his hand and have garlands of darbha grass prepared;
I shall now describe the characteristics of the enclosing sticks (paridhi): they should be straight, free from blemishes, and auspicious.
There should be three enclosing rings (paridhis), each thirty-two finger-breadths in length;
one should surround [the fire] thrice with darbha grass, each [strand] thirty-six finger-breadths in length.

One should tie [the grass] clockwise with a measurement of four finger-breadths; one should prepare four such seats. Now listen to [the description of] the vessel for clarified butter and the other implements.
The vessel for clarified butter (ājyasthālī), the praṇītā vessel, and likewise the prokṣaṇī vessel—
each should have a width of six finger-breadths and a height of two finger-breadths.
I shall describe the characteristics of the sacrificial fuel (samidh): it should be twelve finger-breadths in length;
the clarified butter (ājya) should fill the offering-spoon (sruva), which is one cubit in measure.
Below that and above that, [one should offer] sesame seeds and so forth in the measure of a shell (śukti);
food in the measure of an axle (akṣa), and indeed molasses in that same measure. (82)
The oblation of liquid substances is offered with the *sruva* ladle, while other substances are offered by hand;
furthermore, a small vessel (*sthalikā*) should be made measuring exactly one cubit in size. || 83 ||
Below that and above that,
the best of preceptors should construct the height of the pedestal and the three-legged stand according to his means.

I shall describe the characteristics of the *kūrca* (grass-bundles): the lowest is made with three *darbha* blades, the middle with five *darbha* blades, and the highest with seven *darbha* blades. (85)
It should be joined with a clockwise twist and knotted at its tip; thus the characteristic of the *kūrca* has been declared. Now hear the characteristics of the cloths. || 86 ||
The lowest [size] should be eight cubits, the middle ten cubits, and the highest is declared to be twelve; the width is five tālas.
The characteristics of the cloth have already been described; now hear the rule for the canopy:
it should be six or seven *tālas* in length and eight *tālas* in width.

The characteristics of the canopy have been declared in this very sequence; the characteristics of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) have also been declared. Now, listen to the fire-offering for pacification (śāntihoma).
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter in the Vīratantra, concerning the rules for the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and other elements.
O God! How is the śānti-homa performed? O Lord! How is the diśā-homa performed?
O Śambhu! How is the mūrti-homa performed? Tell me, O Supreme Lord! || 1 ||
The Lord.
I shall describe the peace-offering (śānti-homa); listen, O Lotus-seated One!
It may be performed either in the previously mentioned pavilion or in the fire-sanctuary.
One should cause the oblation to be offered in fire-pits or even upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
one should have the fire-pit made either square or circular.
Equipped with three girdles, or else with a single girdle;
having thus resolved upon that very [site], it is made like the surface of a mirror.
Purification, washing, drying, and likewise digestion—
having churned and taken [the essence], it is established by means of the heart.
One should offer wood with the head-mantra and kindle it with the Astra mantra;
having performed the ritual attendance (upasthāna) and the strewing of grass (paristaraṇa) with the head-mantra as well.
One should spread [the grass] with ten blades of darbha in the east,
and likewise spread it in the south, the west, and the north.
Having placed the enclosing sticks (paridhi) in the south, one should place them in the west and the north;
then the preparation of the vessels is performed, and subsequently the oblation is offered in due order.
Having offered fuel-sticks with the Pañcabrahma mantras, clarified butter with the six ancillary mantras (ṣaḍaṅga),
and the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Aghora mantra, one should offer a hundred oblations.
Then, one should offer oblations specifically for the destruction of the substance; this is known as the *śānti-homa*. Now hear about the *diśā-homa* (the offering to the directions).
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, the ritual for the propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*), in the Vīratantra.
Whatever fault may remain unmentioned is pacified by the *śānti* oblation.
O Four-faced One! Listen as I shall now explain the *diśāhoma*. (1)
One should cause the directional fire-offering (diśāhoma) to be performed in the four directions of the palace,
having prepared the mouth of the fire according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Then, O best of Brahmins, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit;
it should be square in the eastern direction among the four directions of the temple.
In the south, it should be shaped like a half-moon; in the west, it should be circular;
and in the north, it should be a lotus-shaped pit, or else a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
A Plakṣa tree in the east, an Udumbara in the south, an Aśvattha in the west, and a Vaṭa in the northern direction. || 5 ||
In this manner, the preceptor likewise offers oblations with such fuel-sticks (samidh),
either a thousand, half of that, or one hundred and eight.
One should offer a hundred oblations starting from Sadyojāta and ending with Īśāna;
one should likewise offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter and sacrificial porridge (caru). || 7 ||
One hundred oblations of rice mixed with sesame seeds should be offered with the Īśāna mantra;
then, at the end of each batch of materials, one should offer an oblation with the Vyāhṛtis.
This is declared to be the Diśāhoma; now hear about the Mūrtihoma.
Having constructed a pavilion in front of Śiva, prepare a sacrificial altar (sthaṇḍila) with rice grains.
One should place the water-pot in the center, together with its cord, its lid, its cloth, its gold, its tuft of kusha grass, and filled with water.
On all sides, one should place eight water-pots and the Eightfold Form (Aṣṭamūrti):
namely, Āditya, Agni, Soma, and Dharaṇī; || 11 ||
One should worship Ākāśa, Vāyu, Varuṇa,
and the sacrificer with perfumes and flowers, starting from the east and extending to the northeast.
O Brahmin, having worshipped with the Pañcabrahma mantra using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should then perform eight oblations in the eight directions outside the water-pots.
The preceptor, together with the Yavana, offers one hundred and eight oblations each of fuel sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, and milk, beginning with the Ishana direction.
Thereafter, one should especially install [the deity] there in the primary image (mūlabera);
subsequently, one should present the sacrificial offering (havir) to Śiva Parameṣṭhin.
This is known as the Mūrtihoma; now hear about the Vāstuhoma, which is performed for a temple, a pavilion, and the rite of installing a Liṅga.
O best of Brahmins, one should indeed cause the Vāstuhoma sacrifice to be performed when installing an image, or when constructing an assembly hall, a well, a pond, or a garden.
It should be performed by one who is a primordial Śaiva or by one who has been initiated;
having prepared the site and made a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) either with earth or with sand. || 18 ||
To the east of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should place a water-vortex;
having filled it with pure water, one should cast the oblation (homa) right there.
One should place it in the center with the western and eastern branches;
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should perform the ritual scratching (ullekhana).
Having first drawn three lines facing east and likewise three facing north with the Aghora-weapon mantra, one should then sprinkle them with water while reciting the Puruṣa mantra.
Having deposited the fire within his heart and likewise performed the ritual salutation, he should strew darbha grass around it, strewing them according to the previously mentioned method.
One should prepare the vessels there outside the fire to the north;
having placed the *praṇītā* water-vessel to the north, one should worship Brahmā to the south.
One should satisfy Indra and the other guardians of the world from their respective regions;
then one should perform the heating of the clarified butter according to the previously stated procedure.
The *sruva* ladle should also be taken up, having been consecrated as before;
it should be placed on the south and the north, and one should set down the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) on the north.
Having placed the *aghora* fuel-sticks, perform the sprinkling (pariṣecana) thereafter;
one should offer the middle portion silently, and the *aghora* mantra itself is to be sacrificed.

One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the cardinal directions from Sadyojāta to Īśāna, as well as in the center; having offered the sacrificial porridge (caru), one should offer clarified butter with the mantra "vāstoṣpate" and the sacred ashes.
For the deities of the site (vāstu), the Aghora mantra is indeed offered;
one should perform the oblation with clarified butter alone, starting from Sadyojāta and ending with Īśāna.
The names of the deities of the site (vāstu) are offered with the word "svāhā" at their end; milk-rice mixed with sugar and thoroughly saturated with clarified butter is presented. (29)
Having offered the bali-oblation to the deities of the site (vāstudeva), one should cast the bali-oblation to the world-protectors (lokapāla);
then the Jaya and other oblations, as well as the Rāṣṭrabhṛt oblations, are offered.

Immediately after that, while reciting the *havyavāha* [verse], one should offer oblations with clarified butter (*ājya*) and sacrificial rice (*caru*), using the mantra "Sviṣṭam agne" (O Agni, well-sacrificed). || 31 ||
The Sviṣṭakṛt offering is then made with clarified butter according to the sequence of "yad asya," after which one should perform the sprinkling around and cause the enclosing sticks to be placed.
He should dismiss the Brahmin and then cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given;
having sprinkled [the area] with consecrated water (praṇītodaka), he should recite the Pavamāna hymns.
There, one should honor the preceptor with garments, grain, gold, and so forth;
in particular, one should present a cow with its calf to the preceptor.
If the preceptor is deprived of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), the ritual act becomes fruitless;
for it is said that the ritual is the body, while the fee is called the life-force.
In a ritual devoid of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), it would be lifeless and fruitless;
therefore, one should always honor the preceptor with every effort. (36)
Listen to the rite known as Vāstuhoma, which accomplishes all forms of worship. || 36½ ||
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Vāstu-homa for the Image," in the Vīratantra.
The Grandfather.
Having prostrated before Śiva according to the prescribed rites, the Grandfather (Brahmā) inquired:
"O Lord, tell me all about the complete method of propitiation."
The Lord.
I shall explain all of that in its entirety; listen, O Four-faced One!
Having first performed the ritual bath with water, one should perform the bath with sacred ash.
And in front of the image, one should smear it with cow dung,
having positioned oneself facing either north or east. (3)
Having placed the ritual broom (kūrca) in that very spot, the preceptor sits down;
then, on the left side of that [seat], he should spread darbha grass.
One should arrange the perfume, flowers, incense, and lamp;
then one should arrange the water for the feet, the water for sipping, and the respectful offering (arghya) with the heart-mantra.
The wise preceptor should cover it with *darbha* grass while reciting the *Īśa-mantra*,
and he should place a conch shell in the middle of the three feet.
Then, one should sprinkle [the area] with water using either a bunch of grass or *kuśa* blades;
thereafter, one should perform exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*).
With the thumb and forefinger, accompanied by the syllable *huṃ* and joined with the syllable *phaṭ*,
one should purify the ten directions.
First, with both hands, he should touch [the body] from the beginning of the letter *ka* to the end of the feet;
then the preceptor, having placed the *īśāna* [mantra] on the thumb and likewise on the index finger, [should proceed].
O best of Brahmins, one should place the remaining fingers with the thumb;
having placed Puruṣa on the index finger, one should place Aghora on the middle finger.
One should place Vāmadeva on the ring finger and Sadyojāta on the little finger;
there, one should perform the assignment of the six limbs according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having placed the heart-mantra upon the heart, one should place the head-mantra upon the head;
having placed the crest-mantra upon the crest, one should place the armor-mantra between the breasts.
One should place the *astra* mantra on the region of the hands and the *netra* mantra on the eyes;
having placed the form of Īśāna on the head, one should place Tatpuruṣa on the face. (13)
Having placed Aghora in the heart, one should assign Vāma to the secret organ;
one should place Sadyojāta on the foot, and indeed install it there specifically.
Having placed Brahmā on the head, one should place Īśvara on the forehead;
the wise man should place Viṣṇu on the mouth and the two Aśvins on the ears.
One should place the Pitṛs in the throat and Indra in the heart;
one should place Āditya on the right arm and Soma on the left.
One should place Agni there in the belly, and one should place Yama in the penis;
Varuṇa is placed on the right knee, and on the other [left knee], Vāyu is said [to be placed]. (17)
O best of Brahmins, one should then place the Viśvedevas on two feet;
this placement of the forms of creation is declared to be the Sṛṣṭinyāsa.
O best of Brahmins! The placement of the Sthitimūrti is declared as the Sthitinyāsa, and that of the Saṃhāramūrtis is called the Saṃhāranyāsa.
One should first project the body itself onto the body of the worshipper;
having thus performed the ritual of projection (nyāsa), one should thereafter begin the worship.
And the images should likewise be placed in front, endowed with the characteristics of the pedestal;
their width should be one *tāla*, and their height should be half of that. || 21 ||
It should be provided with three girdles, or else with a single girdle;
the height of the girdle should be made two finger-breadths according to the measurement of the mother-finger (mātrāṅgula).
The entry [of the deity] should likewise be performed as if made within the belly of a mirror;
and for all the images, one should perform the ritual worship upon the pedestal. || 23 ||
Or, O Brahmin, one should worship an image provided with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
An image may be of two kinds: mobile and immobile. (24)
The mobile [liṅga] is said to be made of metal, while the immobile is of four kinds:
[made] of stone, or of clay, or on a wall-painting, or even on a cloth.
Thus the supreme teacher has declared the fourfold immovable [deities]:
those made of stone and those that are images; one should indeed perform the consecration for them.
One should sprinkle clay images, wall paintings, and cloth paintings;
likewise, one should bathe or sprinkle metal images.
Having installed the image in a temple, or on a wall-painting or a cloth-painting,
one should worship it there upon a pedestal, together with its retinue.
One should cause an offering of food (naivedya) to be presented there and perform the daily festival;
listen now to this other matter concerning the mere installation [of the deity]. || 29 ||
Thus, when an image has been installed in the place of the *liṅga*,
one should not perform the installation of a retinue (*parivāra*), nor should one employ the sacred *bilva* tree.
Once the lion and likewise the lotus have been established,
the best of instructors should then arrange the vīrāsana above them.
One should worship that which is joined with the womb-enclosure (garbhāvaraṇa) according to the prescribed rule;
and that which rests upon the partless (niṣkala), accompanied by the seat-enclosure (āsanāvaraṇa).
One should especially worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth,
whether all the images are present or only one of them remains. (33)
In all activities such as bathing and so forth, one should perform them while seated;
seated there, one should especially worship everything in its entirety.
One should contemplate either the *liṅga* or the image in its own true form; one must not conceive of it in any other form, for if it is so conceived, it leads to destruction. (35)
One should dismiss with the heart everything that has remained from the worship;
likewise, one should wash the cloth and the ornaments—this is called purification. (36)

The wise one should invoke [the deity] with the *sadyojāta* mantra and establish [him] with the *vāmadeva* mantra; he should then offer water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), and water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) just as before.
He should then perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with the *pañcabrahma* mantra.
Having given the garment with the Aghora mantra, one should indeed offer the perfume with the Śiras mantra. || 38 ||
One should offer flowers with the Īśāna mantra, or alternatively, one may offer incense;
one should offer the lamp with the Sadyojāta mantra, and one should present the oblation with the Hṛdaya mantra.
One should offer betel-leaf with the head; in this very manner and sequence, one should worship the inner enclosure of the womb according to the previously stated order.
It must be performed by a Śiva-brahmin, and one should not have it done by anyone else;
the mortal who acts in this way is liberated from all sins. (41)
The complete method of worship has been declared; now hear about the installation of Vighneśa.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, the ritual procedure for the complete worship, in the Vīratantra.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim in due order that which is extracted from the Five Brahmas;
it is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru, for otherwise it is not told at all. (1)
O Four-faced One, listen to that which bestows both liberation and worldly enjoyment upon men;
one should extract [the mantras] in their proper order, beginning with Īśa and ending with Sadyojāta.
On a level stretch of ground, free from depressions and elevations,
one should take up the thirteenth wheel together with the fifteenth.
The first syllable has been declared; likewise, the second is now being told.
Then follows the fourth letter of Vāsava (Ka), and after that, the first letter of Śūla (Śa).
The fifth [syllable] of Varuṇa is joined with the interior of the vajra;
the third of Īśāna is joined with that vajra. (5)
That which is the fourth [syllable] of Ananta, joined with Vajra—
having extracted that very same one again, it is either conjoined with the seed-syllable of Agni.
The fourth [day] belongs to Rajanīkā, while the third belongs to Vāsava;
the third belongs to Varuṇa, accompanied by Vāsava.
The fifth [letter] of Varuṇa is joined with the second Vajra.
Puruhūta...
the Grandfather (Pitāmaha).
O Lord of the Gods! How is the installation of Vighneśa performed in this Tantra?
O Blessed One, I wish to hear all of that; you should deign to speak it.
The Lord.
"Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! That which has been requested by you, I shall explain all of it in its entirety; listen, O Lotus-seated One! || 2 ||
Bhūtas, piśācas, rākṣasas, and likewise asuras,
who desire to consume the world's wealth— one should worship these for the sake of warding off obstacles.
Whether in a village, a city, a town, or even a market settlement,
one should have a temple constructed there according to the procedures prescribed in the scriptures.
Having made the ground level, the best of preceptors should then have it ploughed; having recited the *Vyomavyāpin* mantra, he should indeed cause the field to be ploughed.
O best of Brahmins, one should then sow seeds in that place as well;
and when all have ripened in a fortnight, one should offer them to the herds of cows.
One should extract the splinter from there and then fill it with dust;
having made it like the surface of a mirror, one should smear it with cow dung.
Having worshipped the deities of the site, one should perform all rites under the previously mentioned lunar mansion, conjunction, and karana.
The first brick should be prepared, especially during a fixed zodiac sign;
one should then place that first brick on the right side of the door.
Then one should prepare a seat of darbha grass endowed with the proper characteristics,
made either of stone, bricks, wood, or even clay. (10)
And a temple should be constructed, endowed with the proper characteristics;
one should have it made nine cubits, five cubits, or even three cubits in height.
A wise man should have a celestial chariot (vimāna) constructed together with a half-pavilion;
thereafter, the learned one should have a rampart built according to the requirements of the temple (prāsāda).
One should arrange an offering pedestal (balipīṭha) on the four sides of the temple;
know that it is best when five tālas high, and middling when four tālas.
The lowest [type] is said to be three tālas; its width and height are equal.
Having divided it into sixteen parts, the plinth (upāna) shall consist of one part.
The *jagatī* should be one-fourth part, and the *kumbha* is said to be three parts;
with one part one should make the *paṭṭikā*, and the neck (*grīvā*) likewise consists of three portions.
One should make the fillet with two parts and have the fillet-molding made with one part;
the height of the pedestal should be four parts, and one should fashion a lotus upon it.
I shall describe the images; listen, O Lotus-Seated One!
That made of metal is said to be the best, while that made of stone is middling. (17)
An auspicious image made of inferior wood or clay [brings worldly success];
one made of gold brings good fortune, while silver is for the seeker of liberation.
One desiring a son should use copper; iron is for malevolent rites (abhicāra).
It may also be made of movable metal, or of gems, or even of wood. || 19 ||
242) (a) One should perform the consecration again according to the procedure taught in the scriptures.
That which has been installed for the sake of others is [called] *parārtha*; otherwise, it is said to be *atyārtha*. || 20 ||
And Bṛhodara, Vighneśa, Nāyaka, and Vīra, as well as Gajānana, Gajakarṇa, and Lambodara. || 21 ||
O best of Brahmins, the eight forms are proclaimed as being dear to those who consume [the offerings];
and for each of these forms, [the mantra] is joined with the first letter of its own name. (22)
That which is joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*, preceded by the *praṇava*, is spoken of here;
I shall now describe its *yantra*, which wards off all that is inauspicious. (23)
Having written [the mantra] on birch bark or palm leaves with an auspicious mineral substance prescribed for protection,
one should draw an eight-petaled lotus complete with filaments and pericarp.
With a concentrated mind, one should inscribe the root mantra in the center of the pericarp;
the wise practitioner should then place the syllables of the eight forms upon the eight petals.
One should worship a round pill made of lac, encased in gold,
especially with the root mantra, and perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with it.
Thereafter, one should wear the pill either on the neck or on the hand;
for this indeed removes all diseases, just as a lion [overcomes] an elephant it has gazed upon. (27)
I have declared the extraction of the mantras; now hear the ritual procedure for consecration.
[It should be performed] under the asterisms of Rohiṇī, Āditya (Pūrvaphalgunī), Puṣya, Hasta, Pūṣan (Revatī), and the three Uttarās.
Svātī is declared for installation, as is the constellation Jyeṣṭhā;
it should be performed in a fixed zodiac sign or even in a dual sign. (29)
(b) Four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with a crown and a basket-shaped head-ornament,
whether seated, standing, or even mounted upon a vehicle. (1)
The dance, however, is of the nature of an exposition; it is adorned with all ornaments, endowed with various jewels, and features a sacred thread made of serpents.
Adorned with small bells and anklets, and endowed with all the auspicious marks,
one should fashion an image five tālas in height and have it made beautiful.
Having divided [the height] into five parts, one should make the upper lip half a part, the lower lip three parts, and the height of the feet two parts; thus one should fashion an excellent image.
In his right hand, he holds a goad, while his left hand holds his own tusk;
in his left [other] hand he holds a noose, and in his right [other] hand an *akṣasūtra*.
A ṭaṅka [emblem] should be in the left hand, and he should be seated upon a lotus;
the wise man should have an image fashioned endowed with such characteristics.
At the root of the white Arka tree, one should perform the ritual for the sake of a specific objective;
by means of the six-armed [form] alone, one shall conquer the wheels of enemies.
Having divided the interior space (garbha) into nine parts, the best [sanctum] shall consist of five parts;
the middling, of four parts; and the lowest, of three parts.
Thereafter, one should have an image made measuring two parts or one part;
I shall now describe the sequence of the number of *tālas*, beginning with what is called the inferior *tāla*.
The medium [size] is said to be two tālas, and the superior should be three tālas;
thereafter, the artisan should have it constructed according to the desire of the patron.
I shall proclaim the extraction of the mantra; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
It bestows desires, grants the fruit of liberation, and destroys all sins. (11)
When the ascendant is auspicious, at a favorable moment, and especially under a propitious lunar mansion,
the wise man, having performed a pure bath and attained purification, should then proceed.
Having invoked the Guru right there, one should worship him especially;
one should then inscribe the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'.
Uttering the seed-syllable of Vināyaka in their midst,
[one should place] the third of the second group and the fourth of the first group.
O Lotus-born One, this root mantra of Vighneśvara is said to consist of the third group of seven syllables, conjoined with the Bindu and the Nāda. 15.
The *brahman* is declared to be short, while the limbs of the *ahaṃ* are said to be long.
243) All planets situated in the eighth house are indeed not desired for consecrations.
Regarding the installation of these, it has been stated that it should be done in accordance with one's means. || 20 ||
Then, one should have an image fashioned, endowed with the characteristics previously described;
one should construct a square pavilion in front of the temple.
It should be three, five, six, seven, eight, or nine cubits [in width];
it is provided with sixteen pillars, and its height is according to the measurement of the row.
The seat should be made of khadira wood, or even of jātīstambaka;
likewise, the bamboo staff should be straight and free from blemishes.
The wise one should cause pillars to be erected according to the sequence previously described for the water-shed (prapā).
He should construct an altar in the center; it is said that a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be made all around it.
In the center of the pavilion, one should cause the deposition of jewels to be performed;
having placed a diamond in the east, one should place coral in the southeast.
Having placed an emerald in the south, one should set a pearl in the southwest;
a ruby in the west, and lapis lazuli in the northwest. (36)
One should place an indranīla gem in the north and crystal in the northeast;
one should especially place a māṇikya gem in the center.
But even if gems are not obtained, one should then place gold there;
then, having joined the deity with the heart-mantra, one should proceed.
One should have it well-anointed with oil there and then worship the artisan;
this very procedure should be performed, especially for those made of metal. (39)
But for others, during the installation and so forth, the wise one should perform the ritual placement;
O Lotus-seated One, listen as I describe the opening of the eyes and the consecration! (40)
On a day endowed with an auspicious muhūrta and a favorable asterism, and joined by the two eyes [of the sun and moon],
one should perform the opening of the eyes in the previously described auspicious pavilion.
Then, having smeared the sacrificial ground with cow dung,
prepare it with eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice and half as much of husked rice.
Having scattered [the offerings], one should spread out [the ground] with a new cloth and with *darbha* grass;
having placed the image right there, facing either eastward or northward.
Then the instructor should cover the image with a new cloth;
he should place eight water-filled jars all around it.
Then, one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and incense, along with heart-mantras, as they are provided with garments, accompanied by gold, and endowed with the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti).
One should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) beginning with Indra and ending with Īśāna;
thereafter, the preceptor should perform the eye-consecration oblation (akṣihoma) using clarified butter alone.
Having conceived of Agni as the mouth, one offers oblations with the Netra-mantra;
having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should then perform the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having drawn the two eyes with a golden needle together with the artisans,
the preceptor shall draw a lotus-line and, in its center, a black circle.
Having drawn a circle of light (jyotirmaṇḍala) accompanied by the eye-mantra,
one should then place honey and clarified butter preceded by gold.
One should place honey in a copper vessel or a bronze one;
then, with the mantra "madhuvātā," one should satisfy [the deity] with that honey. || 50 ||
One should offer clarified butter with the mantra "ghṛtam ikṣa," and likewise satisfy [the deity] with ghee;
one should present a cow with her calf while reciting the mantra "gaṇānām."
Then, having uttered the Brahma-mantra, he should show it to the Brāhmaṇas;
there, the Brāhmaṇas should sprinkle it with water containing unbroken rice grains and Kuśa grass.
Having drawn aside the concealed cloth, one should show it to all the people;
O Brahmin, one should sprinkle the water-pots while joined with the Pañcabrahma mantra.
It was accompanied by song and instrumental music, along with the sounds of lutes and flutes;
it was joined with singing and dancing, and filled with shouts of "Victory! (Jaya).
Then, having lifted it up and performed purification, the preceptor [should bathe it] with the five types of earth, the five products of the cow, and the five limbs [of the deity].

There, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited; then, having placed the image with devotion upon a chariot or a palanquin, one should sprinkle it with water using the *pavamāna* hymns.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village, one should cause the image to dwell in water;
then, one should bathe the image with the five products of the cow while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra.

O best of Brahmins, having wrapped it in a new cloth and joined it with the *kūrca* and the *astra-mantra*, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) in water while reciting the root mantra.
Having constructed a water-shed provided with four pillars, the preceptor should place eight jars all around, accompanied by the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras).
One should especially place [the images] together with garments and gold,
for one night, three nights, or even five nights. (60)
On the preceding day, the preceptor, having performed purification and having emerged from the water, should perform the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsana), equipped with all ornaments.
Then, having thoroughly mixed fragrant substances, the preceptor should smear the image,
wrap it in a new cloth, and [consecrate it] with the root mantra.
O Brahmin! One should place eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice in the middle of the altar;
having placed half that amount of *taṇḍula* rice, one should then place half that amount of sesame seeds.
One should spread darbha grass and prepare five types of beds:
those made of eggs, those made of hair, those made of wool, and likewise those made of leather.
The best of those who know the ritual procedures should fashion [the deity] joined with the Lotus-born;
upon that, he should place the seed-syllable accompanied by the *kūrca* mantra. (65)
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, according to the mantra of the heart,
one should place eight jars endowed with [the deity's] forms all around.
O best of Brahmins, one should install Bṛhodara and the others according to their respective names,
provided with garments, covers, gold, and sacrificial grass-bundles (kūrca).
The preceptor should place the principal water-pot between Īśāna and Indra;
having installed Vighneśa there with the root mantra.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should present milk-rice (pāyasa) as an oblation;
furthermore, one should first install the pitchers representing the world-protectors (lokapālas).
p. 247) Thereafter, the fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed, either nine or five times.
One should cause all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) to be made either circular or square. || 70 ||
Between Īśāna and Indra, the principal fire is ordained;
specifically, the Plakṣa, Aśvattha, Nyagrodha, and Bilva [trees] are to be used. (71)
O best of Brahmins, one should offer oblations into the nine sacrificial pits using wood from the Udumbara, Śamī, Apāmārga, Khadira, and Pālāśa trees.
One should perform the fire-oblation in five sacrificial pits located in the four directions and in the northeast;
however, if none of these are available, it may be performed using palāśa wood fuel.

The most excellent preceptor should offer into the fire oblations consisting of sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, sesame seeds, black gram, barley, as well as plantain fruit. (74)
Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, and likewise Tatpuruṣa, as well as the Heart and the Head, are offered with the Śikhā-mantra. (75)
One should offer oblations numbering one hundred, or fifty, or even half of that, for those belonging to the Ādiśaiva tradition;
having offered them again and again, one should touch the image, especially with respect to each ritual substance.
Having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblation at the end of the substances and having sprinkled [the offerings] with water, they are then sacrificed:
sweetmeat balls (*laḍḍuka*), coconut, and *mātuluṅga* fruits. (77)
One should offer all kinds of edible food, including jackfruit, as an oblation to the Gaṇas;
thereafter, one should have the study of the four Vedas performed in the four directions.
Then, at the clear dawn, one should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having brought [the image] to the bathing altar, one should bathe it with the root mantra.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, the wise one should offer oblations of five colors;
he should then install the śilās and other elements both in the site and upon the pedestal. (80)
Having observed some human [form], one should establish it according to the prescribed rites;
O Four-faced One, listen as I shall fully explain the sacrifice.
Having performed his bath according to the rules, the wise man should then enter his dwelling;
there he should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) and subsequently perform the placement of the Brahmans (brahmavinyāsa).
The placement [of mantras] from the thumb to the little finger is declared to be the *sṛṣṭinyāsa*.
Having performed the five [limb-nyāsas] starting from the heart, one should place Vighneśa at the heart. (83)
One should worship Madhu and Mādhava as the gatekeepers;
[offering] water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, fragrance, flowers, and incense. (84)
One should offer a lamp and an oblation, sprinkling them with water while reciting the heart-mantra (hṛdaya). Then, if it is an image made of metal, one should bathe it on every festival day.
If [the deity] is made of stone, then after bathing at the three junctions of the day on every festival (parvan),
the ritual worship should be performed upon a pedestal made of clay or decorated with paintings on a wall.
One should fashion the three seats by the very same path previously described;
one should arrange the lion, the lotus, and the stainless [seat] in their proper sequence.
The preceptor should then invoke Vighneśa with the root mantra—
[the deity] who has four arms, three eyes, and is endowed with a gracious countenance.
Then the preceptor, having discarded the floral remains (nirmālya) with the Śikhā-mantra, [should worship] the one endowed with the elephant face and adorned with various ornaments. 89.
One should offer the water for the feet and other items with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, offer sandalwood paste with the *śiras-mantra*,
flowers with the *śikhā-mantra*, and likewise incense and the lamp with the *vāma-mantra*.
And likewise, the sacrificial oblation with the weapon-mantra, the betel-leaf immediately with the mantra,
and the food for the Gaṇas— with "Gaṇānāṃ tvā"— in this very same sequence.
Afterwards, having worshipped the outer enclosure (āvaraṇa) as well as the inner enclosure (garbhāvaraṇa),
one should worship Puruṣa in the eastern direction and Aghora in the south.
Having placed Sadyojāta in the west and likewise Vāmadeva in the north,
one should place the mantra of Īśāna in the northeast and the Heart-mantra in the southeast.
Having worshipped the *śikhā* (crown) in the southwest, one should worship the *kavaca* (armor) in the northwest;
likewise, the *śiras* (head) in the northeast, and the *netra* (eye) and *astra* (weapon) in the cardinal directions.
Having likewise worshipped the attendants, one should sacrifice a radish before him, as well as to Śukra, Bṛhaspati, and the two Aśvinīs. (95)
And Viśvedevas, O best of Brahmins, likewise in Jyeṣṭhā;
and Śāstā and Durgā, in due order during the circumambulation. (96)
One should especially install them and worship each by its own name;
one should place the wise deity in the northeastern direction and set down the worn floral offering (nirmālya).
Then one should perform the fire-rite (agnikārya) according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures;
and by means of the previously mentioned procedure, one should prepare the mouth of the fire (agnimukha). 98.
The preceptor should offer seven oblations to Vighneśa with the root mantra, using clarified butter mixed with food and accompanied by flowers.
(250) And for all [the deities], one oblation should be offered with their own names;
thereafter, one should perform the daily festival (nityotsava) accompanied by an image of Vighneśa. 100.
Having become celibate and pure, wearing a turban and an upper garment, he should place the image within the vessel while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*. (101)
One should carry [the image] upon one's head and circumambulate the temple;
having washed one's feet, one should then enter the temple. || 102 ||
One should dismiss the Lord of Gods and enter one's own home;
now I shall fully describe the festival—listen, O Lotus-seated One. (103)
Then, one should offer sprouts joined with eight small vessels;
thereafter, one should construct a pavilion in front of the temple.
Having strewn the pavilion with rice, one should place the *pālikās* in the center, together with mung beans, black gram, and mustard seeds. (105)
One should sow [the seeds] with the root mantra; in the center of that, one should place a jar of Soma. Having established it in a well-concealed spot, one should begin the hoisting of the banner.
The banner-cloth should be five cubits or even seven cubits in length;
its width should be equal to the tail, and the top-knot should be half of that.
Having joined together a betel-nut tree or a bamboo pole provided with three sections by means of a staff, one should then hoist the banner. 108.
At night, one should offer the village-oblation (grāmabali) to all the deities, including the spirits (bhūtas),
having constructed a pavilion for the sacrifice either in the northeast or in the southeast.
p.
251) The sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa) should be constructed in the vicinity of the western quarter or near a lake;
it should measure five, six, or seven cubits [in size] and be provided with sixteen pillars. || 110 ||
One should construct a central altar (vedikā) with a height of one tāla;
outside the altar, however, one should cause five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) to be made all around.
Or else, one may establish a single fire; here it is said that the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be circular.
One should place a śālī plant in the center of the altar and surround it with darbha grass.
One should place the obstacle-pot (vighnakumbha) in the center with the root mantra;
one should then arrange eight jars all around in the middle of the śāli rice.
Having covered them with *darbha* grass, one should place eight large jars (*bṛhodara*) and so forth,
provided with cloths, lids, gold, and sacrificial brooms (*kūrca*).

Having worshipped with the root mantra, the preceptor should perform the fire sacrifice (homa), consisting of sacrificial fuel sticks (samit), clarified butter (ājya), sacrificial porridge (caru), parched grain (lāja), and accompanied by cakes (apūpa). || 115 ||
Having offered oblations twenty-five times each for those beginning with Vidyā and ending with Īśāntaka,
and having likewise offered for the Gaṇas, one should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for him.
Then one should offer the village oblation (grāmabali) together with an image of Vighneśa,
along with [the emblems] joined with a trident, a spear, a sword, a staff, and a lotus.
One should especially offer an oblation (bali) accompanied by the five weapons;
the first is called the "night of spirits" (bhūtarātra), and the second is said to be "scent" (gandha).
The third is the Night of the Sages (Ṛṣirātra), while the fourth is the Night of Mantras (Mantrarātra).
The fifth is declared to belong to the Siddhas, and the sixth is said to be that of the Rākṣasas.
The seventh is Vighnarātra; these are the deities of the nights.
For five days beginning with Ṛṣirātra, there shall be the three days starting with Siddha. (120)
One should offer a bali-oblation of rice mixed with clarified butter to Brahmā and the other deities;
at the conclusion of the bali-offering, one should perform the auspicious rite (kautuka) and circumambulate the village.
Then one should perform the powder festival (cūrṇotsava), and thereafter perform the rite of the sacred ford (tīrtha).
There, the preceptor (deśika) should bathe the jar with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Having again performed the water-rites, he should enter toward the temple;
there, with the consecrated jars, he should bathe the primary image (mūlaberaka).
I shall now fully describe the ritual bathing (snapana); listen, O Lotus-seated One!
[One should draw] four threads with their tips pointing eastward, and likewise four with their tips pointing northward. (124)
One should scatter rice there and place a water-pot in the center; then, the best of men, having arranged the jars starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
O Brahmin, one should place Bṛhodara and the others eightfold in the middle;
and in the second enclosure, one should likewise place the deities known as the Vidyeśvaras.
Having worshipped Dharma and the others in sequence with that clarified butter,
especially in the principal jar, one should first place the water for washing the feet (pādya) made of gold in the eastern direction.
One should place the water for sipping (ācamanīya) to the east and the water for respectful offering (arghya) to the south;
the scented water (gandhatoya) to the southwest and the water with kuśa grass to the west.
In the northwest, one should place the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and in the north, milk;
in the northeast, curd is to be placed, within this first enclosure.
Clarified butter, parched grain, and groats, as well as flower-ash, along with the powder of turmeric combined with plantain, sesame, and mustard seeds. (130)
Likewise, in the second enclosure, there are the jackfruit, the coconut, the pomegranate, the citron, and two oranges.

He should perform the ceremonial bath (snapana) in this manner, including the ritual brush (kūrca), the cloth, the sacred substances, and the presiding deity; this is the supreme rite that brings about all peace.
Having extracted the twenty-first family, he goes to the world of the Gaṇas;
for its installation, five niṣkas are required, but for its festival, two niṣkas.
Half a niṣka is the fee for the teacher at the time of the bath;
as for the image-protectors and the retinue, the fee should be given according to one's ability. (134)
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter in the Vīratantra, concerning the ritual for the installation, worship, bathing, and festival of Vighneśa.
Henceforth, I shall explain in due order that which is extracted from the Five Brahmas;
it must be understood from the mouth of the Guru, for otherwise it is not told.
O Four-faced One, listen! It bestows both liberation and worldly enjoyment upon men;
one should extract [the syllables] from Īśa to Sadyojāta in their proper order.
On a level plot of ground, free from depressions and elevations,
one should take up the thirteenth circle together with the fifteenth.
The first syllable has been declared; the second is now being told by me:
it is the fourth letter of Vāsava (Va), preceded by the trident (Śa), exactly as it is. (4)
The fifth [syllable] of Vāruṇa, joined with the end of *vajra*,
and the third of Īśāna, joined with the end of *vajra*. (5)
The fourth [syllable] of Dhanada is joined with Vajra;
having extracted that very same one again, it is placed above the seed-syllable of Agni and Vāsava.
The fourth [day] belongs to Rajanī, while the third belongs to Vāsava;
the third belongs to Varuṇa, accompanied by Vāsava.
The second letter joined with Vajra (A), and the fifth letter of Varuṇa (U).
The second [son] belongs to Puruhūta, while the fifth belongs to Maheśa;
the fourth belongs to Vāsava, and after that, another belongs to Śaṅkara.
The fourth [syllable] of Gadā is joined with Vajra;
the second of Soma is likewise endowed with the sixteenth [vowel]. (10)
The third [syllable] from Śūlin, the Vajra, the fourth of Soma,
the fourth of Pavana, and the six-syllabled [mantra] from Devendra; having taken these along with the Lord of Varuṇa, they are joined with the end of the Cakra.
One should take the fifth letter of the Maṅgala [group], the third of Anila, and the second of Gadā-vāyu, combined with its own position. (13)
The fourth [syllable] of Īśāna, joined with the five wheels of Vāyu, and the second of Puruhūta, combined with what was previously mentioned. (14)
Having extracted the fourth [syllable] of Parjanya, the second of Vāsava,
and the first of Māruta, one forms the Cakra-mudrā. 15.
Having extracted [the mantra] beginning with Varuṇa and joined it with the three Vāsavas,
one should take the second ending of Māruta and join it with Vahni and Āsava.
One should form the first [syllable] with the seed-syllable of Agni; the fourth belongs to Śūla itself;
the fifth belongs to Anila; and the second belongs to Vāsava. (17)
The thirteenth wheel is conjoined with the fourth of Dhanada.
One should take the fifth [syllable] from "Marutaḥ," the eleventh from "Vāsava," the second from "Śaṅkarasya," and that which is joined with the beginning of "Varuṇa. (19)
The previously mentioned syllable is joined with the five seed-syllables of the wheel;
it ends with the second [letter] of Vāsava and the thirteenth [letter] of Vāsava. (20)

The letter preceding *ha* (i.e., *ya*) joined with the end of *ca* (i.e., *ña*), and the end of *sa* (i.e., *ma*) joined with the end of *da* (i.e., *na*), and the fourth letter of *pa* (i.e., *bha*).
Joined with Soma and the rest, and endowed with the sixteenth [vowel],
it is the third [syllable] of Īśāna, joined with Vāsava.
One should extract that very fourth [syllable] from the seed-syllable of the oblation (HŪM);
it is conjoined with the upper part of the seed-syllable of fire (RA) and with the liquor of the moon (SA).
And that which belongs to the Śis [group] is indeed the seed-syllable of Fire (vahni-bījaka), conjoined with the eleventh [vowel] and the fourth of the Maruts (Vāyu). || 24 ||
Joined with Kubera and united with the End of the Twelve;
joined with the Lord of Waters at the end of the fourth, and endowed with the food of Vāsava. (25)
The third [abode] of Īśāna, however, is Vāsa, which is peaceful.
One should extract [the mantra] ending with Kubera or ending with Pañcavaruṇa,
joined with the seed-syllable of Fire and endowed with Vāsava.
Having raised up the sixth [syllable] of Vāsava from the end of Kaubera, and having raised up Anila with the eleventh of Vāsava. (28)
Then, having brought Anila and Kubera, one should join them with the sixteenth [deity], who is formidable and the granter of all desired objects. (29)
Having extracted the Dvādaśānta (the letter *ha*) together with the fifteenth (the vowel *u*), and [the letter] fourth of Dhanada (*va*) joined with the end of Vajra (*ra*). || 30 ||
One should take the fifth [letter] from Anila (the letter *pa*), conjoined with Vāsava (the letter *e*);
then, having extracted the one ending in Varuṇa (the letter *va*), it is joined with the eleventh [letter] of Vāsava (the letter *ka*).
But at the end of Indra’s thunderbolt, [it was] not endowed with that;
having raised up the mace-weapon, it was endowed with Vāsava.
One should take the fifth [vowel] from Varuṇa, joined with the thunderbolt (vajra);
having taken Pavana, it is adorned at the end by [the letter] Na.
Having raised [the mantra] from the word *upaiśāntam* with the eleventh [syllable],
and having raised the end of the trident (*śūla*), one should then place it below the end of the sword (*khaḍga*).
At the end of *vajra*, one should take the letter that is equal to and distinct from [the previous], which is accompanied by *vāsava*;
then, taking the fifth letter of *varuṇa*, it is joined with *vāsava*. (35)
After that, the fifth of Pavana (Sa), then the thirteenth of Vāyavya (Va);
having extracted the one ending with Gadānta (Ta) and adorned it with the fifth of Vajra (Ra). (36)

Having extracted [the mantra] ending with *pāśa* and *anta*, well-adorned by *vahni* (*ra*) and *astāt* (*kṣa*), it is joined with the end of *vajra* (*ha*) and combined with *gadā* (*la*) and *vāsava* (*sa*). (37)
The fifth [syllable] of Varuṇa, joined with the thunderbolt (vajra), is at the rear;
the fifth [syllable] of Pavana is to be taken, joined with the sixteenth. || 38 ||
Having extracted [the mantra] beginning with *agnādi* and adorned with the end of *vajra*, and having extracted [the mantra] ending with *soma* and endowed with the end of *vajra*. (39)
Having extracted the one beginning with *candra* (ca) together with *vāsava* (va),
one should take the fifth of *īśa* (ma) together with *vajra* (la).
One should take the fifth [vowel] of Pavana (the letter *u*) joined with the sixteenth [consonant] (*ṣa*), and likewise extract Vahni (the letter *ra*) combined with Vāsava (the letter *la*). (41)
And having raised the mace-end, which is joined with a thunderbolt,
it is the fourth of Kubera, while that [other] is the third of his.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of fire (ra) conjoined with Vāsava (la), and having extracted that which ends with the moon (u), it is joined with the discus (kha). 43.
Having taken the fifth [syllable] from Nirṛti, joined with the end of Vajra; having extracted the end of Kubera, joined with the beginning of Indra. (44)
The fifth of Pavana, followed by the thirteenth of Vāsava, and the third of Aṅkuśa joined with the thunderbolt itself. (45)
Having extracted [the seed-syllable] ending with Kubera (KṢ), it is joined with that beginning with Indra (L);
and the fourth of Candra (M) is joined with that ending with Vajra (H). (46)
Having extracted Kṛśānu and joined him with Vajra,
and having placed Kubera at the end together with Vāsava, the sword is indeed the fifth.

One should take the fifth [syllable] of the noose-mantra, which is joined with the end of the vajra and accompanied by Vāsava (the letter *sa*), and likewise combined with the mace (the letter *ga*) and Vāsava. || 48 ||
Having extracted the syllable of the wind (ya), the seed-syllable of fire (ra) is then spoken;
it is joined with Vāsava (la) and is indeed the fifth of the winds (sa). (49)

The fifth [syllable] of Varuṇa, joined with Vāsava (A), ending with the noose (Ū), and conjoined with the thunderbolt (K), is followed by the fifth [syllable] of Varuṇa itself, likewise conjoined with the thunderbolt (K). || 50 ||
The fifth [vowel] of Pavana (the letter *u*) is declared to be joined with the sixteenth [consonant] (*ṣa*);
having extracted it ending with Īśāna (*ha*), it is adorned with Vajra (*kṣa*).
Furthermore, the fourth seed-syllable of Dhanada (Kubera) is indeed the fire-seed (Ra), which is then joined above with Vāsava (La). (52)
Having extracted the fifth of the wind [seed-syllable] (ha) and joined it with the end of the twelve (m),
one should then add the fifth of fire (ra) conjoined with the thunderbolt (k).
The fifth of Pāśa is said to be conjoined with the End of the Twelve;
and the fourth of Pavana is endowed with Vāsava. (54)

The fourth [syllable] of Dhanada (the Lord of Wealth), conjoined with the sixteenth vowel, bestows virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation upon those beginning with Sadyojāta and ending with Īśāna. || 55 ||
This extraction of the Brahman has been proclaimed; now hear of the Vijaya mandala.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Extraction of Brahmā," in the Vīratantra.
Having bowed his head to the God, the Grandfather (Brahmā) asked:
"O Moon-Adorned One! Tell me thus about the Vijaya-maṇḍala."
The Lord.
O Grandfather! I shall describe the supreme Vijaya-maṇḍala, which removes all sins, yields the fruit of all worship, and is equal to all sacrifices.
It bestows victory upon all the gods, it is the circle of victory,
and by those who practice its recitation, it grants the state of Brahman.
Resorting to Viṣṇu as her second [support], endowed with the power of Viṣṇu,
she conquered all his means through the hymns addressed to the Lord.
Therefore, with every effort, a wise man should cause it to be given to men;
however, he should avoid those of other castes among the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
Under the constellation Ārdrā, one should deposit it there within a mandala;
having bathed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should offer the great sacrificial oblation (mahāhavis).
The teacher should draw a Brahma-maṇḍala favorable to him;
he should smear the area in front of the temple with cow dung. (7)
