For a Brāhmaṇa it is twelve finger-breadths, for a Kṣatriya ten finger-breadths,
for a Vaiśya eight finger-breadths, and for Śūdras six finger-breadths.
In the case of women of each respective caste, the mandala should be reduced by one finger-breadth; there, in the center, one should place a lotus flower.
Having constructed a water-station (prapā) with special care, one should, by means of its power, place the lunar disc there and arrange a maṇḍala, either a thousand [petals] or half of that.
One should cause betel-leaf to be offered separately to the teacher and to the people;
daily, thirty, fifty, or one hundred and eight [leaves].

On the previous day, having thus performed the ritual for a year with the mandala endowed with the characteristic marks in the presence of Śiva, one should extract the previously mentioned constellation.
Or for three years, or five, six, seven, or eight ways; according to one's faith and the available time, there should be constant worship of the maṇḍala.
Above that, at the end of the ear-rings (kuṇḍala), the planting of the sprout is most excellent;
[the vessels] are the *pālikā*, the *ghaṭikā*, and the *śarāva* in due order.
The sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) above that should be provided with a water-pot (kumbhavardhana);
it should consist of eight droṇas of śāli rice, and half of that amount of husked rice (taṇḍula). || 15 ||
One should prepare half of that [space] for sesame seeds, using seven types of seeds and measuring six finger-breadths;
having offered the sprouts, it should be provided with blazing lamps.
The highest [merit] is obtained at the three junctions of the day; the middling at two junctions; and the lowest at one junction—provided it is always accompanied by a lamp. (17)
In this manner, one should first worship the primary image (mūlabera) of Soma and Arka;
thus one should perform [the rites] for seven days and conduct the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) at night.
In front of the temple, one should construct a square pavilion,
provided with sixteen pillars and equipped with four doors.
One should cause the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) ceremony to be performed there and begin the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*).
One should worship Umā and Maheśa in the water-pot (*kumbha*), and the primary image (*mūlabimba*) as well. || 20 ||
One should tie the *kautuka* (sacred thread) there, or perform the *adhivāsana* (consecration);
then, upon that, one should prepare the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and place the water-pot (*kuṃbha*).
Combined with fragrant substances and richly adorned with garlands, it is filled in a jar with uśīra,
sandalwood, camphor, and saffron.
Having stirred [the offering] with cardamom, cloves, nutmeg, and cinnamon, one should worship it well;
moreover, one should perform a special fire-oblation (homa) using all these substances combined.
One should place water-pots there, covered with cloth and containing gold;
one should especially worship them together with threads and tufts of kusha grass.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should prepare the sacrificial offering (havis) and perform the adoration of the primary image (mūlabera).
Then, at the clear dawn, the preceptor (deśika), having performed his ablutions, should proceed.
One should perform a special worship accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments,
combined with dance and song, and with hymns and auspicious recitations.
Having uttered the word "Jaya" amidst sounds of "Hara," one should then perform the ceremonial bathing according to the path prescribed in the scriptures. || 27 ||
At the conclusion of the ablution, one should prepare the oblation and present the great offering;
for the gods there is a golden plate, while for Umā and Maheśvara there is the auspicious fish.
Especially the primary image should be joined with a silk ball;
one should cause a small vessel, a staff-bell, and a large bell to be given.
One should likewise cause a cloth joined with the *namanī* [formula] to be offered to Śiva;
having drawn seven mandalas, one should worship the seven worlds well.
Having performed the viewing of the mandala and [the ritual] for the women observing the vow,
one should prepare a separate mandala for each woman using one prastha of rice.
In this same manner, one should likewise [offer] a mountain of rice, or a mountain of blue [sugar],
or a mountain of gold, or even a mountain of salt.
One should fashion a mountain of silver, or indeed a mountain of beans,
or likewise a mountain of mung beans, or even a mountain of the seven precious substances.
Having beheld the mountains with the names of the female warriors of the army, one should first honor the Preceptor with garments, rings, and other such gifts. (34)
The fee for the teacher (ācārya) shall be one niṣka for the lowest, two niṣkas for the middle, and three niṣkas for the highest. || 35 ||
One should cause clothing to be given to all the attendants;
everything should be provided with items dedicated to Maheśvara, and one should honor those born of the arms (the Kṣatriyas). || 36 ||
One should give to Caṇḍeśvara and worship him especially;
at that time, one should cause clothing, grain, betel, and sandalwood to be offered. (37)
In his presence, one should cause all the people, including women, to offer [the gift];
one should cause everyone to be surrounded [by a screen], and then enter that house. || 38 ||
One should cause food and drink to be given to everyone, down to the outcaste Caṇḍālas;
then, under the constellation Ārdrā, one should worship the Lord of Gods.
A woman who acts in this manner goes to the world of Śiva;
having uplifted twenty-one generations of her lineage, she goes to the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, the Ritual for the Vijaya-maṇḍala, in the Vīra-tantra.
The Grandfather.
O Lord! O Master! Tell me all of that—the correct definition of the *liṅga* and the very procedure for its installation—for I wish to hear it. (1)
The Lord.
Now, O Brahmin, I shall describe to you the supreme characteristics of the linga:
that made of stone, that made of gems, that made of minerals, and likewise that made of wood. (2)
The liṅga is said to be of six kinds, including those made of clay and those that are momentary;
the stone liṅga is of four kinds, and likewise, the one born of jewels is of seven kinds.
That which is born of metal is said to be of eight kinds; that which is born of wood is declared to be sixteenfold.
That which is made of clay is said to be of two kinds, and the ephemeral [image] is declared to be sevenfold. (4)
White, red, yellow, and black—thus the stone-made liṅga is said to be of four kinds; now the characteristics of the material are being described. (5)
That which resembles cow’s milk, or resembles a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon, is declared to be very white; endowed with these characteristics, it bestows victory.
Yellow, resembling gold or like the powder of turmeric,
and endowed with the characteristics of a stone, it bestows wealth, grain, and happiness.

That which resembles black gram (*māṣa*) and guggulu resin, as well as that which resembles buffalo-eyes (*mahiṣākṣa*), and that which has the appearance of a bumblebee (*bhṛṅga*) or mung bean (*mudga*), is known to bring success in worship.
A black stone, however, bestows all perfections upon everyone;
it also grants an abundance of grain to Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
Reddish-black stone grants victory to both Brahmins and kings;
white stone is declared to be auspicious on the first day of the lunar fortnight, especially for Brahmins.
Māṇikya, coral, lapis lazuli, crystal,
emerald, topaz, and sapphire— these indeed are the varieties of gems.
Māṇikya is said to bestow prosperity, while coral (pravāla) is a cause for subjugation;
lapis lazuli (vaiḍūrya) is for attraction, and crystal (sphaṭika) grants an increase in progeny.
Emerald brings about enmity, while topaz effects immobilization;
such shall be the fruit of gems produced from jewels when employed in various undertakings. (13)
Gold is said to bestow prosperity, silver grants a kingdom,
copper is for the sake of the abundance of sons, and bell-metal causes enmity.
For expulsion, iron mixed with copper is used; iron causes destruction;
lead causes disease; [silver] increases longevity. (15)
Thus has that which consists of metal been described; next, that which is made of wood is declared:
namely, *devadāru*, the *śamī* tree, the *pippala*, and likewise sandalwood.
The wood for the seat should be from the Khadira, Bakula, or Śiṃśupā tree, as well as from the Madhūka, Padma, Ḍuṇḍūka, or Karṇikāra. (17)
The tinduka, the kārañja, as well as the plakṣa and the udumbara—these are the four groups [of trees] resulting from the sequence of the twice-born castes. (18)
Earthen [liṅgas] are said to be of two kinds, distinguished as baked and unbaked;
likewise, there are those made of sand, cow dung, food, flour, clay, and fruit. (19)
And fresh butter—these seven are declared to be momentary [in their results]:
sand for those desiring liberation, and cow dung for the destruction of disease. (20)
For one desiring food, food [prepared from] flour is prescribed, which bestows nourishment;
that made from cow-products (gaula) is said to grant affection and yield the fruit of the accomplishment of desired goals. (21)
Joy and fresh butter shall be the fruit of momentary [deities];
however, one should not perform the binding of the pedestal for momentary lingas.
At the time of departure, those who examine various omens for good and evil fortune [should be consulted]. || 22 ½ ||
The daughter of a Brahmin, elephant, variegated meat,
a full water-pot, fruit, a lamp,
white flowers, curd, a cow, and a bull.
And a banner, a kettledrum, and a clay drum—these are auspicious. || 23 ½ ||
(266) A broken water-pot, a corpse, scattered hair, and inauspiciousness; the form of a donkey or a *preta*;
all-enemy, fallen, inexhaustible suffering, and constant ill fortune for one setting out on a journey. (24½)
A good omen would lead to movement, while a bad omen results in staying put. || 25 ||
The preceptor, adorned with garments and ornaments along with the artisans,
having performed [the rites] in that place, stands facing east on the path.

Then, having circumambulated [the site], one should examine the defects and non-defects in the water that has been stirred up, as well as the smell of the mud and bones, and the letters of the syllables [inscribed] therein.

She who, by means of a different sequence, places those situated in evil positions and those in good positions [in their proper order], and who possesses a mouth that is crooked, full of *arkarā* sounds, and a cavernous throat like a worn-out drum. 28.
A wise man should avoid stones that have lines, dots, or blemishes;
for the form [of a stone] is traditionally said to be of three kinds, like the foot of a measuring cord, or like a line.
Above that, it is joined with one resembling a date-palm leaf;
the bamboo-staff has the shape of a hand and is provided with spider-legs.
The *hirikā* is said to be of five types, resembling the tip of a sugar cane.
The *kalaṅka* resembles a black disease or is similar to black soil.
The Śikhī [kalpa] has five forms; the Kali [yuga] is of three kinds.
Trāsa is like crystal, and the two shells are like human fat.
The various types of *trāsa* (trembling) are to be known; the fourth is called the *bindu*.
It has the appearance of a rose-apple fruit (*jambūphala*) and resembles the crest of a peacock's plume. (33)
The Bindurekhā is fully described; it is said to be of three kinds, all pure.
The pure [Bindurekhā] resembles gold, while that which is like bronze resembles iron.
(267) It may resemble a cave or a pit and be the cause of all defects.
When it is black, black [qualities] perish; when white, there is a pleasant fragrance. || 35 ||
The Bhīrikā [plant] on the Black Mountain is shown to be white in color;
it is auspicious, having the form of a date-palm leaf and a cluster of dūrvā grass.
That which is made by a maiden does not accept [the offering] for the sake of grain, cattle, or food;
it should be known as "Kālaka," which bestows disease, while "Trāsara" increases the kingdom. (37)
With the *bindu*, there is the loss of a son; with the *vimalās*, all suffer from misery.
A cave destroys grain, and its impurity (*tanmala*) likewise [destroys it]. (38)
Having thus examined it in many ways, one should take a stone endowed with the proper characteristics; a stone of a single color bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (39)
If it possesses many colors, it brings about all defects;
[the stones are classified as] female, male, and neuter, young, old, or middle-aged. (40)

Having characterized the definition by means of the threefold divisions and the threefold distinctions, those ending in the sound of a bell are masculine, while those devoid of vowels are neuter. || 41 ||
Regarding the sound of clapping on the stone: that stone which produces a sound like a young woman is known as "yuvati";
that which produces a long sound is known as "vṛddhā," and that which is short-sounding is known as "bālā. || 42 ||
The liṅga should be made with a masculine word, and the pedestal (piṇḍikā) should be made with a neuter word;
one should especially make the base-stone (pādādhānaśilā) with a neuter word.
The temple (harmyakam) is determined by the measurement of the liṅga, which follows the proportions of the palace;
that liṅga whose interior space is half the size of the house is called the smallest (kanyasam).
A linga with nine parts and five sections is called medium;
one with five parts and three sections is called superior. (45)
One should specifically place precious metals according to the sequence starting with the Brāhmaṇas;
gold bestows prosperity, and silver shall grant sovereignty.
A copper [liṅga] should be known as bestowing sons; bell-metal (kāṃsya) is indeed a cause of nourishment;
this bronze (paittala) liṅga is said to be known for the destruction of disease. (47)
If one must effect destruction by causing it to be carried away into a chasm,
like a finger or similar object, that is said to be the "birth" (end) of all things.
I shall describe the jewel-liṅga; listen, O Four-faced One!
[These consist of] crystal, emerald, ruby, and the padmarāga gem. (49)
One should likewise cause pearls, sapphires, lapis lazuli, coral, sapphire, topaz, and diamonds to be fashioned.

(That which is faultless, endowed with jewels, and likewise obtained through worship) should be known as nourishing for one's own nature; that spoken by others is said to grant the desire for liberation. 51.
One should have all the vajras fashioned according to their own respective measurements;
for all the jewels, a pedestal made of metal is prescribed.
The gopura should be four parts, and the pit (śvabhra) one part, equal to that;
the width of the pedestal (pīṭha) is said to be one-third of the height of the liṅga.
One-third of the height of the pedestal (pīṭha) shall be the length of the cow’s mouth (gomukha);
it may be circular or square, divided into sixteen parts.
The *ghṛtavāri* should be one part, and the *paṭṭikā* one and a half parts;
the *padmatuṇḍa* should be one-fourth part, and the *valaya* two parts. (55)
The lower lotus is five parts, and the fillet (paṭṭikā) is one and a half parts;
thus the pedestal (pīṭha) is fully described, and now the fruit of the [deity’s] standing posture is stated.
Sphaṭika brings about the increase of sons; marakata shall be the bestower of nourishment;
māṇikya is to be known as the giver of liberation; and padmarāga is for the sake of wealth. (57)
A pearl brings the acquisition of wealth, while a sapphire brings all success;
a lapis lazuli increases longevity, and a coral brings the subjugation of the kingdom.
Stambhana is the puṣparāga, while ākarṣaṇa is the vajra;
in this very sequence, the characteristics of the gems are to be known. (59)
O best of Brahmins! One should have the Bāṇaliṅga fashioned according to the proper measurements.
Thus, the two types [of liṅgas] have been described; now hear about the installation of the mobile [liṅga]. || 60 ||
In Rohiṇī, Punarvasu, Puṣya, and Mṛgaśiras, as well as in Hasta, Revatī, Svātī, and the three Uttaras. (61)
However, if the zodiac sign is fixed (sthirarāśi), it should be performed; or one may arrange it for both types.
One should construct a square pavilion in front of the temple.
One should smear with cow dung a platform provided with sixteen pillars;
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) of rice, one should place small bowls (pālikās) upon it.
O best of Brahmins! One should place the Pālikās in the four directions in due order, specifically after nine days, seven days, or five days.

First, one should offer the [seed-]sprouts according to the previously mentioned procedure; having constructed the pavilion for the consecration, the most excellent of men should perform the preliminary rite as prescribed. (65)
On the bank of a river, or on wood, or especially on a mountain;
in a garden, in a pure place, or especially in a house. || 66 ||
It should be three cubits, five cubits, or even seven cubits [in width];
it should be provided with sixteen pillars, and there shall be a pedestal in the center.
The preceptor should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the four directions and in the northeast;
the pit should have as many corners as the pedestal has corners.
For a linga with a circular pedestal, a circular kuṇḍa is prescribed here;
the wise man should adorn the pavilion according to the procedure previously mentioned.
There, the preceptor should wash the image with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
adorn it with flowers and garlands, and perform a circumambulation of the village.

Alternatively, the best of preceptors should perform the circumambulation of the celestial chariot (vimāna) and enter the pavilion; there, he should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) in the water.
One should place eight water-pots, provided with cloths and gold, and associated with the Vidyeśvaras, starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
The preceptor should offer the bali-offering to the world-protectors with their respective mantras;
then, having emerged from the water on the previous day, he should wash the liṅga.
Having entered the pavilion there, one should bathe [the deity] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
having performed a special purification, one should then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
One should place śālī rice, amounting to eight droṇas, in the center of the altar;
having placed half of that amount of rice, one should place half the amount of rice in sesame seeds. (75)
Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, one should strew it with *darbha* grass;
then, having prepared the bed in five ways according to the method previously described.
O best of Brahmins! [The cloth] may be born from an egg, such as the plumage of birds;
or it may be "shorn-born" (muṇḍaja), such as fine silk (dukūla) or even cotton. || 77 ||
A woolen cloth made from hair is prescribed;
it may also be made from tree bark, for it is ordained that it may be made of leather as well. (78)
O best of Brahmins, one should likewise cause the left-hand [image] to be made with *kuśa* grass;
one should then have the Lord laid upon the bed with the *Prāsāda* mantra.
Having thoroughly mixed all the fragrances, one should smear the liṅga itself;
then, with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), one should place the pedestal in the western enclosure and lay [the image] upon the bed.
Taking a new water-pot, one should wrap it with a thread;
having filled it with pure water, one should cover it with a shallow bowl.
Prior to the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the Liṅga, one should worship the archways (toraṇas) with the Hṛdaya-mantra;
having placed the pitcher at the door, one should worship the guardians of the gates.
O Brahmin, one should duly install the pitchers of the world-protectors, beginning with Indra and ending with Īśāna, specifically by means of their respective names.
O Brahmin, one should place the Śiva-pitcher and the Vardhanī vessel in the northeast;
the most excellent preceptor should install the Vardhanī with the seed-syllable of Gaurī.
The preceptor should place eight water-pots starting from the east and ending with the northeast;
he should also fashion the ten weapons out of gold itself. (85)
Having cast [the materials] into the middle of the pitcher while reciting the Astra-mantra,
one should install the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) there by their respective names and according to the mantra.
One should worship well with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps;
one should offer milk-rice as an oblation while reciting the mantra of the heart.
Then one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the prescribed characteristics,
using sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), cooked rice (caru), parched grain (lāja), mustard seeds (sarṣapa), barley (yava), and sesame seeds (tila).
O best of Brahmins, mung beans and black gram are offered again in succession;
likewise, sacrificial fuel sticks are offered with the Īśa-mantra, and clarified butter with the Puruṣa-mantra. (89)

Having offered the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Aghora mantra, and likewise the parched grains (lāja) with the Vāma mantra, one should offer mustard seeds with the Sadyojāta mantra and barley with the Hṛdaya mantra.
Having offered sesame seeds with the *śiras* mantra and mung beans together with the *śikhā* mantra, ghee is indeed offered with the mantra "ghṛtam ikṣe. (91)
Having offered the sacrificial oblation (caru) with the mantra "āpo rājā," the preceptor should keep a vigil there at night and examine the dreams.
Then, at the clear dawn, he should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
the most excellent of preceptors should maintain either a single fire or five fires.
In the rite of oblation (homa), the fire must be kindled by the preceptor himself;
a wise man should not perform the oblation without fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (caru).
Reciting the *Havyavāha* [mantra], one should offer oblations of *citta*, *jaya*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* [mantras], combined with all the ritual substances. (95)
Immediately thereafter, one should offer oblations with the mantra "sviṣṭam agne";
having offered these, at the conclusion, one should specifically offer with the mantra "yad asya".
Thereafter, one should raise the liṅga and place it upon the bathing altar;
then the wise practitioner, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the path prescribed for the placement of mantras, [should proceed]. 97.
One should bathe the Śiva-pitcher, as well as the Vardhanī vessel and the pedestal.
One should place the [liṅgas] ending with Khaṇḍa in the infinite directions upon the top of the liṅga;
there, one should cause the bathing to be performed one hundred and eight or fifty times.
Then the learned one should perform the consecration with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
he should offer an oblation of five colors and then cause betel to be given.
Thereafter, one should worship the preceptor, and then worship the guardians of the images;
the mortal who acts in this manner shall attain the world of Śiva. || 101 ||
Listen now to the description of the installation of the mobile liṅga together with Umā. || 101½ ||
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, the procedure for the consecration of the mobile liṅga, in the Vīratantra.
Having prostrated before Śiva according to the prescribed rites, the Grandfather (Brahmā) inquired:
"O Supreme Lord! Tell me about the establishment of the forms of creation."
The Lord.
I shall explain all of that in its entirety; listen, O Four-faced One!
It concerns the welfare of Umā and Skanda, as well as the comfortable posture (sukhāsana).
Kalyāṇasundara, Candraśekhara, and Gaṅgādhara—these five are said here to be the forms of creation. || 3 ||
I shall describe their establishment, endowed with its defining characteristics,
as well as the creation of their forms, their worship, their abiding, their course, and their cessation.
Lord Īśvara accepts the worship of Umā just as he does the consecration;
[this applies under the asterisms] of Yama, Rohiṇī, Āditya, Puṣya, Indu, Hasta, Pauṣṇa, and the three Uttarās.
The Svātī asterism is prescribed for the installation [of the deity], provided it is free from planetary influence in the eighth house;
the rite should be performed in a fixed zodiacal sign (sthira-rāśi) or even in a dual sign (ubha-rāśi).
The offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) is described according to the previously mentioned procedure;
one should then offer the sprouts prior to the asterism of the consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
On the ninth day, or the seventh, or especially on the fifth day,
one should then have a pavilion constructed in front of the temple.
Five, six, or seven cubits, or ten cubits for the medium size;
likewise eleven, twelve, or thirteen cubits.
Alternatively, the ten and the five are said to be the three supreme [groups];
O best of gods, I shall now declare the seers, meters, and deities.
Vyāsa, Vasiṣṭha, and Jāmadagnya Kāśyapa;
Bhāradvāja and Bhṛgu, as well as Aṅgiras and Gautama. || 11 ||
O Brahmin of good vows, listen now to the meters of the pavilions in their proper order:
the Triṣṭubh, the Anuṣṭubh, and likewise the Prakṛti. (12)
The Jagatī, the Catvarī, and likewise the Aticatvarī—this indeed is prescribed as the highest of the high among the meters. || 13 ||
Indra, and then Kubera, Soma, and likewise Varuṇa;
Vighneśa, Kubera, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. || 14 ||

O best of Brahmins! Having identified the presiding deities (adhidevatās) of these deities within the pavilion in their proper order, one should perform the rite according to the prescribed injunctions.
The pillar should be fashioned from black stone, or indeed from other stones, or even from wood;
it must be made by a craftsman endowed with the proper characteristics.
The Bakula, the Śirīṣa, or even a sacrificial tree;
or a tree suitable for a seat, such as the Kramuka or one sacred to Viṣṇu. || 17 ||
A jackfruit, a coconut, or a ketaka [flower], which is straight, free from blemishes, and devoid of hollows or cavities. || 18 ||
Having carefully measured the length of the body,
as well as its width and height, one should cause a temple pinnacle (kūṭa), a pavilion (maṇṭapa), or even a water-shed (prapā) to be constructed.
One should cause the betel-nut tree or the coconut tree to fall with a moist branch;
having thus constructed the pavilion, one should then prepare the altar in its center.
One should especially arrange sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) all around that very [central pit],
specifically square, half-moon, circular, and likewise lotus-shaped.
The four directions beginning with the east [form the square], while in the corner there should be a triangle (yoni-ākṛti).
Between Īśāna and Indra, it is called the hexagon (ṣaṭkoṇa). || 22 ||
It is declared that one should perform [the rite] at Skanda-kuṇḍa even without [the presence of] Skanda;
and it is likewise declared that [the rite] is performed together with Umā, even when they are seated upon a single throne.
O Lotus-born One! Listen to [the description of] the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) for the God who is seated comfortably:
they may be square, triangular, trapezoidal, or indeed circular.
One should fashion a five-pointed lotus and an eight-sided figure in sequence;
one should then construct a seven-cornered figure between Īśāna and Indra.
I have described the auspicious *sukhāsana*; now listen further.
A four-cornered (*vedāśra*) sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is prescribed in the four directions, starting from the east up to the northeast.
In the corners, there is a circular kuṇḍa and a five-cornered one for the Śiva-fire;
this is declared to be Kalyāṇasundara and is called Candraśekhara.
In the four directions, there should be square, bow-shaped, and circular fire-pits;
in the corners, however, there should be a circular pit and an eight-cornered pit for the Śiva-fire.
O observer of noble vows, I shall describe the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) for the embodiment of Gaṅgādhara:
place eight comfortable seats in the directions and the fire of Śiva in an eight-cornered shape.
For these deities, however, a separate seat is prescribed here;
for the Goddess who is seated on a single seat, the shape of the yoni indeed [is formed] in the intermediate directions.
In this very manner, O Lotus-born One, one should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) step by step;
having covered it above with canopies, one should plant banners in the eight directions.
Having drawn an elephant, a goat, a buffalo, a lion, a fish, a black horse, a cow, and a bull in the center of the banner, one should then place them in the eight directions. (32)
The first is the arrangement of jewels, the second is the opening of the eyes, the third is the purification of the image, and the fourth is the circumambulation of the village. || 33 ||
The fifth is the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsana), the sixth is the pavilion (maṇḍapa),
the seventh is the bed (śayana), and the eighth is indeed the fire-oblation (homa).
The ninth is the giving of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇādāna), and the tenth is the installation (sthāpana). These ten have been declared here; now hear their distinctions.
In the pavilion previously described, or else upon the footprint of Satyaka,
one should perform a smearing with cow dung and then scatter rice there.
Having placed half a measure of śāli rice, one should place half a measure of sesame seeds;
then, having spread darbha grass around it, it should be covered with a new cloth.
Upon that, one should place a pedestal and cause nine pits to be made.
One should place a vajra in the Brahma-pit, and an indranīla gem in the eastern pit.
One should place emerald in the southeast, beryl to the south of that, topaz in the southwest, and pearl in the west. (39)
One should place crystal in the northwest, coral from the northern region, and a great sapphire in the northeast; thus one should arrange [the gems] for the deity. (40)
One should not perform the ritual for the Goddess, especially the placement of jewels;
rather, one should subsequently deposit gold in the four directions and in the center.
Having placed gold upon Skanda, one should then cause it to be well-polished;
there, one should wash the image again with water mixed with sour gruel (āmleṇa). || 42 ||
One should perform the opening of the eyes on a day conjoined with the two stars of the eye;
indeed, the opening of the eyes is said to take place when the sun is in its station.
One should prepare a sacrificial mound there using eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice,
half as much rice again, and half as much sesame seeds.
One should place a cloth upon it and spread it over with *darbha* grass; specifically, one should install Umā together with Skanda upon that [image]. (45)
Then, having recited the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) while [the image] is covered with a cloth,
one should place honey and clarified butter into a copper or bronze vessel.
One should place a *prahara* [of gold] there, joined with a golden needle;
then, one should arrange eight water-pots all around, starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
Having filled [the vessels] with pure water, provided them with threads and cloths,
and equipped them with threads and covers, [he should place] the deities presiding over the world-protectors.
The artisan should strike there, specifically the line of the eyelashes;
having drawn the black circle, he should then draw the circle of light.
There, one should honor the artisan and cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
[the offering] should be joined with golden nail-clippings and accompanied by golden dūrvā grass.
Having recollected the Netra-mantra, one should touch the eyes themselves;
thereafter, one should specifically perform the Akṣi-homa (eye-oblation) in front of it.
In front of the image, there should be a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) divided into three parts;
one should perform the rite of the "mouth of fire" (agnimukha) according to the very path previously described. || 52 ||
With clarified butter and sacrificial porridge (caru), one offers oblations using the Netra-mantra;
each is offered in sequence exactly one hundred and eight times.
And in the northern [fire], O best of Brahmins, Gaurī is offered with the Netra-mantra;
likewise, in the middle [fire], Skanda is offered with the Skanda-mantra. || 54 ||
At that time, one should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), sprinkle with the Pavamāna hymns,
and satisfy [the deity] with honey and clarified butter using gold, fingernails, and dūrvā grass.
With the mantra "madhuvātā ṛtāya," one should indeed satisfy [the deity] with honey;
and with the mantra "ghṛtam ikṣe," one should likewise satisfy [the deity] with clarified butter. || 56 ||
One should show a cow with her calf according to the *bhavya* mantra;
there, one should show the Brahmins according to the *brahmajajñāna* mantra.
The preceptor of Skanda should show him the seven maidens, especially the goddess Umā, as well as the celibate students (brahmacārins).
One should show [the deity] with the *brahmajajñāna* mantra and the *prāsāda* mantra;
having sprinkled [it] with the *āpo hi ṣṭhā* mantra, it should be accompanied by the *arghya* offering.
Having drawn aside the concealing cloth, he should show it to all the people;
then he should perform the consecration joined with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
And the place of Satyaka is called the site for the image;
one should bathe it with pure water while reciting the mantra beginning with "śuddhair uttiṣṭha."
One should have the proclamation of "an auspicious day" (puṇyāha) made there and sprinkle [the area] with the Pavamāna hymns;
one should perform a circumambulation of the village, adorned with all ornaments. (62)
Then, having placed the image upon a chariot or a palanquin,
accompanied by songs and instrumental music, and joined by the sounds of conch shells and kettledrums (63).
Adorned with various banners and equipped with various crests,
he should perform a circumambulation of the village together with various groups of devotees.
One should enter there with the *nandī* and other [musical instruments]; perform the ritual immersion in water (*jalādhivāsana*), having gone specifically to the bank of a river, a pond, or a lake.
Having made the bank level, one should smear it with cow-dung;
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) of rice, one should place the image there.
Having removed the withered offerings, one should then bathe the image,
wrapping it in a new cloth and providing it with a kūrca.
And furthermore, O best of Brahmins, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the image in water,
having especially constructed a water-shed provided with four doors.
One should place eight jars, starting from the east and ending with the northeast,
provided with cloths, covered lids, and accompanied by the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras).
One should offer the bali-oblation to the world-protectors (lokapālas) every day,
especially for one night, three nights, or even five nights.
Disease arises when the lamp is extinguished; therefore, one should maintain the lamp.
One should perform the Vāstuhoma during the day, endowed with the proper characteristics.
And at the end of the day, O best of Brahmins, the preceptor, having emerged from the water,
should enter the temple, remaining there in the station of Puṣpadanta. (72)

One should bathe [the deities] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the Vyomavyāpin mantra; then one should bathe the Goddess with the Gaurī-bīja and Guha with the Skanda-bīja.
Having bathed with pure water, one should then bathe [the image] preceded by fragrant substances, including uśīra, sandalwood, cardamom, and cloves. (74)
Furthermore, one should tie a protective thread (kautuka) made of either gold thread or cotton;
then, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), endowed with the proper characteristics.
Then one should scatter sixteen *droṇas* of *śāli* rice;
having placed half of that amount of husked rice (*taṇḍula*), one should place half of that amount of sesame seeds (*tila*).
Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, one should spread it with *darbha* grass;
there, one should worship the archways and arrange the pitchers at the doors.
Outside the altar, however, one should arrange ten water-pots all around,
provided with cloths and lids, and presided over by the deities of the world-protectors.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and then cause an oblation (naivedya) to be presented;
thereafter, one should prepare a bed with the five [elements], beginning with the egg-born, in their proper sequence.
That which is provided with the feathers of birds is proclaimed as *rasajña*;
that which is made of linen or cotton is proclaimed as *muṇḍaja*. (80)
That which is joined with a jewel-woolen cloth is proclaimed as being made of wool;
that which is fashioned from tree bark is prescribed as being made of leather.
Silk is said to be produced from the left [side]; the fivefold bed is now described.
One should prepare the fivefold bed with the mantra of the Five Brahmans. (82)
Having wrapped it with a new cloth, one should cover the *kautuka*;
joined with this covering, one should lay Śiva upon the bed.
The best of teachers should place the secretions of the goddess with the Gaurī-bīja at the root of Skanda; he should place the head toward the east and the feet toward the west.
Having covered it with a new cloth, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
then, taking nine jars, one should wrap them with three threads.
Having filled it with pure water and covered it with a shallow bowl,
one should join it with the five jewels and wrap it with a pair of cloths.

In the north-eastern direction of the image, one should place the Śiva-pitcher (śivakumbha) together with the five Brahmans (pañcabrahma), accompanied by the mantra and the temple-structure (prāsāda).
One should place the *vardhanī* vessel on his left, conjoined with the seed-syllable of Gaurī;
one should place the *skandakumbha* in the center with the mantra of Skanda's root-verse. || 88 ||
Having assigned those respective seed-syllables, he should especially honor that preceptor with garments, covered vessels, gold, and bundles of kusha grass.
One should likewise install the eight Lords of Knowledge (Aṣṭavidyeśvaras) in the directions starting from the east,
as well as Ambikā and Umādevī, the consort of Īśa.
Gaṇāmbikā, likewise Skandamātā, Prajñā, Agasutā, and Pārvatī as well; || 91 ||
One should install the deities in the intermediate space, and especially in the *vardhanī* vessel:
Kumāra, Guha, and likewise Subrahmaṇya. (92)
One should likewise place the commander-in-chief, the foremost of the gods, the son of Hara,
as well as Kārttikeya, who was born from the forest of reeds.
In this very manner, having laid aside the ritual offerings there together with the noble ones, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and incense using their respective seed-syllables.
It should be fashioned from gold itself, and one should arrange the weapons there;
[one should also place] cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg, *jātīphala*, and *mura*.
One should place the small vessel joined with the [main] vessel into the center of the water-jar;
in this same manner, one should arrange them in sequence within the *vardhanī* and the excellent water-jars.
Thereafter, one should present the sacrificial offering (havir) for each [deity] as prescribed;
then, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) endowed with its proper characteristics. || 97 ||
The Palāśa tree is in the eastern part, and likewise the Aśvattha in the south;
the Cakra tree is in the west, and the Udumbara in the north.
Between Īśāna and Indra, one should offer ten thousand fuel-sticks of the Palāśa tree, together with those of the Śamī, Apāmārga, and Bilva trees. (99)
And the Plakṣa tree is likewise joined in the triangle beginning with the southeast;
likewise, Palāśa fuel-sticks are placed between the north and northeast.
O best of Brahmins! Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, sesame seeds, mung beans, and black gram—these are said here to be the nine substances. (101)
The fuel-sticks (*samidhaḥ*) are offered with the *sadyojāta* mantra, and the clarified butter (*ājya*) is offered with the *vāmadeva* mantra.
Having offered the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the *aghora* mantra, one should offer the parched grain (*lāja*) with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra. (102)
One should offer mustard seeds with the Īśa-mantra, barley with the Hṛdaya-mantra, sesame seeds with the Śiras-mantra, and mung beans with the Śiva-mantra.
One should offer a bean with the Kavaca mantra, as well as ghee and molasses; likewise, the sacrificial porridge (caru) is offered with the Tryambaka mantra.
One should perform the oblation of parched grain (lājahoma) with the mantra "āporāje";
in this manner, the preceptor should offer the oblations in sequence with their respective mantras. || 105 ||
The best of preceptors should specifically offer one hundred and eight, or fifty, or twenty-five oblations for each substance. (106)
One should have the rite of fire-oblation (homa) performed by a Śaiva preceptor;
at the end of each substance [offered], one should then touch the image.
Having offered the *vyāhṛtis* at the conclusion of the substances, an oblation is made for the gods and the ancestors;
thereafter, one should perform the recitation of the four Vedas in the four directions.
The Śrīrudra is in the eastern part, the Hotṛ hymns in the south,
the Camaka in the west, and likewise the Pavamāna in the north.
And in the four directions of the house, having performed with devotion a dance accompanied by courtesans and joined by a devotee of Maheśvara, || 110 ||
Immediately thereafter, while reciting the mantra "sviṣṭam agne," one should offer oblations into the fire, which is joined with all the ritual substances.
In this very manner, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) during the night in due sequence;
then, at the clear dawn, the preceptor (deśika), having performed his ablutions, [should proceed]. (112)

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the path taught for the placement of mantras, the wise one should proceed; in the rite of consecration (pratiṣṭhā), which has the nature of emanation, the "placement of emanation" (sṛṣṭinyāsa) is prescribed.
Then, one should perform the Vāsana-homa in the primary fire;
having offered fuel-sticks (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), sacrificial porridge (caru), and parched grain (lājā), one should offer fifteen oblations (āhuti).
The sacrificial fuel (samidh) is offered in sequence with the Īśāna mantra;
the clarified butter (ājya) is to be offered with the Sadyojāta mantra, and one should offer the cooked rice (caru) with the Hṛdaya mantra. || 115 ||
The fifteen oblations should be offered in sequence with parched grain using the left hand;
no one else should perform the homa, for it is offered by the preceptor alone.
Then, the groups beginning with the mind (citta) are offered here in sequence;
having offered these, one should then perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the mantra "yad asya. || 117 ||
The preceptor, being most excellent, should perform the fire-oblation in the Śiva, Umā, and Skanda pools;
he should then give the sacrificial fee to the teacher according to the path prescribed in the scriptures.
Clad in a new garment, wearing a turban and an upper cloth,
he should offer the five-fold ornamentation to the crest-lock, the ears, and likewise the neck.
With both hands and the two feet—these are called the five limbs (pañcāṅga).
The lowest [fine] is ten niṣkas, while the middle [fine] shall be double that.
Three times that amount is declared as the excellent fee for the preceptor;
half of that for the instructor, and half of that for the Vāstuhoma.
To all the image-keepers (mūrtipas), however, one should give half of that as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
thereafter, one should cause twice that amount to be given as the fee for the astrologer (daivajña).
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the reciters, those who follow the tantras, and the chanters shall be half of that given to the image-protectors;
for the attendants and their retinues, the sacrificial fee shall be according to one's capacity.
The initiated Śivayogin and the Samaya-practitioner should perform the worship; then, at an auspicious moment and a favorable planetary conjunction, they should raise the deity.
Having reached the bathing altar, one should place [the vessel] upon a wooden plank;
having performed the offering of ghee to the head with golden dūrvā sprouts and unbroken grains of rice (akṣata). || 125 ||

And one should place ghee mixed [with the substance] upon the head at the feet of the deity, conjoined with the Pañcabrahma-mantras according to the path prescribed for the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa). || 126 ||
Having recited the *vyomavyāpin* mantra, one should bathe the *śivakumbha* with the *prāsāda* mantra, conjoined with the *brahmāṅga* [mantras]. || 127 ||
O best of Brahmins, one should especially bathe the Vardhanī vessel with the Gaurī-bīja mantra,
and one should consecrate the Skanda-pitcher with the root-mantra of Skanda.
One should install them starting from the east and ending at the northeast;
if the goddess's *vardhanī* vessel is present, it should be installed together with her upon the seat.
One should bathe the three preceptors at one time;
there, one should cause the ritual bathing to be performed and then have the food offering presented.
Afterwards, one should cause betel-leaf to be offered, and then feed the Brāhmaṇas;
one should feed seven maidens and also feed those who observe celibacy (brahmacārins). || 131 ||
The Buddhist, the Jain, the Śaiva, the Pāśupata,
as well as the Kāpāla and the Pāñcarātra— these six are remembered as the *samayas*. (132)
On this day, one should cause food to be given to all, down to the very Caṇḍālas;
there, one should feed the Śaivas, and thereafter, one should feed those who observe the religious observances (samayins).
One should hold a great festival at night for five or seven days;
the mortal who performs it in this manner shall attain the world of Śiva.
At the outset, having relied upon a qualified practitioner, one should have him perform everything pertaining to the consecration; then, one should cause all of it to be presented to the preceptor.
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter in the Vīra-tantra, titled "The Ritual for the Installation of the Icon of the Creative Emanation."
O Lord of Gods, O Master! For the sake of favoring me, you ought to tell me here, according to the scriptures, what the nature of stability, form, and consecration is. (1)
The Lord.
I shall tell you all of that in its entirety; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
Rohiṇī, Punarvasu, Tiṣya, and likewise Mṛgaśiras; || 2 ||

Under Hasta, Revatī, Svātī, Citrā, and the three Uttaras, as well as in the fixed signs of the zodiac, one should perform [the rite]; one may cause it to be performed under either of these two [conditions]. || 3 ||
If all the planets are situated in the eighth house, one should never perform [the rite];
likewise, one should avoid the bull as a vehicle and the Ardhanārī form.
Kirāta, Vīreśa, and likewise Bhikṣāṭana—
these are the five forms, which are declared to be the forms of persistence (sthitimūrti).
In front of the temple, one should construct a square pavilion measuring five,
six, seven, eight, or nine cubits.
Having prepared a betel-nut wood, a bamboo, or likewise a ketaki or coconut wood—
straight and free from blemishes— with the proper proportions for its length and height.
Having covered it with mango branches and provided with canopies and banners,
one should draw the vehicle of a world-protector there in the middle of the banner.
Having arranged [the materials] in their respective places in due order,
the preceptor covers them with garlands of *darbha* grass and adorns them with strings of pearls.

One should construct a central altar; the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is said to be situated all around it. To the east, however, it should be square, while that of Agni should be shaped like a leaf of the Aśvattha tree.
In the southern direction it is square, and triangular in the domain of Nirṛti;
in the western direction it is circular, and five-cornered in the northwestern direction.
Having placed a lotus upon the moon, one should fashion a seven-cornered [figure] in the northeast;
between Indra and Īśāna, however, one should cause an eight-cornered [figure] to be made.
On a single seat, there should be a lotus and a vulva (yoni) in the intermediate directions;
between Īśāna and Indra, one should place a six-cornered bull.
The bull is declared to be the vehicle; now listen to [the description of] Ardhanārī.
In the four directions starting from the east, there should be a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
In the four directions starting from the southeast (āgneya), one should cause [the forms] beginning with the yoni-shape to be made;
Ardhanārīśvara is proclaimed, and Kirātārjuna is mentioned.
A square, a triangle, a bow, and a triangle; a circle, a pentagon, a lotus, a heptagon, and an octagon. (16)

O best of Brahmins, in the center, within the eight-cornered [mandala] extending from the east to the northeast, there is a seat; and in the southeast and other directions, there are yoni-shaped [seats].
(The lotus with five rounded petals, the lotus, and the seven-cornered one)—this has been declared as the Kirātārjuna; now hear the Vīreśa according to its true nature. || 18 ||
In the four directions, there is a square, a bow, a circle, and a lotus;
as well as a pipal tree, a triangle, a pentagon, and an octagon.
One should install these [deities] starting from the southeast (Āgneya) up to the center between Indra and Īśāna;
the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be seven-cornered. Now, Vīreśa is described.
Indeed, the Kuṇḍa for the alms-round was made like that of Vīreśa;
and between Soma and Īśāna is the circular Hariṇā-kuṇḍa.
Between the Indra and Agni [directions], one should fashion a Bhūta-kuṇḍa in the shape of a triangle;
in this very same sequence, the wise man should construct the sacrificial pits.
The preceptor, together with the artisans, should perform the ritual placement of jewels (ratnanyāsa);
or rather, the ritual placement of jewels should be performed upon the footprint of Satyaka.
One should scatter śāli rice there, and place grains of rice and sesame seeds; one should then set down the image there, covered with a new cloth.
Having placed a ruby in the center, one should place [the others] around it in due order:
an indranīla, a vaiḍūrya, a crystal, or a marakata.
Ruby, coral, diamond, and pearl are said [to be the gems];
reciting the five Brahmans, one should place these in the directions starting from the east. (26)
One should cause the placement of jewels upon the lion-throne and for the Goddess;
and one should install Ardhanārīśvara specifically in the portion belonging to Śiva.
One should have it well-anointed there, and then wash the image;
one should perform the opening of the eyes on a day when the moon is in conjunction with the constellation Viśākhā (the pair of eyes).
The opening of the eyes is said to take place at the very station of the Sun;
one should place the deity upon a layer of rice, covered with a concealed cloth.
The artisan shall perform the opening of the eye with a golden needle;
one should honor the artisan there and then dismiss the artisan.
Then one should prepare another cloth and have the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited;
thereafter, one should place eight water-pots (kalaśas) starting from the east and ending in the northeast.

[He should offer] vessels together with cloths, together with lids, together with gold, and together with kūrca-grass; as well as gold, a nail-scraper, dūrvā grass, a vessel of ghee, and an empty vessel.
Then the preceptor, having become pure and clad in new garments,
adorned with the five-fold ornaments, should sprinkle the image.
Then, having performed the eye-homa specifically before the image,
one should offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter, sacrificial porridge (caru), and the netra-mantra.
The wise practitioner should offer honey and clarified butter for the libation, accompanied by the eye-mantra, while holding golden-nailed dūrvā grass and touching his eyes from the left side.
One should satisfy [the deity] with a vessel filled with honey while reciting "madhuvātā";
having offered ghee and molasses, and having satisfied [him] with ghee, one should present a cow together with its calf. || 36 ||
Then, with the mantra "brahmajajñānam," he should show [the image] to the Brahmins;
having removed the concealed cloth, he should show it to all the people.
Or even when seated on a single seat, one should display that very [substance] with its respective mantra;
having recited the *pavamāna* verse, there is the consecration with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
One should bathe [the deity] with pure water accompanied by the five Brahma-mantras;
then one should perform the circumambulation of the village on either a chariot or a palanquin.
Adorned with all the [auspicious] marks and beautified by song, dance, and other [performances],
one should smear with cow dung either the bank of a river or the shore of a pond.
One should bathe [the deity] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the Vyomavyāpin mantra.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) in water;
one should cover it with a cloth and with a tuft of grass (kūrca).

O best of Brahmins, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the image in water reaching up to the neck; having constructed a water-shed, one should then place eight jars there.
He [should worship] the presiding deities of the lords of knowledge (vidyeśvara), together with garments and gold,
for one night, or three nights, or even five nights.
Having emerged from the water on the previous day, he should enter the pavilion again;
during the day, he should perform the Vāstu-homa accompanied by the prescribed characteristics.
Having placed [the image] upon the pedestal of Puṣpadanta, one should perform the consecration with the five products of the cow;
having recited the Vyomavyāpin mantra, one should bathe it with fragrant waters. (46)
One should tie the unjoined golden thread as an auspicious amulet with the Hṛdaya-mantra;
then, having thoroughly mixed all the fragrances, one should smear them upon the image.
Having covered it with a new cloth and provided with a tuft of kusha grass,
one should strew the altar with two bhāras of rice.
Having placed half a measure of śāli rice, one should place half a measure of rice and [the remainder] as sesame;
one should scatter parched grain and darbha grass, and arrange the offerings beginning with the "egg-born" (birds).
One should have the deity lie upon the bed with the head toward the east and the face turned upward;
having covered [the deity] above with a cloth, one should perform the Vyomavyāpin mantra and the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga).
In the north-eastern direction of the image, one should place the Śiva-pitcher (śivakumbha) and the vardhanī;
one should establish the Śiva-pitcher and establish the Śiva-vardhanī.
Then, with the previously mentioned mantra, one should place eight jars containing five gems and cloth, starting from the east and ending in the northeast.

He should place the jars of the World-Protectors (Lokapālas) around the outside of that [central vessel], which contains the presiding deities of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), covered with cloths.

Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth using their respective root mantras, the preceptor [should perform the rites] for the Goddess seated on a single seat, as well as for the intermediate spaces and the *vardhanī* vessel. (54)
Then, one should place a water-pot for each [deity] on the right side of the image;
furthermore, [one should place branches of] the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Vaṭa trees in the directions starting from the east.
(293) One offers into the principal fire using *śamī*, *khadira*, *bilva*, *arka*, and *palāśa* wood; with the *gaurī* and the bull, the offering is made specifically with *palāśa*.
Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridges,
along with thorns, black gram, sesame seeds, barley, and mustard— these nine substances are offered as oblations.
Clarified butter is offered with the *samidhānīśa* mantra using the left hand;
having offered the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the *puruṣa* mantra, one likewise offers parched grains (*lāja*) with the *ghora* mantra.
One should offer roasted flour with the Sadyojāta mantra, black gram with the Hṛdaya mantra,
and sesame seeds with the Śiras mantra, performing one hundred and eight oblations for each.
The five Brahmans and the six limbs are offered with their respective mantras;
the first syllable, both short and long, is said to be the Brahman-limbs.
Having offered clarified butter with the Tryambaka mantra, one should offer the sacrificial porridge (caru) to the deity with the formula "devasya tvā.
Then, having offered the Vyāhṛtis at the conclusion of the materials, one should touch the image.
At the clear dawn, having performed his ablutions, the preceptor should specifically perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the established method.
Then the preceptor, joined by the instructor and the image-makers,
having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) accompanied by all the ritual substances, [should proceed].
Having recited the mantra "Havyavāham" and "Sviṣṭam agne," one should then perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Īśāna mantra.
Then, according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should give the teacher his sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
thereafter, one should worship the instructor, the guardians of the images (mūrtipās), and all the ritual officiants (padārthins).
One should raise the image and place it upon the bathing altar;
according to the method of the *sthitimārga*, one should arrange thirty-eight jars.
One should arrange a seat there,
as well as the various elements such as song and dance, and circumambulate the temple.
One should recite the Vyomavyāpin mantra together with the five Brahmans and the six limbs;
having installed [the deity] with the Prāsāda mantra, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should bathe [the deity] with the Śiva-kumbha and other vessels while reciting their respective root mantras;
then, one should worship [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as with garments and ornaments.
One should offer an oblation of five colors and then cause betel-leaf to be given;
one should feed the Brāhmaṇas there and then feed the devotees of Śiva.
This has been declared as the form of maintenance; now hear about withdrawal and re-establishment.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, on the Installation of the Form of Stability, in the Vīra-tantra.
Having bowed his head to the God, the Grandfather (Brahmā) inquired: "O Supreme Lord, what indeed is the installation of those whose forms are for the purpose of withdrawal? (1)
The Lord.
I shall describe all of that in its entirety; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
[I shall speak of] the dance of Kāmāri and likewise the burning of Time (Kāladāha).
The slaying of Gaja, the destruction of Tripura, and likewise the killing of Jalandhara;
in the sixth [chapter], the installation of the forms of the Destroyers (Saṃhāramūrtis) is described here.
Rohiṇī, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Mṛgaśiras, Hastā, Revatī, Svātī, and the three Uttarās. (4)
One should establish [the seeds] in a stable zodiac sign, provided it is free from planets in the eighth house;
one should offer the sprouts either on the ninth or the seventh day after the initial rite.
Then, one should properly construct a pavilion directly in front of the temple;
it should also be built to the south and the north, endowed with all the required characteristics.
O best of Brahmins, one should likewise cause a temple pinnacle (kūṭa), a water-shed (prapā), or even a pavilion (maṇṭapa) to be constructed; and make it consist of eighty-one squares.
In the center of the nine squares, there is a pedestal with a height of one *ratni*;
outside of that, on all sides within the human area, the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is prescribed.
The fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa) may be square, a half-moon, triangular, circular, hexagonal, lotus-shaped, or even heptagonal. || 9 ||
O best of Brahmins, one should place [the syllables] in order in the eight directions starting from the east;
and one should construct an octagon between the northeast and the east.
Such indeed would be the form of the dance, which captivates the senses; now hear of it further:
[it may be] square, hexagonal, triangular, or pentagonal. || 11 ||
One should arrange these circles in the cardinal directions and fashion the remainder as follows:
one should construct a seven-cornered figure between Īśāna and Indra.
For the slayer of Gaja, a quadrangular pit (kuṇḍa) is prescribed in the four directions;
likewise, for the slayer of Tripura, there is a square and a triangle in the cardinal directions.
p.
296) And likewise, following this very sequence after the slaying of Jalandhara, one should then cause a seven-sided [structure] to be made between Īśāna and Indra. || 14 ||
Having constructed the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in this very manner, the preceptor should then cause the placement of jewels (ratnanyāsa) to be performed upon the site of Satyaka.
One should scatter śāli rice there and place grains of rice and sesame;
upon that, one should especially install the deity consisting of ninety-six [parts].
Vajra, emerald, lapis lazuli, coral, puṣṭika, ruby, and likewise topaz; || 17 ||
O best of Brahmins, the preceptor should place an indranīla gem in the eastern and other directions,
and having established a māṇikya gem in the center with the Śiva-mantra.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should place the image there;
then, with very glossy rice, one should perform the auspicious ceremony and cause it to be recited.
One should perform the worship of the preceptor and then worship the artisan;
this is declared to be the "Depositing of Jewels" (ratnanyāsa), and the "Unveiling of the Eyes" (netramokṣaṇa) is now described.
One should perform the opening of the eyes at the very station of the Sun, on a day endowed with both [auspicious] eyes, and likewise under a favorable astrological moment (lagna). || 21 ||
One should prepare a sacrificial mound with rice and spread it over with darbha grass;
then, one should place the form of the dance upon it while reciting the Śiva mantras.
One should place eight water-pots, presided over by the deities of the world-protectors (lokapāla), covered with a cloth and facing either eastward or [the other direction].
O Brahmin, he should then have a craftsman strike those brooms and their covers, which are wrapped in cloth, with a golden needle. (24)
The line of eyelashes and the black circle should be drawn;
having inscribed the circle of light, it should be joined with the eye-mantra.
Then, O best of Brahmins, one should perform the eye-homa with clarified butter along with the sacrificial porridge (caru), separately reciting the eye-mantra one hundred and eight times for each.
At that time, one should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana) to be recited;
O Brahmin, one should satisfy [the deity] with gold, dūrvā grass, honey, and clarified butter. || 27 ||
Adorned with golden claws and provided with a palace, one should place clarified butter in either a copper or a bronze vessel. (28)
O Brahmin! one should satisfy [the ancestors] with honey using the mantra "madhuvāta," and one should likewise satisfy them with clarified butter using the mantra "ghṛtamikṣa. || 29 ||
Having brought a cow together with her calf into the presence of Nṛttarūpa,
he should specifically show the cow while reciting the Bhavya mantra.
There, one should show the Brahmins [the image] with the mantra "brahmajajñānam";
moreover, one should especially sprinkle it with the ninety-six-syllable mantra.
One should sprinkle it with water containing unbroken grains while reciting the Śiva mantra;
then, having removed the concealing cloth, one should show it to the people.
Having performed a special purification by sprinkling the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the Pavamāna mantra, one should especially attend to the lutes.
Then, with the mantra *śuddhair ukta*, he should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made;
he should then perform a circumambulation of the village while adorned with all ornaments. (34)
One should cause the image to be placed in water reaching up to the neck;
having specially prepared a water-shed (prapā), one should then arrange the jars there.
He [placed] garments, covered vessels, and threads in the eight directions for one night,
three nights, five, or seven nights.
Afterwards, one should worship the astrologer, and then worship the devotees;
one should place [the image] upon the bathing altar in the northeast quarter of the pavilion.
Then, having discarded the floral remains (nirmālya), one should sprinkle [the deity] with pure water;
one should perform the offering of ghee upon the head with gold, dūrvā sprouts, and unbroken rice grains (akṣata).
One should wash [it] with pure water accompanied by the mantra consisting of ninety-six syllables, which is joined with the Śiva-mantra; one should then prepare [the ritual substances].
One should place the five Brahmans in order from the crown of the head down to the feet;
then one should perform the placement of the thirty-eight Kalās along with the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga).
At an auspicious moment, under a favorable lunar mansion, and accompanied by a favorable karaṇa, at a good conjunction and a favorable lagna.
One should install the pitchers called Śiva with the Śiva-mantra,
and one should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) with the ninety-six-fold mantra.
O best of Brahmins! One should bathe Umākumbha and the pedestal (pīṭha) as well;
or one should consecrate them with water from the jars (kalaśa) starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
One should perform the ritual bathing with the *pañcabrahma* mantra according to the prescribed rule,
and one should especially worship [the deity] endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics. (44)
Thereafter, one should present the sacrificial offering (havis) and then cause betel-leaf to be given;
finally, one should cause all the implements for the consecration to be bestowed upon the preceptor (ācārya). || 45 ||
There, one should feed the Brahmins who have performed the investigation and the attendants;
one should also feed the devotees of Śiva there according to one's capacity, along with sacrificial fees.
The mortal who acts in this manner is liberated from all sins;
as long as the ocean of curd remains undiminished, that man dwells in the city of Rudra.
O best of Brahmins! From that day onwards, one should perform a festival;
however, during these first three triads [of days], the rite of hoisting the banner (dhvajārohaṇa) is not performed.
The hoisting of the banner is prescribed either on the seventh day or on the ninth;
when performed in this manner, it brings about great peace and bestows happiness upon the king and the kingdom. (49)
The mortal who acts in this manner goes to the world of Śiva. || 49 ½ ||
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter of the Vīratantra, the ritual procedure for the installation of the form of withdrawal.
Having prostrated again, Brahmā spoke to the Supreme Lord:
"O Supreme Lord, tell me how the installation of Gaurī is performed! (1)
The Lord.
O Four-faced One, listen to all of this in brief:
Rohiṇī, Punarvasu, Puṣya, and likewise Mṛgaśiras. (2)
Hasta, Revatī, Svātī, and the three Uttaras—
these should be performed when the moon is in a fixed zodiac sign (sthirarāśi), provided it is the eighth lunar day and free from malefic planets.
I shall describe the form of the Goddess; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
She has two eyes, a beautiful face, excellent breasts, and is in the full bloom of youth.
Having two hands and two feet, with her hand holding a blue lotus, wearing a basket-shaped crown, and adorned with all ornaments. || 5 ||
Clad in garments of fine silk, endowed with the Channavīra [ornament], and joined with anklets upon her feet— this is described here as the form of the Goddess.
One should construct a square pavilion in front of the temple;
then, one should have that pavilion built according to the characteristics previously described.
Having established eighty-one squares, there are nine altars in the center;
the pit in the middle of that [central area], occupying three squares, is said to be the central *kuṇḍa*.
From the east to the northeast, the womb [of the mandala] should be fashioned in the shape of an ashvattha leaf,
according to the characteristics and in accordance with the previously stated procedure.
The placement of jewels (ratnanyāsa) should not be performed, especially for the goddess Umā;
instead, gold should be deposited there in the eight directions in due order.
O best of Brahmins, one should perform a very affectionate rite there with the Gaurī-gāyatrī mantra, joined with the third letter of the second group [the labials].
The third of the seventh [letter], joined with the fourth of the first [letter] and combined with the Bindu and Nāda, is here called the root mantra.

The third [syllable] of the second [group], however, is the Brahma-syllable extracted in sequence; these short ones are designated as the Brahma-syllables, while the long ones are said to be the limbs (aṅgas). || 13 ||
On a day conjoined with the two stars of the Netra constellation, one should perform the rite of Nayana-mokṣaṇa;
furthermore, one should smear the footprint of the Sun with cow-dung.
With eight *droṇas* of rice, one should prepare a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*);
having placed half of that amount of rice, one should place half of that amount of sesame seeds.
Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, one should strew it with *darbha* grass;
one should place a new cloth there and then install the image.
One should wrap the Goddess with a cloth, joined with a concealed veil;
one should then place eight jars all around, beginning with the left and so forth.
Then, using a golden needle, one should draw the line of the eyelashes;
having drawn the black circle, one should then draw the circle of light.
Afterwards, one should honor the artisan and then dismiss his weapons;
having wrapped it in cloth, that [image] of the Goddess should be joined with a concealed curtain.
One should place eight jars all around, beginning with the left and so forth. || 19 ||
Then one should perform the Akṣihoma, especially with clarified butter alone;
having prepared the mouth of the fire, one should offer oblations fifty times.
Having offered oblations with the Netra-mantra, the sacrificial porridge (caru) is offered in that very same place;
or else, one should fill a copper or bronze vessel with ghee and honey.
Having recited the Netra-mantra one hundred times, and having combined it with *hiraṇyanakha*,
one should then satisfy [the deity] with honey using the mantra "madhu vātā ṛtāya."
Having offered clarified butter and molasses, and having satisfied [the deity], one should apply the Netra-mantra.
With the Bhavya-mantra, one should present a cow with its calf. || 23 ||
There, one should show the Brahmins and show the seven maidens;
one should also show the heap of grain accompanied by the Netra-mantra. || 24 ||
Having removed the concealed cloth, O best of Brahmins, one should show it to all people and perform the consecration with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 25 ||
Having adorned that goddess, one should perform a circumambulation of the village,
or [of a place] on the bank of a river or a pond, which has been smeared with cow dung.
Having placed the pedestal right there, one should set Gaurī upon it;
bathe her with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and perform the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsana). || 27 ||
Having wrapped [the image] in a new cloth and provided it with a tuft of kusha grass,
the preceptor should place the Goddess in the midst of water using the seed-syllable of Gaurī.
Then, one should place the *vardhanī* vessel from the east to the northeast;
it should be provided with a cloth and a lid, and one should also place the [deities] beginning with Vāmā.
And having constructed a water-shed above that, it is prescribed that he should remain there provided with lamps for one night,
three nights, or even five nights.
Having emerged from the water on the previous day, one should enter the temple;
one should bathe the deity with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and clothe it in a new garment.
There, in the middle of the altar, one should place eight *droṇas* of rice;
having placed half of that amount of husked grain (*taṇḍula*), one should place half of that amount of sesame seeds.
(303) One should strew the bed with *darbha* grass and with eggs and so forth;
upon that, the preceptor should place the Goddess Gaurī with the root mantra.
One should specifically place the head toward the east and the feet toward the west;
then, having covered it with a cloth, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
Taking a new vardhanī vessel, one should wrap it with thread; each [vessel] should be filled with pure water and wrapped in cloth. (35)
In the northeastern direction of the divine [mandala], one should place the principal *vardhanī* vessel,
equipped with a *kūrca* grass-bundle and a lid, while reciting the mantra consisting of the seed-syllable of Gaurī.
One should place eight *vardhanīs* starting from the east and ending at the northeast;
each should be provided with a cloth, and gold should be placed within the principal one.
Having worshipped Gaurī in the center, one should worship the nine Śaktis starting from the east up to the northeast, and Manonmanī in the region of Īśa (the northeast).
Then, one should place the form of the weapons of the castes into the *vardhanī* vessel,
and worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the mantra of Gaurī’s root.
One should offer an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa) and present betel-leaf;
thereafter, one should perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) nine or five times.
With the mantra rooted in Gaurī, one should offer oblations in sequence: fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, mung beans, black gram, and likewise barley. || 41 ||

Clarified butter is offered with the Gāyatrī mantra, the sacrificial porridge (caru) likewise with the Hṛdaya mantra, parched grain (lāja) with the Śiras mantra, and mung beans (mudga) are offered with the Vāma mantra. || 42 ||
One should offer a *māṣa* bean with the *sadyojāta* mantra, and barley with the *īśāna* mantra; in this very same sequence, one hundred oblations should be offered for each. (43)
With the mantra "ghṛtam ikṣa," one should perform a hundred oblations with clarified butter alone;
then, with the mantra "devasya tvā," one should offer an oblation of food.

Then, having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblation at the conclusion of each substance, one should touch the image while it is endowed with all the substances, using the mantra beginning with "havyavāha. (45)
Immediately following that, one should offer oblations with the mantra "sviṣṭam agne.
Then, the night vigil (jāgara) is described as being accompanied by dance and song.
Then, one should perform the study of the four Vedas in the four directions;
there, one should mutter the root-mantra of Gaurī in the four directions beginning with the southeast (āgneya).
Then, at the clear dawn, having performed his bath,
the preceptor should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of emanation according to the path prescribed for the placement of mantras.

Then, the best of preceptors should perform the *vāsanahoma* according to the prescribed rite; he should offer oblations of sacrificial wood (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and cooked rice (*caru*). (49)

Having offered one hundred oblations to Gaurī with the root-mantra of Gāyatrī and separately with the *hṛdaya* mantra, at the conclusion, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is made in due order with the verse beginning "yad asya."
One should give a fee to the preceptor consisting of ornaments for the five limbs,
along with garments, jewelry, cows, land, gold, and so forth.
There, one should worship the ritual objects (padārthas), and the instructor (upadeṣṭā) should also be worshipped.
Then, having gazed upon the Goddess for a moment, one should gradually cause her to rise.
Having placed [the deity] upon the bathing altar, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
then, by means of the sequence of the *sṛṣṭinyāsa*, one should perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*) upon the limbs of the Goddess. (53)
Perform the circumambulation of the Pradhāna, the Vardhanī, and the Vimāna;
one should especially bathe [the deity] while recollecting the root-mantra of Gaurī.
One should bathe the eight Vardhanīs with the five Brahmans and the six limbs; thereafter, one should cause the ceremonial bath (snapana) to be performed according to the extent of one's means.
One should offer an oblation of five colors and then cause betel-leaf to be given;
one should feed the Brāhmaṇas there and also feed seven young girls.
Thereafter, he should especially perform auspicious rites in the pavilion;
having smeared it with cow dung, he should then scatter rice grains upon it.
Having placed it well upon rice, and likewise on a human footprint,
one should establish the Goddess on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and place her in the southern direction.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before him, he should perform the rite of the "mouth of fire" (agnimukha);
having invoked Viṣṇu there, he should offer [the oblation] preceded by water.
Then, joined with the Gaurī-bīja and combined with the Brahmā-aṅga,
one should touch the stone with the mantra beginning with "tiṣṭha" (stand firm) at the heart.
Having filled the teacher’s hand with parched grains (lāja) while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra,
one should cause the oblation of parched grains (lājahoma) to be performed with the Īśāna-mantra.
Then, having performed a circumambulation, one should offer fried grain oblations (lājahoma) again and again;
specifically, having offered them three times, one should likewise offer with the mantras beginning with "citta."
Having performed the final oblation with the mantra *yadasya*, one should immediately offer [the next] thereafter;
this is declared to be the "separated seat" (*bhinnāsana*). Now hear about the "united seat" (*sahāsana*). (63)
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, the ritual procedure for the installation of Gaurī, in the Vīratantra.
