I shall describe the installation of the sandals; listen, O Four-faced One!
One should have them made of gold, silver, copper, or even iron.
One should especially have it made either of ivory or of wood;
I shall now duly describe its characteristics in their proper order.
The length of the sandals is declared to be twelve finger-breadths for the best, nine finger-breadths for the middling, and seven finger-breadths for the lowest.
Its width should be half of that, and in its center, half of that again;
the height should be three finger-breadths or more, starting from one finger-breadth.
A foot-rest should be made, and above that, a circular base is prescribed;
then one should have sandals fashioned, endowed with such characteristics as these.
Having adorned the perimeter with rubies and other precious gems, one should,
in the event that gems are unavailable, have it made with gold and the like.
I shall now proclaim the ritual for consecration within the auspicious pavilion previously described; one should perform the purification of the pavilion according to one's means. (7)
One should perform the Vāstu-homa for the quarters according to the prescribed characteristics,
having encircled it with garlands of Darbha grass and provided it with four arches (toraṇas).
Having erected banners in the eight directions, adorned with canopies,
decorated with strings of pearls, and beautified with garlands of flowers; (9)
The altar-platform (vedikā) should be made with the height of a jeweled pinnacle and its surface like the belly of a mirror;
then, one should place eight *droṇas* of rice in its center.
Having placed half a measure of śāli rice, one should place half a measure of rice and [the remaining] half a measure of sesame seeds;
having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, one should strew it with darbha grass.
Then the wise one should prepare a bed there for the Lord of Gods with eggs and other materials; having emerged from the water and performed especially thorough purification.
There, standing upon the footprint of Puṣpadanta, he should enter the temple;
and the preceptor, having become pure, should wrap [the image] in a new cloth.
Wearing a turban and an upper garment, and adorned with all ornaments,
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon all the limbs using the seed-syllable of the preceptor.
When joined with the instructor, it is called the "two teachers":
the instructor is said to be the body, and the teacher is said to be the living soul (jīva). || 15 ||
O Brahmin, it should be made enduring and capable of bestowing all prosperity;
the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) should be performed according to the prescribed characteristics.
There, one should touch with both hands from the letter *ka* to the end of the feet;
then, one should sequentially place the five Brahmans, starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger.
One should perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in sequence, starting from the middle finger and ending with the index finger;
furthermore, one should specifically place the weapon-mantra (astra) upon the palms of the hands.
One should then project the thirty-eight kalās upon the preceptor;
having cast off the state of being a worldly being, one should contemplate, "I am Śiva. (19)
One should bathe the image with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the Śiva-mantras;
thereafter, one should tie the protective amulet (kautuka), joined with a golden thread.
Having thoroughly mixed two palas of camphor with saffron and sandalwood, one should smear it all over [the image]. || 21 ||
At an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction, one should have Śiva laid upon the bed;
then, having covered the entire image with a new cloth.
One should worship with the *prāsāda* mantra, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
then, having taken up a new water-pot, one should wrap it with a thread.
Having filled it with pure water, he [should place] that vessel together with its brush,
its lid, its cloth, its gold, and endowed with the five gems.
One should place the Viṇika and other items joined with the actual substance;
one should install the Śiva-kumbha in the northeastern direction of the image.
Having worshipped Śiva in the Śiva-kumbha with the five Brahmans and the six limbs,
one should place the Vardhanī vessel to its left, established with the Gaurī-bīja.
From the east up to the northeast, it should be joined with the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras).
Then one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) during the day, likewise in the central square where there is no deviation.
Thereafter, the oblation should be performed according to the prescribed characteristics. || 28 ||
The palāśa, aśvattha, bilva, udumbara, and plakṣa;
as well as khadira, śamī, and likewise apāmārga. (29)
These [fires], beginning with the eastern one, are in order; and in the center, there is indeed the Pālāśa fire.
Among all oblations whatsoever, the Pālāśa is said to be in the center.
O best of Brahmins! Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, sesame seeds, mung beans, and black gram—these nine substances are mentioned here.
The *samidhs* are indeed the heart, and the clarified butter (*ājya*) is said to be the head;
the *caru* oblation is the crest-lock (*śikhā*), and the parched grains (*lājās*) are with the armor (*kavaca*).

Then, having offered a mustard seed with the Netra mantra and barley grains with the Astra mantra, one should offer sesame seeds with the Īśāna mantra and mung beans are offered with the Sadyojāta mantra. (33)
One should offer a *māṣa* with the left hand, following this very sequence;
[offering] a thousand, or half of that, or even half of that again. (34)
One hundred and eight, or even one hundred, oblations should likewise be offered to Tirīśa, Vijaya, Ugra, and Atidhāśrīma; these are the deities of the fire sacrifice (homa).
Vāmī, Jyeṣṭhī, Kālī, and likewise Kalavikaraṇī;
Balavikaraṇī, Balapramathinī, and Sarvabhūtamanonmanī. (36)
O best of Brahmins! The names of the Śaktis in the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are stated in due order.
After touching the image at the conclusion of the ritual materials, [one should worship] with the five Brahmans and the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
Then, one should perform the recitation of the four Vedas in the four directions;
likewise, the Vyoman-prāsāda mantra and the Brahma-aṅga mantra.
Then, initiated brāhmaṇas should recite [mantras] in the four directions;
those three joints [of the ritual] were filled with dancing. || 39 ||
Immediately thereafter, while reciting the mantra "Sviṣṭam agne," one should offer oblations into the fire, which is joined with all the ritual substances.
The mind and other faculties, Jaya and the others, and the Rāṣṭrabhṛt offerings are sacrificed;
O Brahmin, they are sacrificed in sequence, and thereafter one should offer the Vyāhṛtis.
The Śiva-initiation should be bestowed upon one who possesses the [proper] characteristics;
those who carry out the Śiva-initiation know that it includes the attendants and the ritual implements. 42.
When this has been done, O best of Brahmins, it brings happiness to the king and the kingdom;
then the *avasāna-homa* is offered into the principal fire.
The Sviṣṭakṛt offering is made in sequence with the mantra beginning "yad asya karmaṇaḥ," and at dawn, one should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and all others in every respect.
One should first honor the preceptor with garments, rings, and other such gifts;
one should especially bestow upon the preceptor the fivefold ornaments.
The fee for the teacher (ācārya) is declared to be ten niṣkas for the lowest grade, double that for the middle grade, and triple that for the highest grade. 46.
O auspicious lady, the sacrificial fee for the image-protectors (mūrtipās) shall be one-tenth of that [total],
while the fee for the chanters of hymns, the Adhvaryu priests, and others shall be half of that.
Having performed the smearing with cow-dung, one should arrange [the site] in the center of a lotus;
in the eastern direction of the lotus, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is said to be triangular.
Having performed the purification of the sandals there, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited;
then, having sprinkled them with the *pavamāna* [mantra], one should proceed with the pure materials that have been prepared. (49)
One should scatter half of that amount of rice there, along with sesame seeds;
one should place two sandals in the middle upon a new cloth.
Having covered [the vessel] with a new cloth, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
then, among the groups ending with the class of spirits (bhūta), one should unite the fire.
That [seed-syllable] joined with the two eyes (kṣa), conjoined with the letter of death (ra), and mounted upon Śiva and Viṣṇu (ha) is called the seed-syllable of the sandals (pādukā-bīja). || 52 ||
Having recollected this mantra, one should place [the deity] facing the east;
the two deities Śrī and Bhūmi are likewise proclaimed to be in the southern direction. (53)
Taking a new *vardhanī* vessel wrapped with thread,
one should fill it with pure water along with *kūrca* grass-bundles and a lid.

He should place garments joined with gold starting from the east and ending at the northeast; then, O Lord of the Quarters, he should place the *pādukā* in the northeastern direction and the *vardhanī* thereafter.
One should install [the deities] starting from the east and ending with the northeast according to the powers of speech (vādi-śakti);
however, one should specifically install Manonmanī as the primary [deity]. || 56 ||
One should properly arrange perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps;
thereafter, the fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed according to the previously mentioned procedure.

At the conclusion of the fire-oblation, one should sprinkle [the area] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the Sadyojāta mantra; then, at an auspicious moment and a favorable planetary conjunction, one should install the Vardhanī vessel.
One should install [the deities] starting from the east and ending with the northeast using the root mantra;
having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) using the Śiva-mantra. || 59 ||
Thereafter, one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented, and then cause betel-leaf (tāmbūla) to be offered;
first, one should worship the preceptor (ācārya), and then the attendants (paricārakas).
One should feed the devotees of Śiva and give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) according to their caste;
at the proper time, one should perform the daily festival and circumambulation.
Whether walking in front or behind, he should proceed for the sake of prosperity;
having carried [the sandals], the student (brahmacārī) should then worship the two sandals.
Above the sandals, one should fashion a silver weapon;
the mortal who acts in this manner shall attain the world of Śiva.
The installation of the sandals has been declared; now hear about the installation of the painting.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, the procedure for the installation of the sandals, in the Vīratantra.
Having paid homage to Sureśāna, the Grandfather (Brahmā) inquired:
"O Supreme Lord! Tell me, what is the installation of a painted image (citrapratiṣṭhā) for a deity? || 1 ||
The Lord.
I shall describe all of that in its entirety; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
Know that painting is of three kinds; now hear their distinctions.
O best of Brahmins, one should have an image made even of stone, or indeed have it executed as a painting—whether on clay, joined with a trident, or on a wall-painting or a cloth scroll. (3)
These three types have been described; now listen to the procedure for installation.
In the presence of the painting, construct a pavilion for the consecration. (4)
One should cause the placement of jewels to be performed for both stone and clay [images];
and the placement of jewels must especially be performed for the goddess Umā.
Having constructed the consecration pavilion endowed with the proper characteristics,
the altar (vedikā) is placed in the Brahma-section, while the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is said to be in the human section.
O best of Brahmins, one should have all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) made either circular or square;
however, if they are for the Goddess, O lord of sages, the yoni should be shaped like a leaf of the holy fig tree (aśvattha).
Seated on a single seat, one should perform the opening of the eyes of the Goddess in the four corners of the womb-diagram on a day joined with the lunar mansion of the pair of eyes (Punarvasu).
And according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should begin the opening of the eyes;
the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsana) is not prescribed here, so one should then have it lie upon its bed.
One should perform the Vāstu-homa during the day, endowed with the proper characteristics;
one should spread [the sacrificial grass] in the middle of the altar, provided with a load of rice.
Having placed half a measure of śāli rice, one should place half of that in sesame seeds;
then one should spread darbha grass to form an eight-petaled lotus with its pericarp.
Having recollected each of those with its respective mantra, one should prepare five types of beds;
there, one should cause [the deity] to lie upon a mirror covered with a concealed cloth.
From the east to the northeast, one should install the Vidyeśvaras;
and specifically, one should install the [Śaktis] of the Goddess, beginning with Vāmā. || 13 ||
Having worshipped it with garments, a cover, gold, and a ritual grass mat (kūrca), along with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should present milk-rice (pāyasa). || 15 ||
Then one should perform the fire oblation (homa) together with fuel-sticks of the palāśa tree,
as well as sacrificial wood, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge (caru), parched grain (lāja), mustard seeds, and sesame seeds.
And indeed, O best of Brahmins, seven substances including black gram (māṣa) are offered;
having offered fuel-sticks with the Sadyojāta mantra and clarified butter with the Hṛdaya mantra.
The *caru* should be offered with the left hand, the parched grain (*lājaka*) with the *śiras* mantra, the mustard seeds with the *netra* mantra, and the mung beans with the *īśāna* mantra. || 18 ||
Having offered a māṣa with the eye-mantra, one hundred and eight times for each,
while reciting the Havyavāha mantra, [one should offer] combined with all the ritual substances.
Immediately after that, he should offer oblations with the mantra "Sviṣṭam agne.
Then, at the clear dawn, the preceptor shall perform his bath.
Then, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon one's own body according to the path prescribed for mantras;
thereafter, one should perform the oblation (homa) with clarified butter and an offering of cooked rice (caru).
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations for each specific substance,
he should then have the four Vedas recited by those learned in the four Vedas in the four directions.
The expiation, however, should be offered with the *cittādi* and *jayādi* mantras;
having offered these, one should subsequently offer the oblation with the verse beginning "yad asya. || 23 ||

The teacher should be given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) together with ornaments for the five limbs; furthermore, one should especially worship those who perform the oblations and the ritual materials. (24)
Then, one should dig a water-vessel in front of the image;
having placed a mirror upon it, it should be consecrated with the root mantra.
One should sprinkle the painted image, and then bathe it in a mirror;
furthermore, one should especially bathe the principal water-pot. || 26 ||
One should bathe [the deity] starting from the east and ending at the northeast with their respective mantras;
thereafter, one should present the sacrificial offering and then cause betel to be given.
One should feed the Brāhmaṇas there, and then one should feed the devotees of Śiva;
for this is indeed the sequence for the installation of all the deities.
It should be performed with its respective mantra; there is no distinction in the ritual procedure.
One should cause all the materials for the consecration to be presented to the preceptor. || 29 ||
"The installation of the painting has been explained; now hear the installation of the image on a wooden plank.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter of the *Vīra-tantra*, the ritual procedure for the consecration of paintings.
Having first prostrated before the God of gods, the Grandfather (Brahmā) asked:
"O Supreme Lord, tell me: what is the procedure for the installation of the celestial chariot? || 1 ||
The Lord said: "O Four-faced One! Listen as I shall declare all of that in its entirety.
Rohiṇī, Punarvasu, Puṣya, and likewise Mṛgaśiras. (2)
Hasta, Revatī, Svātī, and the three Uttaras;
as well as the second, fifth, twelfth, or thirteenth lunar days. (3)
It should be performed during a fixed zodiacal sign when the eighth house is devoid of planets;
at such times as these, carry out the installation of the celestial chariot.
The offering of the sprouts is said to take place on the fifth day or the seventh night,
specifically after having constructed a water-shed (prapā) in front of the temple itself.
Then, one should have a pavilion constructed in the manner previously described;
in its center, one should make an altar that is one cubit in height.
Outside oneself, however, a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is prescribed for all people;
now listen to the descriptions of the Nāgara, Drāviḍa, and Vesara types.
A quadrangle, a vulva-shape, a half-moon, a triangle, a circle, a pentagon, a lotus, and an octagon. || 8 ||
O Brahmin, the Vesara is proclaimed; now follows the fifth type of sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
It is said that the pits should be arranged in the four directions and in the northeast, as previously described.
It was provided with four gateways, adorned with garlands of *darbha* grass,
furnished with canopies and banners, and decorated with flower garlands.
For a temple, a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the four directions is prescribed for Kubera, while that of the Drāviḍa style is circular.
Then one should have sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) made, shaped like a half-moon with a raised rim; to its east, a water-whirlpool (jalāvarta) should be fashioned, adorned with cloths and garlands.
Having filled them with pure water and placed them upon rice,
one should set them down there in the four directions with the heart mantra.
One should perform the Vāstuhoma during the day, endowed with the proper characteristics;
and the preceptor, having become pure, should be wrapped in a new garment.
Wearing a turban and an upper garment, he should smear the temple with fragrant substances;
he should especially encircle the temple with garlands of darbha grass.

One should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited there, sprinkle with the *pavamāna* mantra, and offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to the deities of the site (*vāstu*) according to the previously mentioned procedure. || 16 ||
One should wrap the temple with a new cloth while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra;
one should then hang [the cloth] with a new cloth while reciting the *prāsāda* mantra.
One should likewise encircle the stūpa with a garland of darbha grass and flowers;
the temple-consecration fire-sacrifice (prāsādahoma) should be performed, especially within the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha).
With the mantra "mama āpya," one hundred oblations of clarified butter (ājya) are offered;
with the mantra of Īśa, fuel-sticks (samidh) are offered, and clarified butter is offered with the Vāma mantra. || 19 ||
Having offered a *caru* oblation with the heart-mantra one hundred times,
one should likewise perform oblations in the four directions according to the sequence of the peace-offering (*śāntihoma*).

Then, one should perform recitation by means of the four Vedas in the four directions; likewise, the temple itself [is established] through the fire-oblation (homa). Now listen to [the description of] the seat of Śiva.
One should smear the altar in the previously mentioned pavilion with cow dung and scatter upon it two *bhāras* of rice.
Having placed half-measures of śāli rice, one should place half-measures of sesame seeds;
having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, one should strew it with *darbha* grass. (23)
Having taken nine jars, one should wrap them with thread;
having filled them with pure water, they should be provided with cloths and bunches of kuśa grass.
O Brahmin! One should place the primary pitcher in the center according to the sequence;
having taken up the nine pitchers, one should encircle them with a thread.
The second [syllable] consists of the seventh [consonant] together with the final group [of consonants], joined with the fourteenth vowel and endowed with the bindu and nāda. || 26 ||
O best of Brahmins! The root mantra of the celestial chariot (vimāna) is now declared here;
one should indeed place it within the primary water-pot (pradhānakalaśa). || 27 ||
In the center, the deity Śiva is joined by the Vidyeśvaras;
Viṣṇu with his water-pot is in the east, and Dakṣiṇāmūrti is in the south.
The origin of the Liṅga is in the western quarter, while Pitāmaha is in the north;
and in the four directions starting from the east belongs Śivavidyeśvara.
The wise one should place Vighneśa in the center and install Agni;
and specifically, he should install Durgā in the north.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using their respective root mantras, the preceptor should thereafter present the sacrificial oblation and then cause betel to be offered.
Then one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with palāśa fuel-sticks,
along with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge (caru), parched grains (lāja), mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds.
(319) Bamboo, black gram, green gram, and pigeon pea, joined with the eleventh;
from the northeast (īśāna) ending with the southeast (sadyojāta), joined with the three by means of the heart-mantra. || 33 ||
Either one hundred and eight or fifty oblations are offered;
having offered the seed-syllable of the celestial chariot (*vimāna*) for all [deities], one hundred oblations are likewise made.
At the clear dawn, having performed worship, the preceptor should perform his bath;
specifically, he should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the path prescribed for the placement of mantras.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal, as well as the other [rites] such as nyāsa;
thereafter, the most excellent teacher should perform the ritual of perfuming (vāsana) and the fire-oblation (homa).
One hundred oblations of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice should be offered with the Prāsāda mantra;
twenty-five oblations combined with the seed-syllable of the Vimāna are prescribed.
Immediately thereafter, while reciting the mantra "Sviṣṭam agne," one should offer oblations into the fire, which is provided with all the necessary materials.
The *cittādi*, the *jayādi*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings are sacrificed; having sacrificed these, one should then perform the final *pūrṇāhuti* with the verse "yad asya" at the end.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, accompanied by ornaments for the five limbs;
then, O best of Brahmins, one should carry the pitcher over the head.
Standing atop the temple, one should perform circumambulation of the celestial chariot (vimāna) while reciting the mantra that pervades the sky and is joined with the base of the vimāna. 41.
One should bathe the water-pot itself with the five Brahmans and the six limbs;
one should bathe it starting from the east up to the northeast, using their respective mantras.
O best of Brahmins, one should bathe the forms of the directions with their respective mantras;
having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should especially offer sacrificial oblations.
One should feed the Brāhmaṇas there and also feed the devotees of Śiva; O best of Brahmins, one should cause seven maidens to be given garments and other gifts.
The installation of celestial chariots has been declared; now hear about the installation of human [images].
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, the procedure for the installation of the celestial chariot (*vimāna*), in the *Vīratantra*.
The Grandfather.
Having paid homage to the Lord of the World, the Grandfather (Brahmā) inquired:
"Who is it that establishes humans [in their duties], having been filled with the knowledge of Śiva? || 1 ||
O Lord, tell me about the establishment of the sages and the kings!
[Thus spoke] Īśvara.
I shall declare all of that in its entirety; listen, O Four-faced One! || 2 ||
One should have images and other such objects fashioned from all the castes in both the direct and inverse orders, as well as those perfected through the grace of Śiva.
It may be made of gold or silver, or of copper, or of bell-metal;
it may also be made of stone, wood, clay, or even painted.
Having divided the door into nine parts, one should construct the height of each image as one part,
measuring four, five, or six tālas according to the mātrā-aṅgula.
It should be made seven, eight, or nine *tālas* in height, endowed with the [proper] characteristics; for indeed, whatever form arises at the time of Śiva’s grace, that is what should be fashioned.
O Brahmin, one should have that image made standing or indeed seated;
for sages, it should be in the form of a sage, while for kings, it should be like a king. (7)
Having performed it in this manner according to the injunctions, one should install them according to the prescribed rite:
Ilā, Piṅgalā, and likewise Suṣumnā. (8)
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, the illustrious Pūṣā,
Alaṃpuruṣā, Ruhī, and Śaṅkhinī is remembered as the tenth.
These ten channels are proclaimed as the carriers of the vital breaths: Vimalā, Ghoṣaṇī, Pṛthivī, and likewise Āvinī; || 10 ||
Tejovatī, Vāyuvegī, Gaganī, Mardanī, as well as Śodhanī, Vyādhinī, Rasāvatī, and Mudvatī. || 11 ||
Sraṃsanī, [the others], Śabda, Sparśā, Nakulā, and likewise Sarvagā—these are the twenty-eight channels combined together. (12)
Then one should place the principal channels within that very form;
O Lotus-seated One, listen as I proclaim its mantra. (13)
One should take the second letter of one's own name, or even the second letter of the second [name];
then the second letter of the seventh [vowel] and the fourteenth letter of the first [vowel]. (14)
The human seed-syllable (mānuṣa-bīja) is said to be joined with the bindu and nāda.
The short vowels are declared to be Brahmā; one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the long vowels as the limbs.
In this very same manner, one should likewise establish the mounts of the Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Asuras, Siddhas, and deities.
(322) One established upon a lotus should perform the deposition of jewels;
the best of teachers should deposit either nine jewels or five jewels. 17.
Having constructed a pavilion as before, endowed with the proper characteristics, one should install the Goddess in the center; the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is said to be around her.

A square, a bow-shaped [crescent], a circle, a triangle, and an eight-cornered [octagon]—these are located in the four directions starting from the east, and the eight corners starting from the northeast. || 19 ||
One should place rice in the center of the altar and then install the image;
one should perform the rites of opening the eyes and consecration according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) in water for either one night or three nights; then the wise man [should proceed].
Having emerged from the water, one should bathe [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) on the preceding day;
thereafter, one should perform the Vāstu-homa according to the prescribed characteristics.
One should strew the altar with śāli rice and place half as much sesame;
the bed should be prepared with five cotton covers and wrapped in cloth.
One should place the image upon the bed, covered with a concealed cloth;
and likewise, O Brahmin, one should apply the twenty-five [syllables] to the body.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space;
as well as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth. || 25 ||
Speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ as the fifth;
and hearing, skin, eyes, tongue, and the nose as the fifth. || 26 ||
Then, one should place the twenty-five principles within the body: mind, ego, intellect, primordial nature (prakṛti), and likewise the person (puruṣa). || 27 ||
One should perform the *sṛṣṭinyāsa* according to the path prescribed for the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*);
having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should thereafter place the water-pots (*kumbha*).
One should place the images, along with their cloths, covers, gold, and brushes,
on the right side, and position the water-pot with the root mantra.
One jar should be established on the northern part of the image;
one should then place eight jars starting from the east and extending to the northeast.
One should assign Prāṇa, Apāna, Vyāna, Udāna, and Samāna, as well as Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, and Devadatta, to the directions starting from the east. (31)
One should place the image of Devadatta in the southern jar;
having placed Dhanañjaya in the northern one, one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) as the food offering (naivedya) and then cause betel-leaf (tāmbūla) to be given;
thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) together with palāśa fuel-sticks.
There, being disciplined, one should prepare the Śiva-fire; it carries [the oblation] and the offering is cast into it:
fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds.
One hundred oblations each should be offered with *śālinī*, *vāraga*, and *dhūmacampaka*, accompanied by the five Brahmans and the six limbs.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with all the ritual substances while reciting the root mantra;
thereafter, one should have the study of the four Vedas conducted in the four directions.
Then, having repeatedly transformed the mind and the other faculties into the Victors and so forth, one should touch [them];
thereafter, at the clear dawn, the preceptor shall perform his bath. (37)
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of emanation according to the path prescribed for the placement of mantras;
thereafter, one should perform the homa of latent impressions (vāsanā) together with sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), and the sacrificial porridge (caru).
O best of Brahmins! Having offered one hundred oblations for each [verse] with the root mantra, at the end, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is performed in due order with the verse beginning "yad asya. (39)
Then one should give the teacher his fee and worship the ritual materials;
having worshipped the instructor according to the path prescribed in the scriptures. (40)
Having raised the image, one should place it upon the bathing altar;
then, according to the method prescribed for the placement of mantras, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of emanation (sṛṣṭi-nyāsa).
One should bathe the pitcher of Devadatta with the root mantra,
and perform breath-retentions (kumbhaka) beginning from the vital breath (prāṇa) using the five Brahmans and the six limbs.
Then the wise one should bathe [the deity]; by performing the ritual sipping (ācamana), he becomes purified.
He should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) as the food offering (naivedya) and then cause betel-leaf (tāmbūla) to be given.
There, one should feed Brāhmaṇas who are devoted solely to Śiva;
then, one should cause gold and garments to be given to all of them.
The installation of the human [image] has been declared; now hear about the installation of the pedestal (piṇḍikā). || 44 ½ ||
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, the "Rite for the Installation of Humans," in the Vīratantra.
Having prostrated before Śiva according to the prescribed rites, the Grandfather (Brahmā) inquired:
"O Lord, tell me all that regarding the installation of the *piṇḍikā*. (1)
I shall describe all of that in its entirety; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
One should construct a square pavilion in front of the temple.
It should be five, seven, eight, or even nine cubits in size,
provided with sixteen pillars and equipped with four doors.
In the center, one should construct a platform one palm-span high,
covered with a canopy and draped with banners in the cardinal directions.
Having encircled it with garlands of *darbha* grass and adorned it with archways (*toraṇa*),
one should scatter there *śāli* rice, husked rice, and sesame seeds.
One should place a pedestal consisting of five squares upon that;
O Brahmin, one should then wash the pedestal with the Prāsāda mantra.
One should not wash the pedestal with water from the eight types of clay while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, nor with earth from an anthill, a pond, or likewise from the roots of *kuśa* grass.
In a river, in a mountainous region, in a cow-pen, or from an elephant's tusk—
the wise man should cleanse the sacred clay (brahmamṛd) in a pure place.
One should wrap the pedestal with cloth and place it upon a heap of rice;
there, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited by those who proclaim well-being and auspiciousness.
Having taken the *vardhanīs* and the nine [vessels], one should wrap them with a triple thread;
having filled them with pure water, one should place them outside the pedestal.
(326) One should place gems, new cloth, betel nut, and *takkola* into the *vardhanī* vessel there, starting from the east and ending in the northeast. || 11 ||
One should place the principal *vardhanī* vessel in the northeast direction of the pedestal,
together with a *kūrca* grass-bundle, gold, and a pair of garments, each placed separately.
Having first placed Vāmī in the east, Jyeṣṭhā in the south-eastern quarter,
Raudrī in the south, and Kālī in the region of Nirṛti.
One should specifically install Kalavikariṇī in the west (Vāruṇī), Balavikaraṇī in the northwest (Vāyavya),
and Balapramathinī in the north (Saumya).
One should install Sarvabhūtadamanī starting from the northeast (Īśa) in due order;
having installed the goddess Manonmanī in the center, one should worship her with perfumes and other offerings.
Then one should offer milk-rice as the food offering (naivedya) and provide betel-leaf;
thereafter, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
As many-sided as the pedestal (pīṭha) may be, so many-sided should the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) be;
O Brahmin, for a circular pedestal, a circular pit is prescribed here.
The sacrificial fuel (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), cooked rice (caru), parched grain (lāja), bamboo, mung beans (mudga), and mustard seeds—
one should offer the fuel with the Sadyojāta mantra and the clarified butter with the Vāmadeva mantra.
Having offered the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Aghora mantra, he should offer parched grain (lāja) with the Heart-mantra;
likewise, he should offer bamboo-shoots (veṇu) with the Īśāna mantra and mung beans (mudga) with the Śiras mantra.
One hundred and eight mustard seeds should be offered individually with the *śikhā* mantra;
furthermore, one hundred oblations for each should be made with the *gaurī* seed-mantra.
Immediately after that, while reciting the mantra "sviṣṭam agne," one should offer oblations into the fire, which is joined with all the ritual substances. (21)
Having repeatedly offered oblations, one should touch the limbs with the *prasṛti* mudrā:
the foot is said to be the *upāna*, and likewise the shank and the lower leg are the *jagatī*.
The *kumuda* is said to be the waist, while the *paṭṭikā* is the navel;
the neck is said to be the heart, and the *paṭṭikā* is indeed the navel. (23)
The ears are said to be the heart, and the navel is the plank;
the neck is said to be the heart, and the two arms are the upper dwarf.
A band for the neck, a band for the face, and one worn upon the heart and the hair;
in this manner, one should fashion their form upon the lotus-seat.
Having performed the oblation with the mantra "yad asya" at the end, one should offer it immediately thereafter;
then, at dawn, during a clear moment and an auspicious conjunction of stars.
Having worshipped the preceptor, one should then worship the artisan;
thereafter, the preceptor, together with the artisans, shall enter the inner sanctum.
One should fashion a bull out of clay, with its hooves and horns made of gold,
accompanied by the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra and the Prāsāda mantra.
One should draw out the pedestal itself with the horn of a bull;
one should then dismiss the pedestal there by casting it into the midst of the water.
Having abandoned the Śaiva pedestal, one should recite the mantra of the Prāsāda,
which consists of ninety-six syllables and pervades the void.
Having joined the pedestal (pīṭha) with the linga, one should then make it very smooth;
an eight-fold bond (aṣṭabandha) should be fashioned, endowed with the proper characteristics. || 31 ||
Lac, beeswax, sugar, and likewise sarja resin;
in the Vāyu-ketu [yantra], brick powder is similar to thick oil. (32)
O best of Brahmins! having made them equal, half [the amount] of oil is prescribed;
one should have it cooked in a copper vessel specifically, together with a craftsman.
One should place cooked food between the Linga and the pedestal;
the mortal who acts in this way is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 34 ||
O best of Brahmins! Having washed it, half of the oil is prescribed [to be used].
One should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited there, and sprinkle it with water while reciting the *pavamāna* hymns.
Having placed those respective portions, one should prepare the tip of the thread.
Then one should place everything that was set upon the altar into the vardhanī vessel;
in the midst of that, one should construct an altar raised to the measure of one aratni.
One should perform the wrapping of the body with a garland of *darbha* grass, joined with four arches; one should cover it above with a canopy.
Having placed banners in the eight directions accompanied by the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala),
one should cause nine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) to be constructed all around the exterior of the altar.
Furthermore, O Brahmin, an altar (sthaṇḍila) endowed with the proper characteristics must be prepared; each specific shape of that seat is here called a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The wise man should scatter especially eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice;
having placed half of that amount of husked rice, he should place half of that amount of sesame seeds.
Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus and strewn it with *darbha* grass,
one should perform the *yātrā-homa* sacrifice in front of the location of the child. (41)
The wise man should place before it the Śiva-pitcher (śivakumbha) and the vardhanī vessel,
along with a thread, a lid, cloth, and gold.
One should place the nine gems, together with all the ritual substances, in the center;
and on all sides, eight jars accompanied by the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras).
Recalling that respective mantra, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
and the preceptor, having become pure, should carry the jar upon his head. (44)
Dressed in new garments, wearing a turban and an upper cloth,
he should perform a circumambulation of the celestial chariot (vimāna) and then place it in the center of the altar.
One should install the Vidyeśvaras from the east up to the northeast;
having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should present milk-rice as an oblation.
Having thoroughly mixed cardamom, cloves, black pepper, uśīra, and sandalwood, one should then specifically rub the mixture onto the liṅga.
Having wrapped both the linga and its pedestal with a new cloth,
the preceptor should then perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the prescribed characteristics.
Palāśa, khadira, aśvattha, plakṣa, and nyagrodha, as well as udumbara, apāmārga, and especially khadira again. (49)
It has been proclaimed in sequence from the east up to the northeast;
one should then place the *śamī* tree between the northeast and Indra.
One hundred and eight, fifty, or twenty-five—
palāśa wood is prescribed here for the fuel of all these fire-offerings.
One should offer sacrificial fuel (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), cooked rice (caru), parched grain (lāja), mung beans, black gram, and mustard seeds;
the fuel-stick with the Sadyo-mantra, and likewise the clarified butter with the Vaktra-mantra.
Having offered the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Aghora mantra, one should offer parched grains (lāja) with the Vāma mantra;
with the Netra mantra alone, there should be mung beans (mudga), while the black gram (māṣa) is said to be for the Hṛdaya mantra.
With the Īśāna mantra, mustard seeds are offered;
with the Prāsāda mantra, twenty-five of each are offered.
Reciting the mantra with the seed-syllable of Gaurī twenty-five times for each [substance],
he should offer them all combined into the fire while pronouncing the Havyavāha [mantra].
Immediately after that, one should offer oblations with the mantra "sviṣṭam agne," followed by the Jaya and other offerings, the Abhyātāna, and the Rāṣṭrabhṛt oblations.
Having performed the oblation at the end with the verse "yadasya," the Sviṣṭakṛt offering is made in due order;
thereafter, one should perform the recitation of the four Vedas in the four directions.
One should recite the Śrī Rudra and then the Pavamāna;
having recited the Puruṣasūkta, one should likewise be endowed with a hymn of praise.
Then, at the clear dawn, having performed his ablutions, the preceptor, dressed in new garments,
wearing a turban and an upper cloth, [proceeded].
Having become tranquil in mind, one should bathe the top of the liṅga with earrings, pendants, necklaces, and likewise with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and rings. 60.
One should bathe [the deity] upon the pedestal with the Gaurī-bīja using the *vardhanī* vessel.
Then, one should bathe the Vidyeśas, starting from the east and ending in the northeast. || 61 ||
One should perform the ceremonial bathing there with one hundred and eight, fifty, or twenty-five [verses], according to the extent of one's available wealth.
One should worship well with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps;
thereafter, one should offer sacrificial food (havis) and then present betel-leaf (tāmbūla).
One should feed the Brāhmaṇas there, and then one should feed the devotees of Śiva.
The installation of the pedestal has thus been described; now hear about the sprinkling with water.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, the procedure for the installation of the pedestal, in the Vīratantra. || 70 ||
Having prostrated before the Lord of the World, Brahmā asks Śaṅkara:
"O Supreme Lord, tell me, what is this sprinkling with water? (1)
The Lord.
I shall explain all of that in its entirety; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
Furthermore, during the construction of the temple, the artisan should then perform the ritual touching (sparśayet).
Furthermore, during the ritual of establishing the pedestal (pīṭhabandha), one may touch outcasts (caṇḍāla) and others;
likewise when there is a fall [of the image], when it is defiled, when it has been touched [by the impure], or when the worship is neglected. || 3 ||
During such times as these, perform the sprinkling with water;
after three nights, on the fifth day, or in seven days, one should begin the rite of offering sprouts.
The *pālikā*, the *ghaṭikā*, and the *śarāva* should each be of three sizes: eight, sixteen, or twenty-four [units].
One should sow seeds there according to the previously mentioned procedure;
one should construct a square pavilion in front of the temple.
It should be nine cubits, eight cubits, or twelve cubits in size,
provided with sixteen pillars and adorned with four doors.

In the portion of Brahmā, there should be an altar (vedī), and it is said that a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be situated all around it; likewise, there should be equal divisions and a circular shape, as well as a predominance of Śiva.
Beyond that, however, it is described by means of the fourfold vigor;
O Lotus-born One, the characteristic of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) of equal sections is found in the [text on] characteristics.
One should indeed make squares in the cardinal directions and circles in the intermediate directions;
however, one should cause an eight-cornered figure to be made between Indra and Īśāna.
This has been declared as the equal portion; now hear that which is superior to Śiva:
the square, the womb, the half-moon, and the triangle. || 11 ||
The circle is indeed five-cornered, the lotus is six-cornered,
and there is a seven-cornered [figure] in the northeast, following the sequence of increasing from the east onwards.
Thereafter, all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) pertaining to the superiority of Śiva shall be declared;
O Four-faced One, listen now to the sacrificial pits of the Trairāśika system.

O best of Brahmins! One should cause a circular sacrificial pit (vṛttakuṇḍa) to be constructed in the cardinal and intermediate directions for a self-manifested liṅga or one installed by the great sages.
Or, in the case of a Liṅga established by the gods, there is no fixed measurement of its form;
at the time of their consecration (prokṣaṇa), it should be according to the shape of each respective pedestal.
Thus the shape of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) has been declared; now hear concerning the proportions.
The preceptor should construct the pit according to the measurements previously stated. (16)
In this very manner, one should have a pavilion constructed;
then, having smeared it with cow dung, it should be provided with archways and banners.
Adorned with a garland of *darbha* grass and decorated with strings of pearls,
one should place upon the altar two *bhāra* measures of rice.
Having placed half a measure of śāli rice, one should place half a measure of sesame seeds;
having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, one should strew it with darbha grass.
Cardamom, cloves, black pepper, nimba, nutmeg, and mura;
sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, uśīra, combined with saffron. (20)
Having stirred [the mixture], one should smear the liṅga and wrap it with a new cloth;
one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) there and bathe it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should place a golden thread or cotton upon the rice;
thereafter, one should bind the protective amulet (kautuka) with the Hṛdaya mantra.
Having likewise gone to the place of the child, one should perform the journey-homa;
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before it with śāli rice, paddy, and sesame seeds.
Endowed with the five Brahmans and accompanied by the six limbs,
one should place the Vardhanī vessel on its left side with the seed-syllable of Gaurī.

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before that [vessel], which is covered with cloth, joined with gold, provided with a brush (kūrca), and equipped with a lid, he should perform the *yātrā-homa* (the oblation for the journey). || 25 ||
(334) One should prepare the Śiva-fire there, and the oblation is offered with the fire-mouth as the opening.
There shall be one hundred oblations each of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge. || 26 ||

The fuel sticks are offered with the Sadyojāta mantra, and the clarified butter is offered with the Vāmadeva mantra; having offered sesame seeds with the Īśāna mantra and then touched the liṅga, the wise man [proceeds].

O Lord of Heroes! Having offered the oblation of the mind and so forth, as well as the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for him, the ten mudrās should be bestowed, endowed with their defining characteristics. || 28 ||
Then, holding the auspicious water-pot (śivakumbha) upon his head in front of him,
the learned man should enter the pavilion and proceed to the center of the altar.
The best of teachers, having thus established the eight jars surrounded by the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras) in the location of the child, should perform the rite accordingly.
I shall speak of this other matter; listen, O Four-faced One!
Having taken nine jars that have been wrapped with thread, [one should proceed].
Having filled the jars with pure water and placed them within the mandala,
they should be joined with five kinds of jewels and wrapped in a pair of cloths.
He should place the brooms and the lids in the center of the altar;
he should install them with the five Brahmans, the limbs of Śiva, and the Śiva-mantra.
One should place the *vardhanī* vessel on his left with the seed-syllable of Gaurī;
it should be provided with cloths, gold, sacrificial grass (*kūrca*), and a lid. (34)
One should place eight jars in order, starting from the east and ending with the northeast;
having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should present milk-rice as an oblation.
Then the fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with sacrificial materials such as fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and so forth:
fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice (caru), parched grain (lāja), mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds. (36)
The nine substances combined with mung beans and black gram are described here:
the Palāśa tree in the eastern quarter and the Udumbara tree in the south-eastern direction.
One should place the Aśvattha tree in the south, the Śamī in the region of Nirṛti (the southwest),
the Khadira in the west, and the Bilva in the northwest.
One should offer oblations into the principal fire with fuel-sticks of *plakṣa* wood in the northern direction and *arka* wood in the northeast, as well as with *palāśa* fuel-sticks. (39)
Then, one should perform the study of the four Vedas in the four directions;
having recited the hymn and mantra, one should then recite the Pavamāna.

The fuel-stick (samidh) is offered immediately with the mantra; the clarified butter (ājya) is offered with the Vāma-mantra; the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Tatpuruṣa-mantra itself; and indeed, the parched grains (lāja) with the Ghora-mantra. || 41 ||
One should offer mustard seeds with the Heart-mantra, barley grains with the Head-mantra, sesame seeds with the Tuft-mantra, and mung beans with the Armor-mantra. (42)
Then, one should offer a māṣa grain by means of the Netra-mantra in successive order;
having offered the Vyāhṛtis at the conclusion of the substances, one should touch the liṅga on all sides.
Immediately after that, while reciting the *havyavāha* [mantra] joined with all the substances, one should offer oblations with the mantra "sviṣṭam agne. (44)
One should offer clarified butter one hundred and eight times with the Tṛyambaka mantra;
the Caru oblation is offered once each with the mantras "Āpo rājā" and "Idaṃ viṣṇoḥ."
Then, at the clear dawn, the preceptor, having performed his ablutions,
should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon his own body according to the method prescribed for the placement of mantras.
Then the best of preceptors should perform the vāsana-homa,
and having prepared all the ritual substances, he should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Then one should give the teacher his fee and worship those who have served at his feet;
thereafter, having removed the vessel from the Linga that has become stale from the previous worship.
One should bathe [the deity] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the five Brahmans,
and then provide the five seats according to the previously mentioned procedure.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the five Brahmans on the liṅga, and then perform the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
Having placed the great mantra Vyomavyāpin upon the top of the liṅga, [one should proceed].
At an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction, one should carry the jar on one's head;
one should perform a circumambulation of the celestial chariot (vimāna) and cause it to enter the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha).
Having recited the *Vyomavyāpin* mantra together with the Brahma-aṅgas,
one should bathe the Śiva-pitcher with the *Gaurī-bīja* and the *Vardhanī* pitcher with the same.
Having bathed the jars of the Lords of Knowledge with their respective mantras, the preceptor should perform the ceremonial bathing there according to the extent of his resources.
One should worship the god and goddess with various garments and garlands;
one should offer oblations of five colors and then cause betel-leaf to be given.
There he should feed the Brāhmaṇas; then he should feed the devotees of Śiva (Śaivas). He should give gifts to the Brāhmaṇas and others, as well as to the Śaivas who serve as attendants. || 55 ||
The mortal who acts in this manner shall attain the world of Śiva. || 55 ½ ||
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, the ritual procedure for sprinkling with water, in the Vīratantra.
Having bowed to the Blessed One, Brahmā indeed spoke these words:
"O Lord! Tell me all about the installation of the Bull (Vṛṣabha)—what is it? || 1 ||
The Lord.
I shall explain all of that in its entirety; listen, O Four-faced One!
According to the measurement of the *pūjāṃśa*, the lowest type of bull (*vṛṣabha*) is determined.
Having divided the portion for worship into five parts,
that which is endowed with one part and joined with the portion for worship shall be the middle bull.
The bull should be excellent if its portion for worship exceeds two parts;
or else, as it is said, it should be measured according to the womb (garbha) in the proper manner. || 4 ||
The characteristic measurement of the bull, however, begins with one part and ends at nine parts;
alternatively, according to the measure of *tāla*, the lowest [measurement] shall be three *tālas*.
The medium [size] should be four tālas, while the best should be five tālas;
it may be made of gold, silver, copper, clay, or stone.
The height of the bull should be nine parts, while the length of its face should be two parts;
the neck should be made one part, and the length of the back six parts.
The peak of the horn should not occupy even a single part [of the base], but should be curved on the exterior;
at the two junctions, it should have a lower portion and indeed take the shape of a cow's mouth.
The nose is joined with eight [parts], as are the two rows of teeth;
it is endowed with two ears and adorned with the form of small bells. (9)
The height of the pedestal (pīṭha) is one part; the tāṭī is said to be half a part.
From the base (pāda), there are four parts, and the bālaka is four parts.
The circumference of the knee is thus one and a half parts, while the width of the base of the thigh is said to be nine parts; the width of the upper part of the thigh is stated to be two parts.
Then, one should have a bull fashioned with these characteristics;
whether it be made of stone, clay, or metal, one should perform the insertion of gems.
Vajra, vaidūrya, and likewise padmarāga,
as well as indranīla and other gems, [should be placed] in the four directions starting from the east.
Having placed a smooth coral in the center, one should then have it made very glossy;
the wise man should then wash the bull and cause the proclamation of a "day of merit" (puṇyāha) to be recited.
On the day corresponding to the pair of eyes (the twelfth), one should perform the rite of opening the eyes;
following the previously mentioned procedure, one should carry out the eye-homa and other such rites.
One should perform the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsana) and wrap [the image] with a new cloth;
one should then perform the immersion in water while reciting the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra. || 16 ||
Having emerged from the water together with the eight jars accompanied by the world-protectors (lokapālas), he should enter the temple on the preceding day. (Then... || 17 ||
One should construct the pavilion for the auspicious fire according to the previously mentioned procedure;
one should construct an altar in the center, and it is said that there should be a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) all around it.
And in the four directions, it is said here that there is a circular *kuṇḍa* in the northeast;
[the seed-syllable] is the fourth of the seventh group, and from that group, the third. (19)
Endowed with fourteen syllables and accompanied by Bindu and Nāda, this should be known as the root of Vṛṣabha; having offered it, it is here called Brahma.
O Brahmin, one should place śāli rice, grain, and sesame seeds in the center of the altar; above that, one should place [the vessel] provided with five woolen blankets.
O Brahmin, the preceptor should have [the disciple] lie upon the bed with the root mantra;
he should then place the ritual jars all around, covered by a cloth.
In the northeastern direction of the bull,
the best of preceptors should install the bull-pitcher with the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra.
He [should offer] a garment and the five jewels; there, the bull is the deity.
One should [worship] the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyēśvaras) as the presiding deities of the external pitcher.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and present milk-rice (pāyasa) as an oblation;
thereafter, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) together with fuel-sticks of the Palāśa tree.

The mantras for the sacrificial fuel (samit), clarified butter (ājya), cooked rice (caru), and parched grain (lāja), combined with mustard seeds, are here stated in sequence, beginning with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta. (26)
One should offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter with the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra;
then, having touched the bull at the conclusion of the ritual materials, one should subsequently offer the Vyāhṛtis.
Having offered a hundred oblations of *caru* with the *gaur dhenu bhavya* mantra,
one should then perform the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the *havyavāha* and other mantras.
O Brahmin, one should establish the bull with the mantra at the base of the bull;
likewise, one should bathe the Pañcabrahma and the water-pot with the Gāyatrī.
One should especially offer the sacrificial oblation (havir) and then cause betel-leaf to be given;
thereafter, one should give the teacher his fee (dakṣiṇā) and then worship the ritual materials (padārthas). || 30 ||
One should feed the Brāhmaṇas there and feed all the people as well;
the mortal who acts in this way goes to the world of Śiva. || 31 ||
The installation of the bull has been declared; now hear concerning the installation of the fire.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, the ritual for the installation of the Bull, in the Vīratantra.
Having first prostrated before the God of gods, the Grandfather (Brahmā) inquired:
"O Lord of gods! O Master! Tell me all about the installation of the sacred fire."
The Lord.
I shall explain all of that in its entirety; listen, O Four-faced One!
In the south-eastern quarter of the temple, the fire-pavilion (agnivimāna) is prescribed.

The measurement for the height of the image, which constitutes the portion for the worship of the primary deity (mūlabera), is now declared; alternatively, it may be determined by dividing the measurement of the sanctum (garbha) into nine parts.
The best of instructors should make each [measurement] equal;
the lowest is known to be two tālas, while the middling should be three tālas.
The height of the image is said to be four tālas at the maximum;
it has one heart, three feet, four horns, and two heads.
He has seven tongues, seven hands, and four eyes;
he is seated upon a lotus throne and is endowed with hair standing erect. (6)
One should place the *sruva* ladle and the trident-topped staff in the right hand;
likewise, the *sruva* and the *akṣatomara* weapon should be placed in the left hands. (7)
With one [hand], he should offer an oblation to the gods with the right hand.
Thus has the characteristic of installation been briefly explained; now listen.
The placement of jewels should be performed as follows: a vajra in the east, likewise;
emerald in the south, and coral in the west. (9)
Having placed a lapis lazuli gem in the northern [position], one should place a ruby in the middle;
on a day joined with two eyes (the second), one should perform the opening of the eyes and the rite of liberation.
The third letter of the [third] class and the fourth letter of the first class, joined with Bindu and Nāda, is declared to be the root of Agni. (11)
The short [syllable] is declared to be Brahmā, and the long [syllable] is said to be Viṣṇu;
one should perform the opening and closing of the eyes according to the previously mentioned rule.
One should bathe it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and then perform a circumambulation of the village;
one should then carry out the ritual immersion in water for it with the root mantra.
For one night, three nights, or even five nights,
construct the aforementioned pavilion right in front of the temple.
One should construct a central altar; the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is said to be around it.
In the four directions and in the northeast, the triangular pit is prescribed. || 15 ||
Having emerged from the water on the previous day, one should bathe [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should install it in a single direction with the root-mantra of Agni. || 16 ||
One should place śāli rice in the center of the altar and place rice grains and sesame seeds;
having prepared the bed with five [materials], one should then install the image.
One should perform the placement of the pitcher (kumbhanyāsa) joined with a concealed cloth;
on its left side, however, there is the increasing [of the rite] by means of the seed-syllable *svāhā*.
One should sequentially place eight jars starting from the east and ending in the northeast:
Hutāśana, Pāvaka, Anala, and Havyavāhana. (19)
One should specifically install Jvalana, Saptajihva, Tapana, and Mahānasa in the directions from the east to the northeast.
Then, having provided [the vessels] along with cloths, gold, sacrificial grass (kūrca),
and lids, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) accompanied by fuel-sticks of the Palāśa tree.

The sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, sesame seeds, mung beans, black gram, wild rice, and bilva fruit shall constitute the eleven [offerings]. || 22 ||
Furthermore, one should perform the oblation in sequence with the five Brahmans and the six limbs;
then, at the clear dawn, the preceptor shall perform his bath.
This is the form of withdrawal, which is called the placement of withdrawal (saṃhāranyāsa).
Then follows the oblation for the purification of latent impressions (vāsanā), consisting of sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and the caru-oblation.
O best of Brahmins, with the root mantra, the wise one should offer a hundred oblations for each [deity] and then install the image facing west in the celestial chariot (vimāna).
One should bathe [the deity] with the root mantra and then install the *vardhanī* vessel;
one should likewise bathe the *kumbha* pitcher with the respective mantras of their own names.
Thereafter, one should present the sacrificial offering (havis) and then cause betel-leaf to be given;
one should feed the Brāhmaṇas there, as well as the attendants and those who have come from afar.
One should worship the preceptor first, and thereafter worship the ritual materials;
the installation of the fire has been described, now hear about the installation of the Mothers.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, the ritual for the installation of the fire, in the Vīratantra.
Having bowed his head to the God, Brahmā questioned Śaṅkara:
"O Lord, tell me all about the installation of the Mothers."
The Lord.
I shall declare all of that in its entirety; listen, O Four-faced One!
[They are] Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī. || 2 ||
Having fashioned images of Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, Vīrabhadra, and Vighneśa, one should install them according to the prescribed ritual.
A wise person should have an image of Agni made, measuring one cubit,
with four arms and two eyes, seated upon a lotus throne.
Vīrabhadra, who holds a black axe in his left and right hands, has been described by me; now listen to Brāhmī as well. || 5 ||
Four-armed, three-eyed, with beautiful breasts and in the full bloom of youth;
in her right and left hands, she holds a rosary and a water-pot. (6)
Above the lotus seat, one should likewise fashion Brahmāṇī,
who has three eyes and four arms, and who wears a crown of matted hair.
To the right, one should have Māheśvarī depicted, seated upon a lotus posture, with a black axe held in her right hand.
She has two eyes and two arms, possesses beautiful breasts, and is in the full bloom of youth;
in her right and left hands, she holds a rosary and a water-pot.
One should likewise have Kaumārī fashioned, adorned with a crown,
two-eyed, four-armed, and holding a conch, a discus, and a mace.
One should have fashioned the goddess Vaiṣṇavī, who wears a basket-shaped crown, possesses beautiful breasts, and is in the prime of youth; thereafter, listen to [the description of] Vārāhī. || 11 ||
The goddess has two eyes and four arms, holding a plow and a pestle as weapons;
she is adorned with a crown and possesses the face of a boar.
Then one should have an image of Vārāhī fashioned, endowed with tusks, possessing four arms and two eyes, and endowed with a dark complexion. (13)
Then one should have Indrāṇī fashioned holding a vajra and a tomara;
then one should have Vighneśa fashioned with four arms and three eyes.
The syllables ya-ra-la-va-śa-ṣa-sa-ha, followed by the letter Ga, which is Gaṇapati, joined with Māyā (the letter I) and Nala (the letter Ra), and further endowed with Bindu and Nāda. 15.
This is declared to be the root mantra, which bestows the fruits of all desires.
The short [syllables] are designated as Brahmā, while the long ones are said to be the limbs (aṅgas).

This is declared to be the deposition of the jewels (ratnanyāsa), the five jewels for all [deities]. One should perform the opening and the releasing according to the very path previously described. 17.
One should perform the Akṣihoma with clarified butter using the Netra-mantra, offering a hundred oblations;
then one should carry out the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsana) according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having emerged from the water on the previous day, he should enter the temple;
he should construct the pavilion as before, according to the very same procedure previously described. (19)
In the middle of that, one should construct an altar; around it, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is said to be [prepared].
It may be square, a yoni-shaped pit, a half-moon, or triangular. || 20 ||
Having assigned [the directions] starting from the east in sequence, one should arrange these sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas): circular, pentagonal, lotus-shaped, and octagonal.
Between Indra and Īśāna, one should cause the seven-faced Gaṇādhipa to pronounce the auspicious day (puṇyāha), and there one should sprinkle [the site] with water while reciting the Pavamāna hymns.
One should strew the altar with śāli rice and place grains of rice and sesame seeds there;
one should prepare a bed with five [types of grain] and then place [the image] upon it.
Having established Brahmāṇī in the center, one should place Māheśvarī in the east;
one should place Kaumārī in the region of fire (the southeast), and Vaiṣṇavī in the south.
One should place Vārāhī in the southwest and Aindrāṇī in the west;
Cāmuṇḍī in the northwest, and Vīrabhadra in the north.
Having placed Gaṇapati in the northeast, covered with a concealed cloth,
the preceptor should then place the ritual jars on the left side of that very [deity]. (26)
The preceptor should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using their respective mantras;
the learned one should then wrap them in cloth, joined with gold.
Thereafter, one should present the sacrificial offering and then cause betel-leaf to be given;
after that, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the prescribed characteristics.
Each of these— palāśa fuel-sticks, sacrificial wood, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds— is joined with one hundred and eight offerings.
With mudga, māṣa, bilva, and combined with plantain fruit, one should perform one hundred oblations for each using the Pañcabrahma mantras along with the six limbs (Ṣaḍaṅga). || 30 ||
With the mantra "ghṛtam ikṣā," twenty-five oblations are offered;
thereafter, one should perform Vedic recitation in the four directions by those versed in the four Vedas.
Then, at the clear dawn, the preceptor, having performed his ablutions,
shall perform the Vāsanahoma, consisting of sacrificial fuel and clarified butter.
O best of Brahmins! Having offered one hundred oblations for each [deity] with the root mantra, he should at the end touch the image, especially each of the ritual substances.
The best of preceptors should place the image there facing west, behind the hero; he should place the goddesses facing north.
Then, one should install Vighneśa facing east;
having taken the consecration pitcher, one should bathe [the deity] with their respective mantras.
One should especially offer sacrificial oblations (havis), and thereafter cause betel leaves to be distributed.
One should feed the Brāhmaṇas there, and one should also feed seven young girls. || 36 ||
The installation of the Mothers has been declared; now hear about the installation of Kumāra.
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, the Ritual for the Installation of the Mothers, in the Vīra-tantra.
Having prostrated before the Lord of the World, Brahmā spoke these words:
"O Lord! Tell me everything regarding the installation of Kumāra."
The Lord.
I shall explain all of that in its entirety; listen, O Four-faced One!
The height of the image should be equal to the elevation of the portion of the altar.
Having divided the womb (garbha) into nine parts,
one should have each individual elevation made at four, five, or even six tālas.
Three-eyed, four-armed, peaceful, and endowed with a crown;
his hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and he holds a rosary and a water-pot.
This bestower of well-being is indeed situated in the center of the lotus, facing eastward;
and the two goddesses, Jayā and Vijayā, are always stationed at his sides.
Then one should place either a peacock, a cock, or an elephant;
thereafter, one should have an image fashioned endowed with these characteristics.
The third from the eighth group, the second from the seventh group, and the fourth of the first group, endowed with the bindu and nāda. (7)
This is declared to be the root mantra, difficult to obtain even for the gods.
The short vowels are called Brahman, and the long ones are said to be the limbs (*aṅga*). (8)
The wise should perform the placement of jewels starting from the east in due order:
diamond, emerald, lapis lazuli, and coral.
Having placed [the gems] in the four directions, one should place an emerald (indranīla) in the center;
there, one should have the eye made very smooth, and perform the opening.
Then, O gentle one, one should draw the eye with a golden needle;
having performed the eye-consecration rite (akṣihoma), one should offer a hundred oblations with the mantra of the eye itself. || 11 ||
One should satisfy [the deity] with the mantra "madhu vātā" while it is covered by a cloth;
having satisfied [it] with the mantra "ghṛtam ikṣu," one should present a cow together with its calf.
One should perform [the rites] with Jaya and Vijayā using the root mantra.
The unsurpassed seed-syllable of Jaya is joined with the Bindu and Nāda;
it is the fourth letter of the seventh group, conjoined with the principle of Māyā. (14)
The seed-syllable of Vijayā is said to be joined with Bindu and Nāda;
one should show it to the Brāhmaṇas there and then have them recite the Puṇyāha.

One should bathe the image with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and wash it while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra; then, clothed in new garments, one should perform a circumambulation of the village.
O best of Brahmins, having performed the ritual immersion in water for three or five nights with the root mantra, [the image] should be covered with a concealed cloth.

On the previous day, having emerged from the water, one should bathe the eight jars situated on all sides— which have the world-protectors as their presiding deities— with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice during the day, and thereafter have a pavilion constructed;
one should place the altar in the center, and it is said that sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should be arranged all around it.
One should make a quadrangular [fire-pit] in the four directions, starting from the southeast;
and between Indra and Īśāna, one should make a triangular fire-pit.
Likewise, between Soma and Īśāna, one should scatter rice upon the altar in the form of a five-cornered figure consisting of dots,
and place grains of rice and sesame seeds.

Having prepared the bed with the five [articles] accompanied by the root mantra, one should lay her down in the middle of the altar; it is prescribed that she should lie with her head toward the east.
Then one should place Jayā and Vijayā on the two sides;
one should bind the protective thread (kautuka) in the east with the Hṛdaya mantra.
One should place the *skandakumbha* (the jar of Skanda) in the north-eastern direction of the image;
one should then place Jayā and Vijayā on the two sides in due order.
One should place eight jars in sequence, starting from the east and ending in the northeast, each covered with cloth, containing gold, provided with a tuft of hair, and furnished with a lid.
And Kumāra, and Guha, and likewise Subrahmaṇya, as well as the commander-in-chief, the foremost of the gods, and likewise the son of Hara. || 26 ||
One should also install Śaravaṇodbhava and Kārttikeya, worshipping them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, by means of their respective names and mantras. (27)
Afterwards, one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented, and then cause betel-leaf (tāmbūla) to be offered.
Thereafter, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) together with fuel-sticks (samidh) of the Palāśa tree.
Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, sesame seeds, along with rice, nīvāra, wheat, and mung beans. (29)
Having specifically offered oblations in sequence with the five Brahmans and the six limbs,
one should especially offer one hundred oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra of Skanda.
Then, at the clear dawn, the preceptor, having performed his ablutions,
should perform the Vāsanahoma, consisting of sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and caru-oblation.
O best of Brahmins, one should offer fifteen oblations with the root mantra;
thereafter, one should perform Vedic recitation in the four directions by means of the four Vedas.
Immediately thereafter, while reciting the mantra "Sviṣṭam agne," one should offer oblations into the fire which is provided with all the ritual substances.
The supreme preceptor should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* with the mantra "yadasya" and,
having raised the Goddess from her bed, perform the *sṛṣṭinyāsa*.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, along with ornaments for the five limbs;
one should especially bathe the Skanda-pitcher with the root-mantra of Skanda.

One should establish Jayā and Vijayā with their respective root mantras; however, the invocation (āvāhana) should be performed with the Vāmadeva mantra, while the installation (sthāpana) should be done with the Sadyojāta mantra. || 36 ||
The consecration is performed with the Īśāna mantra;
likewise, the offering of fragrance and other substances is made with the Hṛdaya mantra, and the flower with the Śiras mantra.
One should never cause garments and all other such things to be offered within the heart;
one should never offer the food offering (naivedya) within the heart, but rather perform the perpetual festival (nityotsava). || 38 ||
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) on a small platform, one should worship it with perfumes and flowers;
then, having gone before the image, one should subsequently remain for a moment.
One should enter the Ālaya; therein, the indicative sign is now described.
One should perform a festival there, endowed with the proper characteristics. (40)
The installation of the Skandas has been described; now hear the installation of Jyeṣṭhā.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, the ritual for the installation of Skanda, in the Vīratantra.
Having prostrated before the Lord of the World, Brahmā questioned Śaṅkara:
"O Lord! Tell me all about the installation of Jyeṣṭhā."
The Lord.
I shall explain all of that in its entirety; listen, O Four-faced One!
The height of the image is stated according to the measure of the pūjāṃśa.
Having divided the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) into nine parts, each image should have a height of one part;
the height of the image may be four, five, or six tālas.
Having two hands and two eyes, endowed with a gentle countenance,
she is adorned with a crown and clothed in red garments.
She stands upon a lotus seat with her two feet slightly tucked under;
on her right side she is joined by her son, and she possesses the face of a boar.
On the left, she should be joined by her daughter; on her head and hands, one should thus fashion the form of the Goddess endowed with these characteristics. (6)
Facing eastward and joined with the banner of the crow (Kākadhvaja),
I shall proclaim the root mantra of the second [deity], which is the third [mantra].
The second of the seventh [syllable] and the fourth of the first,
joined with Bindu and Nāda, is known as Jyeṣṭhāmūla.
The short [vowels] are declared to be Brahman, while the long ones are said to be the unguents;
the eleventh of the first [group], joined with the bindu and endowed with nāda.
This should be known as the seed-mantra of the son; now hear the seed-mantra of the daughter: taking the fifth letter from the fifth [vowel], it is endowed with the Bindu and the Nāda. (10)
This is known as the seed-syllable of the Daughter; now hear the true procedure for its installation.
One must perform the ritual placement of jewels, specifically the five gems at the base.

One should perform the rite of opening the eyes (nayana) and the rite of liberation (mokṣaṇa), accompanied by the five Brahmans; thereafter, one should perform the eye-homa (akṣihoma) with clarified butter alone, consisting of one hundred oblations.
The preceptor should satisfy [the deity] with honey and clarified butter, and show it a cow together with its calf;
then he should perform the ritual immersion in water with the root mantra.
The jars representing the world-protectors, joined with a concealed cloth,
[should remain] for one night, three nights, or even five nights.
