Having emerged from the water on the previous day, one should bathe [the deity] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in a beautiful pavilion as previously described, which is provided with a central altar.
One should have sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) constructed there, either nine or five;
one should have all the sacrificial pits made either circular or square. || 16 ||
O son, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be in the southeast, while the pit for the daughter should be in the southwest;
one should perform the Vāstu-homa during the day, endowed with the proper characteristics.
One should place rice, grain, and sesame seeds in the center of the altar;
having prepared a bed with the five [substances], one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
In the eastern direction of the image, one should place Jyeṣṭhā with a water-pot in due order;
on the right and left sides, however, [one should place] the son together with the daughter.
One should place eight jars in sequence from the east to the northeast;
one should also place the crow in sequence, conjoined with the powers beginning with Vāmā.
One should [place] a crow joined with the powers of Vāmā and the others, along with an earthen jar of the fire-element (āgneya),
provided with cloth, a lid, gold, and a bunch of kuśa grass.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should present milk-rice (pāyasa);
thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) together with fuel-sticks of the Palāśa tree.
Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, sesame seeds, along with śāli rice, nīvāra, wheat, and mung beans—endowed with these very items. (23)
O best of Brahmins, having offered oblations according to the sequence with the five Brahmans and the six limbs, one should finally offer one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra.
Then, at the clear dawn, having performed his ablutions, the preceptor should have the study of the four Vedas conducted in the four directions.

Then, one should perform the oblation for the purification of latent impressions (*vāsanā-homa*), consisting of sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and cooked rice (*caru*), which should be offered with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) at one hundred oblations each. (26)
Having offered the oblation with the mantra "yadasya" at the end, and having then offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
one should raise the Goddess from her bed and establish her in a human station.
Taking the principal pitcher, he should establish it again with the root mantra;
then he should bathe the pitchers of Śakti with the five Brahmans and the limbs of Śiva.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and present milk-rice as an oblation;
one should feed the Brāhmaṇas there, and then specifically feed those who are devotees of Śiva.
I shall describe the procedure for daily worship; listen, O Four-faced One!
One should perform the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa) by means of the five Brahmans.
One should cause the water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), and the water for sipping (ācamanīya) to be given with the Hṛdaya mantra;
one should invoke [the deity] with the Sadyojāta mantra, and the installation should be performed with the Vāmadeva mantra.
One should perform the consecration with the root mantra and worship with the heart mantra;
one should offer the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the heart mantra and conduct the daily festival.
Thereafter, I shall describe the great festival of the hoisting of the banner;
the flagstaff is prescribed to be equal in height to the entire elevation of the temple.
Having performed the sounding of the drum and the offering of the ritual sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), || 34 ||
Then, one should perform the festival according to the sequence of the Śivotsava;
thereafter, one should offer the village-oblation (grāmabali) consisting of pure food accompanied by *pratisama*.
The first is the *bhūtarātra*, the second is the *gaṇarātraka*,
the third is the *ṛṣirātra*, and the fourth is called the *gandha*. (36)
The fifth is the Night of Brahmā (brahmarātra), the sixth is the Night of Kali (kalirātra), and the seventh night is the Portion of the Eldest (jyeṣṭhāṃśa); these are the deities of the nights.

Then, having performed the ritual at the sacred ford (tīrtha), the wise man should celebrate a powder festival (cūrṇotsava) and have a ceremonial bath (snapana) performed there for the image endowed with all auspicious marks.
Whether one hundred and eight, fifty, or twenty-five times—
any mortal who performs it in this manner shall attain a meritorious state.
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, the Ritual for the Installation of Jyeṣṭhā, in the Vīra Tantra.
Having first prostrated before the Lord of the World, Brahmā questioned Śaṅkara:
"O Lord, tell me all about the various types of ritual ablutions."
The Lord.
I shall tell you all of that in its entirety; listen, O Four-faced One! [This applies] during an eclipse, at the equinox, at the solstice, and during the Vyatīpāta yoga.
At the commencement of the sixty-four [festivals], at the installation, and at the conclusion of the festival;
when wonders have arisen, and when the occasion for expiation and the like occurs. (3)
In all such cases as these, one should have the ceremonial bathing performed there;
and in front of the temple, one should construct a square pavilion.
Three cubits or five cubits, or likewise six, seven, eight, or nine;
or eleven cubits, or even thirteen cubits.
Then one should have a pavilion constructed measuring fifteen cubits;
the first three [measures] are established as inferior, and the other is middling. (6)
O twice-born one! That which was previously declared is now being stated by me according to its ninefold division;
O Lotus-seated One, listen as I speak of the seers, the meters, and the deities.
That which is joined with Agastya, endowed with the Jagatī meter, and conjoined with Āditya is called the "Triad of the Supreme. (8)
That which is joined with Vasiṣṭha is called the Śakvarī metre;
that which is joined with Vighneśa is called the middle triad.
That which is composed by Vyāsa, endowed with the Anuṣṭubh metre, and joined with that very metre, is called the triad of lower [texts]. (10)
Having made it square and level, one should construct either a water-shed (prapā) or a pavilion (maṇṭapa);
the pavilion should consist of nine or thirty-six [parts] and be joined with limbs.
Either sixteen or twelve [cubits], according to the previously stated rule;
then, one should have a pavilion constructed according to the previously stated rule.
"Know that there are three inferior [levels], one middling, and another which is superior;
it has been declared in nine divisions, and now it is being proclaimed by me, O twice-born! (13)
Out of affection for you, O Prajāpati, [I have prepared] this canopy, adorned with strings of pearls, which covers the space above with the sages, meters, and deities.
Having placed banners in the eight directions, one should then draw the world-protectors;
[the mandala] should be provided with four doors and endowed with four archways.
Having encircled it with garlands of *darbha* grass and joined it with coconut fruits,
it is adorned with the weapons of the deities, the armor, and the lamps of the eyes. || 16 ||
Adorned with flower garlands and endowed with all ornaments,
together with a thousand pitchers, it is called the most excellent of the excellent.
One joined with five hundred would be the best middling;
two hundred and fifty is called the lowest of the best. (18)
One hundred and eight is said to be the medium-superior;
eighty-one, however, is specifically the medium [number] for the medium [type]. (19)
Thus the ninefold [classification] has been declared; now hear about the most excellent of the excellent.
At an auspicious moment and a favorable astrological conjunction, one should have the laying of the foundation lines performed.
O best of Brahmins, on the night [of the ritual], it should be fashioned from rice flour, endowed with the auspicious marks,
measuring forty-eight [units].

The thread should be divided into four parts; one should place the sacrificial offerings with their tips pointing eastward, and likewise with their tips pointing northward, following this very sequence.
O best of Brahmins! The interval between them should be one *tāla* according to the measure of a finger (*mātrāṅgula*);
in the middle there should be twenty-five, and the surrounding path (*vīthikā*) should be twice that.
Having established fifteen [units] on the outside, there are two squares for the pathway;
having placed two squares on the outside, there are five squares at intervals within.
In this very same sequence, one should likewise eliminate the ritual procedures in order, starting from the east, then the south, the west, and likewise the north. (25)
O Brahmin! Having removed the eight arrays from all sides of the central [array],
one should establish the placement of the arrays within the other array according to the sequence.
O Brahmin! Outside of that, on all sides, the place for the water-pots (kalaśas) is prescribed;
there one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited and should sprinkle with the Pavamāna hymns. || 27 ||
One should scatter rice there, endowed with the auspicious marks;
having placed [the grains] against each jar, it shall become the most excellent half-offering.
Two *prasthas* are declared to be the medium size, and one *prastha* is said to be the lowest;
in this very manner, one should not cause even a smaller [measure] to be made. (29)
O Śiva, O best of Brahmins! If [the vessel] is deficient, it will grant fear of disease and affliction;
therefore, having placed half a measure of śāli rice, one should place half a measure of sesame seeds.
If it is deficient in sesame and rice, there will be affliction by fever and other ailments;
one should then spread an eight-petaled lotus made of *darbha* grass.
One should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited there, saying, "By means of pure and upright [vessels].
I shall now describe the procedure for the water-pots (*kalaśa*), the best of which is filled with a *droṇa* measure.
The medium [vessel] should be filled with one śiva-measure, while the inferior should be one āḍhaka;
it should be uncooked or cooked, but one should avoid that which is deficient or of the wrong time. || 33 ||
In this very manner, having carefully taken hold of the jars,
one should wrap the triple-stranded cord around them like the eye of an elephant.
O Brahmin, one should wash it with water and place it upon *darbha* grass while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*;
then, one should immerse it in the middle of a vessel filled with pure water containing *kūrca* grass.
One should place the water-pot (kumbha) in the center with the Prāsāda mantra;
furthermore, one should place that very pot upon the five seats.
The wise one should place the *vardhanī* vessel with the mantra of the seed-syllable of Gaurī, having worshipped it with scents, flowers, and so forth, while reciting the *vyomavyāpin* mantra. (37)
One should especially worship the Śiva-pot with the Vardhanī;
then, one should place the eight pots in sequence from the east to the northeast.
One should worship those joined with the Vidyeśvaras using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
and the most excellent preceptor should place gold for the Vidyeśvaras. (39)
Having wrapped them with a pair of cloths, the jars are established;
the best is ten cubits [in height], while the middling is eight cubits.
The length of the cloth is said here to be six or seven *tālas* at the minimum;
its width, however, should be four *tālas*, and one should wrap the jars in sequence with it. (41)
One should not place cardamom, cloves, camphor, the three types of sacrificial sesame, and *mura*— all ground together— into the heart during the *deśakumbhaka*.
The best of instructors should arrange the ritual jars starting from the east according to the formation;
he should then worship them with cloths, incense, lamps, and perfumes.
One should place each of all the jars with the heart mantra;
having placed the central array, one should place the positions for the outer array.
One should place twenty-five water-pots (kumbhas) around the ritual arrangement (vyūha);
one should place clarified butter (ājya) in the east and curd (dadhi) in the southeast (āgneyī).
One should place cow urine in the southern direction, milk in the region of Nirṛti, honey in the western direction,
and sugar-cane juice in the northwestern direction. (46)
One should place cow dung in the northern part and yellow orpiment (gorocanā) in the northeast;
then, in this very manner, one should place them for each of the Vyūhas.
Then, one should place mudga, māṣa, śimba, barley, bamboo seeds, priyaṅgu, mustard, and śāli rice in the intermediate directions.
The wise one with limbs like a goat, the adamantine-bodied, the crusher;
the pervasive lord, the imperishable teacher, the wielder of the Pināka bow, and the sovereign of the Pramathas. || 49 ||
The wise one should place Mṛtyu in the south, and then Hara, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Karta, and Kāraka, starting from the east and proceeding in a clockwise direction.
One should fill all the jars with these substances; O best of Brahmins, in their absence, one should deposit whatever is available.
Outside of that, one should likewise arrange twenty-four arrays,
and then place twenty-five water-pots (kalaśas) in sequence within each array.
Cardamom, cloves, *takkola*, neem, nutmeg, *mura*, costus, saffron, and likewise *raghumāñci*. (53)
The breadfruit tree together with the plantain, as well as sugarcane and water; uśīra, sandalwood, and likewise tṛṇa, kaccola, and jambaka. || 54 ||
Realgar, yellow orpiment, water with flowers, water with fruits, lodhra, and saffron—these twenty-four [substances] combined together. (55)
p.
361) As far as the consecrated pitcher extends, so far [extends] the water within the Vaiśvānara [circle].
Agni, Rudra, Udbhūtāśī, Piṅgala, and Hara [are located] from the pit (khātataḥ). || 56 ||
Jvalana, Dahana, Babhru, Bhasmāntaka, Kṣayāntaka;
together with śāli rice, nīvāra grain, wheat, and priyaṅgu. (57)
Just as it is offered in sequence with the five Brahmans and the six limbs, [it is offered] with the Triyambaka mantra... || 58 ||
And iron and saffron, combined twenty-four [times]. || 59 ||
Up to the knotted pitcher (grathitakalaśa) and the inner water,
there is the renowned Kālarudra as well as Sarvadharmapati.
He is proclaimed as the uniter, the director, and the ordainer;
he is the world beyond, the manifest world, the three-eyed one adorned with serpents.
Viśvaklinna, Udbhāsena, and Dharmakṛt are indeed proclaimed;
they are celebrated as belonging to each respective manifestation (vyūha) of these deities. || 62 ||
The preceptor, having placed the water in the jars together with the substances and the deity,
should install Śiva and Umā while facing the east.
But for the other deities, one should worship the water-pots with scents, flowers, and so forth, facing toward Śiva.
One should wrap all [the images] with cloth and place gold right there;
then one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the prescribed characteristics.
As many-sided as the pedestal may be, so many-sided should the sacrificial mound (sthaṇṭila) be;
it should be provided with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, and all other necessary materials.
Immediately after that, one should offer oblations with the mantra "sviṣṭam agne," and specifically perform the homas for the *citta* and others, as well as the *jaya* and others.

Having performed the oblation with the mantra "yadasya," one should immediately thereafter offer oblations with fragrant flowers and other items, having worshipped both the Śiva-kumbha and the Vardhanī vessel.
Having summoned all the gods accompanied by the sound of hymns of praise,
one should then perform the recitation of the four Vedas in the four directions.
One should perform the installation (nyāsa) upon one's own body in due order according to the sequence of emanation;
then, having reached the primary image (mūlabera), one should dismiss the remains of the offerings (nirmālya).
Clad in new garments, wearing a turban and an upper robe,
the wise man, seated upon the fivefold seat, should meditate upon Śiva above him.
One should carry the water-pot upon the head and likewise cause the *vardhanī* vessel to be carried;
then, having gone to the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) together with the temple (*prāsāda*).
Having recited the Vyomavyāpin mantra, one should establish the Śiva-kumbha with the five Brahmans and the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga); one should then place the pedestal upon the Vardhanī vessel.
One should bathe [the deity] with eight jars, starting from the east and ending in the northeast;
one should then install the Supreme Lord according to the procedure for installation.
Having bathed [the deity] with coconut water and purified the ground,
one should offer a garment with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and likewise cause fragrant flowers to be offered.
Afterwards, one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented; then, one should cause betel-leaf (tāmbūla) to be offered.
One should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor (ācārya) and then worship the ritual materials (padārtha). || 76 ||
One should cause all the implements for the ritual bathing to be presented to the preceptor;
the mortal who acts in this manner shall attain the world of Śiva. (77)
"The thousand-pitcher rite has been declared; now hear about the five-hundred [pitchers].
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter of the Vīra-tantra, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Thousand Pitchers."
Having bowed down to the Blessed One, the Grandfather (Brahmā) indeed inquired:
"O Supreme Lord, tell me who it is that performs the bath of five hundred? || 1 ||
The Lord.
I shall describe all of that in its entirety; let it be heard, O Four-faced One!
One should construct a square pavilion in front of the temple.
Adorned with a canopy above and beautified by garlands of darbha grass, it was provided with four archways and decorated with garlands of darbha grass. || 3 ||
Then, having adorned it with strings of pearls, one should decorate the pavilion, which is endowed with the eight auspicious symbols and hung with banners reaching toward the quarters.
Having performed the smearing with cow dung, one should cause the laying out of the lines;
one should arrange thirty lines joined together, with their tips pointing toward the east.
The preeminent instructor should likewise place [the lines] with their tips pointing upward;
in the center, there is a nine-square lotus with eight petals and a pericarp.
And for the sake of the doors, one should reduce one square in each of the four directions;
outside of that, however, five squares are situated all around.
In this very manner, one should perform the rite according to the prescribed characteristics;
there, one should scatter an *āḍhaka* of rice for each water-pot.
Having placed half a measure of śāli rice, one should place half a measure of sesame seeds.
Having drawn an eight-petalled lotus, one should strew it with darbha grass.
One should wrap it with a triple-stranded thread like the eye of an elephant;
then, having filled the jar with pure water, one should take it into the pavilion.
One should install the Śiva-kumbha with the Prāsāda mantra;
one should install the Vardhanī to its left with the Gaurī-bīja.
Having wrapped it with a pair of garments, one should wrap it again with a double layer;
having placed a tuft of grass right there, one should deposit the nine gems.
The most excellent preceptor should place the five jewels in the *vardhanī* vessel;
having installed Śiva in the *śivakumbha*, he should install Manonmanī in the *vardhanī*.
Having surrounded the eight jars on all sides with the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) and wrapped them in a pair of cloths, one should place gold right there.
Having thus [described] the first enclosure, now hear of the second enclosure;
in the second enclosure, one should likewise install seventy-six [deities].
The best of preceptors should arrange five enclosures, four additional ones, and eighty pitchers.
At the sixth enclosure, the wise one should likewise arrange the water-pots;
at the third enclosure, he should arrange twenty-eight. (17)
In the fourth enclosure, one should likewise place ninety-two [pots],
and in the seventh enclosure, one should arrange one hundred kumbhas.
And one should place one hundred and eight *kūrca* grass-bundles, joined with water-pots filled with pure water, in the eighth enclosure.
One should place the jars upon the rice with the *hṛdaya* mantra;
they say that one with the *kūrca* [grass-bundle] facing upward is for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), while one with the *kūrca* facing downward is for pacification (*śāntika*).
Therefore, having prepared [this] for all [purposes], it is called *ābhicārika* (sorcery).
It is combined with the fruits of cardamom (*elā*), cloves (*lavaṅga*), *takkola*, neem (*nimbu*), and jasmine (*jātī*). || 21 ||
One should place uśīra and sandalwood in the first enclosure;
likewise, cow urine, cow dung, curd, milk, and ghee. (22)
Likewise, one should provide Rocana, Carkara, and honey, together with mustard seeds, mung beans, black gram, and Priyaṅgu. || 23 ||
Now listen as I describe the deities to be assigned in the second enclosure:
Aja, Kāpāli, Buddhi, Vajradeha, and Pramardana. (24)
One should place Vibhūti, Avyaya, Śāstṛ, Pinākī, Tridaśādhipa,
Agnīrudra, and Hutāśa in the second enclosure (āvāraṇa).
Having assigned camphor, giribera, tṛṇaka, colajambuka,
and [the rest] to the third enclosure, now hear [the assignment] for the deities.
Having sequentially assigned the deities Jvalana, Dahana, Babhru, Bhasmāntaka, and Kṣayāntaka to the corners beginning with the southeast (āgneya), [one should worship them]. (27)
Having assigned Dhātṛ, Pūrvā, Takkola, Punnāga, Jāti, and Pāṭalī in the fourth enclosure, now hear [the names] of the deities. || 28 ||
And the renowned Kālarudra, who is likewise surrounded by dharma and adharma;
having joined him together with the joined one, one should place him in the fifth enclosure (āvaraṇa). || 29 ||
Having mentally prepared the five seats, one should bathe the Śiva-pitcher;
there, one should recite the Vyomavyāpin mantra together with the Brahma-mantras and the ancillaries.
Then, one should place [the vessel] upon the pedestal with the Gaurībīja mantra in the Vardhanī;
thereafter, one should bathe the jars according to the prescribed procedure for installation.
One should offer an oblation of five colors and then cause betel-leaf to be given;
one should give the preceptor’s fee (dakṣiṇā) together with ornaments for the five limbs.
One should cause all the implements for the ritual bathing to be given to the preceptor;
the mortal who acts in this manner shall attain the world of Śiva.
"The five-hundred-fold ablution has been declared; now hear the fifty-two hundred-fold [ablution].
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter of the *Vīratantra*, titled "The Procedure for the Five-Hundred-fold Ablution."
The Grandfather.
O Lord! What is the nature of this ablution consisting of two hundred and fifty [verses]? O Master, tell me all of that. || 1 ||
The Lord.
I shall describe all of that in its entirety; listen, O Four-faced One!
In front of the temple, there should be a square pavilion.
One should have the layout of the lines made adorned with all ornaments,
and there should be twenty-two lines facing toward the east.
Likewise, facing north, with an interval of one palm’s length,
there should be a nine-foot lotus with eight petals and a pericarp.
One should decrease three paces all around the exterior of the lotus;
and outside that enclosure, one should decrease two paces.
And for the sake of the doors, one should reduce the area by one square in each of the four directions;
thus, two hundred and fifty squares remain situated there.
One should scatter rice there along with grains and sesame seeds;
one should spread Darbha grass over it and worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having carefully taken up the jars provided with cords,
one should wrap them with a triple-stranded cord, like the eye of an elephant.
On the previous day, there should be the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) by means of the palace-mantra;
having taken up a water-vessel, one should sprinkle the water with the heart-mantra.
With water purified by a cloth and blended with fragrant substances, combined with cardamom, cloves, nutmeg, uśīra, and sandalwood; (10)
One should place the Śiva-pitcher, joined with five substances and mixed with fragrant materials, while reciting the Vyomavyāpin mantra.
One should place the *vadhanī* on his left with the seed-syllable of Gaurī;
all around, one should arrange eight jars accompanied by the Vidyeśvaras.
Having wrapped it with a pair of garments, one should wrap the Viṇika and others;
[the gems] are diamond, emerald, lapis lazuli, and coral.
One should place the five jewels— the puṣyarāga, gomedha, indranīla,
and pearl— into the Śiva-kumbha and the vardhanī.
O Brahmin, one should place gold into the pitcher of Vidyeśa;
there, one should arrange the outer enclosure consisting of thirty-six pitchers.
One should place Siddhārtha, sesame, mudga beans, and śimba seeds;
[the deities are] Kapālīśa, Vajrapāṇi, Pinākī, and Tridaśādhipa. (16)
These deities have been declared; one should install them in the second enclosure (āvaraṇa).
And in the third enclosure, one should likewise place sixty jars (kalaśas).
One should place cardamom, cloves, jasmine, and likewise takkola;
as well as jackfruit, plantain, and citron fruits. || 18 ||
One should place two oranges and water with fruit;
likewise, one should place [the images of] Yama, Mṛtyuhara, Dhātṛ, and Dharmapati. (19)
These deities are also declared; one should place them in the fourth enclosure (āvaraṇa).
Then, in the fifth enclosure, one should place seventy-six [deities].
One should place murā, māṃjīva, kuṣṭha, and indeed nimba;
likewise Kālarudra, Hutāśa, Jvalana, and Dahana. (21)
These deities are also proclaimed; one should install them in the fifth enclosure (āvaraṇa).
One should place the substance together with the deity in each corner. || 22 ||
Then the fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed in the four directions or the eight directions;
having offered fuel-sticks with the Heart-mantra, one should likewise offer the oblation with the Head-mantra.
Having offered the sacrificial oblation (caru) with the Śikhā-mantra, and the parched grains (lāja) with the Kavaca-mantra,
one should likewise offer mustard seeds with the Netra-mantra.
Having become tranquil in mind, one should offer a hundred oblations for each [deity],
reciting the name of the Fire-god while combining all the ritual substances.
Immediately after that, one should offer oblations with the mantra "Sviṣṭam agne," and then one should engage in study in the various directions and recite the hymn-mantra.
Then one should give the teacher his fee and worship the ritual substances;
one should then bathe the Śiva-pitcher with the Prāsāda mantra.
Having bathed in the first enclosure, one should bathe again in the second enclosure;
thereafter, the third enclosure, and then again the fourth enclosure. (28)
Thereafter, for the fifth enclosure, one should offer oblations of five colors with the five Brahmans and the six limbs, and then cause betel-leaf to be offered.
The mortal who performs it in this manner shall attain the world of Śiva.
Two hundred and fifty [verses] are declared; this is called the threefold excellent [recitation].
O Brahmin! Listen to the one hundred and eight [names] for the middle triad. || 30½ ||
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, the procedure for the bath of two hundred and fifty [verses], in the Vīratantra.
The Grandfather.
"O Lord! What is the supreme form of bathing for the medium [level], O Master?
Please explain all of this in brief, as well as the one hundred and eight [forms]. (1)
I shall describe all of that in its entirety; listen, O Four-faced One!
One should construct a square pavilion in front of the temple.
In the beautiful pavilion previously described, adorned above with celestial chariots, provided with four archways, and encircled by garlands of *darbha* grass; || 3 ||
Having placed banners in the eight directions adorned with hanging garlands of flowers,
one should wrap the pillars there and smear them with cow dung.
The line for the cord should be drawn with an interval of one tāla;
indeed, the line for the cord is of two kinds: that for pacifying rites and likewise that for nourishing rites.
One should lay down fourteen threads with their tips pointing eastward, and likewise with their tips pointing northward; these are the specifications for the threads.

O best of Brahmins, having stood upon the nine squares in the center, one should place the squares for the boundaries; then, in the four directions, one should likewise place the squares for the purpose of the doors.
Outside that outer enclosure, the ritual is prescribed all around;
outside of that, however, there are two squares situated on every side.
In this very manner, the rite for pacification (śāntika) is performed in due order.
Now I shall declare another matter, which is called the installation of the wheel (cakrasthāpana). || 9 ||
O best of Brahmins, one should cause the pair of threads to be laid down with their tips pointing eastward;
likewise, they should point northward, with an interval of exactly one tāla between them.
O Brahmin, one should whirl them like the full moon at a distance of three *tāla*s; the interval between them in the eastern direction, O Brahmin, should be the measure of one *tāla*. (11)
Then, having rotated the eight-fold pattern, there are four paths;
having placed four jars, the rite for prosperity (pauṣṭika) is here described.
One should especially reduce [the measurements] in the four directions for the sake of the doors;
there, one should scatter rice in abundance around each of the jars.
Having placed half a measure of śāli rice, one should place half a measure of rice and [the remaining] half a measure of sesame seeds;
then, having strewn darbha grass around, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
Then, one should have the water-pots brought there; subsequently, having taken earth from a pure place with the *astra-mantra*, its drying should be performed with the left hand.
The wise man, endowed with all auspicious characteristics, should burn [the offering] with the Īśāna mantra;
however, it is prescribed that the lowest quality [offering] consists of a full āḍhaka measure.
The medium [vessel] should be completely filled with ashes, while the best should be filled with a *droṇa* measure;
one should avoid those that are cracked, black, hollow, or split apart.
One should wrap the jars with thread so that they resemble the eyes of an elephant;
then, O best of Brahmins, one should likewise wrap the shallow bowl with thread.
One should wash it in water alone and not place it upon *darbha* grass;
O Brahmin, one should fill the principal pitcher with pure water.
One should cast the five jewels (pañcaratna) therein and wrap it with a pair of garments;
one should place Rudra at the mouth of the jar and Viṣṇu in its center.
On the back is known Prajāpati; the sacred fords (tīrthas) are said to be the belly.
One should install the Śiva-pitcher in the middle by means of the Prāsāda [mantra]. || 21 ||
One should place the *vardhanī* vessel on his left with the seed-syllable of Gaurī; having worshipped Śiva in the *śivakumbha* and Gaurī herself in the *vardhanī*. (22)
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should place the jars of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśa);
one should arrange the eight jars starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
These, provided with cloth, gold, and kūrca-grass, and filled with water, constitute the first enclosure; now hear about the second enclosure.
Having placed twelve water-pots, listen now to the substances [to be placed within them]:
water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), the respectful offering (arghya), cow urine, cow dung, and milk. || 25 ||
Curd and clarified butter are declared as the eighth; one should place them in the second enclosure.
And in the third enclosure, one should place the twenty-four Kalās.
Sandalwood, saffron, kuṣṭha, laghumāñcī, uraṅgula, parched grain flour, śamī, nīvāra, and coconut. || 27 ||
One should place twenty jars containing honey, sugarcane juice, bilva fruit, kuśa grass, barley, sesame seeds, camphor, and jackfruit.
Vibhūti, Avyaya, Śāstṛ, Pinākin, Tridaśādhipa, Agni, Rudra, Hutāśa, Piṅgala, Khātaka, and Hara. || 29 ||
Jvalana, Dahana, Babhru, Bhasman, Antaka, and Kṣayāntaka—
these deities are also said to be placed in the water within the jars.
The third enclosure has been described; now hear of the fourth enclosure.
One should place forty-four jars in the fourth enclosure. (31)
Loha, priyaṅgu flower, clove, fruit-mallikā, ivory, dūrvā grass, takkola, puṃnāga, jasmine, and pāṭalī. || 32 ||
Parṇakā, śatapatrī, oil, musk, gorocanā, vyāghranakhī, śatāvarī, mañjiṣṭhā, and nāgakesara. (33)
Fresh butter, Drāvila, Sāgandhapattra, Dhātakī, Bhītā, Sahadevī, Viṣṇukrānti, and Suvarcalā; || 34 ||
Balabhadrī, Mahābhadrī, Apāmārga, Indu, and Vallikā. || 35 ||
The best of teachers should place Rudraparṇī and Mahālakṣmī, together with Dhūr and Dhūreṇa, in the fourth enclosure.
The southern [deity] is Mṛtyuhara, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and Kartr;
he is likewise renowned as Kālarudra and the Lord of Dharma and Adharma.
The uniter and the disuniter, likewise in the southwest and the west;
the slayer and the one of cruel gaze, with an erect penis and mighty arms. (38)
Virūpākṣa, Dhūmrakarṇa, Lohita, Daṃṣṭrabāhula, Atiścala, Pāśahasta, and Mahābala. (39)
Jayabhadra, Mahābāhu, Bālānta, Baḍavāmukha, Vibhīṣaṇa, Mahāvega, and likewise Laghuvega. || 40 ||
Subtle, sharp, ending in destruction, subsequently peaceful, and five-crested;
he has matted hair, is borne by clouds, and wears a crown of matted locks. (41)
O best of Brahmins, one should place within the water-jars images of Nānārūpadhara, as well as the handsome Nidhīśa, and likewise Dhanu. (42)
The *vardhanī* vessel for Śiva should indeed face eastward,
while those for the other deities should face toward Śiva.
This has been taught as the rite for pacification; now hear concerning the rite for nourishment.
One should place eight [deities] in the first enclosure and twelve in the second.
O best of Brahmins, one should place forty jars for the deities, arranging them in due order according to the previously mentioned method.
O best of Brahmins! the wise one should also perform the placement [of the deities] in the fifth enclosure;
thereafter, a fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed in the four directions with Palāśa wood.
Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, and mustard seeds are offered;
having offered them in sequence from Sadyojāta to Īśāna according to the Śiva-vratas. (47)
Having recited "Vyomavyāpin" twenty-five times for each [syllable],
fifty oblations are offered in sequence with the Prāsāda mantra.
Then, one should offer oblations sequentially with the mind and so forth, beginning with victory;
having offered these, one should subsequently perform the oblation with the mantra "tadasya" at the end.
One should wrap each and every jar with a pair of cloths;
then one should give the teacher's fee (dakṣiṇā) and worship the ritual materials.
Having entered the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), one should discard the withered floral offerings (nirmālya).
Afterwards, having prepared the five seats (pañcāsana), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the process of emanation (sṛṣṭi). || 51 ||
Having raised the Śiva-pitcher, one should bathe [the deity] upon the top of the Liṅga;
one should then bathe the Vardhanī on its left side with the Gaurī-mantra.
There, one should mutter the *vyomavyāpin* mantra and install the *śivakumbha*;
then, one should bathe the jar with the five Brahmans and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Having bathed at the first enclosure, and likewise at the second and third,
having bathed at the fourth and fifth, one should proceed in this very order.
One should offer an oblation of five colors and present betel;
the mortal who acts in this manner shall attain the world of Śiva.
"In this way, [the rites] are middling and excellent; now hear the eighty-one [deities].
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, the procedure for the hundred-and-eight ablutions, in the *Vīratantra*.
Having paid homage to the Lord of the World, the Grandfather (Brahmā) inquired:
"O God! How is it that there are eighty-one [kalpas]? O Lord, tell me all of that."
The Lord.
"Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! That which has been requested by you, I shall explain all of it in its entirety; listen, O four-faced one! || 2 ||
In front of the temple, the most excellent preceptor should construct a square pavilion according to the very same procedure previously described.
Having carefully taken up the water-pots, one should wrap them with the thread itself;
having filled them with pure water, they are placed upon shallow bowls. (4)
There, one should scatter śāli rice, providing one āḍhaka for each;
having placed half as much unhusked rice (taṇḍula), one should place half as much sesame (tila).
One should spread darbha grass and place the Śiva-kumbha;
one should place the Vardhanī vessel with the Prāsāda mantra and the Gaurī-bīja.
And one should indeed place it all around, O best of Brahmins, together with water-pots.
It should be joined with the lords of knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), provided with cloth, and accompanied by gold;
the lowest [size] should be eight cubits, while the middle [size] should be nine cubits.
The best [image] is ten cubits long and four tālas wide;
an ancient one causes the loss of sons, and one with hair causes the loss of wealth. (9)
One should not have [the vessel] made white, red, yellow, or variegated.
One should place a new pitcher in the east and a new pitcher in the southeast.
The wise man should place nine jars in the south, a group of nine in the southwest,
a group of nine in the west, and a group of nine in the northwest.
Having placed one set of nine [vessels] there, he should place another set of nine in the northeast;
these should be filled with water, provided with cloths, covered with lids, and accompanied by bunches of kuśa grass.
One should place [these] upon the heart, especially upon rice;
[namely] iron, priyaṅgu flowers, cloves, and mallikā fruit.
Dāntā, dūrvā grass, takkola, punnāga, jasmine, pāṭalī, parṇaka, śatapatra, oil, musk, and gorocanā. (14)
Vyāghranakhī, śatāvarī, mañjiṣṭhā, nāgakeśara, rajanī, bhadrakoṣṭha, sarala, and kṛṣṇamālikā. (15)
Bhītā, Sahadevī, Viṣṇukrānti, Suvarcalā, Siṃhī, Śaṅkhapuṣpī, Lakṣmī, and the land-lotus (sthalāravindaka). || 16 ||
Balabhadrī, Mahābhadrī, Apāmārgenduvallikā, Rudraparṇī, Mahālakṣmī, Dhūr, and Dhūreṇa—[these are] combined together. || 17 ||
One should place these substances, combined together, into the jars;
[and likewise] on the bank of a river, in a cow-pen, at an anthill, and at the horn of a bull.
One should take earth from the tusk of a boar or an elephant and from the root of a lotus,
place it into the jar of the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa), and combine it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
O Brahmin, one should install [the deities] in the eastern group of nine in sequence;
likewise, one should install them in sequence in the western group of nine.
O Brahmin, one should place Vāyu in the ninth square and Kumāra;
having invoked Viṣṇu in the north, [one should place him] in the region of Caṇḍīśa.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should then perform the oblation on the fourteenth day,
consisting of sacrificial fuel sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, and parched grain, combined with mustard seeds.
Having recited the *Vyomavyāpin* mantra one hundred and eight times individually for each [deity] from Sadyojāta to Īśāna, he should then offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter.
Having performed the final oblation with the mantra *yad asya*,
one should immediately thereafter sprinkle the Śiva-kumbha while reciting the *Vyomavyāpin* mantra. (24)
The best of preceptors should bathe [the deity] in the *vardhanī* vessel with the *gaurī* seed-syllable;
the wise one should bathe the jars with the five Brahmans and the six limbs.
One should offer an oblation of five colors and then cause betel to be given;
thereafter, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and worship the ritual materials.
The mortal who acts in this manner shall attain the world of Śiva.
Thus the eighty-one have been declared; now hear the forty-nine.
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, the procedure for the eighty-one-fold ablution, in the Vīratantra. 81.
The Grandfather.
Having bowed his head to the God, Brahmā questioned Śaṅkara:
"O Lord, tell me all that which consists of forty-nine crores."
The Lord.
I shall tell you all of that in its entirety; listen, O Four-faced One!
One should construct a square pavilion in front of the temple.
It was provided with four archways, adorned with four gates,
encircled by garlands of *darbha* grass, and beautified by a canopy.
Equipped with banners and adorned with strings of pearls,
one should apply a coating of cow dung and then perform the laying of the foundation lines.
Ten threads with their tips pointing eastward and likewise ten with their tips pointing northward;
having established nine squares in the center, there shall be one [square] outside that for the walkway.
It should be constructed with eight gates and endowed with the proper characteristics,
having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) of *śāli* rice according to the previously mentioned procedure. (6)
Having placed half a measure of śāli rice and likewise half a measure of rice for sesame,
and having prepared eight squares in the center, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should place the Śiva-pitcher in the center, endowed with the five jewels,
provided with two cloths, together with a bunch of kuśa grass, and covered with a lid.
Having placed six water-pots in the cardinal directions and four indeed in the intermediate directions,
one should arrange those pots there, provided with cloths and lids.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, clarified butter, curd, and likewise milk;
sandalwood, saffron, as well as māñji, murā, and aṅgula. || 10 ||
Lāja, girivera, tṛṇakaccola, jambuka, śatapuṣpa, as well as vyāghrī, dhātrī, pūrvā, and harītakī. || 11 ||
Hitā, sahadevī, mātuluṅga, dāḍimī,
haṃsapuṣpā, gandhapuṣpā, and mahādroṇī— [these] combined together.
The wise one should place green gram, black gram, and mustard seeds in the jars;
[the deities are] Aja, Kapālī, Buddhi, Vajradeha, and Pramardana.
Vibhūti, Avyaya, Śāstṛ, Pinākin, Tridaśādhipa, Agnīrudra, Hutāśin, Piṅgala, Pādaka, and Hari. || 14 ||
Jvalana, Dahana, Bhadra, Bhasmāntaka, Kṣayāntaka, Yāmya, Mṛtyuhara, Dhātṛ (Vidhātṛ), and Karṇakārikā. 15.
Kālarudra is reckoned as the lord of dharma and adharma;
he is proclaimed as the uniter, the disuniter, and the ordainer. (16)
He is the foremost of the hosts, the one of virtuous conduct, Śarva, Śambhu, Maheśvara, the renowned Kālarudra, the Creator, and likewise the Lord of Dharma. (17)
The slayer, the one with a cruel gaze, the one with hair standing erect, the long-armed, the odd-eyed, the smoke-colored, the red, the tusked, or the wise one (Budha). 18.
He holds a noose in his hand, possesses great awakening, has a dark throat, and is four-armed;
he is the protector of spirits, the guardian of the world, and likewise the guardian of the field. (19)
Likewise, those who cause happiness and suffering, as well as [the others], are declared to be deities; one should place them within the water in the pitchers.
Then the fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed in the four cardinal directions and the intermediate directions;
or alternatively, a single oblation may be offered in the northeast together with fuel-sticks of the Palāśa tree.
Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, sesame seeds, rice, millet, wheat, and mung beans—these were provided together. (22)
The wise one, having offered oblations to the five Brahmans and the six limbs in succession,
should then perform the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the verse "yad asya" at the conclusion of the offerings.
Having recited the *vyomavyāpin* mantra, one should bathe the Śiva-kumbha;
one should bathe the Śiva-kumbha in the *vardhanī* vessel with the seed-syllable of Gaurī.
One should bathe [the deity] upon the pedestal with the Gaurī-bīja using the Vardhanī vessel;
one should bathe all the pitchers with the Pañcabrahma and Ṣaḍaṅga mantras.
Afterwards, one should present the sacrificial offering (havis), and then cause betel to be given.
The mortal who acts in this manner is glorified in the world of Śiva. (26)
"Fifty-nine have been declared; now hear the twenty-five.
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, the procedure for the forty-nine ablutions, in the Vīratantra. 82.
The Grandfather.
Having first prostrated before the God of gods, the Grandfather (Brahmā) inquired:
"O Supreme Lord! Tell me about the twenty-five-fold ceremonial bath."
The Lord.
I shall describe all of that in its entirety; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
One should construct a square pavilion in front of the temple.
It was provided with four gateways, adorned with garlands of darbha grass,
covered above by a canopy, and hung with banners in every direction.
Then, one should have a pavilion constructed, adorned with all ornaments;
having applied a coating of cow dung, one should then perform the laying out of the ritual lines.
There should be eight lines oriented toward the east and likewise eight toward the north;
standing upon the central nine squares, one should discard the single square outside of that.
Then, one should scatter śāli rice upon that [altar] which is provided with eight pathways; one should arrange either an āḍhaka, half of that, or a prastha of śāli rice.
O best of Brahmins, one should place rice upon each of the jars;
having placed half as much sesame as rice, one should then spread darbha grass around them.
One should place the Śiva-pitcher in the center and wrap it with a pair of cloths;
it should be provided with the five jewels, along with a tuft of grass and a lid.
With the seed-syllable of Gaurī, one should place the Vardhanī vessel together with cloth and gold;
then, one should arrange the eight jars starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
Having placed gold there, together with the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśvara),
it should be accompanied by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), along with a cloth and a lid.
O best of Brahmins! One should place twelve water-pots (kalaśas) in the four cardinal directions;
it is said that there should be four pots in the corners beginning with the southeast (āgneya).
Sandalwood, saffron, uśīra, and mudge, as well as cardamom, cloves, black pepper, timbu, nutmeg, and aṅgula. || 12 ||
Laghu-māñcīra, the sixth being saffron (kuṅkuma), as well as dāntā, dūrvā grass, takkola, puṃnāga, jasmine (jāti), and pāṭalī. || 13 ||
Having placed the *loghra*, the *priyaṅgu*, and the coconut in their proper sequence, starting from the east and ending with the northeast (Īśāna). || 13 ||

The Unborn, the Skull-bearer, Intelligence, the Adamantine-bodied, the Destroyer, the All-pervading, the Imperishable, the Teacher, the Wielder of the Pināka bow, and the Lord of the Thirty-three gods. || 14 ||
Agni, Rudra, Hutāśa, Piṅgala, Khātaka, Hara, Jvalana, Dahana, Babhru, Bhasmāntaka, and Kṣayāntaka. || 15 ||
O best of Brahmins! Yāmya, Mṛtyuhara, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Kartṛ, Kāraka, and Kālarudra are the presiding deities (adhidevatās) of the water-pot (kalaśa). || 16 ||
Having worshipped with incense, flowers, and so forth by means of the mantra consisting of each deity's own name,
one should then perform the fire oblation (homa) together with fuel-sticks of the Palāśa tree.
One should have a vessel made there, endowed with the proper characteristics;
[and one should prepare] sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds.
Rice, along with barley, wheat, and bamboo,
is offered in sequence according to the five Brahmans and the six limbs.
Having offered it at the end, one should then perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the mantra "yad asya...";
one should give the preceptor a sacrificial fee consisting of garments, gold, and rings.
One should bathe the Śiva-pitcher with the Prāsāda mantra;
however, one should especially bathe the Vardhanī vessel with the Gaurī-bīja.
Then, having recited the "Vyomavyāpin" mantra, one should bathe the ritual jars;
thereafter, one should offer five-colored oblations and cause betel-leaf to be presented.
The mortal who performs this in such a manner shall attain the world of Śiva.
Twenty-five [verses] have been declared; now hear the sixteenth from here on. || 23 ||
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, the procedure for the twenty-fivefold ablution, in the Vīratantra.
The Grandfather.
Having prostrated before the Blessed One, the Grandfather indeed questioned him:
"O Supreme Lord, tell me, what is the purpose of the sixteen jars? (1)
The Lord.
I shall explain all of that in its entirety; listen, O Four-faced One!
One should construct a square pavilion in front of the temple.
Having encircled it with garlands of *darbha* grass and adorned it with four archways,
one should cover it from above with a canopy suspended by cords made of silk.
The wise man should wrap it with cloths and adorn it with strings of pearls;
having equipped it with all ornaments, he should then perform the laying of the foundation lines.
There should be eight lines with their tips pointing eastward, and likewise eight with their tips pointing northward;
having established nine squares in the center, one should discard the square surrounding it.
Provided with eight pathways, it stands with one square outside;
there, one should scatter *śāli* rice according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having placed half a measure of śāli rice, one should place half of that amount of sesame seeds;
one should then strew it with darbha grass and worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
The best of preceptors should place the Śiva-pitcher in the center with the Prāsāda mantra, and he should install the Vardhanī vessel in the northeast with the Gaurī-bīja.
One should place three jars in the four cardinal directions,
and one should place four jars in the corners beginning with the southeast (āgneya).
Having worshipped Śiva in the auspicious water-pot (śivakumbha), which is endowed with four jewels, wrapped in a pair of cloths, and adorned with small bells; || 10 ||
Having placed the Gaurī and Vardhanī vessels, along with cloth and gold, as well as cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and clarified butter; || 11 ||
One should likewise place uśīra and candana together with kuṣṭha,
arranging them in due order from Sadyojāta up to Īśāna.
Having offered the final oblation with the mantra "yadasya," one should then perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
One should then bathe the Śiva-pitcher while reciting the "Vyomavyāpin" mantra. (13)
One should especially bathe the Vardhanī vessel with the Gaurī-bīja mantra;
thereafter, one should install the ritual jars (kalaśas) using the Pañcabrahma and Ṣaḍaṅga mantras.
One should offer milk-rice as the food offering (naivedya) and present betel-leaf;
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor (ācārya), consisting of garments, gold, and rings.
"For the inferior [type of practitioner], the middle [method] has been declared; now hear concerning the nine jars.
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Sixteen Ablutions," in the Vīra-tantra.
The Grandfather.
Having bowed down to the Blessed One Śaṅkara, he indeed inquired:
"O God! O Supreme Lord! Tell me, how is it that there are nine jars? || 1 ||
The Lord.
I shall explain all of that in its entirety; listen, O Four-faced One!
One should construct a square pavilion in front of the temple.
It was provided with four gates, adorned with four archways,
covered by a canopy above, and hung with banners in every direction.
Having encircled it with garlands of *darbha* grass and adorned it with strings of pearls,
one should smear it with cow dung while it is furnished with all ornaments.
One should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited there, and one should also recite the *Svasti-sūkta*.
The laying of the foundation lines (*sūtrapāta*) should be performed; the six lines should run toward the east as the head.
It should likewise have its tips pointing upward and be provided with eight gates;
one should scatter an *āḍhaka* of rice there for each jar.
Having placed half-measures of śāli rice, one should place half-measures of sesame seeds;
then, having strewn it with darbha grass, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus.
One should place the Śiva-pitcher in the center with the Prāsāda mantra;
it should be provided with cloth, the five gems, a tuft of grass, and a lid.
The best of preceptors should place the *vardhanī* vessels with the *gaurī* seed-syllable;
they should be filled with scented water and provided with cloth and gold.
One should place eight water-pots starting from the east and ending with the northeast.
In the east, one should place cow’s urine, and in the southeast, cow dung.
Having placed milk in the south, one should arrange curd in the west;
having established clarified butter in the north, and a lotus made of kuśa grass in the southwest.
In the northwest, there is fruit and water; in the northeast, there should be yellow pigment (rocanā).
One should install the eight Lords of Knowledge (Aṣṭavidyeśvaras) starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using their respective mantras;
thereafter, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) together with palāśa fuel-sticks.
Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds—endowed with these seven substances and joined with the five Brahmans. || 14 ||
The heart, together with the head, is offered in sequence;
having offered these, at the end, the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation is offered in order with the verse beginning "yad asya."
Then, one should arrange the forms of the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgalas) all around; thereafter,
one should give the preceptor a sacrificial fee consisting of garments, gold, and rings.
Having recited the *Vyomavyāpin* mantra, one should bathe [the deity] with the Śiva-pitchers;
[one should bathe] the Vardhanī vessel with the *Gaurī*-seed mantra and with the respective mantras of Ananta and the others.
Thereafter, one should present the sacrificial offering (havis) and then cause betel-leaf (tāmbūla) to be given.
This is declared to be the lowest of the low; now hear about the "cold-pitcher" (śītakumbha). || 18 ||
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, the ritual for the bathing of the nine jars, in the Vīratantra.
The Grandfather.
O Lord! How is the Śītakumbha [rite] performed, and what indeed is its ritual procedure?
O Blessed One, you ought to explain all of this in brief.
The Lord.
I shall declare all of that in its entirety; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
It is for the destruction of fever and pestilence, and the eradication of all misfortunes.
A vessel filled with thirty-two prasthas is called the best;
thirty of those is declared the middling, and twenty-eight the lowest.
O best of Brahmins, the width of the face is said to be eight finger-breadths;
it should be endowed with the radiance and luster of the image, and one must avoid a disfigured or inauspicious time.
One should wrap it with a triple-stranded thread like the eye of an elephant;
one should wash it with the Heart-mantra and place it upon the Darbha grass.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before Śiva with eight droṇas of śāli rice,
one should place half that amount of rice grains and half that amount of sesame seeds.
Having drawn an eight-petalled lotus, one should strew it with *darbha* grass; then,
one should fill the water-jar with water purified by a cloth.
One should place cardamom, cloves, *takkola*, nutmeg, jasmine, and *jātī* fruit, along with *uśīra* and sandalwood, into the middle of the jar while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having wrapped it in a pair of garments and adorned it with various gems—
namely, a diamond, a ruby, lapis lazuli, and likewise a pearl— (9)
One should place it, joined with coral, into the middle of the jar,
together with a tuft of grass, a lid, and provided with a garland of flowers.
One should place the pitcher upon the rice while reciting the Vyomavyāpin mantra;
one should worship it with perfumes and flowers using the Pañcabrahma mantras along with the Ṣaḍaṅga mantras.
One should contemplate the water in the pitcher as being nectar;
having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) during the first part of the night, accompanied by dance and song.
Thereafter, one should present the sacrificial offering (havis) and then cause betel-leaf to be given.
In this very manner, one should place the water-pot (kumbha), with Śiva as its presiding deity (adhidevatā). || 13 ||
One should perform the Vāstuhoma during the day, endowed with the proper characteristics;
O Brāhmaṇa, one should cause the Śāntihoma to be performed in the vicinity of the water-pot.
The twice-born man should perform the study of the four Vedas in the four directions;
in this very manner, he should also place the secondary water-pot (upakumbha).
Then, at the clear dawn, having performed his ablutions,
the preceptor should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of emanation according to the path prescribed for the placement of mantras.
O best of Brahmins, having there conceived of the three-footed pedestal made from sacrificial wood, it is said that [the base] above the liṅga should be one cubit in height. (17)

It should have a circumference of twelve finger-breadths; one should fashion it using the *mātrāṅgula* measurement, making it straight, free from blemishes, and provided with three seats (*viṣṭhara*).
The preceptor should make a hollow in the middle of it measuring one tāla;
he should then place two supports on the sides and one behind.
Then, one should make a hole in the back of the jar itself;
having inserted a tube there, four finger-breadths in length.
One should certainly not do so with gold; rather, one should join it beneath the jar.
Then, having recited the *vyomavyāpin* mantra, one should place the water-pot upon it.
One should have it performed for three days, five days, or even seven days; flowing upon the head day and night, it cuts away all defects.
Thereafter, one should offer a great oblation, and then cause betel-leaf to be given;
subsequently, at twilight, one should perform worship according to the previously mentioned procedure.

O Brahmin! One should pour water from the secondary jar (upakumbha) into the cool-water jar (śītakumbha). And at the end of the day, O best of Brahmins, perform the descent of the jars (kumbhāvarohaṇa).
The ceremonial bathing (snapana) should be performed there according to the previously mentioned procedure;
one should give the preceptor (ācārya) a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of garments, gold, and rings.
One should feed the Brahmins there, as well as the attendants who seek alms;
one should feed the devotees of Śiva there, and then feed those who observe the religious observances (samaya).
The procedure for the cold-water jar has been declared; now hear the procedure for the extraordinary rites. (26½)
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, the Ritual of the Cold Pitcher, in the Vīra Tantra.
Having paid homage to the Lord of the World, the Grandfather (Brahmā) inquired:
"O Lord, what is the method for [performing] wonders? Tell me all of that."
The Lord.
I shall declare all of that in its entirety; listen, O Four-faced One!
[When] there is an earthquake, a conflagration of the quarters, or when a comet appears; || 2 ||
Having bathed with a thousand jars for the pacification of that defect,
one should perform the propitiation of the planets during times of drought and similar calamities.
One should construct a pavilion in front of Śiva according to the previously mentioned procedure;
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice, one should then arrange grains of rice upon it.
O best of Brahmins, one should place either a broom made of kuśa grass or a bundle [of grass] measuring one tāla in height; and indeed, three such items should be placed in the middle.
From the east to the northeast, the *kūrca* [grass-bundle] is prescribed for three;
one should place it in the middle of those three and also for the planets.
Having placed Āditya in the center, one should install Śukra in the east;
Candramas in the south-eastern direction, and Aṅgāraka in the south.
Having placed Rāhu in the southwest and Śanaiścara in the west,
one should place Ketu in the northwest and Bṛhaspati in the north.
The best of preceptors should also place Budha in the northeast;
the god Īśvara is the presiding deity of Bhāskara, and he faces directly toward the east.
The deity of Umācandra is Deva; that of Aṅgāraka is Skanda;
that of Rāhu is Kāliṅgadeva; and likewise, the deity of Śani is Yama.
Ketu, Citragupta, Brahmadeva, Bṛhaspati, Budha, and Viṣṇu as the deity— these are the presiding deities of the planets.
Fire, water, and earth; Viṣṇu and Indra as deities;
Indrāṇī, Prajāpati, and the serpents; and Brahmā as the presiding deities. || 12 ||
Having then invoked the deity with the *sadya* mantra joined with *bhūḥ* and *bhuvaḥ*,
O best of Brahmins, prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) for them to the east using sand.
Having conceived of Agni as the mouth [of the sacrifice], one should worship him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
the orb of the Sun should be circular, and that of Venus five-cornered.
Some, however, say it is square for Mars,
triangular for Rāhu, and shaped like a winnowing basket for Saturn, as well as bow-shaped.
The banner of Bṛhaspati should be known as triangular, while that of Budha is square and long; thus it is said by the Blessed One.
In this very manner, the best of preceptors should prepare either a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or a leveled altar (sthaṇḍila), and worship it with flowers of their respective colors.
One should know that *arka* belongs to Āditya, and *palāśa* to Soma;
*khadira* belongs to Aṅgāraka, and *apāmārga* to Budha.
For Bṛhaspati, the fuel should be of the Aśvattha tree; for Śukra, it should be of the Udumbara.
One should know that for Śanaiścara it is the Śamī, and for Rāhu, the oblation of Dūrvā grass is prescribed. (19)
For the concluding oblation (ketoḥ), one should use *kuśa* sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*), or in their absence, *palāśa* sticks;
either one hundred and eight or twenty-eight [should be offered].
O best of Brahmins! Now each [oblation] is offered in succession;
one initiated by Śiva should perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) endowed with these characteristics. || 21 ||
With the *prāsāda* mantra, endowed with truth,
and with the mantra "He is the Lord of these," an oblation is offered specifically to Āditya.
Mindāha, Viśvatastha, Indra, and Nairṛti from there;
this is declared as the Śukra-homa. Then Āpyāya spoke to Soma. || 23 ||
The Soma-homa is proclaimed to be performed with the mantra "Gaurīmimāya. And for Aṅgāraka, the oblation is offered with the mantra beginning "Agnirmūrdhā" and "Somatā. (24)
"Gaurī yat te devi," "nṛttir āpadya," "caiva rāhu," "śanno devī," and "prajāpate"—the fire-oblation (homa) for Śani is thus proclaimed. || 25 ||
The oblation for Ketu is said here to be "brahmajajñānaṃ" (the knowledge born of Brahman);
the oblation for Āditya is said to be the Bṛhat-sāman and the knowledge of the Ācārya.
The oblation for Viṣṇu is said to be "Udbudhyasva," and that for Budha is accompanied by the Pañcabrahma, the Ṣaḍaṅga, and the Prāsāda mantras. || 27 ||
The pacification of the planets (grahaśānti) is here described as an oblation performed with the seed-syllable of Śiva;
furthermore, a bath with milk should be performed, especially with the Śrī Rudra mantra. (28)
Afterwards, one should worship the preceptor; then the affliction of the planets is released.
There will be excessive rain there, and thereafter it brings about an abundance of food. (29)
When the constellation Puccha is visible at night accompanied by Indra’s bow (a rainbow),
and when a great pestilence has broken out, one should perform the thousandfold ritual bath.
When fever and other ailments arise from the wind, one should cause a jar of cold water to be prepared;
listen to the truth regarding what occurs when blood-born women appear, O Grandfather. (31)
If a *piṇḍikā* appears in the middle of the *liṅga* due to the emergence of a red maiden, the village or field of kings will certainly meet with destruction. (32)
In the eastern quarter there shall be the destruction of living beings; in the southeast, there shall be the loss of grain;
in the southern quarter, there shall be the loss of vehicles; and in the southwest, there shall be the destruction of one's wife.
In the western quarter and at the very threshold, there shall be the destruction of quadrupeds;
in the northwestern quarter one encounters fever and epilepsy, and in the northern quarter one shall incur disease.
One should cause the destruction of the king and his ministers, especially in the northeast;
if it is seen in the Nirmālya-kunda, there will be the ruin of the king and the kingdom. (35)
If the fire-chamber is placed in the kitchen, it causes harm to the preceptor;
if in the grain-room, there will be destruction; and if at the gate, it brings ruin to the household.
In this very manner, it is said that there are five enclosures;
for Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, they should be within the inner circle. || 37 ||
The destruction of Vaiśyas is seen even when it occurs in the inner enclosure;
likewise, when it occurs in the middle enclosure, the Śūdras shall meet with ruin. (38)
Furthermore, there is the destruction of the four-footed [beasts] when the boundary walls are small;
likewise, there is the destruction of fire and other elements when the boundary walls are large. (39)
When such a phenomenon occurs at the place of the bed, one should predict death;
in this very manner, a terrifying and extraordinary event is seen. (40)
To pacify those defects, one should have [the ground] excavated from that location;
having removed everything there, one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If there is the defect of a tawny cow (kapilā) therein, one should then cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana) to be made;
having established a mound in that place, one should thereafter perform a propitiatory fire-oblation (śānti-homa).
A milk-bath should be performed, especially with the Śrī Rudra hymns;
furthermore, the preceptor should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the procedure as previously described.
Within five days, seven nights, or even nine days, the Savior,
having thus performed this great propitiation for the removal of all defects, [attains his goal].
But when an anthill has arisen upon a palace built by bees,
one should remove everything from there and perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the quarters.
When the stars are visible during the day, one should then bathe the Lord of the Gods with a thousand jars of water and offer the great sacrificial oblation.
If an owl or similar creature is seen above the temple,
one should perform a rite for an auspicious day there and sprinkle it with water consecrated by the Pavamāna hymns.
There, an ablution (snapana) should be performed and a propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma) should be caused to be made;
furthermore, when other portents have arisen, one should then cause an ablution to be performed.
A pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) should be performed for the sake of neutralizing those defects;
the ritual for portents has been declared, and now the Kṛttikādīpa is described. (49)
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, the Procedure for the Miraculous Pacification, in the Vīratantra.
Having prostrated before the Lord of the World, the Grandfather (Brahmā) inquired:
"O Lord, who indeed is the Kṛttikā-lamp? Tell me all of that! (1)
The Lord.
I shall relate all of that in its entirety; listen, O Four-faced One! It concerns the month of Kārttika when it is joined with the lunar mansion Kṛttikā.
Then the best of preceptors should perform the rite of the lamp under Kṛttikā;
for if the lamp under Kṛttikā is omitted, fever and pestilence will prevail.
Drought may occur there; therefore, a lamp is employed.
Having made a wick from new cloth combined with cotton, [one should offer it].
Having requested these, one should place the length and the circumference— these two—
into the vessel filled with auspiciousness, while reciting the heart-mantra.
Having combined it with cow’s ghee or again with pure oil,
one should place it upon the summit of the temple while reciting the Hṛdaya mantra.
I shall describe the lamp-post; listen, O Four-faced One! It may be made of sandalwood, or campaka, or betel-nut wood, or indeed of bamboo. || 7 ||
One should have it made in the shape of a plantain tree, a coconut, or a bilva fruit; or even like a palace, or as high as the throat.
It should be the height of a pigeon or five cubits;
having joined this with the lamp, [the measurements are] fifty or twenty-five.
The artisan should fashion it as four or eight rows;
there, he should wrap it with cloth and drench it thoroughly with ghee.
O best of Brahmins, having offered a lamp with the Sadyojāta mantra, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) there according to the extent of one's means.
One should especially hold [the image] with the head facing the Vāmadeva direction;
one should perform the circumambulation of the temple and cause it to enter the inner sanctum.
Having placed it in the maṇḍala as before, one should then sprinkle it with water;
the preceptor should then give a sacrificial fee consisting of garments, gold, and rings.
O best of Brahmins, one should join Śiva with a lamp upon the summit of the palace; O best of Brahmins, one should join the lamp-stand with the lamp of Viṣṇu.
One should join the lamps of the inner sanctum and other areas with the Brahma-lamp;
one should join all the lamps everywhere with the Prāsāda mantra. || 15 ||
One should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented to the God, and then cause betel-leaf (tāmbūla) to be offered;
accompanied by various lamps, perform a great festival at night.
It was accompanied by dance and song, adorned with various peacock feathers,
frequented by ancient courtesans, and joined by female attendants and slave-girls.
One should enter the Ālaya and then follow the sequence of serving food there;
the mortal who acts in this manner shall attain the world of Śiva. || 18 ||
It should be performed with tree oil, especially during festivals and the like; this is specifically called the Kṛttikā-lamp. Now hear about the foremost food offering (agrāśana). || 19 ||
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, the Ritual for the Kṛttikā Lamp, in the Vīratantra.
Having bowed his head to the God, the Grandfather (Brahmā) questioned him: "O Lord! How does one obtain the first portion of food? Tell me all that, O Master! (1)
The Lord.
I shall relate all of that in its entirety; listen, O Four-faced One!
On an auspicious and propitious moment, the acquisition of the ground should take place.
Furthermore, under the constellations Uttara-phalgunī, Maghā, Svātī, Puṣya, Anurādhā, Ārdrā,
and Bharaṇī in the month of Caitra, one should perform the entry onto the ground.
The odd lunar days (tithis) are to be known as [auspicious], with the exception of the ninth;
the second and tenth are to be accepted, as are the signs of Taurus, Scorpio, and Cancer.
Tuesday is the best day for entering a new house, while Mercury and Jupiter are middling;
thus the entry into a dwelling has been declared, and now the work of agriculture is being described.
One should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited there and worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
[the asterisms] Mūla, Punarvasu, Rohiṇī, and the three Uttaras [are favorable]. (6)
O best of Brahmins, the constellations Revatī, Puṣya, and Hastā are honored for agricultural activities;
however, one should avoid the ninth lunar day (navamī) in agricultural work.
Wednesday is praised for Venus, the Sun, Mercury, and Jupiter;
as well as when the ascendant is Taurus, Cancer, Pisces, Gemini, or Leo. (8)
(398) This commencement of agriculture has been specifically declared according to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*):
likewise, two bulls that are white, red, or tawny, and whose noses have not been cut, [are auspicious]. (9)
Having bound it together with a pair [of ropes], or even with a strong middle rope,
one should fasten the plow using a go-carma cord.
One should perform all rites with the Heart-mantra;
one should cause the ground to settle as previously described by means of the Sadyojāta mantra.
One should perform the sowing of seeds when conjoined with an auspicious lunar mansion:
namely, Mūla, Anurādhā, Hasta, Maghā, Rohiṇī, and Revatī. (12)
Viśākhā, the three Uttarās, Svātī, Caitrī (Anurādhā), Śravaṇa, and the constellation Śatabhiṣaj are commended for sowing seeds. (13)
The fifth, the seventh, the full moon day, the thirteenth,
the eleventh, and the third lunar days are praised for the rite of sowing seeds.
The Naga, Simha, Arka, Mina, and Makara are honored;
Yamakumbha and Tulā are middling; one should avoid all the rest.
The decan (drekkāṇa) and other divisions of Venus, the Moon, Jupiter, and Mercury are auspicious;
in this very manner, the sowing of the seed is described. || 16 ||
Having placed the image upon a palanquin, or indeed upon an elephant, horse, or chariot, he should enter the ground and remain facing the east. (17)
Having leveled the ground before him, he should offer an oblation to the deities of the directions;
then the wise man should fashion an image of the earth out of clay, with its head facing east.
(399) One who has two hands and two feet, beautiful breasts, and is in the prime of youth—
there one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited and cause people to offer betel-leaf. || 19 ||
The fourth letter from the sixth group, joined with the sixth letter from the first group, and conjoined with Bindu and Nāda—this is called the root mantra here. (20)
Having recited this mantra, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
one should present an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa) accompanied by parched grain (lāja) and cakes (apūpa). || 21 ||
Thereafter, one should cause betel-leaf to be offered, accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments;
likewise, one should offer a handful of rice powder while reciting the root mantra.
"O Vasundharā!"—thus the father addressed the goddess Śrī, who held a lotus flower in her joined palms:
"Salutations to you, O auspicious one! May you always be present here for the sake of agricultural work. (23)
Having recited this mantra, the sowing of seeds should be performed;
thereafter, one should worship the preceptor, and after that, one should worship the astrologer.
One should cause all the people there, especially [the children], to receive seeds;
then, together with the devotees, one should enter the temple.
The sowing of the seed has been declared; now the "first meal" (agrāśana) is described here:
it should be accompanied by an image of Caṇḍeśa and provided with all kinds of musical instruments. || 26 ||
Having reached a field of grain, one should begin the harvesting of the grain,
especially under the asterism Rohiṇī when it extends three cubits further north.
In Scorpio or Cancer as well, the wise man should perform this [rite] in the same manner;
he should then take hold of a parrot with the weapon-mantra and carry it on his head.

One should perform a circumambulation of the village accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments; [the deity], well-heated by the rays of the sun, should be placed in a mortar that has been split open. (29)
One should perform all rites with the *hṛdaya-mantra*;
likewise, [the asterisms] Hasta, Śravaṇa, Revatī, and Aśvinī are auspicious. (30)
Mūla, Rohiṇī, Svātī, Viśākhā, Punarvasū, Śraviṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, Anurādhā, and the three Uttarās; || 31 ||
Mṛgaśīrṣa and Puṣya are praised for eating; however, Aries, Scorpio, and Pisces are to be avoided, while the remaining signs are honored.
In this very manner, one should especially offer to Śiva rice mixed with sugar and joined with coconut fruits.
Having recited the *vyomavyāpin* mantra, the wise one should offer it to Śivā;
and for all images as well, he should likewise offer the *akṣama*.
The attendants who have been sought out should be presented to the preceptor;
after thus making this announcement, one should then cause betel to be offered.

One should give the preceptor a sacrificial fee consisting of garments, gold, and rings; this is declared to be the "foremost meal. Now hear concerning the "establishment of the child" (bālasthāpana). || 36 ||
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, the Rite of the Foremost Food, in the Vīratantra.
Having paid homage to the Lord of the World, Brahmā questioned Śaṅkara: "O God! How is the state of childhood? O Lord, tell all of that to me. (1)
The Lord.
I shall describe the site for the child; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
It may be according to the measurement of the door or, again, according to the measurement of the wall.
Furthermore, one indeed fashions a preliminary linga (bālaliṅga) according to the measurement of a liṅga or again according to the measurement of a palm (tāla),
whether it be made of stone or wood.
The height of the door should be nine [units], and there should be nine [units] for each image;
one should make the height of the portion for worship nine [units], provided with the various directions.
The middle [measure] is said to be three tālas, while the lowest is two tālas. || 5 ||
In this very manner, one should fashion the emblem of a child;
by that measurement, the supreme portion of the emblem must be made.
The width of the liṅga is three parts; the width of the pedestal (pīṭha) and so forth is now stated.
The lowest [pedestal] shall consist of one part of Brahmā, while the middle one is said to be... [one part of Viṣṇu]. || 7 ||
Above, however, there should be the portion of Śiva; Śiva should be in the shape of an umbrella.
The thread for the liṅga must be made, and the stalk should indeed be fashioned according to the ritual rule. || 8 ||
Likewise, a *bāla-liṅga* should be fashioned from aśvattha, udumbara, bilva, or śamī wood, following this very same sequence.
