The location for the child (bālasthāna) is said here to be established in the eastern direction of the temple, or in the southeast, or even in front, or likewise in the west.
One should have a pavilion, a maṇḍapa, or even a temple constructed, measuring three cubits, five cubits, or even seven cubits [in size]. || 11 ||
(402) Having protected [the site] for three-quarters, half, or even just the face [of the ground], on the left side of the place of the Child (Bālasthāna)... || 12 ||
One should construct a middle altar; it is said to be circular or square, or otherwise [rectangular]. || 13 ||
Then, one should first cause the installation in the eastern part of the main temple;
having placed the Śiva-kumbha and the Vardhanī vessel upon the pedestal.
Having invoked the Lord of the Gods of gods—provided with cloth, gold, a tuft of hair, and a lid—one should worship Him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. || 15 ||
Having recited the *vyomavyāpin* mantra combined with the Brahma-aṅgas, O Brahmin, one should perform the rite here on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) as previously described. || 16 ||
Having established the fire-mouth and offered oblations to Śiva and Agni in due order,
one should then properly construct a pavilion in front of the temple.
One should cause it to be made, endowed with the proper characteristics, either to the south or to the north.
One should cause a temple pinnacle (kūṭa) or a water-shed (prapā) to be constructed, or otherwise, perform the consecration of the pavilion (maṇṭapa) according to one's means; then,
at night, one should perform the Vāstu-homa sacrifice endowed with the prescribed characteristics.
Having encircled it with garlands of *darbha* grass, adorned with four archways,
having fixed banners in the eight directions, and beautified with canopies;
Adorned with strings of pearls and beautified by garlands of flowers,
the altar was made one cubit in height and as smooth as the surface of a mirror.
Then, one should place eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice in the center of that;
having placed half as much unhusked rice (*taṇḍula*), one should place half as much sesame (*tila*).
Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus and strewn it with *darbha* grass,
the wise one should then prepare a bed there using eggs and other such materials.
Having emerged from the water and performed purification especially for the Lord of Gods,
one should enter the temple, standing there at the station of Puṣpadanta.
And the preceptor, having become pure, wrapped in a new cloth,
wearing a turban and an upper garment, and adorned with all ornaments;
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon all the limbs using the primary seed-mantra;
this, when conjoined with the instructor, is called the "pair of teachers" (*ācāryadvaya*).
The teacher is said to be the body and the disciple is said to be the life-force;
when these two are united, O Brahmin, they bring about all forms of prosperity.

One should perform the ritual placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa), endowed with its proper characteristics; there, one should touch [the body] with both hands, beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with the letter *pa*.
One should place the five Brahmans in sequence from the thumb to the little finger;
one should then place the six limbs in sequence from the middle fingers to the index fingers.
One should specifically place the Astra-mantra on the palms of the hands;
having placed Īśāna on the head, one should place Tatpuruṣa on the face.
Having placed Aghora in the heart, one should assign Vāma to the secret place;
one should especially install Sadyojāta mantra upon the two feet.
The supreme teacher should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the thirty-eight kalās;
having cast off the state of being a mere material being, he should contemplate, "I am Śiva."
One should establish the image with the five products of the cow while reciting the Śiva-mantra;
one should bind the protective thread (kautuka), joined with a golden thread, with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Having mixed the three fruits, camphor, uśīra, and sandalwood together,
one should smear it all over [the image] on every side.
At an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction, one should have Śiva laid upon the bed,
having covered all the limbs of the image with a new cloth.
One should worship with the *prāsāda* mantra, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having taken nine jars, one should encircle them with three threads;
they should be filled with pure water and provided with a bundle of *kūrca* grass and lids.
One should arrange the vīṇikā and other items together with cloth, gold, the five precious gems, and various other materials.
One should place the Śiva-kumbha in the northeast direction of the image;
having worshipped Śiva in the Śiva-kumbha with the five Brahmans and the six limbs.
One should place the *vardhanī* vessel to his left with the seed-syllable of Gaurī;
[the area] from the east to the northeast should be joined by the eight Vidyeśvaras.
Outside of that, however, one should place the water-pots (kumbha) for the world-protectors (lokapāla) all around;
one should install them with their respective mantras and worship them with perfumes and flowers.
Having fashioned a weapon out of gold, the preceptor should place it within the central pitcher;
he should likewise place gold within the pitchers of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras).
Thereafter, one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented along with betel-leaf;
then, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) at the junctions of the quarters and the center.
Palāśa, aśvattha, bilva, udumbara, and likewise plakṣa; khādira, śamī, and apāmārga as well.
These [fires] starting from the east [should be arranged] in sequence, and in the center, the Pālāśa fire alone;
for all homas, the fuel (idhma) must likewise be of the Pālāśa tree.
O best of Brahmins, fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, sesame seeds,
mung beans, and black gram— these are called the nine substances here.
The *samidhs* are said to be in the heart, and the clarified butter (*ājya*) is the head;
the oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) is with the crest-lock (*śikhā*), and the parched grains (*lājās*) are indeed with the armor (*kavaca*).
Having offered a mustard seed with the Netra-mantra, and likewise barley with the Astra-mantra,
having offered sesame with the Īśāna-mantra, the mung bean is offered with the Sadyojāta-mantra.
One should offer a single māṣa with the left hand, following this very sequence;
[offering] a thousand, or half of that, or even half of that again.
Or one hundred and eight, or fifty, or twenty-five;
or sixteen, or twelve, or specifically ten in number.
At the end of each substance, one should then offer a *vyāhṛti* oblation;
[the deities are] Bhava, Śarva, Paśupati, Īśāna, and likewise Vijaya.
Ugra, Rudra, and Bhīma— these are the deities of the fire-oblation (homa).
[The goddesses] Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, and Kalavikaraṇī.
O best of Brahmins, the powers (śaktis) and presiding deities (adhidevatās) in the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), in due order, are Balavikaraṇī, Balapramathinī, and Sarvabhūtamanonmanī.
Having touched the image at the end of the ritual substances, one should then perform the recitation with the five Brahmans and the six limbs,
and with the four Vedas in the four directions.
Now hear the mantra for the celestial palace (vyomaprāsāda) and the Brahma-limbs;
one should then prepare the bathing altar in the northeastern direction of the pavilion.
Having raised the Lord from the bed, one should place him upon the sacrificial altar for the ritual bath.

The Ritual for the Installation of the Kumāra (in the Tiruvāḍudurai Kośa): In this chapter, several additional verses are seen here and there; in total, twenty verses exist in excess. Therefore, this complete chapter is written below.
Brahmā said:
Having prostrated before the Lord of the World, Brahmā spoke these words:
"O Lord, tell me all about the installation of Kumāra."
Īśvara said:
O Four-faced One, listen; I shall declare all that in its entirety.
The height of the image should be equal to the elevation of the portion of the altar used for worship.
Having divided the *garbha* (inner sanctum) into nine parts,
one should construct each individual elevation (*ucchraya*) at four, five, or even six *tālas*.
Three-eyed, four-armed, peaceful, and endowed with a crown;
his hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and he holds a rosary and a water-pot.
He is well-established in the center of the lotus, facing directly toward the east;
and the two goddesses, Jayā and Vijayā, are always stationed at his sides.
One should place either a peacock, a cock, or an elephant in front;
a wise man should have an image fashioned endowed with these characteristics.
The third from the eighth group, the third from the seventh group,
and the fourth of the first group, endowed with the bindu and nāda.
This is declared to be the root mantra, difficult even for the gods to obtain;
the short vowels are said to be Brahmā, while the long vowels are called the limbs (aṅgas).
The wise should perform the deposition of jewels in the directions starting from the east in due order:
the diamond, the emerald, the lapis lazuli, and the coral.
Having placed [the gems] in the four directions, one should have the central [gem], an indranīla, made very smooth; there, perform the opening of the eyes.
Then, with a golden needle, one should paint a gentle gaze;
having performed the eye-consecration rite (akṣihoma), one should offer a hundred oblations with the Netra-mantra.
One should satisfy [the deity] with the *madhuvāta* mantra while it is joined with a concealed cloth;
having satisfied [it] with the *ghṛtaṃ mimikṣe* mantra, one should show a cow together with its calf.
One should perform [the rite] for Jayā and Vijayā with the root mantra;
for the second, however, one should use the third [mantra] conjoined with Māyā and Anala.
The unsurpassed seed-syllable of Jaya is conjoined with Bindu and Nāda;
it is the fourth letter of the seventh group, endowed with the principle of Māyā.
The seed-syllable of Vijayā is said to be joined with Bindu and Nāda;
one should show it to the Brāhmaṇas there and then have them recite the Puṇyāha.

One should bathe the image with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and wash it while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra; one should then clothe it in new garments and perform a circumambulation of the village.
One should perform the consecration of the water for three nights, five nights,
or for a single watch of the night, while reciting the root mantra and keeping it covered with a cloth.
Having emerged from the water, one should first bathe the eight jars placed on all sides— presided over by the world-protectors— with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in the east.
Then, having performed the Vāstuhoma sacrifice,
one should have a pavilion constructed in front of the temple according to the previously mentioned procedure.
One should construct a central altar; it is said that there should be sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) all around it—
square in the four cardinal directions and circular in the intermediate directions, beginning with the southeast.
One should construct a triangular pit (kuṇḍa) between Indra and Īśāna;
and for victory, a five-cornered one between Soma and Īśāna.
Alternatively, one may fashion a hexagon in another manner;
one should fashion a triangular pit (kuṇḍa) and cause two śaktis to be made.
One should strew the altar with *śāli* rice, and place *taṇḍula* rice and sesame seeds;
one should then prepare the fivefold bed in due order with skins and other materials.
One should cause [the deity] to lie down in the middle of the altar with the head toward the east and the face turned upward;
one should then place Jayā and Vijayā on both sides.
First, one should bind the protective thread (kautuka) with the Hṛdaya mantra;
then, one should place the Skanda-pitcher (skandakumbha) in the northeastern direction of the image.
One should duly place eight jars, provided with cloths, gold, tufts of hair, and lids, starting from the east and extending to the northeast.
And Kumāra, and Guha, and likewise Subrahmaṇya,
the commander-in-chief, the foremost of the gods, and likewise the son of Hara.
One should also install Śaravaṇodbhava and Kārttikeya,
worshipping them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, by means of their respective names and mantras.
Thereafter, one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented, and then cause betel-leaf (tāmbūla) to be offered;
after that, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the procedure prescribed for the fire ritual.
Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, sesame seeds, along with śāli rice, nīvāra, wheat, and mung beans— all these combined together.
Having performed the oblations specifically in sequence with the five Brahmans and the six limbs,
one should offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter using the root mantra of Skanda.
The oblation should be offered together with the officiating priests (ṛtvij), and their food should be one-tenth of that [offering].
One should perform a thousand oblations with the six-syllable mantra.
The expiation is performed with one hundred oblations using the Aghora mantra;
likewise, there shall be one hundred oblations each for the Jaya and Vijayā mantras.
One should perform the Jaya and other oblations, the installation of the fire, and the Rāṣṭrabhṛt offerings in their proper sequence;
then, at the clear dawn, the preceptor shall perform his bath.
Then, O best of Brahmins, one should offer fifteen oblations for the concluding fire-sacrifice (avasānahoma), consisting of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice, using the root mantra.
Then, one should perform the study of the four Vedas in the four directions while reciting the Havyavāha mantra,
accompanied by all the ritual substances.
Immediately after that, the best of preceptors should offer the oblation with the mantra "sviṣṭam agne," and then he should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the mantra "yad asya."

Having performed the oblation according to the rules of worship, one should carry out the rites for the two jars at the four doors and so forth, precisely according to the procedure prescribed for the installation of a Śiva-liṅga.
Having raised the deity from the bed, one should perform the *sṛṣṭinyāsa*;
then one should perform the *garbhanyāsa*, and place [the deity] upon the seventh step.
Having bound it very firmly, one should dismiss the artisan;
one should give the preceptor’s fee (dakṣiṇā) together with ornaments for the five limbs.
One should especially bathe the *skandakumbha* with the root-mantra of Skanda;
likewise, one should bathe Jayā and Vijayā with their respective root-mantras.
One should perform the installation of the power (śakti) of Skanda with the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra;
thereafter, one should present the sacrificial oblation and then cause betel-leaf to be offered.
One should feed the Brahmins there, and then one should feed the devotees of Śiva;
one should worship according to the prescribed rite and perform the Sṛṣṭinyāsa.
One should invoke with the Sadyojāta mantra, establish [the deity] with the Vāmadeva mantra,
and perform the consecration with the Īśāna mantra.
One should offer incense with the heart-mantra and likewise flowers with the head-mantra;
all items such as clothing, incense, and so forth, one should cause to be offered with the heart-mantra.

One should never place the food offering (naivedya) in the heart; rather, one should perform the perpetual festival by placing rice grains on a small stand and worshipping them with perfumes and flowers.
The image should go forward first, but afterwards one should abandon the momentary;
one should enter the abode there—this is here called the "caused" [process].
One should cause a festival to be held there for one day, or even for three days,
or for five days, or for seven days, or for nine days, in successive order.
One should perform the raising of the banner, using either a *kramuka* tree or a bamboo;
it should be joined with three staffs, with a bamboo fixed at its top.
The cloth should be five or seven cubits in length on all sides;
one should depict a peacock with its crest at the center.
One should place five water-pots and indeed raise a banner;
one should beat a drum there—this is called the rite of offering sprouts.
One should construct the sacrificial hall either in the northeast or in the southeast;
in the center, one should fashion a circular altar using the five types of colored powders.
One should place the ritual jars there according to the previously mentioned procedure:
first is the Bhūtarātra, and second is the Gaṇarātra.
The third is indeed the Ṛṣirātra, while the fourth is called the Gāndharva;
the fifth is the Brahmarātra, and the sixth is the Viṣṇurātra.
The seventh is Skandarātra; these are the deities of the nights.
Beginning at evening, one should perform the ritual at the sacred ford (tīrtha) at dawn.
One should offer a special oblation (bali) accompanied by an image, endowed with the appropriate insignia, and consisting of pure food.

Then, having performed the powder festival (cūrṇotsava), one should bathe [the deity] at the time of the sacred occasion (tīrthakāla). There, one should cause the ceremonial bath (snapana) to be performed one hundred and eight times in succession.
After the descent of the banner, one should dismiss the deities of the joints;
thereafter, one should perform the festival of silence and carry out only what is necessary for one's capacity.
Afterwards, one should especially cause the portion for Sumitra to be performed;
then one should worship the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings.
For the devotees and attendants, one should act according to their means; as prescribed for the festival, so should one do, performing everything until the conclusion of the pilgrimage site.
One should have the ceremonial bathing performed there for the one endowed with the proper characteristics;
the installation of Skanda has thus been described—now hear about the installation of the human [image].
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for the installation of Guha in the glorious Vīra Tantra, the compendium of six thousand verses.
